Foundations · CV
These four pieces are the verbs of every convolutional network: convolution slides a small learned stencil across the image to detect edges and textures, activation bends those linear scans into nonlinear decisions so the network can learn curves rather than straight lines, normalization rescales the signal at each layer so gradients neither explode nor fade, and transposed convolution runs the stencil in reverse to grow coarse features back up to a full-resolution map. Master these and the rest of modern vision — the encoder that compresses a CT scan, the decoder that paints a pixel-perfect tumor mask — is just clever ways of stacking and tuning them. This is the bedrock layer of the medical-imaging stack: every U-Net, every segmentation backbone, every diffusion model is built from exactly these primitives.
Before transformers, a network only saw a pixel and its immediate neighbors; here we instead chop the scan into tokens and let every piece talk to every other piece, with attention deciding who is worth listening to — so a tumor edge can directly consult a far-away organ boundary in a single step. This family is the engine room of modern vision: patch embedding turns a volume into a sequence, self- and multi-head attention build the global picture, Swin keeps the cost from exploding on big 3D images, and cross- and temporal attention let a U-Net fuse encoder/decoder features or compare a scan against last month's. It is what lets a model reason about long-range context — the difference between labeling each voxel in isolation and understanding the whole anatomy at once.
These are the load-bearing pieces that turn a generic feature extractor into a network that can actually draw a tumor: the U-Net shape that funnels a scan down to "what is this?" and back up to "where exactly?", deep supervision that pushes a training signal into the deepest layers, sliding-window inference that streams a 240³ scan through a model that only ever sees small crops, and an output head that emits overlapping regions instead of mutually-exclusive classes. Each one is less a fancy idea than a hard-won fix for a real obstacle — vanishing gradients, GPUs too small for a whole brain, anatomy that nests rather than partitions. Together they are the skeleton of essentially every modern medical-image segmenter, and getting them right is what separates a model that scores well on paper from one a radiologist can trust voxel-by-voxel.
Every segmentation network learns by chasing a single number — its loss — and in tumor imaging that number has to survive a brutal fact: cancer voxels are a tiny minority, so a model can score 99% "accurate" by labelling everything background. These widgets show the fix the whole field converged on — pairing Dice, which rewards raw overlap and ignores how big the background is, with cross-entropy for per-voxel calibration and Focal to pour gradient onto the hard, ambiguous tumor rim instead of the easy interior. Get this objective right and the same Dice score becomes both the thing you optimize and the headline metric reviewers judge you on; get it wrong and the model quietly learns to ignore the lesion you actually care about.
A model that draws a tumor outline will hand you that mask with total swagger — even when it's wrong — so this family asks the harder questions: how sure should we be, and does the error actually matter? MC-Dropout and predictive entropy turn one network into a crowd of opinions to expose where it's secretly guessing; calibration & ECE check whether a stated "90% confident" is honest or just inflated by easy background voxels; and HD95 plus connected components catch the failures a Dice score smiles right past — a stray boundary spike or a phantom second lesion. In medical imaging and any high-stakes CV system, this is the layer between a pretty prediction and one a clinician can actually trust and act on.
This is the pipeline's last mile: the moment a segmentation mask stops being pretty pixels and becomes a decision a doctor can act on — split the mask into individual lesions, measure each one's longest diameter, sum them, and read off whether the tumor shrank, grew, vanished, or held steady. RECIST 1.1 is the standardized rulebook (CR / PR / SD / PD, the ≥30% and ≥20% thresholds) that oncologists and regulators trust, so getting it right is what turns a clever model into something that can actually change treatment. It is also where small upstream errors get amplified into the wrong verdict, which is exactly why this clinical-endpoint layer — not the Dice score — is the number that ultimately matters.
These models all learn to see before anyone tells them what they're looking at: instead of memorizing human labels, they invent their own homework — hide part of an image and guess it back, match a photo to its caption, or destroy a picture with noise and reconstruct it — and in doing so soak up a general sense of shape, texture, and meaning from raw pixels alone. That self-taught backbone is exactly what makes them the foundation of the modern stack: pretrain once on millions of unlabeled scans, then fine-tune on the few hundred annotated tumors you actually have. In medical imaging, where expert labels are scarce and expensive, this is the difference between a model that needs a radiologist to hand-mark everything and one that already understands anatomy before it ever sees a single ground-truth mask.
A pathology slide is a gigapixel mosaic of stained tissue — sometimes a hundred thousand pixels wide, often labelled only at the level of a whole patient — so the central challenge here is bridging an enormous, dye-tinted image to a single clinical verdict. These widgets walk that ladder: tiling the slide into a memory-friendly pyramid, separating the H&E dyes back into pure stains, segmenting and counting individual cells, learning from one label spread across thousands of patches (multiple-instance learning), and finally compressing morphology into geometric embeddings via foundation models. Together they form the backbone of computational pathology — the part of the medical-imaging stack that turns the microscope, the field where so much diagnosis and prognosis is still decided, into something a neural network can actually read.
The plain transformer was just the starting point; this family is the set of upgrades that turned it into a workhorse for images and long sequences. You'll see how a transformer first ingests a picture and learns where each patch sits (the [CLS] token and positional encoding), then three tricks that beat the cost of doing so at scale — Mixture-of-Experts buys capacity by waking only a few sub-networks per token, state-space models swap quadratic attention for a linear-time scan, and FlashAttention computes the exact same softmax without ever writing the giant N×N matrix to memory. These matter for OncoSeg precisely because medical data is huge: a 128³ volume flattens to ~2 million tokens and longitudinal scans stack many timepoints, so these are the moves that make a transformer affordable on real 3D and temporal imaging.
A world model is a network that learns the rules of how things change — feed it the current state and an action, and it dreams the next moment, so an agent can rehearse a thousand futures inside its own head instead of paying for them in the real world. The four ideas here are variations on that dream: JEPA predicts the future as compact latent features rather than wasteful pixels; classic world models and Dreamer roll those latents forward frame by frame so a policy can learn to act purely by imagining; and Genie shows you can grow a controllable, playable world from raw unlabeled video alone. This family matters because it turns passive video into a predictive simulator — the same machinery that lets a robot plan, a game engine generate itself, or, in medical imaging, a model anticipate how a tumor or organ will deform across time from sparse, unlabeled scans.
These widgets reveal what happens when a model can both see and talk: each word it reads or writes quietly tugs on specific pixels, so "the nodule in the upper-left lobe" lights up exactly that region of the scan rather than the whole image. Visual chain-of-thought pushes this further — instead of blurting an answer, the model is made to point first, then reason in steps, leaving a visible trail of where it looked and why, which is the difference between a black-box guess and an explanation a radiologist can audit. This family is the bridge between modern vision-language models (CLIP, LLaVA, GPT-4V-style systems) and trustworthy medical AI: it's how a report-generating or diagnosis-assisting model grounds its claims in evidence you can actually check.
A Vision-Language-Action model collapses the whole robot pipeline — see, understand, act — into one network: feed it a camera frame and a plain-English instruction like "pick up the red block," and it spits out motor commands directly, with no separate planner in between. The trick is that those continuous gripper and end-effector moves are chopped into discrete bins, so steering a robot arm becomes the exact same next-token prediction a language model already does — letting models like RT-2, OpenVLA, and π0 inherit the scale and common sense of internet-trained transformers. It matters because it's the leading recipe for general-purpose embodied AI, and it reframes a perception stack like OncoSeg as the eyes of such a system: whatever turns raw voxels into clean object and region representations is exactly the front-end a downstream policy — robot or clinician — has to act on.
These widgets are all about teaching a network to live in 3D physical space instead of a flat grid of pixels: how to bake a whole scene into a field you can re-render from any angle (NeRF, Gaussian splatting), how to label or learn directly on unordered points and occupancy volumes (PointNet, occupancy grids), how to act in that space by denoising a plan (diffusion policy), and how to bolt the actual laws of physics onto a loss so the answer can't violate them (PINNs). The common thread is geometry and dynamics as first-class citizens — the model reasons about where things are and how they move, then bridges the gap between simulator and reality through domain randomization. This family is the engine room of robotics, autonomous driving, and surgical/interventional AI; for a system like OncoSeg it is the path from a static 2D-slice mindset toward true volumetric reasoning and physics-aware reconstruction.
A state-of-the-art tumor-segmentation network can weigh hundreds of megabytes and demand a datacenter GPU — but the scanner is at the bedside, the data can't leave the hospital, and the radiologist wants an answer in seconds. This family is the toolkit for shrinking, speeding up, and democratizing big models: quantization and pruning strip away bits and weights, distillation and LoRA pour a giant's knowledge into something small and cheap to tune, federated learning trains across sites without moving a single patient scan, and mixed precision makes even the training run faster on the hardware you already have. These are the tricks that move a model from a research paper onto a real CT console — the unglamorous, decisive last mile that decides whether AI ever touches a patient.
A whole-slide image is a billion-pixel landscape where the diagnosis lives in two places a plain patch-classifier ignores: the spatial arrangement of cells and the colour physics of the dye. These two widgets attack both — a cell-graph GNN turns each nucleus into a node and lets message-passing read the tumor microenvironment (an immune-infiltrated tumor cell looks different from a lonely one), while Macenko stain normalization deconvolves H&E into its optical-density stain basis to scrub out the lab-to-lab colour cast before the network ever sees it. This is the unglamorous-but-decisive plumbing of modern computational pathology: it's what lets a model trained on one hospital's purple-ish scanner still work on another's, and what lets it reason about tissue as a structured neighbourhood rather than a bag of isolated crops.
A freshly initialized network is just noise; training is the loop that drags it downhill toward predictions that match reality. These widgets open up that loop one gear at a time — backprop sending blame backward through every layer, the optimizer deciding how big and which-way each step lands, the learning-rate schedule warming up then cooling off, residual connections keeping the gradient signal alive in very deep nets, and augmentation plus early stopping fighting the constant temptation to memorize instead of generalize. This is the unglamorous engine room behind every modern CV model: in medical imaging, where labeled scans are scarce and a model that overfits one scanner can quietly fail on the next, getting these knobs right is often the difference between a tool that generalizes to a new hospital and one that doesn't.
Before networks learned features, vision engineers hand-built them — and these five tools are the canonical kit: blur an image to pick a scale, walk the gradients to find edges, clean a mask with morphology, stack the picture into a pyramid to see it coarse-to-fine, and chase pixels between frames to read motion. The thread tying them together is the idea that a picture is a signal you can filter, differentiate, and rescale, so structure pops out without any training data. They are not museum pieces: Gaussian scale space lives inside every CNN's receptive field, pyramids became feature-pyramid networks, morphology still scrubs the raw output of a segmentation model, and optical flow is the workhorse behind tumor tracking across CT/MRI time-points — so knowing these makes the deep stack feel less like magic and more like a smart, learned version of the same moves.
Segmentation paints every pixel; detection instead asks "what is here, and where is its box?" — and these five widgets walk the whole journey from how a box is scored to how boxes are produced. You start with IoU, the overlap ruler every detector is graded by, then NMS to thin a swarm of guesses down to one box per lesion; anchor boxes and the Feature Pyramid Network show the classic recipe — tile the image with priors at every scale and classify-plus-nudge each one — while DETR tears that up and predicts the whole set of objects at once with a transformer, no hand-tuned anchors or NMS at all. This family is the backbone of finding-and-counting tasks across the modern stack: from autonomous-driving perception to flagging and tallying lesions, nuclei, or nodules on a scan, where "how many, how big, did it grow?" is exactly the clinical question.
A CT or MRI scanner never photographs the body — it measures shadows and echoes (X-ray projections that pile up into a sinogram, or spatial frequencies that fill k-space) and then solves for the picture, turning many views back into a slice via filtered backprojection or an inverse Fourier transform. This family is the physics layer beneath every pixel your network sees: it explains why a scan looks the way it does, how to line two studies up across time or modality (registration guided by mutual information), and how a ±2000 HU world gets squeezed into 256 greys by windowing. Understanding it is what separates treating a CT as a generic JPEG from reading it as the calibrated physical measurement it actually is — the difference between a model that overfits scanner quirks and one that measures real tumor change.
These three are all answers to the same question: how do you make a machine dream up a plausible scan, lesion, or face it has never seen? Each starts from pure noise and learns a different route to realism — a GAN trains a forger against a detective until the fakes pass, a VAE squeezes data into a smooth latent space you can sample and steer, and flow matching learns a velocity field that carries noise to data along nearly straight paths. In modern CV they power text-to-image and the diffusion family; in medical imaging they are the workhorses for augmenting scarce labeled tumors, harmonizing scans across scanners, denoising low-dose CT, and filling in missing modalities — turning "we don't have enough data" into something you can generate.
A model that says "tumour" is useless until you can answer how often is it right, when it's wrong what does it confuse, and how sure are we of that number? — and these five tools are the toolkit for exactly that. ROC/AUC, precision-recall-F1, and the confusion matrix turn a pile of predictions into honest performance you can argue about, while the bootstrap and k-fold cross-validation wrap every score in an error bar so you know whether a "2% improvement" is real or just luck on one lucky split. In medical imaging this family is the difference between a demo and a deliverable: regulators, radiologists, and reviewers all want not just a number but a defensible, uncertainty-aware claim about how the model behaves on the rare voxels that actually matter.
A trained network can call a scan "malignant" with high confidence, but a doctor needs to know which pixels it stared at to get there — these tools open that black box. Each works backward from a decision to a heatmap over the input: Grad-CAM follows gradients into a CNN's last feature maps, integrated gradients accumulates credit along a path from a blank baseline so even saturated neurons get their due, and attention rollout chains a ViT's attention matrices to trace what a patch token was really looking at. In medical imaging this is where trust, debugging, and regulatory sign-off live: a model that points at the actual lesion is one a radiologist can stand behind, and one whose spurious shortcuts you can catch before they reach a patient.
A trained network turns every image, tumor, or cell into a long list of numbers living in a space too high-dimensional to picture — and these four tools are how you tame that space. PCA rotates it to find the directions that actually carry signal, t-SNE/UMAP flatten it into a 2-D map where neighbors stay neighbors, k-means carves it into groups by similarity alone, and InfoNCE goes one level deeper — it shapes the space in the first place, pulling matching views together and pushing mismatches apart without ever seeing a label. This family is the connective tissue of modern CV: it powers the self-supervised pretraining behind foundation models, and in medical imaging it lets you sanity-check what a model learned, discover tumor subtypes nobody annotated, and cluster patients when labels are scarce or expensive.
Everything else in this lab learns from a fixed answer key; here the network learns from consequences that unfold over time — it acts, sees a reward, and rewrites its own behavior. Policy gradient nudges a policy toward actions that paid off, value iteration lets reward propagate backward from outcomes so a planner can look ahead, and recurrence shows why carrying a memory across many steps is so fragile that gating had to be invented. This family is the engine behind RLHF that tunes assistants like Claude and the sequence models that predict tokens — and downstream of a segmenter it is exactly how you'd frame treatment-response follow-up: when to scan, wait, or escalate as a tumor's state evolves.
A trained net hands you a confident answer for every pixel — but says nothing about when to trust it, and out of the box its 99% is often really 70%. This family is the cheap, mostly bolt-on layer that turns raw scores into honest, deployable predictions: temperature scaling rescales over-confident probabilities with a single learned knob, conformal prediction swaps the brittle top-1 label for a set with a hard coverage guarantee, deep ensembles let disagreeing copies of the same model surface their own uncertainty, and test-time augmentation averages several views for a free accuracy bump. In medical imaging this is the difference between a black box and a tool a radiologist can act on — a model that knows when to say "look again" is what separates a demo from something that ships into the clinic.
Once a segmentation model has found and measured the tumors, something still has to talk — narrate the findings, compare them to the prior scan, draft the RECIST report. That talking is an LLM running token by token, and this family covers the four tricks that make it fast, cheap, and trustworthy: BPE turns the messy text going in into tokens; the KV-cache stops the model from re-reading the whole context on every word; speculative decoding lets a tiny model race ahead and the big one merely fact-check, for the exact same output at 2-3× the speed; and RAG chains the answer to retrieved evidence so it cites the chart instead of hallucinating a measurement. Together they are the difference between a demo that stalls and a report generator that streams grounded, auditable text at the clinical workstation — the inference layer that sits downstream of every modern vision model with a language head.
In medical imaging the model is rarely the bottleneck — the data and the training signal are. Expert tumor masks cost minutes each, every annotator draws boundaries differently, and a shared encoder must keep two squabbling tasks honest. These widgets are the levers on that side of the bench: which scans to send to the radiologist next (active learning), how to keep learning when labels lie (robust loss), how to manufacture a steady moving target out of a jittery student (the EMA teacher behind Mean-Teacher and DINO), and how to stop a loud loss from hijacking the gradient of a quiet one (uncertainty weighting). Master these and you squeeze more out of a few hundred labeled cases than a fancier network ever buys you — which is exactly why data-centric tricks now decide who ships a clinical model and who doesn't.
Every network is really a graph of who-talks-to-whom, and these widgets show that the wiring — not just the weights — decides what each unit can see and what it costs. Stack too many graph message-passing rounds and every node blurs into the same gray (over-smoothing); stretch a convolution to a full 3D kernel and you buy z-context at a cubic blow-up in params, FLOPs, and memory — which is exactly why 2.5D and anisotropic kernels exist. This family is the architect's toolkit behind GNNs and volumetric CNNs alike: in a 3D medical-imaging stack like OncoSeg it is the knob that trades how far a layer reaches against whether the batch still fits on the GPU.
cnn_decoder.py — local detail via convolution
Left: input patch. A 3×3 kernel slides over it. Right: feature response.

Convolution — the decoder's local craftsman

A tiny learnable kernel slides over the image, computing a weighted sum at each position. It is the core operation of every CNN and excels at local structure — edges, gradients, texture — exactly what places a crisp tumor boundary.

OncoSeg's decoder is CNN, not transformer, on purpose: after the Swin encoder decides what and roughly where, convolutions reconstruct the exact voxel edges. Training learns these kernel weights.
3×3×3 in 3Dstride 1learnable weightsweight sharing
💡 Why it mattersConvolution applies the same small learnable kernel at every spatial location, so a network captures local structure — edges, gradients, texture — with weight sharing and translation equivariance instead of a separate weight per pixel. That parameter efficiency and locality is exactly what lets a decoder reconstruct crisp, voxel-accurate object boundaries (like a tumor edge) rather than just a blurry blob.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the core building block of essentially all CNNs: ImageNet classifiers (ResNet, ConvNeXt), object detectors (YOLO), and the decoders of segmentation networks that turn coarse features into pixel-accurate masks. In medical imaging it underpins nnU-Net and MONAI 3D segmentation pipelines, and many transformer/SSM models still keep convolutional stems, patch-embeddings, and decoders precisely because conv is unmatched at local detail.
Cutting-edge / SOTAnnU-Net (DKFZ)ConvNeXt V2 (Meta)MONAI (Project MONAI)EfficientNetV2 (Google)DeepLabv3+ (Google)YOLO11 (Ultralytics)
▸ Code PyTorch — nn.Conv3d (the decoder conv) + the sliding sum-of-products it computes▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

# OncoSeg decoder block: a learnable 3x3x3 kernel slides over the volume (stride 1),
# weight-shared across every voxel. y[b,co,z,y,x] = sum_{ci,kz,ky,kx} w * x + bias
conv = nn.Conv3d(in_channels=class="n">32, out_channels=class="n">64,
                 kernel_size=class="n">3, stride=class="n">1, padding=class="n">1, bias=True)  # padding=1 keeps D,H,W

x = torch.randn(class="n">2, class="n">32, class="n">16, class="n">16, class="n">16)        # (B, C_in, D, H, W)
y = conv(x)                                # (2, 64, 16, 16, 16) — same spatial size
y = F.leaky_relu(y, negative_slope=class="n">0.1)   # the decoder's nonlinearity

# --- the actual sliding sum-of-products one cell does (unrolled, for intuition) ---
w, b = conv.weight, conv.bias              # w: (64, 32, 3, 3, 3)
xp = F.pad(x, (class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1))          # zero-pad so the kernel fits at borders
patch = xp[class="n">0, :, class="n">0:class="n">3, class="n">0:class="n">3, class="n">0:class="n">3]            # 32x3x3x3 receptive field at output voxel (0,0,0)
out000 = (w[class="n">0] * patch).sum() + b[class="n">0]       # one weighted sum == one number in feature map
assert torch.allclose(out000, conv(x)[class="n">0, class="n">0, class="n">0, class="n">0, class="n">0], atol=class="n">1e-5)
nonlinearity — ReLU · LeakyReLU · GELU · Sigmoid
f(x) curves. Without a nonlinearity, stacked layers collapse to one linear map.

Activation functions — where the network gets its power

Between linear layers sits a nonlinearity. ReLU = max(0,x) is cheap but can "die". LeakyReLU keeps a small negative slope (used in OncoSeg's decoder convs). GELU is the smooth gate inside the transformer FFN. Sigmoid squashes logits to (0,1) probabilities at the output head.

Each maps to a real spot in the code: LeakyReLU in cnn_decoder, GELU in the cross-attention FFN, sigmoid on the 3-channel output. Stack linear layers with no activation and you can only ever learn a straight line.
1.00
💡 Why it mattersActivation functions inject the nonlinearity that lets a network compose simple layers into arbitrarily complex functions — without them, any stack of linear layers collapses into a single linear map with no representational power. The specific choice (ReLU, GELU, SiLU/Swish, GLU variants) also governs gradient flow, sparsity, and training stability, directly affecting whether deep nets converge and how well they generalize.
▸ Where it’s usedThey sit inside every modern architecture: ReLU/LeakyReLU in CNNs and U-Net segmentation backbones (nnU-Net, MONAI medical-imaging models), GELU in Transformers/ViTs (BERT, GPT, DINOv2), and SwiGLU gated feed-forward blocks in current LLMs (Llama 3, PaLM). The activation choice is a routine but consequential design knob in tasks from tumor segmentation and image classification to large-scale language modeling.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs▶
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = torch.randn(class="n">8, class="n">64, class="n">16, class="n">16, class="n">16)          # (N, C, D, H, W) feature map

# The four nonlinearities the widget plots — idiomatic API + the formula it computes:
relu  = F.relu(x)                            # max(0, x)            — cheap, can "die" at x<0
leaky = F.leaky_relu(x, negative_slope=class="n">0.1)  # x>0? x : 0.1*x       — OncoSeg decoder convs
gelu  = F.gelu(x)                            # x * Φ(x), Φ = N(0,1) cdf (exact erf; default approximate='none')
sig   = torch.sigmoid(x)                     # 1/(1+e^-x) ∈ (0,1)  — squashes logits → probabilities

# From-scratch equivalents (what the library calls actually do):
assert torch.allclose(leaky, torch.where(x > class="n">0, x, class="n">0.1 * x))
assert torch.allclose(gelu,  x * class="n">0.5 * (class="n">1 + torch.erf(x / class="n">2**class="n">0.5)), atol=class="n">1e-6)
assert torch.allclose(sig,   class="n">1 / (class="n">1 + torch.exp(-x)),               atol=class="n">1e-6)

# As layers inside a block — nonlinearity BETWEEN linears, else they collapse to one matrix:
block = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(class="n">64, class="n">64, class="n">3, padding=class="n">1), nn.LeakyReLU(class="n">0.1, inplace=True))
feats  = block(x)                            # (8, 64, 16, 16, 16) hidden feature map
head   = nn.Conv3d(class="n">64, class="n">1, kernel_size=class="n">1)     # 1×1 seg head → 1-channel tumor logits
logits = head(feats)
probs  = torch.sigmoid(logits)               # (8, 1, 16, 16, 16) per-voxel tumor probability
InstanceNorm3d / LayerNorm — stabilizing activations
Raw feature distribution (amber) → normalized to mean 0, var 1 (teal).

Normalization — keeping signals well-behaved

Deep nets train poorly when activations drift to huge or tiny scales. Normalization re-centers a group of values to mean 0, variance 1, then lets the network re-scale with learnable γ, β. The differences are which values get grouped.

OncoSeg uses InstanceNorm3d in the decoder (per-channel, per-sample — robust to the tiny batch sizes forced by 3D volumes) and LayerNorm inside the transformer blocks. BatchNorm, which averages across the batch, is fragile when batch=1 or 2.
1.5
1.8
💡 Why it mattersWithout normalization, layer inputs drift in scale and distribution as weights update (internal covariate shift), which slows convergence, forces tiny learning rates, and makes deep nets unstable; normalizing activations to a controlled mean/variance smooths the loss landscape and lets you train far deeper models reliably. It also reduces sensitivity to weight initialization and acts as a mild regularizer.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is ubiquitous: BatchNorm in CNNs (ResNet, nnU-Net medical segmentation), LayerNorm/RMSNorm in every Transformer (GPT, LLaMA, ViT), GroupNorm/InstanceNorm for small-batch 3D medical imaging and style transfer, and is the backbone of stable diffusion and large-scale LLM pretraining. Modern LLMs use pre-norm RMSNorm to keep gradients well-behaved across hundreds of layers.
Cutting-edge / SOTARMSNorm (used in LLaMA 3 / Qwen)LayerNorm (Transformers, ViT)BatchNorm (ResNet)GroupNorm (used in nnU-Net, diffusion U-Nets)InstanceNorm (style transfer / medical imaging)QK-Norm (stabilizing large-scale attention)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs in the decoder (InstanceNorm3d) and transformer (LayerNorm)▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn

x = torch.randn(class="n">2, class="n">16, class="n">8, class="n">32, class="n">32) * class="n">1.8 + class="n">1.5   # (N, C, D, H, W): drifted μ≈1.5, σ≈1.8

# --- InstanceNorm3d: OncoSeg decoder. Normalize per-sample, per-channel over (D,H,W) ---
inorm = nn.InstanceNorm3d(class="n">16, affine=True, eps=class="n">1e-5)   # learnable γ, β per channel
y = inorm(x)                                           # standardized over (D,H,W), then γ·x̂+β (γ=1,β=0 at init)

# from-scratch equivalent — exactly what the widget animates (pre-affine standardization):
dims = (class="n">2, class="n">3, class="n">4)                                        # reduce over D,H,W only
mu  = x.mean(dim=dims, keepdim=True)
var = x.var(dim=dims, keepdim=True, unbiased=False)
y_manual = (x - mu) / torch.sqrt(var + class="n">1e-5)           # x̂ = (x − μ) / √(σ²+ε); mean≈0, var≈1
# affine: γ, β shaped (1,C,1,1,1) would scale/shift x̂ here (then y_manual matches inorm(x))

# --- LayerNorm: OncoSeg transformer blocks. Normalize each token over its feature dim ---
tokens = torch.randn(class="n">2, class="n">256, class="n">768)                      # (batch, seq, dim)
lnorm  = nn.LayerNorm(class="n">768)                             # μ,σ over last axis, per token; eps=1e-5
z = lnorm(tokens)                                      # batch-size-robust → safe at batch=1
ConvTranspose3d — learnable upsampling in the decoder
Each low-res cell paints a scaled copy of the kernel into the high-res grid; overlaps sum.

Transposed convolution — rebuilding resolution

The encoder shrank the volume 32×. To produce a full-resolution mask the decoder must grow it back. A transposed conv (a.k.a. "deconv") does the reverse of striding: every input cell is multiplied by a learnable kernel and stamped into a larger output, with overlaps added.

This is the ConvTranspose3d(stride=2)ConvTranspose3d(stride=2)ConvTranspose3d(stride=2) in every decoder stage, plus a final 4× head to undo the patch-embed downsample. Unlike fixed interpolation, the kernel is learned — so upsampling itself can sharpen edges.
2
💡 Why it mattersPooling and strided convolutions shrink feature maps to capture context, but dense tasks like segmentation need a per-pixel output at the original resolution — transposed convolution provides a learnable upsampling operator (a backward-strided convolution) that recovers spatial detail, instead of fixed interpolation that cannot adapt to the data.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the standard decoder/up-sampling block in encoder-decoder segmentation networks (U-Net and 3D U-Net for organ and tumor delineation in CT/MRI), in semantic-segmentation FCNs, and in the generator of convolutional GANs (DCGAN, StyleGAN) and super-resolution models that synthesize images from low-dimensional features. Note that many modern decoders now prefer bilinear upsample + conv to avoid checkerboard artifacts.
Cutting-edge / SOTAnnU-Net (DKFZ)U-Net / 3D U-NetMONAI (Project MONAI)Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN, Long et al.)DCGANStyleGAN (NVIDIA)
▸ Code PyTorch — ConvTranspose3d, the learnable stride-2 upsample in the decoder▶
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

# Decoder upsample: stride-2 transpose conv DOUBLES each spatial dim AND projects 64->32, kernel learned
up = nn.ConvTranspose3d(in_channels=class="n">64, out_channels=class="n">32, kernel_size=class="n">2, stride=class="n">2)
x = torch.randn(class="n">1, class="n">64, class="n">8, class="n">8, class="n">8)          # [B, C_in, D, H, W]
y = up(x)                                # -> [1, 32, 16, 16, 16]  (out = (in-1)*stride + k)

# What it really does: it's the *transpose* of conv's input->output map (a.k.a. fractionally-strided).
# Each input voxel SCATTERS a learned kernel onto the output grid; overlaps sum.
# Equivalent to the gradient of a stride-2 Conv3d w.r.t. its input.
# NOTE weight layout is [C_in, C_out, k, k, k] = [64, 32, 2,2,2] -- opposite of Conv3d's [C_out, C_in, ...].
y_eq = F.conv_transpose3d(x, up.weight, up.bias, stride=class="n">2)
assert torch.allclose(y, y_eq, atol=class="n">1e-5)

# Cheaper, non-learnable alternative (fixed interp) -- but it ONLY upsamples; it keeps 64 channels,
# so to match `up` you must add a learned projection. This "resize-conv" also avoids checkerboard artifacts:
proj = nn.Conv3d(class="n">64, class="n">32, kernel_size=class="n">1)
y_interp = proj(F.interpolate(x, scale_factor=class="n">2, mode=class=class="s">"s">class="s">'trilinear', align_corners=False))  # -> [1,32,16,16,16]
# Transpose-conv fuses upsample+projection in one learnable op; resize-conv decouples them (no checkerboard).
swin_encoder.py — patch_size (4,4,4) tokenization
The volume is cut into non-overlapping patches; each becomes one token vector.

Patch embedding — turning a volume into tokens

A transformer eats a sequence, not a grid. Patch embedding slices the image into fixed p×p×p patches and linearly projects each into a embed_dim-vector "token". A 128³ volume with patch 4 becomes a 32³ grid of tokens.

This is the very first layer of the Swin encoder (patchsize=(4,4,4)patch_size=(4,4,4)patchs​ize=(4,4,4)). Bigger patches = fewer tokens = cheaper but coarser. It's why the encoder's finest feature map is at H/4, and why the decoder needs a 4× head to get back to voxels.
4
💡 Why it mattersTransformers operate on a sequence of tokens, but a raw 3D volume is a dense grid of voxels far too large to attend over directly; patch embedding solves this by slicing the volume into fixed-size 3D patches and linearly projecting each into a token vector, cutting sequence length by the patch volume (e.g. a 16³ patch is one token instead of 4096 voxels). This makes self-attention tractable, injects a lightweight inductive bias about local structure, and gives the model a learnable, content-adaptive embedding instead of fixed handcrafted features.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the input stem of essentially every vision and volumetric transformer: image classification and self-supervised pretraining (ViT, DINOv2, MAE), promptable segmentation (Segment Anything), and 3D medical-imaging models that tokenize CT/MRI volumes into 16³ patches for organ and tumor segmentation (UNETR, Swin UNETR, MONAI). The same patchify-then-project step also underlies video transformers and diffusion transformers (DiT) that operate on latent patches.
Cutting-edge / SOTAViT (Google)DINOv2 (Meta)Segment Anything 2 (Meta)Swin UNETR / UNETR (MONAI, NVIDIA)DiT — Diffusion Transformer (Meta/Berkeley)MAE — Masked Autoencoder (Meta)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (Conv3d with kernel=stride=patch)▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn

# Patch embedding = a strided conv whose kernel == stride == patch_size,
# so each non-overlapping 4x4x4 voxel block -> one embed_dim token (no overlap).
B, C, P, embed_dim = class="n">2, class="n">4, (class="n">4, class="n">4, class="n">4), class="n">48          # 4 MRI channels -> 48-d tokens
x = torch.randn(B, C, class="n">128, class="n">128, class="n">128)              # [B, C, H, W, D]

proj = nn.Conv3d(C, embed_dim, kernel_size=P, stride=P)   # the line MONAI/ViT actually run
tokens = proj(x)                                  # [B, 48, 32, 32, 32]  (H/4, W/4, D/4)

# From scratch, the conv on patch p is just a learned linear map of the flattened block:
#   token = W @ p.flatten() + b,  W: [embed_dim, C*4*4*4] = [48, 256]
#   -> each token-dim reads C*4*4*4 = 256 weights (total W params = 48*256 = 12288)
seq = tokens.flatten(class="n">2).transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2)           # [B, 32*32*32, 48] = (B, N_tokens, embed_dim)
seq = nn.LayerNorm(embed_dim)(seq)                # Swin/ViT normalize each token
assert seq.shape == (B, class="n">32 * class="n">32 * class="n">32, embed_dim)  # 32768 tokens, 48 features each
scaled_dot_product_attention.ipynb
Click a query token (left). Edge opacity = attention weight after softmax.

Self-Attention: every voxel asks every other voxel "how relevant are you?"

Each token emits a Query, a Key and a Value. Relevance between a query i and key j is their dot product qi⋅kjq_{i}\cdot k_{j}qi​⋅kj​, scaled by 1/d1/\sqrt{d}1/d​, then passed through softmax so the weights for one query sum to 1. The output is the softmax-weighted sum of Values.

Why it matters here: a CNN only sees a local neighborhood. Attention lets a voxel on one side of the brain directly reference tissue on the other — essential for deciding whether two bright blobs belong to one tumor.
1.00

Low temperature → softmax sharpens to "hard" attention (one neighbor wins). High → diffuse, averaging attention. This is exactly the scale=headdim−0.5scale = head_dim^{-0.5}scale=headd​im−0.5 term in cross_attention_skip.py:30.

Q·Kᵀsoftmax(dim=-1)·Vmulti-head
💡 Why it mattersSelf-attention lets every token (or voxel) directly weigh its relevance to every other one via query-key dot products, so a model can capture long-range dependencies in a single layer instead of slowly propagating information through stacked convolutions or recurrence. This dynamic, content-based routing — not fixed local kernels — is what gives Transformers their global receptive field and parallelizable training.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the core mechanism behind all modern LLMs (GPT, Claude, Llama) and vision/medical-imaging foundation models — ViTs, Segment Anything, and 3D Swin/TransUNet-style tumor and organ segmentation in MONAI. The same attention drives DINOv2 self-supervised features and SAM-2 promptable segmentation now used for interactive lesion delineation in radiology.
Cutting-edge / SOTATransformer / "Attention Is All You Need" (Google)FlashAttention-3 (Dao et al.)Vision Transformer / DINOv2 (Meta)Segment Anything 2 (Meta)Swin Transformer / TransUNet (medical seg, MONAI)vLLM (PagedAttention serving)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (fused kernel + the formula it computes)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# Q,K,V: (batch, heads, seq, head_dim) — what a transformer block produces
B, H, L, d = class="n">2, class="n">8, class="n">64, class="n">32
q = torch.randn(B, H, L, d)
k = torch.randn(B, H, L, d)
v = torch.randn(B, H, L, d)

# Idiomatic: fused, numerically-stable, optionally Flash/causal kernels
out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=False)  # (B,H,L,d)

# The exact formula the widget animates — softmax(QKᵀ/√d) · V:
scale = class="n">1.0 / d ** class="n">0.5                       # = head_dim^{-0.5}
scores = (q @ k.transpose(-class="n">2, -class="n">1)) * scale    # (B,H,L,L) raw affinities
attn = scores.softmax(dim=-class="n">1)                 # rows sum to 1 → weights
out_manual = attn @ v                         # weighted sum of Values

assert torch.allclose(out, out_manual, atol=class="n">1e-5)  # same result
num_heads — parallel attention subspaces
The channel dim splits into H heads; each head attends differently, then they concat.

Multi-head attention — many questions at once

Instead of one attention map, the embed_dim is split into H heads of size d/Hd/Hd/H. Each head computes its own Q·Kᵀ·V in a different subspace, so one head can track "bright edges" while another tracks "spatial proximity". Outputs are concatenated and projected.

OncoSeg scales heads with depth: numheads=(3,6,12,24)num_heads=(3,6,12,24)numh​eads=(3,6,12,24) across the four Swin stages. Watch how each head specializes on a different feature axis below — more heads = more parallel relationships, at fixed total compute.
4
💡 Why it mattersA single attention map forces the model to mix all token relationships into one weighted average, blurring distinct cues; multi-head attention runs several attention computations in parallel on learned subspace projections so each head can specialize (e.g. local edges, long-range layout, channel/semantic links) and the results are concatenated. This gives the model the capacity to attend to many relationships at once without one pattern washing out another.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the core block of every modern Transformer: LLMs (GPT/Llama/Claude), vision backbones (ViT, DINOv2) and detectors/segmenters (DETR, SAM). In medical imaging it powers Vision-Transformer encoders and hybrid CNN-Transformer models such as TransUNet, Swin-UNETR and UNETR for 3D tumor and organ segmentation on CT/MRI.
Cutting-edge / SOTAAttention Is All You Need (Transformer, Google)FlashAttention-3 (Dao et al.)Vision Transformer / DINOv2 (Google, Meta)Swin-UNETR & UNETR (MONAI / NVIDIA)Segment Anything 2 (Meta)Grouped-Query Attention (Llama 3, Mistral)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (fused QKV → per-head SDPA → concat → output proj)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from einops import rearrange

# x: (B, N, D) tokens.  H heads, each of width d = D // H.
def multi_head_attention(x, Wqkv, Wo, H):
    B, N, D = x.shape
    qkv = x @ Wqkv                                   # (B, N, 3D): fused Q,K,V projection
    q, k, v = qkv.chunk(class="n">3, dim=-class="n">1)
    # split D into H independent subspaces -> (B, H, N, d); each head attends on its own d-dim slice
    q, k, v = (rearrange(t, class="s">"b n (h d) -> b h n d", h=H) for t in (q, k, v))

    # the line that actually runs (fused/flash kernel): softmax(QKᵀ / √d) · V  per head, in parallel
    out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)    # scale = 1/√d = head_dim^-0.5

    # from-scratch equivalent of the kernel above:
    #   d = q.shape[-1]
    #   A = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / d**0.5        # (B,H,N,N) scores, scale = head_dim^-0.5
    #   out = A.softmax(dim=-1) @ v                    # softmax-weighted sum of Values, per head

    out = rearrange(out, class="s">"b h n d -> b n (h d)")     # concat the H heads back to width D
    return out @ Wo                                  # mix heads: final output projection
swin_encoder.py — windowed + shifted attention
Grid = feature map. Colored squares = attention windows. Toggle the shift to see cross-window mixing.

Swin: attention that doesn't explode in cost

Global attention over a 128³ volume is impossible — cost grows as (number of voxels)². Swin restricts attention to small windows (here, square tiles), making cost linear in volume. To let information cross window borders, alternating layers shift the window grid by half a window.

Window-only attention would trap each region in its own tile forever. The shift is what stitches the whole volume together over successive layers — global reach, local cost.
4
💡 Why it mattersVanilla self-attention costs O(n²) in the number of tokens, so it becomes intractable on the long sequences produced by high-resolution images (or 3D volumes). Swin restricts attention to small local windows — making cost linear in image size — and then shifts the window grid between layers so information still flows across window boundaries, recovering a global receptive field without the quadratic blow-up.
▸ Where it’s usedSwin and its successors are go-to backbones for dense prediction at high resolution: object detection and segmentation, and especially medical imaging where Swin UNETR and nnFormer set strong marks on 3D CT/MRI tumor and organ segmentation (e.g. the BraTS and BTCV benchmarks). The window-attention idea also underpins efficient video and document-image transformers.
Cutting-edge / SOTASwin Transformer / SwinV2 (Microsoft)Swin UNETR (NVIDIA / MONAI)nnFormerVideo Swin TransformerMask2Former (with Swin backbone)FlashAttention-3 (complementary exact-attention speedup)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs in a Swin encoder block (W-MSA / SW-MSA)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

def _partition(x, win):                          # (B,H,W,C) -> (nW*B, win*win, C)
    B, H, W, C = x.shape
    x = x.view(B, H // win, win, W // win, win, C)
    return x.permute(class="n">0, class="n">1, class="n">3, class="n">2, class="n">4, class="n">5).reshape(-class="n">1, win * win, C)

def swin_block(x, qkv, proj, win=class="n">4, shift=class="n">0, H=class="n">32, W=class="n">32):  # x:(B,H*W,C); shift=win//2 on alt. layers
    B, _, C = x.shape
    x = x.view(B, H, W, C)
    attn_mask = None
    if shift:                                    # shifted windows straddle previous borders
        x = torch.roll(x, (-shift, -shift), dims=(class="n">1, class="n">2))
        idx, cnt = torch.zeros(class="n">1, H, W, class="n">1), class="n">0     # region ids so wrapped tokens DON'T cross-attend
        for hs in (slice(class="n">0, -win), slice(-win, -shift), slice(-shift, None)):
            for ws in (slice(class="n">0, -win), slice(-win, -shift), slice(-shift, None)):
                idx[:, hs, ws, :] = cnt; cnt += class="n">1
        m = _partition(idx, win).squeeze(-class="n">1)      # (nW, win*win)
        attn_mask = torch.where(m[:, None, :] == m[:, :, None], class="n">0.0, float(class="s">"-inf"))
        attn_mask = attn_mask.repeat(B, class="n">1, class="n">1)     # -> (nW*B, win*win, win*win), additive in softmax
    win_seq = _partition(x, win)
    q, k, v = qkv(win_seq).chunk(class="n">3, dim=-class="n">1)       # NB: real Swin is multi-head + rel-pos bias
    out = proj(F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=attn_mask))  # scale=1/sqrt(C) here
    out = out.view(B, H // win, W // win, win, win, C).permute(class="n">0, class="n">1, class="n">3, class="n">2, class="n">4, class="n">5).reshape(B, H, W, C)
    if shift:
        out = torch.roll(out, (shift, shift), dims=(class="n">1, class="n">2))
    return out.view(B, H * W, C)
cross_attention_skip.py — decoder queries encoder
Top row = encoder features (Keys/Values). Bottom = decoder query. Bars = where the query "looks".

Cross-Attention Skip: a smarter U-Net bridge

A normal U-Net concatenates encoder features into the decoder — every location, indiscriminately. OncoSeg instead makes the decoder the Query and the encoder the Key/Value. The decoder pulls only the encoder positions it actually needs.

Intuition: the decoder is rebuilding a tumor edge and "asks" the encoder — where are the sharp boundaries that match what I'm drawing here? Move the decoder query and watch which encoder columns light up.
0.40
1.6

Residual + FFN wrap the attention (out = dec + attn; out += ffn(norm(out))) so the skip can refine rather than replace the decoder's own estimate.

💡 Why it mattersA plain U-Net skip concatenates or adds every encoder feature into the decoder, dragging along irrelevant context and noise at each resolution. A cross-attention skip instead lets the decoder use its own features as queries and attend over the encoder's keys/values, so it selectively pulls in only the encoder context relevant at each spatial location — sharpening fuzzy boundaries (e.g. tumor edges) that an indiscriminate skip blurs.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the bridge in Transformer-CNN hybrid segmentation networks (this project's Swin-encoder/CNN-decoder OncoSeg, plus UNETR/Swin-UNETR-style 3D medical models for organ and tumor delineation), and the same query-encoder cross-attention powers attention-gated U-Nets and the cross-attention layers that inject text/image conditioning into diffusion U-Nets.
Cutting-edge / SOTAUNETR (NVIDIA/MONAI)Swin-UNETR (NVIDIA/MONAI)Attention U-NetnnFormerStable Diffusion U-Net cross-attentionTransUNet
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs in cross_attention_skip.py▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
# 3D U-Net skip as cross-attention: decoder = Query, encoder = Key/Value.
# enc, dec: [B, C, H, W, D]  ->  flatten voxels to a token sequence [B, N, C]
B, C, H, W, Dd = dec.shape
enc_seq = enc.flatten(class="n">2).transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2)          # [B, N_enc, C_enc]  K/V source
dec_seq = dec.flatten(class="n">2).transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2)          # [B, N_dec, C_dec]  Q source
Q = q_proj(norm_dec(dec_seq))                     # decoder asks the questions -> [B, N_dec, inner]
K = k_proj(norm_enc(enc_seq)); V = v_proj(norm_enc(enc_seq))   # [B, N_enc, inner]
# split heads -> [B, heads, N, head_dim]; inner = n_heads * head_dim (N differs for Q vs K/V)
Q, K, V = (t.reshape(B, t.shape[class="n">1], n_heads, head_dim).transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2) for t in (Q, K, V))
# softmax(QKᵀ / √d_head) · V  — the line the whole widget visualizes
ctx = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V)     # fused; scale = head_dim**-0.5 inside
# from-scratch equivalent:  ctx = (Q @ K.transpose(-2,-1) * head_dim**-0.5).softmax(-1) @ V
ctx = ctx.transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2).reshape(B, -class="n">1, n_heads * head_dim)   # merge heads -> [B, N_dec, inner]
out = dec_seq + out_proj(ctx)                     # out_proj: inner -> C; residual refines decoder
out = out + ffn(norm_out(out))                    # transformer-style FFN block
fused = out.transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2).reshape(B, C, H, W, Dd)  # back to volume [B, C, H, W, D]
temporal_attention.py — baseline vs follow-up fusion
Baseline (t0) and follow-up (t1) bottlenecks; attention + difference highlight change.

Temporal attention — seeing what changed between scans

For longitudinal response, OncoSeg can fuse two timepoints. The follow-up features attend to the baseline (cross-attention), then concatenate the explicit difference t1−t0t1 - t0t1−t0 and project. The model thus represents evolution, not just two static masks.

Operates on the deepest (bottleneck) features. Drag the tumor-growth slider: the difference channel lights up exactly where the lesion expanded — the signal a response classifier wants. temporal_attention.py:40-45.
+35%
💡 Why it mattersA single scan tells you the tumor's current size but not its trajectory, yet treatment response (PD/SD/PR) is defined by change; temporal cross-attention lets follow-up features query the baseline so the model represents how a lesion evolved (grow/shrink/shift) rather than comparing two static masks. Fusing attention with an explicit t1−t0 difference channel hands the response classifier exactly the signal it needs and is robust to alignment noise that a naive voxel subtraction would amplify.
▸ Where it’s usedLongitudinal tumor response and progression-free-survival modeling (RECIST/iRECIST automation), change detection in serial CT/MR and chest X-rays, and disease-progression tracking in MS/Alzheimer brain MRI; the same baseline-vs-follow-up cross-attention pattern also drives remote-sensing change detection and video temporal modeling. In practice it appears as cross-attention fusion blocks added to a segmentation/encoder backbone (e.g. a Swin or U-Net bottleneck) for paired or multi-timepoint studies.
Cutting-edge / SOTATimeSformer (Meta, divided space-time attention)ViViT (Google video transformer)ChangeFormer (siamese transformer change detection)LongiSeg / longitudinal nnU-Net pipelinesVideoMAE V2MONAI (medical-imaging framework)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs in the temporal fusion module▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class TemporalFusion(nn.Module):           # fuses two longitudinal bottlenecks
    def __init__(self, C, heads=class="n">4):
        super().__init__()
        self.h = heads
        self.q, self.k, self.v = (nn.Conv3d(C, C, class="n">1) for _ in range(class="n">3))
        self.proj = nn.Conv3d(class="n">2 * C, C, class="n">1)  # consumes [attended t1 ; (t1 - t0)]

    def forward(self, t0, t1):             # t0,t1: (B,C,D,H,W) deepest features
        B, C, D, H, W = t1.shape
        sh = lambda x: x.flatten(class="n">2).transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2).unflatten(class="n">2, (self.h, C // self.h)).transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2)
        q, k, v = sh(self.q(t1)), sh(self.k(t0)), sh(self.v(t0))  # t1 queries, t0 keys/values
        # cross-attention: softmax(QKᵀ/√d) V  — follow-up attends to baseline
        a = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
        a = a.transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2).reshape(B, D, H, W, C).permute(class="n">0, class="n">4, class="n">1, class="n">2, class="n">3)
        diff = t1 - t0                     # explicit change channel: t1 − t0
        return self.proj(torch.cat([a, diff], dim=class="n">1))  # concat → project back to C
oncoseg.py — encoder ↓ / bottleneck / decoder ↑ with skips
Resolution halves down the encoder, doubles up the decoder; skips bridge equal scales.

The U-Net shape — context down, detail up

Segmentation needs both global context (what is this?) and pixel precision (where exactly?). The U-Net solves this with a contracting encoder, an expanding decoder, and skip connections that hand high-resolution detail across the "U" so the decoder doesn't have to invent it.

OncoSeg's twist: the encoder is a Swin transformer, the decoder is CNN, and the skips are cross-attention (demo 09) instead of plain concatenation. Hover a stage to trace its skip. Channels 48→96→192→384 mirror back down.
2
💡 Why it mattersDense per-pixel prediction needs both global context (what the structure is) and fine spatial detail (exactly where its boundary lies), but downsampling for context destroys the resolution needed for crisp edges. The U-Net solves this with a contracting encoder that builds semantic context, an expanding decoder that recovers resolution, and skip connections that re-inject high-resolution encoder features into the decoder so boundaries stay sharp.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the default backbone for medical image segmentation (brain-tumor, organ, and lesion delineation on MRI/CT, as in this OncoSeg project) and underpins much of biomedical microscopy and satellite/land-cover segmentation. The same encoder-decoder-with-skips shape also powers the denoising networks inside latent diffusion image generators like Stable Diffusion.
Cutting-edge / SOTAnnU-Net (DKFZ)MONAI (Project MONAI)SwinUNETR / UNETR (NVIDIA)TransUNetAttention U-NetStable Diffusion U-Net (Stability AI)
▸ Code PyTorch — the real 3D U-Net forward: encode ↓, bottleneck, decode ↑ with skip concat▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class DoubleConv(nn.Module):                       # the helper the U-Net leans on
    def __init__(self, i, o):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(i, o, class="n">3, padding=class="n">1), nn.BatchNorm3d(o), nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                                 nn.Conv3d(o, o, class="n">3, padding=class="n">1), nn.BatchNorm3d(o), nn.ReLU(inplace=True))
    def forward(self, x): return self.net(x)

class UNet3D(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, chs=(class="n">48, class="n">96, class="n">192, class="n">384)):    # the 48->96->192->384 pyramid
        super().__init__()
        self.down = nn.ModuleList(DoubleConv(i, o) for i, o in zip((class="n">1,)+chs, chs))
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool3d(class="n">2)                                  # resolution halves
        self.up   = nn.ModuleList(nn.ConvTranspose3d(o, i, class="n">2, stride=class="n">2)  # learnable upsample
                                  for i, o in zip(chs[:-class="n">1], chs[class="n">1:]))
        self.dec  = nn.ModuleList(DoubleConv(class="n">2*i, i) for i in chs[:-class="n">1])  # 2*i: after skip concat
        self.head = nn.Conv3d(chs[class="n">0], class="n">3, class="n">1)                          # 1x1 conv -> class logits
    def forward(self, x):                          # x: (B,1,D,H,W); D,H,W ideally divisible by 8
        skips = []
        for i, enc in enumerate(self.down):
            x = enc(x)
            if i < len(self.down) - class="n">1: skips.append(x); x = self.pool(x)
        for up, dec, skip in zip(reversed(self.up), reversed(self.dec), reversed(skips)):
            x = up(x)                                                # double D,H,W
            d = [skip.shape[k] - x.shape[k] for k in (class="n">2, class="n">3, class="n">4)]      # pad if floor-pool left odd sizes
            x = F.pad(x, [d[class="n">2]//class="n">2, d[class="n">2]-d[class="n">2]//class="n">2, d[class="n">1]//class="n">2, d[class="n">1]-d[class="n">1]//class="n">2, d[class="n">0]//class="n">2, d[class="n">0]-d[class="n">0]//class="n">2])
            x = dec(torch.cat([x, skip], dim=class="n">1))                     # bridge equal scales across the "U"
        return self.head(x)                        # (B, 3, D, H, W) segmentation logits
deep_supervision.py — auxiliary losses at every scale
Each decoder stage gets its own prediction head + loss, upsampled and weighted.

Deep supervision — gradients reach every layer

Normally only the final output is scored. Deep supervision attaches a prediction head at each decoder stage and adds their losses (with decreasing weights), so even the deepest, coarsest layers get a direct training signal. This stabilizes training and helps tiny lesions survive downsampling.

Weights normalize to roughly [0.57, 0.29, 0.14] — finest scale counts most. Review caveat: the src library version forgets to interpolate, so its DS loss is shape-broken; only the inline trainer interpolates correctly. losses.py:79-90.
0.50
💡 Why it mattersIn a deep encoder-decoder, gradients backpropagated from a single final output get attenuated before they reach the deepest, coarsest layers, slowing and destabilizing their training. Deep supervision attaches an auxiliary prediction head and loss at each decoder stage, giving every layer a direct gradient signal — this speeds convergence, fights vanishing gradients, and keeps small structures (tiny lesions) discriminable even after heavy downsampling.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is a default ingredient in 3D medical image segmentation — nnU-Net and the MONAI/SegResNet-style decoders apply weighted multi-scale losses (finest scale weighted most) for organ and tumor segmentation in CT/MRI. The same idea (auxiliary intermediate-stage losses) appears more broadly in UNet++/UNet 3+, the original GoogLeNet/Inception auxiliary classifiers, and HRNet-style dense-prediction backbones.
Cutting-edge / SOTAnnU-Net (DKFZ)MONAI / SegResNet (Project MONAI, NVIDIA)UNet++ (Zhou et al.)UNet 3+ (full-scale deep supervision)GoogLeNet/Inception (auxiliary classifiers)Deeply-Supervised Nets (Lee et al., 2015)
▸ Code PyTorch + MONAI — what actually runs in the trainer▶
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from monai.losses import DiceCELoss

# decoder returns coarse->fine logits, one head per stage (1x1 conv, B,C,d,h,w)
logits = decoder(skips)            # e.g. [H/16, H/8, H/4]: logits[0] is COARSEST
loss_fn = DiceCELoss(sigmoid=True) # per-channel BCE+Dice (multi-label head)

# decay**(n-1-i): with coarse->fine logits the FINEST (last) head gets the
# largest weight -> [0.143, 0.286, 0.571]; coarse aux heads get small grad.
n = len(logits)
w = torch.tensor([class="n">0.5 ** (n - class="n">1 - i) for i in range(n)], device=label.device)
w = w / w.sum()                    # finest scale dominates; coarse heads still learn

total = class="n">0.0
for wi, pred in zip(w, logits):
    # upsample each coarse head to the label grid before scoring
    # (nnU-Net instead downsamples the label per-head; both are accepted)
    pred = F.interpolate(pred, size=label.shape[class="n">2:], mode=class="s">"trilinear",
                         align_corners=False)
    total = total + wi * loss_fn(pred, label)   # L = Sum_i w_i * L(up(y_i), y)

total.backward()                   # gradient reaches every decoder stage directly
inference.py — sliding_window_inference over the full scan
An ROI-sized window tiles the full volume with overlap; predictions are blended.

Sliding-window inference — fitting a big scan through a small model

The model trains on 96–128³ ROI crops, but a real scan is 240×240×155. At test time a window of the ROI size slides across the volume with overlap; the overlapping predictions are averaged (Gaussian-weighted) so there are no seams at tile borders.

More overlap = smoother, slower. This is how OncoSeg processes a whole brain without ever holding it in memory at once. Raise the overlap and watch the seam artifacts vanish.
0.25
💡 Why it mattersA model trained on small ROI crops (e.g. 128³) cannot fit a full 240×240×155 scan or a gigapixel slide into GPU memory at once, and naively tiling produces visible seams at patch borders. Sliding-window inference solves both: it slides a fixed-size window across the volume with overlap and blends the overlapping predictions with a Gaussian (center-weighted) overlap-add, giving seamless, memory-bounded full-resolution output.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the standard test-time recipe for 3D medical segmentation (BraTS brain tumor, abdominal CT, whole-body PET) in MONAI and nnU-Net, and the same tile-infer-stitch pattern drives gigapixel histopathology (CAMELYON, TCGA) and high-resolution remote-sensing/satellite segmentation where the full image never fits the model.
Cutting-edge / SOTAMONAI sliding_window_inference (Project MONAI)nnU-Net (DKFZ)TorchIO GridSampler/GridAggregatorSwinUNETR (MONAI)STU-Net (large-scale 3D U-Net)DeepMedic (dense multi-scale patch inference)
▸ Code PyTorch / MONAI — what actually runs at test time▶
import torch
from monai.inferers import sliding_window_inference

# vol: full scan (B, C, 240, 240, 155); model trained on 128^3 ROI crops.
# The real one-liner OncoSeg runs at test time (default overlap is 0.25):
logits = sliding_window_inference(
    inputs=vol, roi_size=(class="n">128, class="n">128, class="n">128), sw_batch_size=class="n">4,
    predictor=model, overlap=class="n">0.25, mode=class="s">"gaussian",  # Gaussian-weighted blend
)                                                     # -> (B, 3, 240, 240, 155)

# What that does under the hood — overlap-add with a per-window importance map.
B, n_cls, roi_size = vol.shape[class="n">0], class="n">3, (class="n">128, class="n">128, class="n">128)
acc  = torch.zeros(B, n_cls, *vol.shape[class="n">2:])  # accumulated weighted logits
wsum = torch.zeros(class="n">1, class="n">1,    *vol.shape[class="n">2:])   # accumulated weights (denominator)
g = gaussian_kernel(roi_size)                 # peak-at-center weight, low at seams
# MONAI stacks up to sw_batch_size windows per forward and shifts edge windows
# back to fit the volume; shown one-at-a-time here for clarity:
for sl in dense_patch_slices(vol.shape[class="n">2:], roi_size, overlap=class="n">0.25):
    pred = model(vol[(..., *sl)])             # forward one ROI window
    acc[(..., *sl)]  += g * pred              # weighted contribution (g broadcasts)
    wsum[(..., *sl)] += g
out = acc / wsum                              # normalize: pred(x) = Σ wᵢ pᵢ / Σ wᵢ
msd labels {1,2,3} → 3 overlapping sigmoid channels TC/WT/ET
Class labels become 3 nested binary regions. Each channel has its own sigmoid.

The output head — multi-label, not multi-class

Brain-tumor regions nest: ET ⊂ TC ⊂ WT. So OncoSeg does not use a 4-way softmax. It derives 3 overlapping binary regions — Tumor Core (labels 2,3), Whole Tumor (1,2,3), Enhancing (3) — and predicts each with an independent sigmoid. The channels need not sum to 1.

This is the BraTS convention and it changes everything downstream: the loss is BCE+Dice per channel, and uncertainty must use binary entropy (demo 18) — a subtle bug-source the review flagged. Toggle a voxel's true class to see which channels fire. train_all.py:71-74.
3
💡 Why it mattersTumor sub-regions physically nest (enhancing ⊂ core ⊂ whole tumor), so a 4-way softmax — which forces classes to be mutually exclusive and sum to 1 — is the wrong inductive bias. An independent sigmoid per region (multi-label) lets a single voxel belong to several regions at once, which is what the BraTS evaluation actually scores and which sets the rest of the pipeline (per-channel BCE+Dice loss, binary rather than categorical entropy for uncertainty).
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the standard output head for brain-tumor segmentation in the BraTS challenge and any nested/overlapping-region task, and more broadly for multi-label dense prediction where a pixel can carry several attributes at once (e.g. co-occurring pathologies on a chest X-ray, or overlapping anatomical structures). Production medical-imaging stacks like MONAI and nnU-Net expose exactly this via sigmoid heads plus per-channel Dice/BCE losses.
Cutting-edge / SOTAnnU-Net (DKFZ)MONAI DiceCELoss / DiceFocalLoss (sigmoid=True)BraTS challenge TC/WT/ET region conventionSegResNet (MONAI / NVIDIA)Swin UNETR (NVIDIA)BCEWithLogitsLoss (PyTorch)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (sigmoid head, not softmax)▶
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

# Label -> 3 overlapping BraTS regions (train_all.py:71-74). TARGET masks NEST: ET ⊂ TC ⊂ WT.
def msd_to_regions(label):                       # label: (B,1,D,H,W) in {0,1,2,3}
    tc = ((label == class="n">2) | (label == class="n">3)).float()   # Tumor Core  = labels {2,3}
    wt = ((label == class="n">1) | (label == class="n">2) | (label == class="n">3)).float()  # Whole Tumor = {1,2,3}
    et = (label == class="n">3).float()                     # Enhancing   = label {3}
    return torch.cat([tc, wt, et], dim=class="n">1)         # (B,3,D,H,W) — order [TC, WT, ET]

# The head: 3 logits, one INDEPENDENT sigmoid each — NOT a 4-way softmax over classes.
head = nn.Conv3d(in_ch, class="n">3, kernel_size=class="n">1)         # decoder features -> 3 region logits
logits = head(features)                           # (B,3,D,H,W)
probs  = torch.sigmoid(logits)                    # p_c = 1/(1+e^-z_c), per channel
#   softmax would force Σ_c p_c = 1 (mutually exclusive); sigmoid lets them overlap, so
#   probs.sum(1) ≠ 1. NOTE: the TARGET masks satisfy ET ⊆ TC ⊆ WT, but the three sigmoids
#   are INDEPENDENT — the model is NOT constrained to p_ET ≤ p_TC ≤ p_WT and often violates
#   it; BraTS pipelines re-impose the hierarchy as a separate post-processing step.
preds = probs > class="n">0.5                               # independent per-channel thresholding

# Loss is therefore PER channel (multi-label): BCE-with-logits + Dice(sigmoid=True), weighted.
bce = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, msd_to_regions(label))
# real DiceCELoss (losses.py): 0.5*MONAI DiceLoss(sigmoid=True) + 0.5*BCEWithLogitsLoss
# uncertainty is BINARY (per-channel) entropy, not categorical softmax entropy.
losses.py — Dice + BCE, and why Focal handles imbalance
Per-voxel loss vs predicted prob for a positive voxel. Focal down-weights easy cases.

The training objective — Dice + cross-entropy (+ Focal)

Tumor voxels are a tiny minority, so plain cross-entropy lets the model "win" by predicting all-background. OncoSeg combines Dice loss (optimizes overlap directly, scale-invariant) with BCE (per-voxel calibration). Focal loss adds a (1−p)γ(1-p)^{}\gamma (1−p)γ factor that shrinks the loss on easy, confident voxels so training focuses on the hard boundary.

Drag γ: at γ=0 Focal = BCE; as γ grows, confidently-correct voxels contribute almost nothing, so gradient budget flows to the ambiguous tumor rim. This is the class-imbalance fix at the heart of medical segmentation.
2.0
💡 Why it mattersIn dense segmentation the foreground (a tumor) is a tiny fraction of voxels, so a plain cross-entropy/BCE loss is minimized by predicting all-background — the model "wins" while finding nothing. Combining region-overlap losses (Dice) that optimize the IoU/Dice metric directly with per-voxel cross-entropy (and a Focal (1−p)γ term that suppresses easy, confident voxels) keeps gradient on the rare, hard tumor-boundary voxels and is the standard fix for extreme class imbalance.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the default training objective for 3D medical segmentation — brain-tumor (BraTS), organ, and lesion delineation in CT/MRI — and powers nnU-Net and MONAI pipelines; the same Dice/Tversky/Focal family is used wherever foreground is rare, e.g. cell/nucleus segmentation and remote-sensing or defect detection.
Cutting-edge / SOTAnnU-Net (DKFZ)MONAI DiceCELoss / DiceFocalLossFocal Loss / RetinaNet (FAIR)Tversky & Focal-Tversky lossBoundary / Hausdorff DT lossUnified Focal loss
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (DiceFocal, 3D sigmoid heads)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

def seg_loss(logits, target, gamma=class="n">2.0, w_dice=class="n">1.0, w_focal=class="n">1.0, eps=class="n">1e-6):
    # logits, target: [B, C, D, H, W]; sigmoid heads → channels are independent
    p = torch.sigmoid(logits)                      # per-voxel tumor probability

    # --- soft Dice loss: 1 - 2|A∩B| / (|A|+|B|), summed over spatial dims ---
    dims = (class="n">2, class="n">3, class="n">4)
    inter = (p * target).sum(dims)
    dice = class="n">1 - (class="n">2 * inter + eps) / (p.sum(dims) + target.sum(dims) + eps)
    dice = dice.mean()

    # --- Focal-BCE: BCE * (1-p_t)^γ  → down-weights easy, confident voxels ---
    bce = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, target, reduction=class="s">"none")
    p_t = p * target + (class="n">1 - p) * (class="n">1 - target)      # prob of true class; soft-label safe
    focal = ((class="n">1 - p_t) ** gamma * bce).mean()      # γ=0 ⇒ plain BCE

    return w_dice * dice + w_focal * focal
    # ≈ monai.losses.DiceFocalLoss(sigmoid=True, gamma=2.0); same family but NOT bit-exact
    # (MONAI's reduction/normalization & include_background defaults differ) — not a drop-in oracle
metrics.py — Dice overlap & why it punishes small lesions
Teal = ground truth. Amber = prediction. Overlap = where both agree. Drag prediction.

Dice: the overlap score that drives everything

Dice = 2⋅∣A∩B∣/(∣A∣+∣B∣)2\cdot |A\cap B| / (|A|+|B|)2⋅∣A∩B∣/(∣A∣+∣B∣) — twice the overlap over the total mask size. 1.0 = perfect, 0 = no overlap. It's the training loss and the headline metric because plain pixel accuracy is useless when 99% of voxels are background.

Shrink the prediction and watch Dice collapse: for a small tumor, missing a handful of voxels costs far more Dice than the same miss on a large one. This is precisely why OncoSeg's worst cases are small-TC tumors — and why the review flags ET (often empty) as producing NaN Dice.
100
20
💡 Why it mattersThe Dice coefficient (2·|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|)) measures mask overlap directly, so it stays meaningful when foreground is a tiny fraction of voxels — exactly the regime where pixel accuracy is useless because predicting all-background already scores ~99%. As a soft, differentiable loss it optimizes overlap end-to-end and is class-imbalance-robust; as a metric it is the headline number for segmentation quality, with the caveat that it punishes small-lesion errors disproportionately and goes undefined when ground truth is empty.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the default loss-and-metric pairing for medical image segmentation — BraTS brain-tumor and KiTS kidney challenges, organ/lesion delineation, and clinical workflows feeding RECIST-style response assessment — and is built into MONAI, nnU-Net, and TotalSegmentator. The Dice family (often combined with cross-entropy or Focal) also appears broadly in cell/microscopy segmentation and any heavily imbalanced dense-prediction task.
Cutting-edge / SOTAnnU-Net (DKFZ)MONAI DiceCELoss/DiceFocalLoss (Project MONAI)TotalSegmentatorGeneralized Dice / GDL (Sudre et al. 2017)Tversky / Focal-Tversky lossSegResNet (MONAI, BraTS winners)
▸ Code PyTorch + MONAI — what actually runs▶
import torch
from monai.metrics import DiceMetric

# pred, gt: (B, C, D, H, W) one-hot (per-channel binary) masks for 3D tumor seg
pred = (logits.sigmoid() > class="n">0.5).float()    # binarize the network output

# --- idiomatic: MONAI Dice per-class, per-volume, then mean ---
metric = DiceMetric(include_background=False, reduction=class="s">"mean")
metric(y_pred=pred, y=gt)
dice = metric.aggregate().item()           # 0-dim tensor -> float in [0, 1]

# --- from-scratch (CLOSE but NOT identical: MONAI returns NaN for absent
#     classes and drops them; here a small epsilon avoids 0/0 instead) ---
dims = (class="n">2, class="n">3, class="n">4)                           # reduce over voxels, keep (B, C)
inter = (pred * gt).sum(dims)              # |A and B|
denom = pred.sum(dims) + gt.sum(dims)      # |A| + |B|
dice_manual = (class="n">2 * inter + class="n">1e-6) / (denom + class="n">1e-6)   # 2|A and B| / (|A|+|B|)

# soft (differentiable) Dice LOSS — no thresholding, logits -> prob
prob = logits.sigmoid()
soft = (class="n">2 * (prob * gt).sum(dims) + class="n">1.) / ((prob + gt).sum(dims) + class="n">1.)
# size-normalized: each class/volume weighs ~equally regardless of lesion
# size, which is why Dice loss is robust to foreground/background imbalance.
dice_loss = class="n">1.0 - soft.mean()
inference.py — Monte-Carlo Dropout uncertainty
Each pass randomly drops units → a slightly different mask. Spread across passes = uncertainty.

MC-Dropout: turning a network into an ensemble

Dropout normally only runs during training. Leave it on at inference and run the model N times: each pass silences a different random subset of units, giving N slightly different masks. The mean is the prediction; the per-voxel disagreement is the uncertainty.

Where passes agree (tumor center) → confident. Where they flicker (the boundary) → the model is honestly telling you "I'm not sure here" — the signal a radiologist would want highlighted.
0.20
12
💡 Why it mattersA standard softmax/sigmoid gives one number with no notion of how trustworthy it is; MC-Dropout (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016) shows that leaving dropout on at inference and averaging N stochastic passes approximates Bayesian model averaging, so the spread across passes becomes a free per-voxel epistemic uncertainty estimate. It is the cheapest way to get an honest "I'm not sure here" signal — one network, a few extra forward passes, no retraining and no ensemble of separately trained models to store.
▸ Where it’s usedWidely used in medical imaging to flag ambiguous tumor boundaries and out-of-distribution scans for radiologist review (MONAI exposes it directly), and more broadly for safety-critical triage in autonomous driving, active learning (querying the most uncertain samples), and as a cheap uncertainty baseline whenever a full deep ensemble is too expensive to train or serve.
Cutting-edge / SOTADropout as a Bayesian Approximation (Gal & Ghahramani, ICML 2016)Deep Ensembles (Lakshminarayanan et al., NeurIPS 2017)TorchUncertaintyUncertainty Baselines (Google)Fortuna (AWS)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs at inference▶
import torch
from torch.nn.modules.dropout import _DropoutNd

@torch.no_grad()
def mc_dropout(model, x, N=class="n">12):                  # x: [B,C,H,W,D]
    model.eval()                                 # BN/InstanceNorm use running stats...
    for m in model.modules():                    # ...but force every Dropout variant on
        if isinstance(m, (_DropoutNd, torch.nn.AlphaDropout)):  # AlphaDropout is NOT a _DropoutNd
            m.train()                            # -> stays stochastic at inference
    # NOTE: leaves dropout in train mode; call model.eval() again for deterministic inference.

    # N stochastic forward passes ~ a cheap ensemble (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016)
    probs = torch.stack([model(x).sigmoid() for _ in range(N)])   # [N,B,1,H,W,D]

    mean = probs.mean(class="n">0)                         # predictive mean  mu = (1/N) sum p_i
    # population sigma (unbiased=False); sample std of MC predictions is TOTAL
    # predictive uncertainty (epistemic + aleatoric), the standard MC-dropout proxy.
    std  = probs.std(class="n">0, unbiased=False)          # per-voxel uncertainty
    # entropy of the mean (alt. uncertainty): H = -[mu*log mu + (1-mu)*log(1-mu)]
    return mean, std
entropy — binary (correct) vs categorical (the inference.py bug)
Entropy vs probability. Maximal at p=0.5 ("coin flip"), zero at 0 or 1.

Predictive entropy — quantifying "how unsure"

Once you have a probability, entropy turns it into a single uncertainty number. For a binary (sigmoid) output it's −p⋅logp−(1−p)⋅log(1−p)-p\cdot log p - (1-p)\cdot log(1-p)−p⋅logp−(1−p)⋅log(1−p) — peaking at p=0.5. The model is most uncertain at the decision boundary.

Review caveat made tangible: OncoSeg's output is sigmoid (independent channels), so binary entropy is correct. But inference.py uses the categorical formula −Σp⋅logp-\Sigma p\cdot log p−Σp⋅logp, which omits the (1−p) mass and gives a different, invalid number. Drag p past 0.5 and compare the two curves.
0.50
💡 Why it mattersA network's softmax/sigmoid can output a confident-looking number even when it's effectively guessing; predictive entropy H = −Σ p log p collapses the whole output distribution into one scalar "how unsure" score, peaking when probability mass is spread evenly and going to zero only when the model commits. This lets you flag low-confidence voxels, slices, or whole scans for human review instead of trusting every prediction equally, and it is the workhorse acquisition signal in active learning.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed to build uncertainty heatmaps in medical segmentation (e.g. flagging ambiguous tumor borders in BraTS, where binary per-channel entropy is the correct form, not categorical), to gate auto-contouring in radiotherapy and trigger "refer to clinician" in diagnostic CAD, and as the core acquisition function for active/semi-supervised learning and out-of-distribution / selective-prediction pipelines. In LLMs the same quantity drives hallucination detection and abstention.
