▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (binary entropy is correct; softmax is the inference.py bug)▶
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

logits = model(x)                      # (B, C, D, H, W) — C independent tumor channels
eps = class="n">1e-7

# CORRECT for sigmoid heads: per-channel BINARY entropy, summed over channels.
# H = -p·log p - (1-p)·log(1-p)  (nats), maximal at p=0.5
p = logits.sigmoid().clamp(eps, class="n">1 - eps)
H_binary = -(p * p.log() + (class="n">1 - p) * (class="n">1 - p).log())   # (B, C, D, H, W)
H_binary = H_binary.sum(dim=class="n">1)                         # aggregate channels -> (B, D, H, W)

# THE inference.py BUG: categorical entropy treats channels as a softmax simplex.
# H = -Σ_c p_c·log p_c  — drops the (1-p) mass, wrong for independent sigmoids.
q = logits.softmax(dim=class="n">1)                              # forces Σ_c q_c = 1 (false here)
H_categorical = -(q * q.clamp_min(eps).log()).sum(dim=class="n">1)

# torch.distributions gives the same categorical value, as a sanity check:
# H_categorical == torch.distributions.Categorical(probs=q.movedim(1, -1)).entropy()
uncertainty_map = H_binary                             # use the binary form for BraTS sigmoid outputs
uncertainty_qualitative_analysis.py — the ECE trap
Reliability diagram. Diagonal = perfect. Bars below = over-confident.

Calibration & ECE — and how background voxels hide a problem

Calibration asks: when the model says "90% sure", is it right 90% of the time? Expected Calibration Error (ECE) averages the gap ∣confidence−accuracy∣|confidence - accuracy|∣confidence−accuracy∣ across confidence bins, weighted by how many voxels fall in each bin.

This is the project's most important finding. Toggle the background mass: when 98% of voxels are easy background, the count-weighted ECE looks tiny (~0.01, "well-calibrated") — even though on the foreground the model is badly over-confident (foreground ECE ≈ 0.49). The headline metric averages the problem away.
0.95
0.50
💡 Why it mattersA model can be accurate yet badly calibrated — its predicted probabilities don't match true correctness rates — so a "0.9" confidence may only be right 60% of the time, which is dangerous when clinicians use those scores to triage or decide. Expected Calibration Error (ECE) quantifies this gap, but in 3D segmentation the overwhelming majority of voxels are easy background; their near-perfect, near-1.0 confidence dominates the bins and drives ECE toward zero, hiding severe miscalibration on the few tumor-boundary voxels that actually matter.
▸ Where it’s usedCalibration is critical wherever probabilities feed downstream decisions: medical-imaging triage and uncertainty-aware tumor/lesion segmentation (foreground-only or boundary-region ECE, reliability diagrams), autonomous-driving perception, and selective prediction / abstention systems. It is standard practice to report foreground-masked ECE plus post-hoc fixes like temperature scaling, and to use uncertainty maps to flag voxels for human review.

▸ Code PyTorch — count-weighted ECE, and the foreground mask that reveals the trap▶
import torch

def ece(probs, labels, n_bins=class="n">10, mask=None):
    # probs: (N,) confidence of the predicted class; labels: (N,) 1 if that prediction was correct
    conf, correct = probs.flatten(), labels.flatten().float()
    if mask is not None:                          # the repo's bug: restrict to foreground voxels
        sel_m = mask.flatten().bool()             # .bool() so a 0/1 int mask selects, not fancy-indexes
        conf, correct = conf[sel_m], correct[sel_m]
    edges = torch.linspace(class="n">0, class="n">1, n_bins + class="n">1, device=conf.device)
    b = torch.bucketize(conf, edges[class="n">1:-class="n">1])        # n_bins bins, indices 0..n_bins-1; 0.0/1.0 in end bins
    out = conf.new_zeros(())
    N = conf.numel()                              # AFTER masking -> weights renormalize over the subset
    for k in range(n_bins):
        s = b == k
        n_k = s.sum()
        if n_k == class="n">0:
            continue
        acc_k  = correct[s].mean()                # observed accuracy in bin k
        conf_k = conf[s].mean()                   # mean claimed confidence
        out += (n_k / N) * (acc_k - conf_k).abs() # ECE = Sum_k (n_k/N)*|acc_k - conf_k|
    return out

# reported, count-weighted ECE looks tiny when 98% of voxels are easy background...
ece_all = ece(probs, correct)
# ...but masking to foreground exposes the over-confidence the headline metric averaged away
ece_fg  = ece(probs, correct, mask=foreground)
metrics.py — boundary error: HD95 vs mean surface distance
Two contours. Lines = each boundary point's distance to the other surface.

Hausdorff HD95 — Dice can't see boundary spikes

Dice measures volume overlap but is blind to shape: a prediction can have great Dice yet a single nasty spur far from the tumor. Hausdorff distance measures the worst boundary disagreement; HD95 uses the 95th percentile to ignore lone outlier voxels, reporting error in millimetres.

This is OncoSeg's secondary metric (15.4mm vs UNet3D's 21.0mm — its most defensible result). Add a boundary spike and watch HD95 jump while Dice barely moves — exactly why both metrics are reported together.
0
💡 Why it mattersDice/IoU are overlap metrics that saturate on large structures and are blind to thin boundary errors — a mask can score 0.95 Dice while a single voxel-thin spike juts far into healthy tissue. HD95 measures the 95th-percentile of surface-to-surface distances (in mm), so it directly penalizes those boundary excursions while the 95% trim discards lone-voxel outliers that make raw Hausdorff unstable.
▸ Where it’s usedHD95 is a mandatory boundary metric in nearly every medical-imaging segmentation challenge — BraTS (brain tumor), KiTS (kidney tumor), AMOS and the Medical Segmentation Decathlon — where surgical/radiotherapy margins make boundary accuracy clinically critical; it is reported alongside Dice for organ-at-risk delineation, tumor contouring, and CMR/cardiac structure analysis.

▸ Code PyTorch + MONAI — what actually runs (with the from-scratch surface-distance formula)▶
import torch, numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import distance_transform_edt as edt, binary_erosion

# pred, gt: (B, C, H, W, D) one-hot binary masks; spacing in mm
spacing = (class="n">1.0, class="n">1.0, class="n">1.0)

# --- idiomatic: MONAI does surface extraction + EDT + percentile for you ---
from monai.metrics import HausdorffDistanceMetric
hd95 = HausdorffDistanceMetric(include_background=False, percentile=class="n">95,
                               reduction=class="s">"mean_batch")
hd95(y_pred=pred, y=gt); print(hd95.aggregate())   # mm, per-channel

# --- from-scratch equivalent (what the animation draws), one 3-D mask pair ---
def surface_dist(a, b, spacing):                    # a, b: 3-D bool arrays
    surf_a = a ^ binary_erosion(a)                  # 1-voxel-thick border of A
    surf_b = b ^ binary_erosion(b)
    dt_b = edt(~surf_b, sampling=spacing)           # dist of every voxel to surface(B)
    return dt_b[surf_a]                             # d(p->B) for each border p of A

a = pred[class="n">0, class="n">0].bool().cpu().numpy()                 # pick one 3-D mask pair
b = gt[class="n">0, class="n">0].bool().cpu().numpy()
d = np.concatenate([surface_dist(a, b, spacing),
                    surface_dist(b, a, spacing)])   # symmetric: both directions
HD95 = np.percentile(d, class="n">95)   # 95th pct of pooled surface distances -> robust to spurs
recist.py — connected components = individual lesions
A binary mask is split into separate blobs; each colored region is one lesion.

Connected components — counting separate lesions

A segmentation mask is just "tumor / not tumor". To apply RECIST you must first split it into individual lesions — connected blobs of foreground voxels (6- or 26-connectivity in 3D). Each component is measured separately; tiny fragments below a size threshold are dropped as noise.

This is the bridge from a raw mask to clinical "target lesions". The diagnose-worst-case analysis counts these too: BRATS_077 had 31 fragmented WT components — a fragmented tumor is harder to segment and to measure. Raise the noise threshold to prune specks.
5
💡 Why it mattersA segmentation network only outputs "tumor / not tumor" per voxel; connected-component labeling is what turns that undifferentiated mask into discrete instances — one integer id per blob — so you can count lesions, measure each one's diameter for RECIST, and prune sub-threshold specks as noise. Without it there is no notion of "how many tumors" or "which lesion grew", only a pile of foreground pixels.
▸ Where it’s usedStandard post-processing in medical-imaging pipelines (lesion/nodule/metastasis counting and longitudinal RECIST tracking, e.g. nnU-Net's "keep largest component"), plus instance segmentation, cell counting in microscopy, connectomics, and any vision task that must convert a semantic mask into countable objects.

▸ Code SciPy/NumPy — what actually runs in recist.py▶
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage

# prob: model SIGMOID PROBABILITIES, shape [D,H,W]; threshold -> binary mask.
# (For raw logits the equivalent cut is 0.0, since sigmoid(0)=0.5.)
mask = prob > class="n">0.5

# 26-connectivity in 3D: voxels touch if they share a face, edge, OR corner.
structure = ndimage.generate_binary_structure(rank=class="n">3, connectivity=class="n">3)  # 3x3x3 all-ones

# label() = flood-fill / union-find sweep: every fg voxel gets the SAME integer id
# as its blob. labels==0 is background; labels==k is the k-th component (lesion).
labels, n_lesions = ndimage.label(mask, structure=structure)   # equivalence-class merge

# from-scratch essence (what label() does under the hood):
#   for each fg voxel v: for each labeled neighbor u: union(v, u)   # disjoint-set
#   then relabel each root -> 1..K  ->  one integer per lesion

# split into per-lesion masks, drop sub-threshold specks by VOLUME.
# NOTE: this is a min-size noise filter, NOT RECIST 1.1 (whose 10 mm is a
# longest-DIAMETER criterion, not a volume cut). spacing=(sz,sy,sx) in mm.
voxel_mm3 = np.prod(spacing)
for k in range(class="n">1, n_lesions + class="n">1):
    lesion = labels == k                           # boolean mask of lesion k
    if lesion.sum() * voxel_mm3 >= MIN_LESION_MM3: # keep measurable-size lesions
        yield lesion
recist.py / classifier.py — diameter → response class
Baseline vs follow-up sum of longest diameters. Zone = RECIST verdict.

RECIST 1.1: turning pixels into a clinical verdict

From the segmentation, measure each target lesion's longest diameter, sum them, and compare follow-up to baseline (and to the smallest-ever "nadir"):

  • CR — all target lesions gone.
  • PR — sum drops ≥ 30% vs baseline.
  • PD — sum rises ≥ 20% vs nadir and ≥ 5mm5mm5mm absolute.
  • SD — anything in between.
-40%
Review caveat: OncoSeg measures the longest diameter only on the single largest-area slice — it can under-measure elongated lesions and flip this verdict. And the README's "validated" longitudinal table is a fixed-seed simulation, not real follow-up scans.
💡 Why it mattersRECIST 1.1 is the standardized rulebook that converts tumor measurements into the response categories (CR/PR/SD/PD) used to decide whether a therapy is working — it picks target lesions, sums their longest diameters, and applies fixed thresholds (≥30% shrinkage = PR, ≥20% growth = PD). It matters because it turns subjective "the tumor looks smaller" reads into a reproducible, regulator-accepted endpoint that drives oncology trial outcomes and treatment decisions; an auto-segmentation model is only clinically useful once its pixel masks are reduced to this verdict.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the primary efficacy endpoint in essentially every solid-tumor clinical trial and in routine oncology follow-up CT/MRI reading, and is increasingly automated by deep-learning segmentation pipelines that measure lesions and emit the response verdict (e.g., lung-cancer, liver-met, and lymphoma trials). Related radiology variants and tooling include iRECIST for immunotherapy, PERCIST for PET, RANO for brain tumors, and segmentation engines like nnU-Net and MONAI feeding automated lesion measurement on platforms such as 3D Slicer.

▸ Code recist.py / classifier.py — what actually runs▶
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage

def sum_longest_diameters(mask, pixdim=(class="n">1.,class="n">1.,class="n">1.)):  # mask: 3D binary [H,W,D]
    lab, n = ndimage.label(mask > class="n">0)                  # split into connected lesions
    diams = []
    for i in range(class="n">1, n + class="n">1):
        les = lab == i
        z = int(np.argmax(les.sum(axis=(class="n">0, class="n">1))))      # largest-area axial slice
        pts = np.argwhere(les[:, :, z]) * np.asarray(pixdim[:class="n">2])  # (row,col)->mm
        d = np.linalg.norm(pts[:, None] - pts[None], axis=-class="n">1).max() if len(pts) > class="n">1 else class="n">0.
        diams.append(d)
    diams = sorted((x for x in diams if x >= class="n">10.), reverse=True)[:class="n">5]  # target lesions
    return float(sum(diams))                          # SLD = Σ longest diameters

def recist_response(base_mask, fu_mask, nadir_sld=None, pixdim=(class="n">1.,class="n">1.,class="n">1.)):
    base = sum_longest_diameters(base_mask, pixdim)
    fu   = sum_longest_diameters(fu_mask, pixdim)
    nadir = min(base, nadir_sld) if nadir_sld is not None else base
    if fu == class="n">0:                                  return class="s">"CR"   # all targets gone
    if base > class="n">0 and nadir > class="n">0:                                 # PD(vs nadir) ranked before PR(vs baseline)
        if (fu - nadir) / nadir >= class="n">0.20 and (fu - nadir) >= class="n">5.0: return class="s">"PD"  # ≥20% AND ≥5mm
        if (fu - base) / base <= -class="n">0.30:          return class="s">"PR"   # ≥30% drop vs baseline
    return class="s">"SD"                                                # otherwise stable
pretrain.py — DINO: emergent [CLS] attention, no labels
Patch grid = the input image. Amber dashed = the object. Teal = where the [CLS] token attends — diffuse early, locked onto the object late.

DINO: attention that finds the object — with zero labels

A Vision Transformer trained self-supervised (DINO: student matches a teacher across crops, no class labels) develops something striking: the [CLS][CLS][CLS] token's attention spontaneously localizes the salient object. Each patch gets an attention weight wi = softmax(β·featurei); we measure how peaked that map is with normalized entropy H = −Σ wi log wi / log N.

Drag training progress: at 0% features are random, so attention is uniform (H = 1.0) and the foreground gets only its fair area share (chance). As pretraining proceeds the inverse-temperature β grows, attention sharpens, entropy falls, and the foreground share races past chance toward ~100% — the object boundary emerges on its own.

Labels are the scarce resource in medical imaging — annotating a 3D tumor is hours of an expert's time. Self-supervised pretraining (DINO-style) is exactly how modern medical foundation models learn rich, object-aware features from oceans of unlabeled CT/MRI, so that fine-tuning a segmenter like OncoSeg needs only a handful of labeled scans. The entropy-drop / foreground-rise you see here is the signal that useful structure was learned before a single mask was ever shown.
0.00
no labelsViT [CLS]emergent localization
💡 Why it mattersDINO shows that a Vision Transformer trained by self-distillation with no labels spontaneously learns where objects are — its [CLS]-token attention maps segment foreground from background, and its features rival supervised ones on k-NN and linear probes. This solves the core bottleneck of medical and scientific imaging, where pixel-level labels are scarce and expensive, by yielding strong general-purpose features and rough object masks for free.
▸ Where it’s usedDINOv2 features power off-the-shelf backbones for classification, retrieval, depth, dense matching, and zero-shot segmentation, and serve as frozen encoders in robotics and remote sensing. In medical imaging they are increasingly used as pretrained encoders for pathology slides, radiology, and retinal images (e.g., RudolfV/UNI-style pathology foundation models), where labels are scarce and the emergent attention gives cheap candidate object/lesion masks.

▸ Code PyTorch — the real DINO self-distillation step (centered-sharpened teacher + EMA update)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
# DINO: student matches sharpened+centered teacher across crops, summed over all
# cross-view pairs (teacher sees 2 globals; student sees all). No labels.
def dino_loss(s_all, t_all, center, ncrops, tps=class="n">0.04, sps=class="n">0.1, m=class="n">0.9):
    s = (s_all / sps).chunk(ncrops)                          # ncrops student chunks
    t = F.softmax((t_all - center) / tps, dim=-class="n">1).detach().chunk(class="n">2)  # 2 teacher globals
    total, n = class="n">0.0, class="n">0
    for iq, q in enumerate(t):                               # over teacher globals
        for v in range(len(s)):
            if v == iq:                                      # skip same-crop pair
                continue
            total += torch.sum(-q * F.log_softmax(s[v], dim=-class="n">1), dim=-class="n">1).mean()
            n += class="n">1
    loss = total / n
    with torch.no_grad():                                    # center = EMA of RAW teacher out
        center = m * center + (class="n">1 - m) * t_all.mean(class="n">0, keepdim=True)
    return loss, center

s_glob, s_loc = student(globals_), student(locals_)          # student: all crops
with torch.no_grad():
    t_out = teacher(globals_)                                # teacher: 2 global crops only
loss, center = dino_loss(torch.cat([s_glob, s_loc]), t_out, center, ncrops)
loss.backward()                                              # only the student gets gradients
opt.step()
with torch.no_grad():                                        # teacher = EMA of student weights
    for pt, ps in zip(teacher.parameters(), student.parameters()):
        pt.data.mul_(class="n">0.996).add_(ps.detach().data, alpha=class="n">1 - class="n">0.996)
# emergent: trained ViT [CLS] head attends to the object (softmax(qK^T/sqrt(d)))
mae_pretrain.py — mask patches, reconstruct the rest
Original → masked input (gray = hidden patches) → reconstruction. Drag the mask ratio.

Masked Autoencoder — learn by filling in the blanks

Cut the image into patches, hide most of them at random, and train the network to reconstruct the missing pixels from the few that remain. The encoder only ever sees the visible patches; a lightweight decoder paints the holes back in. No labels needed — the image is its own supervision.

The headline MAE finding (He et al., 2021): you can mask 75% of patches and still rebuild a plausible image, because natural scans are redundant — a handful of patches carry the gist. That redundancy is exactly why MAE-style self-supervised pretraining works so well for data-hungry 3D medical encoders: a model can learn anatomy from thousands of unlabelled volumes before ever seeing a hand-drawn tumor mask. Drag past 75% and watch the reconstruction stay structurally faithful — the tumor blob survives.

75%
self-supervisedno labelsasymmetric enc/decpretrain → finetune
💡 Why it mattersMasked Autoencoders (He et al., 2021) hide ~75% of image patches and train an asymmetric encoder-decoder to rebuild the rest, forcing the model to learn the underlying structure of a scene rather than copy pixels. Because only the visible 25% of patches feed the heavy encoder, pretraining is several times faster and lets a model learn rich representations from huge unlabelled image/volume collections before any annotation exists — directly attacking the label-scarcity bottleneck.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the default self-supervised recipe for pretraining vision backbones (ViT/Swin) on unlabelled data, and is widely used in medical imaging to pretrain 3D CT/MRI encoders on thousands of unlabelled scans before fine-tuning for tumor or organ segmentation. Extensions reach video understanding, point clouds, audio spectrograms, and multimodal models.

▸ Code PyTorch — MAE pretrain step (He et al. 2021): mask 75%, encode visible only, reconstruct, loss on hidden patches▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

def mae_step(x, target, encoder, decoder, mask_ratio=class="n">0.75):
    # x: (B,N,D) patch embeddings (+pos-embed); target: (B,N,P) pixel patches
    B, N, D = x.shape
    len_keep = int(N * (class="n">1 - mask_ratio))             # keep 25% of patches
    ids_shuffle = torch.argsort(torch.rand(B, N, device=x.device), dim=class="n">1)
    ids_restore = torch.argsort(ids_shuffle, dim=class="n">1)  # to un-shuffle later
    ids_keep = ids_shuffle[:, :len_keep]
    x_vis = torch.gather(x, class="n">1, ids_keep[..., None].expand(-class="n">1, -class="n">1, D))
    z = encoder(x_vis)                               # encoder ONLY sees visible patches
    z = decoder.embed(z)                             # project encoder dim -> decoder dim
    Dd = z.size(-class="n">1)
    mask_tok = decoder.mask_token.expand(B, N - len_keep, -class="n">1)
    z_full = torch.cat([z, mask_tok], dim=class="n">1)
    z_full = torch.gather(z_full, class="n">1, ids_restore[..., None].expand(-class="n">1, -class="n">1, Dd))
    z_full = z_full + decoder.pos_embed              # decoder positional embeddings
    pred = decoder(z_full)                           # reconstruct all N patches
    # binary mask: 1 = was hidden. MSE on the MASKED patches only
    mask = torch.ones(B, N, device=x.device); mask[:, :len_keep] = class="n">0
    mask = torch.gather(mask, class="n">1, ids_restore)
    loss = (((pred - target) ** class="n">2).mean(-class="n">1) * mask).sum() / mask.sum()
    return loss
clip.py — contrastive image↔text cosine alignment
Teal = image embedding (drag the arc). Amber = caption embeddings. Bars = softmax(cosine).

CLIP: matching a picture to the words that describe it

CLIP projects an image and each candidate caption into the same vector space, normalized to unit length. Their agreement is the cosine similarity cos(θ)=img⋅textcos(\theta ) = img\cdot textcos(θ)=img⋅text — which, for unit vectors, is just the dot product. A temperature-scaled softmax over those cosines turns the scores into a probability per caption, and the highest one is the prediction.

This single idea is the engine of zero-shot classification: to label a scan you never trained a classifier on, you embed it once and compare it to text prompts like "an MRI of an enhancing glioma" vs "a normal brain MRI" — no new head, no fine-tuning. The same image↔text bridge is what lets vision-language models draft a radiology report from pixels. Drag the image embedding around the arc and watch the winning caption flip.
0.00
0.10

Low τ → softmax sharpens to a confident single match (CLIP's learned logit-scale is a small τ). High τ → diffuse, hedged probabilities. This is the exact logits=img⋅textT/τlogits = img\cdot text^{T} / \tau logits=img⋅textT/τ term in a CLIP head.

L2-normalizedcosine = dotsoftmax(sim/τ)zero-shot
💡 Why it mattersCLIP learns a shared embedding space for images and text by contrastively pulling matched image-caption pairs together and pushing mismatched ones apart, so a single model can recognize concepts it was never explicitly labeled for. This enables zero-shot classification and retrieval — you just describe a class in words instead of collecting and annotating training examples for it.
▸ Where it’s usedIt powers text-based image search, content moderation, and dataset curation/filtering (e.g. LAION), and serves as the frozen vision encoder behind multimodal LLMs like LLaVA and Stable Diffusion's text conditioning. In medical imaging, CLIP-style image-report contrastive pretraining (e.g. CheXzero, BiomedCLIP) enables zero-shot pathology detection on chest X-rays without explicit disease labels.

▸ Code PyTorch — CLIP zero-shot: normalize, cosine logits / temperature, softmax▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# img_feat: [B, D] from the vision tower, txt_feat: [C, D] from the text tower (C captions)
img_feat = image_encoder(pixels)           # e.g. ViT-B/16  -> [B, 512]
txt_feat = text_encoder(tokenized_prompts) # transformer   -> [C, 512]

# L2-normalize onto the unit hypersphere -> cosine similarity == dot product
img = F.normalize(img_feat, dim=-class="n">1)        # img / ||img||
txt = F.normalize(txt_feat, dim=-class="n">1)        # txt / ||txt||

# CLIP stores a *learned* log-scale param init to log(1/tau); it is applied via .exp().
log_logit_scale = torch.tensor(class="n">1.0 / class="n">0.07).log()                         # = log(1/tau) ~ 2.659 (an nn.Parameter in CLIP)
logit_scale = log_logit_scale.clamp(max=torch.tensor(class="n">100.0).log()).exp() # clamp the LOG, then exp -> ~14.29

# logits = (img . txt^T) * exp(log_scale) == cos/tau -> the exact term the widget scales
logits = logit_scale * img @ txt.t()       # [B, C] cosine sims, temperature-scaled
probs  = logits.softmax(dim=-class="n">1)            # softmax(cos/tau) -> P(caption | image)
pred   = probs.argmax(dim=-class="n">1)              # zero-shot label: the winning prompt

# Contrastive training (symmetric InfoNCE): paired batch -> logits is square [B, B], so B == C.
# targets = torch.arange(B)  # positive pairs on the diagonal
# loss = 0.5 * (F.cross_entropy(logits, targets) + F.cross_entropy(logits.t(), targets))
diffusion.py — forward noising & the reverse score (denoise) direction
Left = noisy x_t (a brain slice + tumor blob). Right = clean target x₀. Amber arrows = the score: where the model pulls each pixel to remove noise.

Diffusion: corrupt with noise, then learn to walk back

A diffusion model defines a forward process that gradually drowns an image in Gaussian noise: xt=αˉ⋅x0+1−αˉ⋅εx_t = \sqrt{}\bar{\alpha}\cdot x_{0} + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}}\cdot \varepsilon xt​=​αˉ⋅x0​+1−αˉ​⋅ε, where αˉ(t)\bar{\alpha}(t)αˉ(t) follows a cosine schedule from ≈1 (clean) at t=0 to ≈0 (pure noise) at t=1. A U-Net is trained to predict the noise ε at any t. Generation runs the process in reverse: estimate ε, subtract a step of it, repeat — climbing the score ∇xlogp(xt)\nabla _{x} log p(x_t)∇x​logp(xt​) back onto the data manifold.

Diffusion is the SOTA engine for image synthesis and augmentation, and is now used as a segmentation prior: conditioning the reverse process can sample or sharpen plausible tumor masks, and the inherent stochasticity yields per-voxel uncertainty — the same signal the MC-Dropout widget estimates by a cruder route. Drag t: as noise rises the slice dissolves, σ grows, SNR drops, and the amber denoise arrows lengthen — that vector field is what the network learns to predict.
0.00
💡 Why it mattersDiffusion turns generative modeling into a stable, tractable regression problem — instead of learning a one-shot mapping to data (which adversarial or autoregressive models struggle with), the network only has to predict the Gaussian noise added at each timestep, and sampling iteratively walks that noise back to climb the data score ∇ log p(x). This gives high-fidelity, mode-covering generation with a simple denoising loss, plus stochasticity that doubles as a free uncertainty signal.
▸ Where it’s usedDiffusion powers production text-to-image and video tools (Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, Sora) and is now standard for data augmentation, super-resolution, and inpainting; in medical imaging it synthesizes scarce labeled scans, reconstructs accelerated MRI/low-dose CT, and serves as a segmentation prior (e.g. sampling plausible tumor masks) whose sample variance yields per-voxel uncertainty.

▸ Code PyTorch — DDPM: forward noising + noise-prediction loss, and the score it implies▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

T = class="n">1000                                              # cosine schedule (Nichol & Dhariwal)
t_grid = torch.arange(T + class="n">1) / T
abar = torch.cos((t_grid + class="n">0.008) / class="n">1.008 * torch.pi / class="n">2) ** class="n">2
abar = (abar / abar[class="n">0]).clamp(class="n">1e-4, class="n">1.0)              # [T+1]: ᾱ(0)=1 → ᾱ(T)≈0

def training_step(unet, x0):                          # x0: [B,C,H,W] clean slice
    B = x0.size(class="n">0)
    t = torch.randint(class="n">1, T + class="n">1, (B,), device=x0.device)   # t∈[1,T]
    ab = abar[t].view(B, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1)
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    xt = ab.sqrt() * x0 + (class="n">1 - ab).sqrt() * eps       # forward: x_t = √ᾱ·x₀ + √(1−ᾱ)·ε
    return F.mse_loss(unet(xt, t), eps)               # ‖ε − ε̂‖²

@torch.no_grad()
def ddpm_step(unet, xt, t):                           # one TRUE reverse step: x_t → x_{t-1}
    ab  = abar[t].view(-class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1)                   # ᾱ_t   (broadcast over [B,C,H,W])
    abp = abar[t - class="n">1].view(-class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1)               # ᾱ_{t-1}
    alpha = ab / abp; beta = class="n">1 - alpha                # per-step α_t, β_t
    eps_hat = unet(xt, t)
    mean = (xt - beta / (class="n">1 - ab).sqrt() * eps_hat) / alpha.sqrt()
    z = torch.randn_like(xt) * (t.view(-class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1) > class="n">1)  # no noise at t=1
    x_prev = mean + beta.sqrt() * z                   # + σ_t·z, σ_t²=β_t
    x0_hat = (xt - (class="n">1 - ab).sqrt() * eps_hat) / ab.sqrt()   # Tweedie estimate of x₀
    return x_prev, x0_hat
deepzoom — gigapixel WSI: resolution pyramid + tile reader
Stylized H&E thumbnail. The grid is the tiling at this pyramid level; one tile is what the GPU actually sees.

The whole-slide pyramid — when the image won't fit in memory

A digitized histology slide is a gigapixel image: scan a glass slide at 40× and you get on the order of 100,000 × 100,000 pixels ≈ 10¹⁰ pixels — about 30 GB raw. No GPU holds that. So the file is stored as a multi-resolution pyramid of fixed-size tiles (DeepZoom convention): level 0 is one coarse thumbnail tile, and each level up quadruples the resolution into 4L4^{L}4L tiles (1, 4, 16, 64, 256, …) — higher level = finer detail = more tiles. You read only the tiles you need, at the zoom you need. (OpenSlide numbers it the other way: its level 0 is full-resolution.)

This is the opposite memory regime from OncoSeg. OncoSeg's MRI is a compact 1283≈2×106128^{3} \approx 2\times 10^{6}1283≈2×106-voxel volume that fits whole on one card — its challenge is 3D context. Histology can't fit at all, so the entire pipeline (tile → infer → stitch) is built around tiling, the same trick OncoSeg uses for inference (demo 13, sliding window) but forced on it from the very first byte.
2
tiles = 4ᴸ~10¹⁰ px~30 GB rawread on demand
💡 Why it mattersA single H&E whole-slide image is a gigapixel raster — often 100,000×100,000 px and many gigabytes uncompressed — so it cannot be loaded into RAM or fed to a GPU whole. Storing it as a tiled multi-resolution pyramid (the same source decoded at 40×, 20×, 10×, … into small JPEG/JP2 tiles) lets software random-access only the tiles it needs at the magnification it needs, making interactive viewing and patch-based deep learning tractable.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins essentially all computational pathology: digital slide viewers and PACS, FDA-cleared diagnostic tools (e.g. Paige Prostate), and patch-sampling pipelines for tumor segmentation, mitosis detection, and weakly-supervised slide-level classification (MIL). The same pyramid/tiling pattern also drives gigapixel satellite and microscopy imagery and web map tiles.

import openslide, numpy as np
from openslide.deepzoom import DeepZoomGenerator

slide = openslide.OpenSlide(class="s">"tumor_001.svs")     # ~100k x 100k px, ~30 GB raw
TS = class="n">256
dz = DeepZoomGenerator(slide, tile_size=TS, overlap=class="n">0)

L = class="n">14                                            # pyramid level (finer = larger L)
cols, rows = dz.level_tiles[L]                    # tile-grid COUNT at this level
assert (cols, rows) == tuple(-(-d // TS) for d in dz.level_dimensions[L])
n_tiles = cols * rows                             # ->4x per level asymptotically (ceil-rounded)

col, row = class="n">0, class="n">0                                   # pick a tile to fetch
tile = dz.get_tile(L, (col, row))                 # RGB PIL region; only INTERIOR tiles are TSxTS
x = np.asarray(tile, dtype=np.float32) / class="n">255.0    # edge col/row are smaller (remainder)!

# stream lazily; pad ragged edge tiles to TSxTS so model() gets a fixed shape
for r in range(rows):
    for c in range(cols):
        patch = np.asarray(dz.get_tile(L, (c, r)))   # (h<=TS, w<=TS, 3), edges are smaller
        h, w = patch.shape[:class="n">2]
        buf = np.zeros((TS, TS, class="n">3), np.uint8); buf[:h, :w] = patch
        # logits = model(to_tensor(buf)); stitch buf[:h,:w] into the level-L mask canvas
color_deconvolution.py — H&E → Hematoxylin + Eosin (Ruifrok)
Left: raw H&E patch. Right: the channel(s) recovered by projecting onto the stain basis.

H&E stain deconvolution — unmixing two dyes

In histology, Hematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple and Eosin stains stroma/cytoplasm pink. The camera only sees their mixture. Each dye absorbs light along a fixed colour direction, so in optical-density space OD=−log10(I/I0)OD = -log_{10}(I/I_{0})OD=−log10​(I/I0​) the two stains form a basis. Inverting that 2-vector basis recovers each dye's concentration per pixel — a linear unmixing, exactly Ruifrok & Johnston (2001).

Stain colour drifts between labs, scanners and batches — the histology analog of MRI intensity drift in demo 03. Deconvolving onto canonical H/E vectors (then renormalizing) is stain normalization: it makes inputs comparable before they hit the network, just like InstanceNorm. Spin the basis angle to mis-set the vectors and watch the nuclei "bleed" into the stroma channel — a wrong basis corrupts every downstream feature.
RGB
0°
OD = −log₁₀(I/I₀)C = M⁻¹·ODH=[.65,.70,.29]E=[.07,.99,.11]
💡 Why it mattersIn H&E whole-slide images, hematoxylin (nuclei, blue-purple) and eosin (cytoplasm/stroma, pink) optically overlap in RGB, so stain deconvolution inverts the Beer-Lambert mixing to recover a per-pixel concentration map for each dye. This both isolates nuclear vs. stromal channels for downstream tasks and underpins stain normalization, which removes the large color variation between scanners and labs that otherwise wrecks model generalization.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed as a near-universal preprocessing step in computational pathology: nuclei segmentation and counting, tumor/mitosis detection, Ki-67 and IHC quantification, and as color-augmentation/normalization to make CNNs and pathology foundation models robust across sites (e.g. CAMELYON, TCGA pipelines). It is built into standard toolkits like scikit-image, TIAToolbox, and HistomicsTK that power clinical-research WSI workflows.

▸ Code skimage / NumPy — what actually runs (Ruifrok color deconvolution)▶
import numpy as np
from skimage.color import separate_stains, hed_from_rgb  # canonical Ruifrok H+E+DAB basis

# --- idiomatic one-liner: deconvolve an RGB patch into [H, E, DAB] concentration maps ---
C = separate_stains(rgb, hed_from_rgb)          # rgb: (H,W,3) float in [0,1]; out (H,W,3)
H_map, E_map = C[..., class="n">0], C[..., class="n">1]             # per-pixel Hematoxylin / Eosin amounts

# --- what that one line really does (Ruifrok & Johnston 2001, as in skimage) ---
M = np.array([[class="n">0.650, class="n">0.704, class="n">0.286],            # H stain vector (nuclei, blue-purple)
              [class="n">0.072, class="n">0.990, class="n">0.105],            # E stain vector (stroma, pink)
              [class="n">0.268, class="n">0.570, class="n">0.776]])           # DAB: measured Ruifrok vector (NOT a cross-product)
M /= np.linalg.norm(M, axis=class="n">1, keepdims=True)   # unit stain vectors; M is NOT orthonormal (cos(H,E)~0.78)
rgb_c = np.maximum(rgb, class="n">1e-6)                    # clamp to avoid log(0); skimage uses 1e-6
OD = np.log(rgb_c) / np.log(class="n">1e-6)               # Beer-Lambert OD (natural log, as skimage does)
# stains mix linearly in OD space: OD = C @ M  ->  unmix by the inverse of the (square) basis
Cf = OD.reshape(-class="n">1, class="n">3) @ np.linalg.inv(M)       # exact solve, full 3-stain inversion (inv(M)==hed_from_rgb)
Cf = np.clip(Cf, class="n">0, None).reshape(rgb.shape)    # concentrations are non-negative
# wrong M (mis-set stain vector) -> nuclei "bleed" into the eosin channel: every downstream feature corrupted
hovernet_idea.py — distance-map watershed splits touching nuclei
Left: one merged semantic mask, shaded by distance-to-edge; black dots = markers. Right: instances after watershed.

Instance segmentation — counting cells, not just labelling tumor

Semantic segmentation answers "is this pixel a nucleus?" — so five touching nuclei come back as one fused blob. Instance segmentation must additionally say which nucleus each pixel belongs to. The classic recipe (and the spirit of HoVer-Net): take the foreground mask, compute its distance transform (each pixel's distance to the nearest edge), keep the high-distance peaks as markers, then run a watershed so every pixel joins its nearest marker.

Drag the threshold and watch the count vs the true 5. Too low → markers merge → the clump stays one object (under-split). The right band → exactly one marker per nucleus → correct count. Too high → the elongated dividing cell's distance ridge breaks into two peaks → over-split. OncoSeg outputs region masks (TC/WT/ET), not per-cell instances — so counting individual lesions or cells is a strictly harder problem layered on top, exactly the gap between a semantic mask and a clinical object count.
0.30
distance transformmarker = h-maximawatershedinstance ≠ semantic
💡 Why it mattersSemantic segmentation only answers "is this pixel a nucleus?", so a clump of touching cells collapses into one blob; instance segmentation assigns each pixel to a specific nucleus, which is what lets you actually count cells, measure per-cell morphology, and compute biomarkers like the Ki-67 proliferation index or tumor-infiltrating-lymphocyte density. Reliable splitting of crowded, overlapping nuclei is the hard part, and is the gateway from a pixel mask to a clinically meaningful object count.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed in computational pathology to count and type nuclei on H&E whole-slide images (tumor cellularity, mitotic counts, immune-cell quantification) and in fluorescence and live-cell microscopy for high-content screening; it underlies challenges like CoNIC/MoNuSeg/PanNuke and clinical readouts such as automated Ki-67 and PD-L1 scoring.

▸ Code scikit-image — distance-transform + marker watershed (the HoVer-Net recipe)▶
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage as ndi
from skimage.feature import peak_local_max
from skimage.segmentation import watershed

def split_nuclei(prob, thr=class="n">0.5, h=class="n">0.30):
    fg = prob > thr                                   # semantic mask: "is this pixel a nucleus?"
    if not fg.any():
        return np.zeros(fg.shape, dtype=np.int32), class="n">0
    dist = ndi.distance_transform_edt(fg)             # d(x) = min_{b in bg} ||x - b||
    dist = ndi.gaussian_filter(dist, class="n">1.0)             # smooth -> suppress spurious local maxima
    # seeds = thresholded local maxima of the distance map (NOT the h-maxima transform);
    # exclude_border=False so nuclei touching the image edge keep their seed
    coords = peak_local_max(dist, threshold_abs=h * dist.max(),
                            labels=fg, exclude_border=False)
    seed = np.zeros(fg.shape, dtype=bool)
    seed[tuple(coords.T)] = True
    markers, n = ndi.label(seed)                      # connected seed pixels -> instance ids
    # watershed FLOODS the surface -dist from the markers; basin boundaries fall on the
    # distance-map valley (ridge of -dist) between nuclei -> space-filling split of the blob
    inst = watershed(-dist, markers, mask=fg)
    return inst, n                                    # NOTE: n = #markers pre-watershed (can over/undershoot
                                                      # realized instances); use len(np.unique(inst))-1 to be exact
# WARNING: this is topographic flooding, NOT a nearest-marker (Voronoi) assignment:
#   inst[x] generally != argmin_m ||x - m||; the cut follows the -dist valley, not equidistance.

Top: 10 patches in one slide (amber = tumor). Bars = softmax attention. Bottom: pooled slide score vs 0.5 threshold.

Multiple-Instance Learning — one label for a whole bag

A gigapixel slide is far too big to label per pixel, but a pathologist can say "this slide is cancer / not". MIL learns from exactly that: the slide is a bag of N patch instances, and only the bag carries a label. The model scores each patch, computes an attention weight ai=softmax(tanh(V⋅hi)⊙sigmoid(U⋅hi))a_{i} = softmax(tanh(V\cdot h_{i}) \odot sigmoid(U\cdot h_{i}))ai​=softmax(tanh(V⋅hi​)⊙sigmoid(U⋅hi​)), and pools them into one prediction z=Σai⋅piz = \Sigma a_{i}\cdot p_{i}z=Σai​⋅pi​ (Ilse et al. 2018, ABMIL).

The MI assumption: a bag is positive if any instance is positive. Drag the slider — with zero tumor patches the slide reads benign; the first tumor patch flips it to malignant and grabs most of the attention. This is how you'd pre-train OncoSeg's encoder on slides/scans labeled only "cancer/not" — no voxel masks — and the attention bars double as a free interpretable heatmap of which patches drove the call.
3
bag → 1 labelsoftmax aᵢ, Σ=1weak supervisionpermutation-invariant
💡 Why it mattersMultiple-Instance Learning lets you train on weak, slide-level labels (e.g. "this biopsy contains tumor") when no pixel- or patch-level annotations exist: an image is a bag of many instances (tissue patches), and the model must predict the bag label even though only an unknown subset of instances is actually positive. This sidesteps the prohibitive cost of exhaustive expert annotation on gigapixel images while still letting attention pinpoint which regions drove the decision.
▸ Where it’s usedThe dominant paradigm for computational pathology on gigapixel whole-slide images — cancer subtyping, grading, biomarker/mutation and treatment-response prediction — where each slide is tiled into thousands of patches and only the diagnosis is known. It also appears in weakly-supervised CT/MRI and mammography screening, video-level action and anomaly detection, and drug-activity prediction from molecule conformers.

▸ Code PyTorch — gated-attention MIL (ABMIL), what actually runs▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class GatedAttentionMIL(nn.Module):           # Ilse et al. 2018 (ABMIL)
    def __init__(self, d=class="n">512, h=class="n">128, L=class="n">256):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(d, L)              # project frozen patch EMBEDDINGS d -> L
        self.V, self.U = nn.Linear(L, h), nn.Linear(L, h)
        self.w = nn.Linear(h, class="n">1)               # attention scorer -> scalar
        self.clf = nn.Linear(L, class="n">1)             # bag classifier

    def forward(self, H):                      # H: (N, d) one slide = bag of N patch embeddings
        h = self.fc(H)                         # (N, L)
        # gated attention: tanh(V h) (elementwise) sigmoid(U h) -> w(.) , Eq.9
        s = self.w(torch.tanh(self.V(h)) * torch.sigmoid(self.U(h)))   # (N, 1)
        a = F.softmax(s, dim=class="n">0)                # over N patches; == softmax(dim=1) of (1,N) transpose
        z = (a * h).sum(dim=class="n">0)                 # (L,)  z = sum_i a_i h_i  (single bag)
        return self.clf(z), a                  # bag logit (1,) + per-patch attention (N,1)

# weak supervision: one label per slide, no pixel/voxel masks; trains batch=1 per bag
logit, attn = GatedAttentionMIL()(torch.randn(class="n">10, class="n">512))
loss = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logit, torch.tensor([class="n">1.]))  # logit & target both (1,)
foundation_model.py — frozen UNI/Virchow embeddings + kNN retrieval
30 H&E patches embedded in feature space. Click or drag to pick a query; lines = its k nearest neighbors. Retrieved class = majority vote.

Pathology foundation models — morphology becomes geometry

A pathology FM (UNI, Virchow, …) is a huge encoder pretrained on millions of unlabeled tissue patches. It maps each patch to a feature vector in which patches that look alike land near each other. Tumor, stroma and immune patches form distinct clusters — so a brand-new patch can be classified just by looking at who its neighbors are.

This is the modern recipe: freeze the foundation encoder and train only a tiny head (here, a parameter-free kNN vote). It is exactly the OncoSeg move — start from a pretrained encoder rather than learning vision from scratch on a few hundred scans. Frozen features that cluster cleanly are the whole game; the head can be almost trivial.

💡 Why it mattersWhole-slide images are gigapixel-scale and scarce in expert labels, so pathology foundation models pretrain self-supervised on millions of unlabeled tissue tiles to turn raw morphology (cells, glands, stromal texture) into a compact geometric embedding space where biologically similar regions cluster together. This lets a single frozen encoder power many downstream tasks with little or no fine-tuning, replacing dozens of bespoke task-specific CNNs.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed for cancer subtyping, grading, biomarker and molecular-status prediction (e.g. MSI, EGFR/IDH mutation), metastasis detection, and survival/prognosis directly from H&E slides, typically via weakly-supervised multiple-instance learning over tile embeddings. Deployed in computational-pathology pipelines for slide retrieval, report generation, and clinical decision support in oncology.

▸ Code PyTorch + timm + sklearn — what actually runs▶
import timm, torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

dev = class="s">"cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else class="s">"cpu"
# 1) Frozen pathology FM (UNI is a timm ViT-L/16, D=1024). No grads, eval mode.
fm = timm.create_model(class="s">"hf-hub:MahmoodLab/UNI", pretrained=True, num_classes=class="n">0).eval().to(dev)
for p in fm.parameters(): p.requires_grad_(False)

@torch.no_grad()                                   # activations never need grad
def embed(x, bs=class="n">256):                              # x: (N,3,224,224) H&E patches
    out = []
    for i in range(class="n">0, len(x), bs):                 # stream in batches -> avoid OOM
        z = fm(x[i:i+bs].to(dev))                   # (b,1024) CLS embedding
        out.append(F.normalize(z, dim=class="n">1).cpu())     # unit vectors -> L2 dist ~ cosine
    return torch.cat(out)

bank = embed(train_patches); y = torch.as_tensor(train_labels)  # tensor for both heads
qz = embed(query)                                  # encode queries ONCE, reuse below
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=class="n">7).fit(bank.numpy(), y.numpy())
pred = knn.predict(qz.numpy())                     # majority vote over k nearest

# from scratch -- exactly what the widget draws:
d = torch.cdist(qz, bank)                          # (Nq,Nbank) pairwise L2 distances
nn = d.topk(class="n">7, largest=False).indices              # k nearest neighbor indices
vote = torch.mode(y[nn], dim=class="n">1).values             # plurality label (ties -> lowest)
vision_transformer.py — [CLS] aggregation + positional encoding
Every patch feeds the [CLS] token (line width = attention weight). PE tags each grid slot. Shuffle the patches and watch.

ViT: the [CLS] token, and why position must be injected

A Vision Transformer cuts the image into patch tokens, prepends one extra learnable [CLS] token, and lets attention run. The [CLS] token attends to every patch and becomes a single global summary vector. But attention has no built-in sense of where a patch was — so each patch token gets a positional encoding added before the first layer.

Without PE, [CLS] pooling is a pure set operation: Σsoftmax(q⋅tokens)⋅values\Sigma softmax(q\cdot token_{s})\cdot value_{s}Σsoftmax(q⋅tokens​)⋅values​ is permutation-invariant, so a scrambled image and the real one produce the identical output (drag PE to 0 and shuffle — ‖Δ‖ stays exactly 0.000). PE breaks that symmetry by binding a position signature to each slot. This is the encoder family behind SAM, DINO and the medical foundation models OncoSeg's Swin transformer descends from.
0.70
[CLS] global token+ positional encodingpermutation-invariant w/o PESAM · DINO backbone
💡 Why it mattersSelf-attention is permutation-invariant and treats image patches as an unordered set, so a Vision Transformer cannot know where a patch sits unless explicit position embeddings are added to each token; the learnable [CLS] token gives a single slot that attends to all patches and aggregates a global image representation for classification. Together they let pure attention (no convolutions) model both what is present and where it is.
▸ Where it’s usedThis patch-token-plus-position design underlies image classification, self-supervised pretraining, and segmentation backbones; in medical imaging ViT encoders power tumor and organ segmentation (e.g. UNETR/Swin-UNETR in MONAI) and serve as the prompt-driven image backbone in interactive tools like Segment Anything. CLS-pooled or patch-token features from DINOv2/CLIP are also reused as off-the-shelf representations for retrieval, detection, and few-shot pathology tasks.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (ViT [CLS] + positional-embedding stem)▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class ViTStem(nn.Module):                       # the [CLS] + positional-encoding stem
    def __init__(self, img=class="n">224, p=class="n">16, C=class="n">3, D=class="n">768):
        super().__init__()
        self.proj = nn.Conv2d(C, D, kernel_size=p, stride=p)   # patchify: (B,3,H,W) -> (B,D,H/p,W/p)
        n = (img // p) ** class="n">2
        self.cls = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(class="n">1, class="n">1, D))          # ONE learnable global token
        self.pos = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(class="n">1, n + class="n">1, D))      # learned PE, +1 slot for [CLS]
        nn.init.trunc_normal_(self.pos, std=class="n">0.02); nn.init.trunc_normal_(self.cls, std=class="n">0.02)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.proj(x).flatten(class="n">2).transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2)            # (B, N, D) patch tokens
        cls = self.cls.expand(x.size(class="n">0), -class="n">1, -class="n">1)               # broadcast [CLS] over batch
        x = torch.cat([cls, x], dim=class="n">1)                         # PREPEND -> (B, N+1, D)
        return x + self.pos                                     # add PE: breaks permutation-invariance

# x = encoder(stem(img));  global summary = x[:, 0]            # the [CLS] row is the image embedding
positional_encoding — sin/cos at geometric frequencies
Top: the 24-d position code for token p (teal=sin, amber=cos, per frequency). Bottom: PE(p)·PE(p+Δ) vs offset Δ — invariant to where p sits.

Positional encoding — telling a transformer where a token is

Self-attention is permutation-blind: shuffle the patch tokens and the math is unchanged. So before attention, each token at index p is stamped with a fixed vector built from sines and cosines at geometrically spaced frequencies ωk=10000(−2k/d)\omega _k = 10000^{}(-2k/d)ωk​=10000(−2k/d): PE[p,2k]=sin(p⋅ωk)PE[p,2k]=sin(p\cdot \omega _k)PE[p,2k]=sin(p⋅ωk​), PE[p,2k+1]=cos(p⋅ωk)PE[p,2k+1]=cos(p\cdot \omega _k)PE[p,2k+1]=cos(p⋅ωk​). Low-k pairs spin fast (fine local position); high-k pairs spin slowly (coarse global position) — like the hands of a set of clocks.

The magic property: PE(p)⋅PE(p+Δ)=Σkcos(ωk⋅Δ)PE(p)\cdot PE(p+\Delta ) = \Sigma _k cos(\omega _k\cdot \Delta )PE(p)⋅PE(p+Δ)=Σk​cos(ωk​⋅Δ) — it depends only on the relative offset Δ, never on the absolute p. That is what lets attention learn "attend to my neighbour" once and apply it everywhere. In OncoSeg this is how the Swin/transformer encoder knows a voxel-patch's location in the 3D grid without convolution's hard-wired locality — and it's the exact idea RoPE generalises by rotating Q/K instead of adding the code.

7
d_model=2412 sin/cos pairsrelative ⇒ dot dep. on Δ onlyRoPE precursor
💡 Why it mattersSelf-attention is permutation-invariant — it sees a bag of tokens with no order — so without injecting position, "the tumor grew" and "grew the tumor" look identical. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) solves this by rotating each query/key vector by an angle proportional to its index, so the attention dot-product depends only on the relative distance between tokens, which generalizes cleanly to sequences (or 3D voxel grids) longer than those seen in training.
▸ Where it’s usedRoPE is the default position scheme in nearly every modern LLM (Llama 3, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek, GPT-NeoX) and powers long-context extension via YaRN/NTK-aware interpolation; the same idea drives Vision Transformers and 3D medical-imaging transformers (e.g. position-aware ViT/Swin backbones in MONAI) where a voxel must know "where" it sits without convolution's built-in locality.

▸ Code PyTorch — sinusoidal PE table + RoPE rotation (what Llama/HF actually run)▶
import torch

def sinusoidal_pe(T, d, base=class="n">10000.0):                     # original "Attention Is All You Need"
    pos = torch.arange(T).unsqueeze(class="n">1).float()             # (T,1)
    w   = base ** (-torch.arange(class="n">0, d, class="n">2).float() / d)     # omega_k = base^(-2k/d), geometric freqs
    pe  = torch.zeros(T, d)
    pe[:, class="n">0::class="n">2] = torch.sin(pos * w)                        # interleaved: sin at even, cos at odd
    pe[:, class="n">1::class="n">2] = torch.cos(pos * w)
    return pe                                              # x = x + pe (added to embeddings)

# RoPE (Llama/HF "rotate_half" layout): rotates the two HALVES of q,k, pairing dim i with i+d/2
def rope_cos_sin(T, d, base=class="n">10000.0):                      # build cos/sin the HF way (NOT sinusoidal_pe)
    w   = base ** (-torch.arange(class="n">0, d, class="n">2).float() / d)     # (d/2,)
    ang = torch.outer(torch.arange(T).float(), w)          # (T,d/2) = p*omega_k
    emb = torch.cat((ang, ang), dim=-class="n">1)                    # (T,d): cos[i]==cos[i+d/2]
    return emb.cos(), emb.sin()

def rotate_half(x):                                        # [x1,x2] -> [-x2,x1], x1/x2 are HALVES
    x1, x2 = x.chunk(class="n">2, dim=-class="n">1)
    return torch.cat((-x2, x1), dim=-class="n">1)

def apply_rope(q, k, cos, sin):                            # cos,sin: (...,T,d) from rope_cos_sin; broadcast over B,H
    q_rot = q * cos + rotate_half(q) * sin                 # rotates pair (q_i, q_{i+d/2}) by p*omega_i
    k_rot = k * cos + rotate_half(k) * sin
    return q_rot, k_rot                                    # then F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q_rot,k_rot,v)
moe_layer.py — sparse gate · top-k routing · load balance
Left: gate scores the token against 8 experts. Center: top-2 light up (run); the rest stay idle. Bottom: per-expert load over a token stream.

Mixture-of-Experts — capacity without the compute bill

A dense layer runs every parameter on every token. A sparse MoE layer holds N expert sub-networks but a tiny gate picks only the top-k per token: logits=Wg⋅xlogits = W^{g}\cdot xlogits=Wg⋅x, then softmax, then keep the k largest and renormalize their weights so they sum to 1. The output is that gated blend of just the k chosen experts — the other N−k do zero compute.

This is how Mixtral 8×7B and DeepSeek-V3 hit frontier quality cheaply: 8 experts of parameters, but only 2 run per token → ~25% of the FLOPs of using all of them. For a 3D medical model the same trick lets you grow specialist capacity (one expert good at edemas, another at enhancing cores) without paying for all of it on every voxel patch. The catch — watch the bottom bars — is load imbalance: a skewed token stream sends most tokens to a few experts, so MoE training adds an auxiliary load-balancing loss to spread tokens out.
20°
24
N=8 expertstop-k=2softmax gatek/N = 25% FLOPsload balance
💡 Why it mattersMixture-of-Experts replaces one dense feed-forward block with many parallel "expert" sub-networks plus a lightweight router that activates only a few per token, so the model's total parameter count (and thus knowledge capacity) can grow 10-50x while the FLOPs spent per token stay roughly fixed. This decouples capacity from compute, letting a trillion-parameter model train and serve at the cost of a much smaller dense one.
▸ Where it’s usedIt powers most frontier open and closed LLMs (Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, Llama 4, GPT-4-class systems) where serving cost matters, and increasingly large vision and multimodal backbones; in research it is being explored for efficient 3D medical-image and pathology foundation models where heterogeneous modalities/organs map naturally onto specialized experts.

▸ Code PyTorch — sparse top-k routing with a load-balancing loss (what actually runs in Mixtral / Switch)▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class MoE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, N=class="n">8, k=class="n">2):
        super().__init__()
        self.k = k
        self.gate = nn.Linear(d, N, bias=False)              # Wᵍ
        self.experts = nn.ModuleList(nn.Linear(d, d) for _ in range(N))

    def forward(self, x):                                    # x: (T, d) token stream
        logits = self.gate(x)                                # = Wᵍ·x  → (T, N)
        probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-class="n">1)
        w, idx = probs.topk(self.k, dim=-class="n">1)                  # keep the k largest experts
        w = w / w.sum(-class="n">1, keepdim=True)                      # renormalize so chosen weights Σ=1
        y = torch.zeros_like(x)
        for slot in range(self.k):                           # only the k chosen experts run → k/N FLOPs
            for e in range(len(self.experts)):
                m = idx[:, slot] == e                        # tokens routed to expert e in this slot
                if m.any():
                    y[m] += w[m, slot, None] * self.experts[e](x[m])
        # auxiliary load-balance loss: encourage uniform routing across experts
        load = F.one_hot(idx, len(self.experts)).float().sum((class="n">0, class="n">1)) / (x.size(class="n">0) * self.k)
        aux = len(self.experts) * (load * probs.mean(class="n">0)).sum()  # Switch-Transformer balancing term
        return y, aux
state_space.py — selective scan hₜ = A·hₜ₋₁ + Bₜ·xₜ vs O(N²) attention
Top: the recurrent state carried left→right through the sequence, gated by content. Bottom: cost ∝ N² (attention) vs ∝ N (SSM).

State-space models — linear-time sequence modeling

Self-attention compares every token to every other token, so its cost grows as N². A state-space model (Mamba) instead carries a single recurrent hidden state: ht=A⋅ht−1+Bt⋅xth_{t} = A\cdot h_{t-1} + B_{t}\cdot x_{t}ht​=A⋅ht−1​+Bt​⋅xt​. It walks the sequence once, updating that state token-by-token — a selective scan — so cost grows only as N, with O(1) memory per step.

What makes it selective: the input gate Bt=σ(w⋅xt)B_{t} = \sigma (w\cdot x_{t})Bt​=σ(w⋅xt​) is content-dependent. The model decides per-token how much of the new input to write into memory, and A sets how long old information lingers. Drag A toward 1 and the state remembers longer; lower it and memory decays fast.

For OncoSeg-style problems this matters whenever the sequence is long: a 128³ volume flattens to ~2 million tokens, and a longitudinal study stacks many timepoints. Quadratic attention is hopeless there, but a linear-time scan stays tractable — the same reason Swin windows (demo 08) cap attention cost. SSMs are the emerging alternative to making long 3D/temporal medical sequences affordable.
24
0.82
recurrent scanO(N) timeO(1) statecontent-dependent gate
💡 Why it mattersState-space models (SSMs) like Mamba process sequences in linear time and constant memory per step, replacing attention's O(n²) cost and the growing KV cache — so they can model very long sequences (hundreds of thousands of tokens, long audio, or high-resolution 3D scans) that quadratic Transformers choke on. The key trick is an input-dependent (selective) state update that decides what to remember or forget, recovering much of attention's content-selectivity while staying recurrent at inference.
▸ Where it’s usedSSMs power long-context language models, genomics (DNA sequence modeling), audio/speech and time-series forecasting, and increasingly vision — including medical imaging, where U-Mamba and SegMamba use Mamba blocks for memory-efficient 3D CT/MRI tumor and organ segmentation on long volumetric token sequences. They are most attractive wherever sequences are very long or streaming and a Transformer's quadratic attention is the bottleneck.

▸ Code PyTorch — fused selective_scan_fn vs. the exact recurrence it runs▶
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F  # needed for softplus/silu
from mamba_ssm.ops.selective_scan_interface import selective_scan_fn

# x:(B,D,L); Delta, B_t, C_t are INPUT-DEPENDENT (the "selective" part)
delta = F.softplus(x_proj_dt(x))             # (B,D,L) data-dependent step Δ_t>0
A = -torch.exp(A_log)                         # (D,N) stable cont. state matrix (A<0)
Bt = x_proj_B(x); Ct = x_proj_C(x)            # (B,N,L) input-dependent B_t, C_t

# Fused scan: discretize + recurrence h=Ā·h+B̄·x, y=C·h, then SiLU gate by z
y = selective_scan_fn(x, delta, A, Bt, Ct, D=D_skip, z=gate, delta_softplus=False)

# --- exact from-scratch equivalent (state kept in fp32, as the kernel does) ---
dA = torch.exp(delta.unsqueeze(-class="n">1) * A[:, None, :])        # Āₜ=exp(Δₜ·A) (B,D,L,N) ZOH
dB = delta.unsqueeze(-class="n">1) * Bt.transpose(class="n">1, class="n">2).unsqueeze(class="n">1) # B̄ₜ=Δₜ·Bₜ   (B,D,L,N)
h = x.new_zeros(x.shape[class="n">0], x.shape[class="n">1], A.shape[class="n">1]).float()# (B,D,N) state, O(1) mem
ys = []
for t in range(x.shape[-class="n">1]):                               # left→right O(L), no N² attn
    h = dA[..., t, :] * h + dB[..., t, :] * x[..., t, None]      # hₜ=Āₜ·hₜ₋₁+B̄ₜ·xₜ
    ys.append(torch.einsum(class="s">'bdn,bn->bd', h, Ct[..., t]))         # yₜ=Cₜ·hₜ
y_ref = torch.stack(ys, dim=-class="n">1).to(x.dtype) + D_skip[None, :, None] * x  # +skip
y_ref = y_ref * F.silu(gate)                # apply the same SiLU gate → matches y above
flash_attention.py — IO-aware tiled attention
Faded cells are never materialized. The amber box is the on-chip tile; only running max m and sum ℓ persist between tiles.

FlashAttention: same softmax, never store the N×N matrix

Plain attention computes the full score matrix S=QKT/dS = QK^{T}/\sqrt{d}S=QKT/d​, writes all N² entries to HBM, runs softmax over each row, then multiplies by V. The bottleneck is not FLOPs — it is shuttling that N² matrix to and from slow GPU memory. FlashAttention streams S in column tiles and keeps each query row's softmax up to date with an online running max m and running sum ℓ\ell ℓ, rescaling by exp(mold−mnew)exp(m_{ol}\mathcal{d} - m_{ne}\mathcal{w})exp(mol​d−mne​w) as each tile arrives. The full row is never held at once.

Why it matters here: OncoSeg attends over large 3D volumes and across baseline/follow-up scans. The attention map alone would be tens of GB — impossible to materialize. Tiling makes peak memory grow with tile size, not with N², which is exactly what lets long-context and large-volume attention run on a real GPU. (Distinct from Swin: that shrinks the receptive field; this keeps full global attention but shrinks the memory/IO.)
4

Slide tile → 16 and the on-chip box covers the whole matrix: no savings, you are back to naive. Slide → 1 and peak memory drops to O(N⋅1)O(N\cdot 1)O(N⋅1). The output is bit-for-bit the same softmax (Δ≈1e-16) at every setting — only the HBM traffic changes.

online softmaxrunning max mrunning sum ℓO(N·tile) memory
💡 Why it mattersPlain attention stores the whole score grid in slow GPU memory and is bound by memory traffic; FlashAttention streams it in blocks with an online running max and sum, so peak memory scales with block size while the result stays mathematically identical
▸ Where it’s usedThe default attention kernel across modern LLM training and serving stacks such as PyTorch SDPA and vLLM, and what makes long context practical; in imaging the same IO-aware tiling lets ViT backbones run over 3D CT or MRI volumes and gigapixel pathology slides

▸ Code PyTorch — F.scaled_dot_product_attention (FlashAttention) + the online-softmax recurrence it fuses▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.nn.attention import sdpa_kernel, SDPBackend

# Force the fused FlashAttention CUDA kernel. NOTE: sdp_kernel(enable_flash=True) does NOT
# do this -- it leaves math+mem_efficient ON, so the NxN-materializing math backend may run;
# it is also deprecated since torch 2.3. sdpa_kernel RESTRICTS dispatch to the listed backend.
with sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION):                # truly restricts to flash
    out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=False)  # q,k,v: (B,H,N,d)

# Reference online-softmax over column tiles of K,V. Per-row state is O(d): max m, sum l, acc.
def flash_attention(q, k, v, tile):                  # streams K/V in blocks of `tile`
    d = q.shape[-class="n">1]; m = q.new_full(q.shape[:-class="n">1], -float(class=class="s">"s">class="s">'inf'))
    l = torch.zeros_like(m); acc = torch.zeros_like(q)
    for j in range(class="n">0, k.shape[-class="n">2], tile):             # one column block at a time
        s = (q @ k[..., j:j+tile, :].transpose(-class="n">1, -class="n">2)) / d**class="n">0.5   # (.,N,tile) tile only
        m_new = torch.maximum(m, s.amax(-class="n">1))          # running max over keys seen so far
        p = torch.exp(s - m_new.unsqueeze(-class="n">1))        # rescaled, numerically stable
        alpha = torch.exp(m - m_new)                  # correction for old accumulator
        l = alpha * l + p.sum(-class="n">1)                      # running denominator l
        acc = alpha.unsqueeze(-class="n">1) * acc + p @ v[..., j:j+tile, :]   # rescale + add block
        m = m_new
    return acc / l.unsqueeze(-class="n">1)                       # final normalize == full softmax
jepa.py — predict the masked region's representation, not its pixels
Left: context visible, amber target masked. Right: JEPA fills the target's LATENT (bars); a pixel MAE only manages a blurry mean.

JEPA: predict in latent space, not pixels

Masked-image models hide a region and ask the network to fill it back in. Pixel MAE predicts the raw pixels — but the exact texture under a mask is largely unknowable, so the best the loss can do is the smooth average, giving a blurry guess. JEPA (I-JEPA / V-JEPA) instead encodes the context, then a predictor outputs the target encoder's latent for the masked block — an abstract feature vector (here: mean, blob-mass, centroid, edge-energy). It is scored by cosine similarity to the true target latent, never by pixel error.

Drag the mask larger: the pixel MSE bar climbs steeply (more high-frequency detail hidden → blurrier) while the latent cosine stays high — the lesion's gist (it's a round bright blob, roughly here) is predictable even when its precise speckle is not. That is the whole point: JEPA learns transferable semantics and discards unpredictable pixel noise. For OncoSeg, this is the pretraining you'd want before fine-tuning on scarce labelled tumors — representations that capture lesion structure, not scanner artefacts.
3
target latent = abstract featurescosine match, not pixel MSEsemantics > detail
💡 Why it mattersJEPA learns by predicting the latent representation of a masked or future part of an input from a visible context, instead of reconstructing raw pixels — so the model spends capacity on abstract, semantically useful structure rather than on noisy, unpredictable low-level detail that pixel/generative objectives waste effort on. This sidesteps representation collapse and the blurriness of pixel reconstruction, yielding encoders that transfer strongly to downstream tasks without labels.
▸ Where it’s usedIt powers self-supervised foundation encoders for images and video that feed classification, detection, and action/world-model tasks (e.g. robot planning via latent rollouts), and the same masked-latent-prediction recipe is attractive in medical imaging, where label-free pretraining on large unlabeled CT/MRI or pathology archives improves downstream tumor and organ segmentation. Latent-prediction pretraining is also being explored for audio and time-series signals.

▸ Code PyTorch — I-JEPA: predict the EMA target encoder's latent (stop-grad), not pixels▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# I-JEPA / V-JEPA: predict the TARGET ENCODER's latent for masked blocks, never pixels.
ctx_tokens  = context_encoder(x, keep_mask=visible)        # encode only visible patches  -> [B, Nv, D]
pred_latent = predictor(ctx_tokens, target_pos=masked)     # query masked positions       -> [B, Nm, D]

with torch.no_grad():                                       # target = stop-grad EMA twin (no pixel decoder)
    tgt_full   = target_encoder(x)                          # full image, momentum weights -> [B, N,  D]
    tgt_full   = F.layer_norm(tgt_full, (tgt_full.size(-class="n">1),))  # NORMALIZE target over feature-dim (real I-JEPA)
    tgt_latent = tgt_full[:, masked]                        # gather just the masked blocks-> [B, Nm, D]

# loss lives in REPRESENTATION space. I-JEPA: smooth-L1 on (LayerNorm'd) latents:
loss = F.smooth_l1_loss(pred_latent, tgt_latent)           # ||predictor(ctx) - sg[LN(target(x))]|| on features, not RGB
# related (not identical) semantic score the panel shows -- normalized cousin, drops magnitude:
# cos = F.cosine_similarity(pred_latent, tgt_latent, dim=-1).mean()

loss.backward()                                             # grads flow ONLY through context_encoder + predictor
optimizer.step()
# update the target encoder as an EMA of the online weights (prevents collapse, no gradient):
for p_t, p_c in zip(target_encoder.parameters(), context_encoder.parameters()):
    p_t.data.mul_(m).add_(p_c.data, alpha=class="n">1 - m)           # m ~ 0.996 -> 1.0 over training
world_model.py — autoregressive rollout & error accumulation
Gray = the true world's orbit. Teal = the model imagining the future, one frame fed back into the next.

World models: imagining the future, one frame at a time

A world model learns the dynamics of a scene: given the current state, predict the next frame. To dream a whole trajectory it runs autoregressively — it feeds its own prediction back in as the next input. A single step is almost perfect; but each frame carries a tiny error, and feeding a slightly-wrong state back in makes the next error a little bigger. Errors compound, so the imagined orbit slowly drifts off the true one.

This drift is the central challenge of model-based RL and video world models (Dreamer, Genie, GAIA). The same idea underlies any longitudinal medical prediction that rolls a model forward in time — predicting how a tumor evolves scan-to-scan: a 1-step forecast is trustworthy, but unrolling many steps without re-grounding on real data accumulates error fast. Slide the horizon and watch the teal trajectory peel away from gray.
8
next-frame predictionfeed output → inputcompounding errordrift
💡 Why it mattersA world model learns the dynamics of an environment — given the current state (and an action), it predicts the next latent state or frame — so an agent can "imagine" rollouts and plan or train inside the model instead of paying for expensive, slow, or unsafe real-world interaction. The catch it exposes is compounding error: each predicted frame feeds the next, so small mistakes snowball over the rollout horizon k, which is why latent-space prediction, stochastic transitions, and KL regularization matter.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed for model-based RL and planning in robotics and games (learning controllers from imagined rollouts), playable/generative game and video "neural simulators," autonomous-driving scene prediction, and sim-to-real pretraining; the same predict-the-next-state idea underlies 4D medical-imaging tasks like longitudinal tumor-growth forecasting and predicting future cardiac/respiratory frames for motion-compensated planning.
Cutting-edge / SOTADreamerV3 (Google DeepMind)Genie / Genie 2 (Google DeepMind)Sora (OpenAI)V-JEPA 2 (Meta)Cosmos world foundation models (NVIDIA)GAIA-1/GAIA-2 (Wayve)
▸ Code PyTorch — teacher-forced training vs. autoregressive dream (error compounds)▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn

# A world model learns next-frame dynamics: s_{t+1} ≈ f_θ(s_t, a_t).
# (Dreamer/Genie do this in a learned latent z_t; we show the loop in state space.)
dynamics = nn.GRUCell(state_dim + action_dim, hidden_dim)
readout  = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, state_dim)

# --- training: TEACHER-FORCED 1-step — always condition on the TRUE s_t ---
# states/actions are BATCH-major: [B, T, *]
h = torch.zeros(B, hidden_dim)
loss = class="n">0.0
for t in range(T - class="n">1):
    h = dynamics(torch.cat([states[:, t], actions[:, t]], -class="n">1), h)   # input = ground truth
    loss = loss + nn.functional.mse_loss(readout(h), states[:, t + class="n">1])

# --- inference: AUTOREGRESSIVE rollout — feed the model's OWN output back in ---
@torch.no_grad()
def imagine(s0, action_plan, k):                 # action_plan BATCH-major: [B, T, action_dim]
    s, h = s0, torch.zeros(s0.size(class="n">0), hidden_dim)
    traj = []
    for i in range(min(k, action_plan.size(class="n">1))):
        h = dynamics(torch.cat([s, action_plan[:, i]], -class="n">1), h)  # s is the PREVIOUS PREDICTION
        s = readout(h)                           # ŝ_{t+1} = f_θ(ŝ_t, a_t)  → error compounds
        traj.append(s)
    return torch.stack(traj, class="n">1)                  # [B, k, state_dim]; drift grows with horizon k
vlm_report.py — vision-language joint attention (image↔text)
Left: 6×6 image patch tokens (grey = anatomy, teal = attention). Right: the report's word tokens. Amber box = peak patch. Pick a word.

Vision-language attention: words that point at pixels

A VLM doesn't keep image and text in separate towers — it lays image patch tokens and word tokens in one sequence and runs the same attention across both. A word's query q dot-products against every patch's key kjk_{j}kj​; softmax(q⋅kj/d)softmax(q\cdot k_{j}/\sqrt{d})softmax(q⋅kj​/d​) is the patch attention map. Pick "tumor", "left", or "bright" and watch that word's attention light up the matching region (teal). "Tumor" finds the lesion; "left" sweeps the left column; "bright" hits the lesion and the bright streak on the right that "tumor" rightly ignores.

This is exactly how a VLM generates a radiology report: each word it emits is grounded by attending back into the image. The grounding map is also the explanation — you can show a clinician which voxels made the model write "enhancing tumor in the left lobe." For OncoSeg, the same image features the Swin encoder produces become the keys a language head attends to when narrating a scan or RECIST response.
one shared sequencecross-modal attentionsoftmax(q·k/√d)text→pixel grounding
💡 Why it mattersCross-attention between text tokens and image patches lets a model ground a word like "tumor" or "the cup on the left" onto the specific pixels it refers to, instead of just classifying the whole image — turning free-form language into spatial pointers. This is what makes open-vocabulary detection, referring segmentation, and visual question answering possible without retraining a fixed label set for every new concept.
▸ Where it’s usedPowers open-vocabulary detection/segmentation (CLIP-style retrieval, "segment by text prompt"), referring-expression grounding, document/chart understanding, and embodied agents that follow language instructions. In medical imaging it underlies report-grounded findings — linking a radiology phrase to the lesion region (e.g. CheXagent, MedSAM-style text-prompted segmentation) for explainable CAD and auto-drafted reports.
Cutting-edge / SOTAGLIP / Grounding DINO (IDEA)Qwen2-VL / Qwen2.5-VL (Alibaba)LLaVA-1.5 / LLaVA-OneVisionFlorence-2 (Microsoft)Grounded-SAM / Grounded-SAM 2 (IDEA Research)CheXagent / MedSAM (medical VLM)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (joint VLM attention + the word→patch grounding map)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# One shared sequence: image patch tokens (6*6=36) + word tokens, same d.
patch_tok = vit_encoder(image)                   # (B, 36, d)  Swin/ViT features
word_tok  = embed(report_ids)                     # (B, T,  d)  report word tokens
seq = torch.cat([patch_tok, word_tok], dim=class="n">1)     # (B, 36+T, d) — NOT two towers

# Project the joint sequence to q,k,v (one weight set spans both modalities).
q, k, v = (seq @ Wq), (seq @ Wk), (seq @ Wv)      # each (B, N, d); single-head for clarity

# Idiomatic fused kernel for the full joint self-attention (scale = 1/√d).
ctx = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)     # softmax(qkᵀ/√d) · v

# Grounding map = ONE word's query over the patch keys.
w     = class="n">36 + word_index                           # pick "tumor" / "left" / "bright"
scale = q.size(-class="n">1) ** class="n">0.5                          # √d, NOT d
qw    = q[:, w:w+class="n">1]                                # (B,1,d) — keep token axis (else broadcasts to (B,B,36)!)
logits = (qw @ k[:, :class="n">36].transpose(-class="n">1, -class="n">2)).squeeze(class="n">1) / scale   # (B,36) = q_w·kⱼ/√d
# NOTE: re-softmax over the 36 patch keys only → rows sum to 1. The *real* joint-attention
# mass token w puts on patches is softmax over ALL N keys (here we renormalize the sub-block).
attn   = F.softmax(logits, dim=-class="n">1)                 # (B,36) patch attention for word w
peak   = attn.argmax(-class="n">1)                           # (B,) amber box = argmax-attended patch
grounding = attn.reshape(-class="n">1, class="n">6, class="n">6)                 # (B,6,6) text→pixel heatmap, one per image
vqa_report.py — grounded visual chain-of-thought (read → attend → reason → answer)
Step 1 read · 2 attend + box the grounded region · 3 sub-conclusion · 4 final answer. The box snaps to the argmax-attended lesion.

Visual chain-of-thought — reason in steps, point before you answer

Ask a vision-language model a question about a scan and it can blurt an answer in one shot — and confidently hallucinate. Grounded visual CoT forces it to think in stages: (1) read the question, (2) attend — compute a softmax over candidate regions and draw a box on the winner, (3) state a sub-conclusion measured from that box, and (4) give a final answer that must cite the box.

Step 2 runs the same scaled-dot-product attention softmax(β⋅q⋅kj/d)softmax(\beta \cdot q\cdot k_{j}/\sqrt{d})softmax(β⋅q⋅kj​/d​) as the self-attention demo (06) — with a sharpening temperature β — where the question is the query, the image regions are keys, and the argmax region becomes the bounding box. Tie to OncoSeg: its real output is a segmented lesion + a measured diameter. A report generator that grounds "the enhancing lesion measures D mm" on that box — instead of guessing — is what cuts hallucination in medical VQA. Drag the step slider to watch the attended region move and the reasoning chain accumulate.
