💡 Why it mattersVLMs that answer in one shot tend to confidently hallucinate — they assert "the lesion is enlarging" without ever looking at it. Visual chain-of-thought forces the model to reason in explicit stages and ground each claim on a region it points to or boxes, so the final answer is auditable and traceable to pixels instead of a free-floating guess.
▸ Where it’s usedIt powers grounded visual question answering, document/chart understanding, GUI and robot agents that must point before they act, and referring/reasoning segmentation. In medical imaging it underpins report generation and grounded VQA, where "the enhancing lesion measures D mm" must cite the exact box or mask it was measured from — the workflow OncoSeg targets for RECIST-style response assessment.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs: attend → argmax → box → cited answer▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# Grounded visual CoT: question (query) attends over region features (keys/values),
# the argmax-attended region becomes the box the answer MUST cite.
def grounded_vcot(q, region_feats, region_boxes, beta=class="n">2.4, scale=None):
    # q:[D]  region_feats(keys/vals):[N,D]  region_boxes:[N,4] (xyxy, in mm-calibrated px)
    d = q.shape[-class="n">1]
    scale = scale if scale is not None else d ** -class="n">0.5    # 1/sqrt(d); keep a caller's scale=0.0
    # NOTE: beta is a CUSTOM sharpening temperature; plain attn = softmax(q.k/sqrt(d)).
    # F.scaled_dot_product_attention has NO beta, so this is NOT its weights when beta != 1.
    scores = beta * (region_feats @ q) * scale           # [N]
    attn   = F.softmax(scores, dim=-class="n">1)                   # [N]
    top    = int(attn.argmax())                          # ground: pick winning region -> draw box
    box    = region_boxes[top]
    # diameter = max extent of the bbox (longest axis), not just width
    diam_mm = max(box[class="n">2] - box[class="n">0], box[class="n">3] - box[class="n">1]).item()
    answer = fclass="s">"Yes - one enhancing lesion, ~{diam_mm:.0f} mm, grounded on region {top}"
    return answer, attn, box

# sanity: q,k define the (scaled, beta-sharpened) softmax the widget's step-2 visualizes
q = torch.tensor([class="n">0.85, class="n">0.95, class="n">0.45]); K = torch.tensor([[.class="n">55,.class="n">20,.class="n">80],[.class="n">92,.class="n">95,.class="n">55],[.class="n">40,.class="n">30,.class="n">18]])
print(grounded_vcot(q, K, torch.tensor([[class="n">274,class="n">174,class="n">326,class="n">226]]*class="n">3))[class="n">1])  # -> region index 1 dominates
vla_policy.py — image + instruction → action tokens
Left: camera view, dashed ring = the instructed target. Right: decoded action-token chunk; amber row = the token executing now.

VLA: one model from pixels to motor commands

A Vision-Language-Action model (RT-2, OpenVLA, π0) takes a camera image plus a language instruction and emits a short chunk of action tokens. Continuous end-effector deltas (dx,dy)(dx, dy)(dx,dy) and the gripper command are discretized into bins — here 256 — so motor control becomes next-token prediction, the same machinery as a language model.

Pick the instruction, then drag timestep: the policy decodes a 6-step plan toward the chosen object, the arm follows each token, and the gripper closes on the final token to grasp.

image+text → tokens256-bin actionsaction chunkterminal grasp
0
Tie-in: a VLA unifies perception, language, and control in one autoregressive policy — but it is only as good as its eyes. A segmentation/perception stack like OncoSeg is exactly that front-end: it turns raw voxels into the object/region representation a downstream policy (or a clinician) acts on. Garbage perception → wrong target token → wrong action.
💡 Why it mattersA VLA (Vision-Language-Action) model collapses the classic perception → planning → control stack into one differentiable network that maps raw camera pixels plus a natural-language instruction directly to robot motor commands, so a single policy can generalize to new objects, scenes, and verbal commands instead of needing a hand-engineered pipeline per task. Pretraining the backbone on internet-scale vision-language data lets the robot inherit semantic and commonsense knowledge (e.g. "pick up the extinct animal"), which pure robot demonstrations alone could never cover.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed for general-purpose robot manipulation and mobile manipulation — table-top pick-and-place, kitchen and warehouse tasks, and language-commanded household robots — and increasingly explored for autonomous driving and embodied AI agents. The same instruction-to-action recipe is being adapted to surgical and interventional robotics, where a model could map endoscopic or ultrasound video plus a clinician's instruction to instrument motion, and to language-guided control of medical-imaging acquisition.

▸ Code PyTorch (OpenVLA-style) — image+instruction decoded to discretized action tokens▶
import torch
NB, AMIN, AMAX = class="n">256, -class="n">1.0, class="n">1.0                       # 256 action classes over [-1,1]
V = lm_head.out_features                               # full LLM vocab size
img_feats = projector(vision_encoder(image))           # (B,P,D) patches -> LLM embed space
prompt    = tokenizer(class="s">"In: pick up the red block\nOut:", return_tensors=class="s">"pt").input_ids
prefix    = torch.cat([img_feats, embed(prompt)], dim=class="n">1)
glob_ids = []                                           # store GLOBAL vocab ids, not local bins
for _ in range(class="n">7):                                     # 7-D chunk: dx dy dz droll dpitch dyaw grip
    h     = backbone(inputs_embeds=prefix)[:, -class="n">1]      # (B, D_hidden)
    bin_logits = lm_head(h)[:, V - NB:]                # last NB vocab slots = action bins
    local = bin_logits.argmax(-class="n">1)                       # (B,) local bin index 0..NB-1
    gid   = local + (V - NB)                            # map to GLOBAL vocab id for embed()
    glob_ids.append(gid)
    prefix = torch.cat([prefix, embed(gid)[:, None]], dim=class="n">1)
bins   = (torch.stack(glob_ids, dim=class="n">1) - (V - NB)).float()   # (B,7) local indices 0..NB-1
# Bin CENTERS, no extra +0.5 (round-forward has none); NB classes span [AMIN,AMAX]:
action = AMIN + bins / (NB - class="n">1) * (AMAX - AMIN)         # consistent inverse of round(...*(NB-1))
action = unnormalize(action, robot_stats)              # per-DIM stats -> meters / radians
dreamer.py — RSSM latent imagination & actor-critic on imagined returns
Left: teal field = reward landscape; coral squares o1–o4 = real frames encoded to latent; teal path = a dream rolled forward in latent space. Right: per-step discounted reward (bars) and accumulating return (coral).

Dreamer: learn to act by imagining in a compact latent

A recurrent state-space model (RSSM) keeps a latent state h_t that evolves recurrently. From a handful of real observations it encodes a posterior latent — the coral squares o1…o4o1\ldots o4o1…o4 landing on the data manifold. From the last real latent z0z_{0}z0​ it then imagines a rollout entirely in latent space: the prior transition ht+1=f(ht,at)h_{t+1}=f(h_t,a_t)ht+1​=f(ht​,at​) predicts the next latent and an actor picks each action, all without decoding a single pixel. A reward/value model scores every imagined latent, and the actor-critic is trained on the imagined discounted return G=Σγtr(zt)G = \Sigma \gamma ^{t} r(z_{t})G=Σγtr(zt​) — never querying the real environment again.

Imagination is cheap precisely because it happens in a small latent, not in raw observations — rolling forward a 30-D state is orders of magnitude cheaper than rendering frames. That "compress to a latent, then reason there" move is exactly what OncoSeg's Swin encoder does: it squeezes a 128³ CT/MR volume into a compact feature state, and every downstream decision (segmentation, RECIST response, a forecast of how a lesion evolves between scans) is computed in that latent rather than in voxel space. Slide the horizon H: the dream sweeps toward the high-reward region and the return accumulates, but later steps are discounted by γt\gamma ^{t}γt so the curve flattens — distant imagined rewards count for less, which is what keeps long-horizon planning stable.
12
encode → posterior latentimagine in latent (no decode)actor-critic on Gdiscount γᵗ
💡 Why it mattersReal environment interaction is slow, costly, or unsafe, yet model-free RL needs millions of trials. Dreamer learns a compact latent world model (an RSSM) from pixels and then trains the policy almost entirely by "imagining" rollouts inside that latent, slashing the number of real interactions needed and letting one fixed configuration solve very different control tasks.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed for sample-efficient control and game-playing (DreamerV3 was the first to mine diamonds in Minecraft from scratch, with one config beating specialists on 150+ tasks) and for real-world robot learning (DayDreamer taught a quadruped to walk in about an hour and arms to do visual pick-and-place). The same imagine-then-act recipe is being explored for embodied agents and could power planning over latent dynamics in safety-critical, hard-to-simulate domains such as surgical robotics and adaptive image-guided treatment.

▸ Code PyTorch — DreamerV3 latent imagination + actor-critic on the λ-return▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
h, z = rssm.posterior(obs[:, :K])          # last grounded RSSM state: (B,Dh),(B,Dz)
states, rewards, values, logps = [], [], [], []
for t in range(H):                          # imagine H steps purely in latent space
    dist = actor(torch.cat([h, z], -class="n">1))
    a = dist.sample()                       # sample (REINFORCE path: NOT reparameterized)
    logps.append(dist.log_prob(a))          # (B,) keep log-prob for the policy gradient
    h = rssm.gru(torch.cat([z, a], -class="n">1), h)
    z = rssm.prior(h).rsample()             # next latent, no pixel decode
    s = torch.cat([h, z], -class="n">1); states.append(s)
    rewards.append(reward_head(s).mean)     # (B,)
    values.append(critic(s).mean)           # (B,)
r, v = torch.stack(rewards), torch.stack(values)   # (H,B)
logp = torch.stack(logps)                          # (H,B)
lam, gamma = class="n">0.95, class="n">0.997
G = v[-class="n">1]; returns = [None]*H
for t in reversed(range(H)):                # bootstrap off the NEXT value v[t+1]
    nextv = v[t + class="n">1] if t + class="n">1 < H else v[-class="n">1]
    G = r[t] + gamma * ((class="n">1 - lam) * nextv + lam * G)
    returns[t] = G
returns = torch.stack(returns).detach()            # (H,B), stop-grad target
adv = (returns - v.detach())                       # baseline = critic at same step
scale = (adv.std() + class="n">1e-8)                          # DreamerV3 normalizes the advantage
actor_loss = -(adv / scale * logp).mean() - class="n">1e-3 * dist.entropy().mean()
critic_loss = F.mse_loss(v, returns)               # twohog/symlog CE in real DreamerV3
genie.py — latent action model + dynamics
Left: infer which latent action z happened between two frames. Right: pick an action, generate the next frame.

Genie: controllable worlds from unlabeled video

Genie learns to turn raw video into a playable simulator — with no action labels at all. It has two halves. A latent action model (LAM) looks at two consecutive frames and infers which of N discrete actions must have occurred between them, compressing the change into one of a tiny set of codes (a VQ codebook, here 4 entries). Then a dynamics model takes the current frame plus a chosen latent action and generates the next frame — so you can drive the world even though nobody ever told it what a "button press" means.

Below, the LAM watches a token slide one tile right and quantizes that change to the nearest codebook vector z. Pick any of the 4 latent actions on the right and the dynamics model deterministically rolls the sprite to the predicted next cell (with toroidal wrap).

The same recipe matters for medical imaging: longitudinal scans are essentially unlabeled "video" of a patient. A Genie-style model could learn the latent moves a tumor makes between scans (grow, shrink, shift) without hand annotation, then let a clinician counterfactually roll a lesion forward under a hypothetical action — a controllable simulator distilled from observation alone, exactly the kind of world model OncoSeg's response-assessment story points toward.
→ right
unsupervised actionsVQ codebooklatent action modellearned dynamics
💡 Why it mattersGenie (Google DeepMind) learns a controllable world model purely from unlabeled video, recovering a latent action space without any action labels — so a frame-by-frame interactive environment emerges from raw footage that has no controller logs. This unlocks the bottleneck in world models and embodied AI: it lets you turn the internet's vast trove of action-free video into playable simulators and unlimited training grounds for agents, instead of needing expensive action-annotated or game-engine data.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed to build interactive, navigable simulators for training and evaluating embodied/game agents in unlimited generated worlds, plus prototyping playable scenes from a single image, sketch, or text prompt; the same learn-dynamics-from-unlabeled-video idea extends to robotics video prediction and, in medical imaging, to forecasting how an organ or contrast bolus evolves across frames in dynamic CINE-MRI or 4D-CT sequences.

▸ Code PyTorch — Genie's latent-action VQ + dynamics, what actually trains▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# --- Latent Action Model: infer WHICH of N discrete actions happened (no labels) ---
def infer_latent_action(frame_prev, frame_cur, encoder, codebook):  # codebook: (N, D)
    z_e = encoder(torch.cat([frame_prev, frame_cur], dim=class="n">1))         # encode the CHANGE -> (B, D)
    d = torch.cdist(z_e, codebook)                                   # (B, N) Euclidean dist; argmin == argmin of ||.||^2
    idx = d.argmin(dim=class="n">1)                                            # chosen discrete latent action -> (B,)
    z_q = codebook[idx]                                              # hard quantized code -> (B, D)
    z_st = z_e + (z_q - z_e).detach()                                # straight-through: fwd=z_q, grad->z_e
    probs = F.softmax(-d, dim=class="n">1)                                     # soft assignment (the bar chart)
    return idx, z_e, z_q, z_st, probs                               # NOTE: also return z_e for the VQ losses

# --- Dynamics model: previous frame + CHOSEN latent action -> reconstruct current frame ---
def predict_next_frame(frame_prev, action_idx, codebook, dynamics):
    z = codebook[action_idx]                                        # hard code lookup (inference, no STE)
    return dynamics(frame_prev, z)                                  # autoregressive token model rolls t-1 -> t

# Train end-to-end on raw video with NO action labels: reconstruct frame_t from (frame_{t-1}, z_st)
idx, z_e, z_q, z_st, probs = infer_latent_action(f_prev, f_cur, encoder, codebook)
pred = dynamics(f_prev, z_st)                                        # use the straight-through code so grad reaches encoder
recon = F.mse_loss(pred, f_cur)
codebook_loss   = F.mse_loss(z_q, z_e.detach())                     # move codes toward encoder (weight 1.0)
commit_loss     = F.mse_loss(z_e, z_q.detach())                     # move encoder toward codes (beta)
loss = recon + codebook_loss + class="n">0.25 * commit_loss                   # standard VQ-VAE / Genie LAM weighting
nerf.py — render one pixel by ray marching the volume integral
Top: the density field σ(x) with the marching ray (dashed) and its sample weights (coral dots) → the rendered pixel swatch. Bottom: per-sample σ·δ (teal bars), transmittance Tᵢ (coral, decaying) and the running accumulated opacity (dashed, rising).

NeRF: turning a 3D field into one pixel by marching a ray

A Neural Radiance Field stores a scene as a function that, for any 3D point, returns a density σ and a view-dependent color c. To render a single pixel you shoot a ray from the eye and take N samples along it. Each slab of length δ\delta δ absorbs light with opacity αᵢ = 1 − e−σᵢδ. How much of that slab's color actually reaches the eye is gated by the transmittance Tᵢ = e−Σj σⱼδ = Πj(1−αⱼ) — the fraction of light that survived everything in front of it.

The final pixel is the transmittance-weighted integral C=ΣTi⋅αi⋅ciC = \Sigma T_{i}\cdot \alpha _{i}\cdot c_{i}C=ΣTi​⋅αi​⋅ci​, and the accumulated opacity Σ Tᵢ·αᵢ = 1 − TN. Drag the slider to sweep the ray across the scene: a ray through empty space stays transparent (T barely decays, opacity ≈ 0); a ray through the dense teal core saturates early (T collapses, weights pile up at the first surface it hits, color locks onto that blob); a ray grazing the deeper coral satellite blends warm. The weights peak exactly at the first opaque surface — that is why NeRF reconstructs sharp geometry rather than a foggy average.

This is the same accumulate-along-a-ray operator that defines CT: a CT projection integrates attenuation Σσiδ\Sigma \sigma _{i}\delta Σσi​δ through tissue, and reconstruction inverts many such rays into a 3D volume. NeRF generalizes it — learning a continuous σ/c field from 2D views and rendering it differentiably — which is precisely the machinery behind learned 3D reconstruction of an organ or lesion from sparse 2D slices/projections, and behind novel-view synthesis for surgical and interventional planning. The transmittance term is also what makes the render occlusion-aware: a deep structure can't contribute color the moment something solid sits in front of it.
0.42
σ densityα=1−e^(−σδ)T=Π(1−α)C=Σ T·α·csame as CT
💡 Why it mattersNeRF reframes 3D as a coordinate-MLP that maps any (x,y,z,viewing-direction) to color and density, then renders a pixel by alpha-compositing samples along a camera ray — so the whole scene is learned purely from posed 2D photos with no mesh, voxel grid, or depth sensor. This solves novel-view synthesis with photorealistic specularities and transparency that classical multi-view stereo and explicit meshes struggle to capture, and the differentiable volume-rendering integral makes the entire pipeline trainable end-to-end by photometric loss.
▸ Where it’s usedIt powers free-viewpoint capture, VFX/relighting, AR/VR scene reconstruction, robotics and autonomous-driving simulation, and Google Maps Immersive View; in medical imaging the same differentiable ray-marching idea underlies sparse-view/limited-angle CT and tomographic reconstruction and intra-operative endoscopic/surgical-scene 3D reconstruction. Its faster successor, 3D Gaussian Splatting, is now the practical workhorse for real-time radiance-field rendering.

▸ Code PyTorch — the volume-rendering integral that actually runs (torch.cumprod transmittance)▶
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def volume_render(sigma, rgb, t):           # sigma:[R,N], rgb:[R,N,3], t:[R,N] sample depths
    delta = t[..., class="n">1:] - t[..., :-class="n">1]        # slab lengths δ_i between adjacent samples
    delta = torch.cat([delta, delta[..., -class="n">1:].clamp(min=class="n">1e10)], -class="n">1)  # last slab → ∞ (background)
    alpha = class="n">1.0 - torch.exp(-F.relu(sigma) * delta)                  # α_i = 1 − e^(−σ_i δ_i)
    # transmittance T_i = Π_{j<i}(1−α_j): exclusive cumulative product of (1−α), light surviving to i
    T = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.ones_like(alpha[..., :class="n">1]),
                                 class="n">1.0 - alpha + class="n">1e-10], -class="n">1), -class="n">1)[..., :-class="n">1]
    w = T * alpha                            # per-sample weight w_i = T_i·α_i (peaks at first surface)
    C = (w[..., None] * torch.sigmoid(rgb)).sum(-class="n">2)   # C = Σ w_i·c_i — transmittance-weighted color
    acc = w.sum(-class="n">1)                          # accumulated opacity = 1 − T_N
    depth = (w * t).sum(-class="n">1)                  # expected ray-termination depth → the reconstructed surface
    return C, acc, depth, w
# train: render rays from a coordinate MLP σ,c = net(x, view_dir); loss = ((C - C_gt)**2).mean()
rasterizer.cu — project 3D gaussians → 2D, sort by depth, α-composite
Left = composited novel view (rasterized). Right = the depth-sorted splat stack; front splats (small depth) are blended first and occlude those behind.

3D Gaussian Splatting — render a scene by stamping fuzzy blobs

Instead of an implicit MLP, the scene is an explicit cloud of 3D gaussians, each with a position, an anisotropic covariance (its 3D shape), a color and an opacity. To synthesize a new view you project every gaussian to a 2D elliptical footprint, sort them front-to-back by depth, and alpha-composite them onto the image — exactly the "over" operator: C=Σici⋅αi⋅TiC = \Sigma _{i} c_{i}\cdot \alpha _{i}\cdot T_{i}C=Σi​ci​⋅αi​⋅Ti​ with transmittance Ti=Πj=1i−1(1−αj)T_{i} = \Pi _{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alpha _{j})Ti​=Πj=1i−1​(1−αj​). Each pixel's splat weight is αi=opacityi⋅exp(−12⋅dTΣ−1d)\alpha _{i} = opacity_{i} \cdot exp(-\tfrac12 \cdot d^{T}\Sigma ^{-1}d)αi​=opacityi​⋅exp(−21​⋅dTΣ−1d) — the projected gaussian evaluated at that pixel.

Drag splats rendered: the renderer adds gaussians in depth order. Early (front) splats lay down color and spend transmittance; once T drops near zero the surface is opaque and farther splats are culled — the same early-termination a real tile rasterizer uses.

The contrast with NeRF (demo on diffusion/JEPA-style implicit models) is the whole point: NeRF answers each pixel by marching a ray and evaluating a per-ray MLP at dozens of sample points — accurate but slow. Gaussian splatting is a single rasterize pass (sort + blend), no network in the loop, so it renders novel views at 100+ FPS. For medical/clinical use that means a 3D capture of a patient's anatomy or a surgical field can be re-viewed interactively in real time, and the explicit gaussians are directly editable (delete, recolor, deform a structure) in a way an opaque MLP volume is not.
14
explicit gaussianssort by depthα-composite (over)rasterize → real-time
💡 Why it matters3D Gaussian Splatting represents a scene as millions of anisotropic Gaussian "blobs" (each with position, covariance, color, and opacity) and rasterizes them via differentiable alpha-blending, giving photorealistic novel-view synthesis at real-time (100+ FPS) rates — a leap over NeRFs, which are accurate but require slow volumetric ray-marching to render. Because the representation is explicit and rasterized rather than queried by an MLP, it trains in minutes and renders interactively, making radiance fields practical for live applications.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed for VR/AR scene capture, digital twins, robotics and SLAM mapping, film/VFX set reconstruction, and product/3D-asset capture from phone video. In medical imaging it is emerging for endoscopic and surgical-scene 3D reconstruction (e.g., deformable tissue from laparoscopy) and for dynamic 4D reconstruction of moving anatomy.

▸ Code PyTorch + gsplat — what actually runs (the over-composite, front→back)▶
import torch
from gsplat import rasterization          # CUDA differentiable splatter (nerfstudio)

# A scene IS the explicit Gaussians — no MLP, unlike NeRF.
N = 100_000
means     = torch.randn(N, class="n">3, device=class="s">"cuda")          # 3D centers  μ
quats     = torch.randn(N, class="n">4, device=class="s">"cuda")          # rotation R (wxyz, auto-normalized)
scales    = torch.rand (N, class="n">3, device=class="s">"cuda") * class="n">0.05   # → Σ = R·diag(s²)·Rᵀ
opacities = torch.rand (N,    device=class="s">"cuda")          # base α o
sh        = torch.randn(N, class="n">16, class="n">3, device=class="s">"cuda")      # view-dep color, SH deg-3 (K=16=(3+1)²)

# project μ,Σ → 2D, depth-sort per 16×16 tile, then α-composite "over" — all on-GPU.
# viewmat: [4,4] WORLD-TO-CAMERA (w2c); K: [3,3] intrinsics.
rgb, alpha, meta = rasterization(means, quats, scales, opacities,
    colors=sh, viewmats=viewmat[None], Ks=K[None],    # [1,4,4], [1,3,3]
    width=class="n">640, height=class="n">480, sh_degree=class="n">3, render_mode=class="s">"RGB")  # rgb: [1,480,640,3]

# The per-pixel kernel each tile runs, front→back (near→far). For ONE pixel's
# depth-sorted splats sorted_a:[M] sorted_c:[M,3] (M = #Gaussians hitting it):
#   αᵢ = oᵢ·exp(-½ (x-μᵢ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x-μᵢ));  Tᵢ = Π_{j<i}(1-αⱼ)  (T₀=1)
#   C  = Σᵢ cᵢ·αᵢ·Tᵢ ;  nearer splats attenuate farther ones, early-stop when T→0.
one_minus = class="n">1.0 - sorted_a                                   # [M]
T = torch.cat([sorted_a.new_ones(class="n">1), torch.cumprod(one_minus, class="n">0)[:-class="n">1]])  # exclusive cumprod
C = (sorted_c * (sorted_a * T).unsqueeze(-class="n">1)).sum(class="n">0)         # Σ cᵢ αᵢ Tᵢ  → [3]
occupancy_grid.py — ray-cast BEV: free · occupied · unknown
Top-down grid. Sensor (teal dot) casts rays: cells before the first hit = free (teal), the hit cell = occupied (coral), everything behind/unseen = unknown (gray).

Occupancy grid — dense 3D labeling in another domain

An autonomous-driving perception stack turns raw sensor returns into a bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid where every voxel is tagged free, occupied, or unknown. The trick is honest ray-casting: along each ray, cells in front of the first return are confidently empty, the return marks an obstacle, and — crucially — everything in the obstacle's shadow stays unknown, because the sensor never saw it.

Drag sensor range: a short range reveals only a small disc, so most of the map is unknown. As range grows the free region expands and more obstacles get hit — until the fractions plateau, because no extra range can see through an obstacle. Drag sweep to watch a rotating lidar paint the map angle-by-angle, each ray independently resolving its own line of sight.

This is the same problem OncoSeg solves, wearing a different hat: predicting a dense per-voxel label over a 3D grid. A BEV occupancy grid is voxel occupancy of a road scene; OncoSeg's segmentation is voxel occupancy of a tumor in an MRI volume. Both must reason about regions they can't directly observe — the lidar's shadow is the radiologist's partial-volume / low-contrast zone — and both express that honestly as unknown / uncertain rather than guessing. The free/occupied/unknown split here is exactly the confident-foreground / confident-background / boundary-uncertainty trichotomy the uncertainty widgets quantify for segmentation.

💡 Why it mattersAn occupancy grid turns noisy, partial range sensing (lidar/radar/camera depth) into a dense per-voxel label — free, occupied, or unknown — giving a self-driving stack a single geometry-complete world model that fuses many sensors and time steps and, crucially, marks unseen/occluded space as unknown rather than guessing. It is the same dense 3D-labeling problem as voxel tumor segmentation: confident-foreground / confident-background / boundary-uncertain maps directly onto occupied / free / unknown, and the lidar's shadow plays the role of the radiologist's partial-volume, low-contrast zone.
▸ Where it’s usedOccupancy networks are now a core perception layer in production autonomous-driving stacks (Tesla's vision-only "occupancy network," Waymo, Wayve, NVIDIA DRIVE) and in robotics for collision-free motion planning, where 3D semantic-occupancy prediction (e.g. the CVPR Occ3D / nuScenes occupancy benchmarks) is an active research frontier. The same dense-voxel, free/occupied/unknown formulation also underlies classic robot mapping (OctoMap) and SLAM, and is conceptually the road-scene twin of volumetric medical-image segmentation.

▸ Code PyTorch — log-odds occupancy grid (inverse sensor model), what actually runs▶
import torch
# Log-odds BEV occupancy grid. State l in R^{H,W}; P(occ)=sigmoid(l).
l = torch.zeros(H, W)                                  # prior log-odds = logit(0.5) = 0
L_FREE, L_OCC = -class="n">0.85, class="n">0.85                            # inverse-sensor-model log-odds
# Ray-march each beam from the sensor to (and including) its measured hit range.
for ang, rng in zip(angles, ranges):                   # rng = lidar return for this beam
    t   = torch.arange(class="n">0., rng + res, res)             # +res so the HIT cell is sampled
    xs  = ((sx + t * torch.cos(ang)) / res).long()     # cell index x along the ray
    ys  = ((sy + t * torch.sin(ang)) / res).long()     # cell index y along the ray
    m   = (xs >= class="n">0) & (xs < W) & (ys >= class="n">0) & (ys < H)   # keep in-bounds cells only
    upd = torch.where(t >= rng - class="n">1e-6, L_OCC, L_FREE)  # last cell (the return) -> occupied
    l[ys[m], xs[m]] += upd[m]                           # Bayesian fusion = adding log-odds
l.clamp_(-class="n">4., class="n">4.)                                      # saturate so the map stays adaptive
# Cells no ray ever touched keep l==0  ->  P=0.5  ->  UNKNOWN (the lidar shadow).
p = torch.sigmoid(l)                                    # back to occupancy probability
label = torch.full_like(l, fill_value=-class="n">1, dtype=torch.long)  # -1 = unknown
label[p < class="n">0.3] = class="n">0    # free
label[p > class="n">0.7] = class="n">1    # occupied
pointnet.py — set input → shared MLP → max-pool → permutation-invariant feature
Left: the fixed point SET, labels = position in the current order. Middle: shared MLP features per point (ink-boxed bar = the per-dim max). Right: global vector g. Step the order — g and its argmax points never move.

PointNet: learning on a SET, not a sequence

A point cloud is an unordered set — there is no canonical "point #0". PointNet handles this with three steps: (1) a shared per-point MLP f(pi)f(p_{i})f(pi​) applied independently with the same weights to every point, (2) a symmetric pool — element-wise max over all points, (3) the resulting global vector g[d]=maxif(pi)[d]g[d] = max_{i} f(p_{i})[d]g[d]=maxi​f(pi​)[d]. Because max over a set ignores order, g is permutation-invariant by construction: g(π⋅X)=g(X)g(\pi \cdot X) = g(X)g(π⋅X)=g(X) for any reordering π.

Step the order control through 6 permutations of the same 8 points. The position labels on the left scramble, the feature columns in the middle slide around — but the global vector g on the right is byte-identical every time, and the physical point that supplies each dimension's max (ink-outlined) is unchanged. Tie to OncoSeg: dense CT/MRI voxels do have a natural grid order, so OncoSeg uses ordered conv + windowed attention. But the instant you work with sparse 3D — point-sampled lesion surfaces, centroid sets, multi-detector fusion, or LiDAR-style sensing with no natural order — you need set-based, permutation-invariant operators. Max-pool is the simplest faithful one.
1 / 6
unordered setshared per-point MLPglobal max-poolg(π·X)=g(X)
💡 Why it mattersPoint clouds (e.g. from LiDAR or surface meshes) are unordered sets with no grid or canonical sequence, so the same shape can be fed in any of N! orderings — PointNet solves this by learning a permutation-invariant function (per-point MLP + symmetric max-pool), letting deep nets operate directly on raw 3D points without voxelizing or imposing a fake ordering.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins 3D shape classification and part/scene segmentation, autonomous-driving LiDAR perception (object detection, drivable-space), robotic grasping and SLAM, and in medical imaging is used on point-sampled organ/tumor surfaces, vessel trees, and surgical-scene reconstructions where a mesh or 3D scan is treated as a set.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (shared 1x1-conv MLP + max over points)▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class PointNetEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim=class="n">3, dims=(class="n">64, class="n">128, class="n">1024)):
        super().__init__()
        # "shared MLP" = 1x1 conv over points: SAME weights applied to every point i
        layers, c = [], in_dim
        for d in dims:
            layers += [nn.Conv1d(c, d, class="n">1), nn.BatchNorm1d(d), nn.ReLU(inplace=True)]
            c = d
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(*layers)          # f(p_i), independent & weight-shared

    def forward(self, x):                          # x: (B, in_dim, N)  N = #points (a SET)
        feats = self.mlp(x)                        # (B, C, N)  per-point features f(p_i)
        g, _ = feats.max(dim=class="n">2)                    # g[d] = max_i f(p_i)[d]  — symmetric pool
        return g                                   # (B, C)  permutation-invariant global vector

enc = PointNetEncoder().eval()                     # eval(): freeze BN so invariance is exact/deterministic
pts = torch.randn(class="n">4, class="n">3, class="n">2048)                      # (B, C=xyz, N)
g = enc(pts)
perm = torch.randperm(class="n">2048)
assert torch.allclose(g, enc(pts[:, :, perm]), atol=class="n">1e-5)  # g(pi.X) == g(X)
augment.py — domain randomization: cover the reality gap
Teal cloud = randomized SIM samples · coral ◆ = the fixed REAL scanner. Widen σ until it is enclosed.

Sim-to-real domain randomization

A model only generalizes to inputs it was effectively trained on. Plot every image as a point in an abstract appearance space (x = texture/contrast, y = brightness/illumination). The training distribution is a cloud of synthetic samples whose appearance we deliberately randomize; its spread is the randomization strength σ\sigma σ. One fixed real sample (coral ◆) sits off to the side — the reality gap.

At small σ\sigma σ the real sample is far outside the cloud (out-of-distribution): the model never saw anything like it, so it fails. Crank σ\sigma σ and the cloud expands; once the support contour (drawn at 2.5σ2.5\sigma 2.5σ) encloses the real point, it becomes in-distribution — the real domain is now just one more sample the network already trained against.

In OncoSeg terms this is the deployment analog of augmenting across MRI/CT scanners and sites. A tumor model trained on one hospital's scanner is out-of-distribution on the next (different bias field, contrast, noise). Randomizing intensity/texture/orientation during training widens the appearance cloud so an unseen scanner lands inside it — bridging the reality gap without collecting labels from every new site. Over-randomize, though, and you waste capacity covering appearances no scanner ever produces.
0.10
support = 2.5σ contourreal fixed at dist 0.46crossover σ ≈ 0.18
💡 Why it mattersCollecting and labeling real-world data for robots or 3D perception is slow, costly, and dangerous, while pure simulation suffers a "reality gap" that breaks transfer. Domain randomization closes that gap by aggressively varying simulated textures, lighting, physics, and sensor noise so the real world looks like just another random sample, letting models trained only in sim work on real hardware zero-shot.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed to train robot manipulation and locomotion policies (e.g. in-hand dexterity, legged-robot walking), autonomous-driving perception, and grasp/pose detection that deploy on real hardware without real-world labels. In medical imaging the same idea powers synthetic-data and heavy-augmentation pipelines so segmentation models generalize across unseen scanners, vendors, and acquisition protocols.

▸ Code MONAI — what actually runs in the training dataloader▶
import torch
from monai.transforms import Compose, RandShiftIntensityd, RandAdjustContrastd, \
    RandGaussianNoised, RandBiasFieldd, RandGaussianSmoothd

# Domain randomization = widen the TRAINING appearance distribution. Each transform
# samples fresh params per volume; `sigma` scales the randomization strength.
sigma = class="n">0.10
randomize = Compose([
    RandShiftIntensityd(keys=class="s">"img", offsets=sigma, prob=class="n">1.0),                  # brightness ~ Uniform(-sigma, sigma)
    RandAdjustContrastd(keys=class="s">"img", gamma=(class="n">1 - class="n">2*sigma, class="n">1 + class="n">2*sigma), prob=class="n">1.0),  # contrast: gamma in (0.8, 1.2)
    RandBiasFieldd(keys=class="s">"img", coeff_range=(class="n">0., sigma), prob=class="n">0.5),             # MRI smooth multiplicative shading
    RandGaussianSmoothd(keys=class="s">"img", sigma_x=(class="n">0., class="n">3*sigma),                     # isotropic acquisition blur
                        sigma_y=(class="n">0., class="n">3*sigma), sigma_z=(class="n">0., class="n">3*sigma), prob=class="n">0.3),
    RandGaussianNoised(keys=class="s">"img", mean=class="n">0.0, std=sigma, prob=class="n">0.5),             # scanner noise ~ N(0, sigma^2)
])
aug = randomize({class="s">"img": vol})[class="s">"img"]   # fresh draw every iteration

# Faithful "from scratch" version. NOTE: gamma is applied to the image RESCALED to [0,1]
# by its ACTUAL min/max (MONAI does this, not a hard clamp), then mapped back — so it works
# on CT/z-scored MRI too. The result is NOT Gaussian: brightness is Uniform, gamma is nonlinear;
# only the additive term is N(0, sigma^2).
#   eps = 1e-7; lo = vol.min(); rng = vol.max() - lo
#   gamma = 1 + (2*torch.rand(1) - 1) * 2*sigma                  # contrast, gamma in [1-2s, 1+2s]
#   x = ((vol - lo) / (rng + eps)) ** gamma * rng + lo           # MONAI contrast (no clamp, rescaled back)
#   x = x + (2*torch.rand(1) - 1) * sigma                        # brightness ~ Uniform(-sigma, sigma)
#   x = x + sigma * torch.randn_like(vol)                        # noise ~ N(0, sigma^2)
diffusion_policy.py — denoise an ACTION trajectory, conditioned on the observation
Faint teal dashes = clean target x₀. Solid line = the path at denoise step k (coral→teal as it cleans). Coral stubs = the per-waypoint denoise pull toward x₀. Bar = noise σ.

Diffusion Policy — generate the plan by denoising it

Instead of emitting one action at a time, a diffusion policy treats the next H-step action trajectory as a single object to generate. It starts from a path of pure Gaussian noise and runs a learned reverse diffusion: at each step k (counting T→0T\to 0T→0) a network predicts the noise and subtracts a slice of it, so the random scribble collapses into a smooth, feasible path that reaches the goal and arcs around the obstacle — all conditioned on the observation.

Each waypoint follows the DDPM relation xk=αˉk⋅x0+1−αˉk⋅εx_{k} = \sqrt{}\bar{\alpha}_{k}\cdot x_{0} + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{k}}\cdot \varepsilon xk​=​αˉk​⋅x0​+1−αˉk​​⋅ε with a cosine schedule for αˉ\bar{\alpha}αˉ. Drag k from T down to 0: the signal weight αˉ\sqrt{}\bar{\alpha}​αˉ rises, the noise level σ=1−αˉ\sigma =\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}}σ=1−αˉ​ falls, the signal-to-noise ratio climbs, and the trajectory snaps onto the clean target. The coral stubs are the denoise direction the model would apply next.

This is SOTA visuomotor control (Chi et al., 2023; π0). It is deliberately distinct from the VLA widget: VLA emits discrete, tokenized actions one bin at a time, whereas a diffusion policy produces a continuous, multimodal whole-trajectory distribution — switch the goal and it commits to a different smooth mode rather than averaging them. The same denoise-a-structured-output recipe is why diffusion is creeping into medical imaging as a segmentation / registration prior: sample plausible masks or deformations rather than regress one blurry mean — and for surgical-robot or auto-contouring deployment, generating a full feasible trajectory beats greedy per-step decoding.
20
reverse diffusioncontinuous trajectorymultimodalcosine ᾱ scheduleobs-conditioned
💡 Why it mattersDiffusion Policy treats action generation as conditional denoising: instead of regressing a single action, it samples a whole action sequence by iteratively denoising noise conditioned on observations. This naturally captures multimodal behavior (multiple valid ways to do a task), produces smooth multi-step plans, and is far more stable to train than GANs or energy-based policies for high-dimensional, continuous robot control.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the dominant approach for visuomotor robot manipulation learned from human demonstrations — bimanual and dexterous tasks, pick-and-place, tool use, and humanoid control — and underpins large robot foundation policies; the same denoising-the-plan idea also appears in motion/trajectory planning and could guide image-conditioned interventions such as surgical-robot or needle-insertion trajectory generation in medical imaging.

▸ Code PyTorch + diffusers — the Diffusion Policy reverse loop that actually runs at inference▶
import torch
from diffusers import DDPMScheduler  # cosine ᾱ schedule, betas precomputed
# clip_sample=True is the DEFAULT and clamps x0_hat (hence the traj) to ±1 each step,
# so actions MUST be normalized to [-1,1]; we set it explicitly to make that contract clear.
sched = DDPMScheduler(num_train_timesteps=class="n">100, beta_schedule=class="s">"squaredcos_cap_v2",
                      clip_sample=True)            # train steps = 100
T = class="n">100                                            # inference steps (full DDPM; use DDIM for fewer)
sched.set_timesteps(T)                             # sched.timesteps: integer grid, high → 0

obs_cond = obs_encoder(obs)                         # condition on the observation o
x = torch.randn(B, H, action_dim, device=dev)       # x_T : trajectory of PURE noise (normalized space)
for k in sched.timesteps:                            # k descends over the inference grid → 0
    eps_hat = net(x, k, global_cond=obs_cond)        # ε_θ(x_k, k | o): predict the noise
    x = sched.step(eps_hat, k, x).prev_sample        # x_{k-1}: rescale + (k>0) re-noise
    # DDPM reverse posterior q(x_{k-1}|x_k,x0) that .step computes (verified vs diffusers):
    #   x0_hat = (x - √(1-ᾱ_k)·eps_hat) / √(ᾱ_k); if clip_sample: x0_hat.clamp_(-1, 1)
    #   with α_k=ᾱ_k/ᾱ_{k-1}, β_k=1-α_k  (cumprod ratios over the strided grid; raw betas iff T==100)
    #   mean = √(ᾱ_{k-1})·β_k/(1-ᾱ_k)·x0_hat + √(α_k)·(1-ᾱ_{k-1})/(1-ᾱ_k)·x
    #   x    = mean + (k>0)·σ_k·torch.randn_like(x)  # add noise except on the last step

action_traj = unnormalize(x)[:, :n_exec]             # de-normalize, then execute first n_exec steps
pinn.py - damped oscillator
Blue=true physical u(t), teal=network fit, coral dots=sparse data, coral shading=local |ODE residual|.

Physics-Informed NN (PINN)

Fit a curve u(t) through a handful of noisy measurements of a damped harmonic oscillator. With only the data term, infinitely many wiggly curves pass near the points — the network happily picks one and overfits between samples. A PINN adds a second loss: the residual of the governing equation r(t) = u″ + 2ζω·u′ + ω²·u, which must be ~0 if u truly obeys the physics. Slide λ to weight that residual. At λ=0 the fit oscillates and r(t) is huge; as λ→1 the only curve that satisfies both the data and the equation is the smooth physical solution.

Total loss = Ldata + λ·Lresidual. The residual is evaluated everywhere via autodiff (here: finite differences), not just at labeled points — so the equation regularizes the gaps where labels are missing. In OncoSeg-style settings with scarce annotations, encoding known biology/physics (smooth boundary growth, conservation, dose kinetics) as a soft constraint stops the model from producing impossible predictions and improves generalization from tiny cohorts.
0.00
λ=0 → overfit, ODE violatedλ→1 → physical solution
💡 Why it mattersPINNs embed the governing PDEs/ODEs of a physical system directly into the loss (as residuals enforced via autodiff), so the network respects conservation laws and boundary conditions instead of just fitting data. This lets them solve forward and inverse problems in sparse- or noisy-data regimes where pure data-driven nets fail and classical mesh solvers are expensive or ill-posed.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed for fluid dynamics, heat transfer, and electromagnetics surrogates, seismic/subsurface inversion, and discovering unknown PDE parameters from measurements. In medical imaging they reconstruct blood-flow fields from sparse 4D-flow MRI, infer tissue stiffness in elastography, and solve patient-specific cardiac/hemodynamics models for digital twins.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (autograd ODE residual)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

zeta, omega, lam = class="n">0.1, class="n">4.0, class="n">1.0          # damping, freq, physics weight λ

def residual(net, t):                     # t: (N,1), requires_grad=True
    u   = net(t)
    # autodiff the network w.r.t. its INPUT to get the time-derivatives
    u_t  = torch.autograd.grad(u,  t, torch.ones_like(u),  create_graph=True)[class="n">0]
    u_tt = torch.autograd.grad(u_t, t, torch.ones_like(u_t), create_graph=True)[class="n">0]
    return u_tt + class="n">2*zeta*omega*u_t + omega**class="n">2 * u   # r(t)=u''+2ζω·u'+ω²·u  (≈0 if physical)

# data term: fit the few noisy measurements
L_data = F.mse_loss(net(t_obs), u_obs)
# physics term: ODE residual driven to 0 at dense COLLOCATION points (no labels needed)
t_col = torch.rand(class="n">256, class="n">1, requires_grad=True) * T
L_res  = (residual(net, t_col) ** class="n">2).mean()        # ‖r(t)‖²

loss = L_data + lam * L_res                         # total = L_data + λ·L_residual
loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
quantize.py - PTQ FP32 -> INT8
Teal grid = 2^b reconstruction levels. Bars = weight histogram, colored by |rounding error| (coral = large). Blue = accuracy vs bit-width.

Quantization: FP32 -> INT8

A trained net stores each weight as a 32-bit float. Post-training quantization snaps those continuous values onto a small grid of integers. With a per-tensor scale s and symmetric mapping, each weight becomes wq=round(w/s)w_q = round(w / s)wq​=round(w/s), an integer in [−2(b−1),2(b−1)−1][-2^{}(b-1), 2^{}(b-1)-1][−2(b−1),2(b−1)−1], and is read back as wq⋅sw_q \cdot swq​⋅s. The choice s=max∣w∣/(2(b−1)−1)s = max|w| / (2^{}(b-1)-1)s=max∣w∣/(2(b−1)−1) spends the whole integer range on the observed weights. A b-bit code has only 2b2^{b}2b levels, so the grid spacing — and the rounding error — doubles for every bit you drop.

Why it matters for OncoSeg: a 3D segmentation backbone is large, but hospitals rarely have datacenter GPUs at the bedside. INT8 makes the weights 4× smaller (8/32 of FP32) and lets integer matmul run on a clinical workstation or edge appliance with near-identical Dice. Push too far, though — the accuracy strip shows INT8 and INT6 sit on a plateau, but at 2-bit the rounding noise swamps the signal and validation accuracy falls off a cliff. The engineering job is finding the lowest bit-width before that knee.
8-bit
w_q = round(w/s)levels = 2^bmem = b/32
💡 Why it mattersQuantization maps FP32 weights and activations to 8-bit integers, cutting memory and bandwidth ~4x and exploiting fast INT8 tensor cores, so the same model fits on a phone, microcontroller, or embedded GPU and runs several times faster at lower power. With calibration or quantization-aware training the accuracy drop is typically under a percent, making it the default lever for deploying deep nets within tight latency and memory budgets.
▸ Where it’s usedINT8 quantization powers on-device inference for mobile vision, ASR and LLMs (TensorRT/TFLite on phones and NVIDIA Jetson edge boxes), and lower-bit variants (INT4/AWQ/GPTQ) make 70B LLMs servable on a single GPU. In medical imaging it lets segmentation and detection models run on portable ultrasound, point-of-care, and FDA-cleared embedded devices where DRAM and battery are limited.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (torch.quantize_per_tensor + the scale/zero-point it wraps)▶
import torch

w = model.layer.weight.detach()          # FP32 tensor to compress
qmin, qmax = -class="n">128, class="n">127                    # INT8 range = [-2^(b-1), 2^(b-1)-1], b=8 (256 levels)

# --- affine (asymmetric) PTQ: scale + zero-point from observed [min,max] ---
s  = (w.max() - w.min()) / (qmax - qmin)  # scale = range / num_steps  (steps = 2^b - 1 = 255)
zp = (qmin - torch.round(w.min() / s)).clamp(qmin, qmax).to(torch.int8)  # integer that maps to 0.0

q  = torch.clamp(torch.round(w / s) + zp, qmin, qmax).to(torch.int8)     # w_q = round(w/s)+zp
w_hat = (q.to(torch.float32) - zp) * s    # dequantize: read back as (w_q - zp)*s

# --- what you actually call in PyTorch (same scale/zero-point semantics) ---
qt = torch.quantize_per_tensor(w, scale=s.item(), zero_point=int(zp), dtype=torch.qint8)
assert torch.allclose(qt.dequantize(), w_hat, atol=s.item())  # matches the manual path

# symmetric variant (zp=0): s = w.abs().max() / qmax; for exact symmetry restrict to qmin=-127
print(fclass="s">"INT8: 4x smaller (class="n">8/class="n">32), max rounding err of affine path ~ s/class="n">2 = {s.item()/class="n">2:.4g}")
compress.py - Magnitude Pruning
Left: weight matrix, teal intensity = |w|; cells below the threshold (coral marker) are zeroed to EMPTY. Right: accuracy vs sparsity.

Magnitude pruning & sparsity

A trained network is mostly dead weight: many connections have a tiny magnitude and barely move the output. Unstructured magnitude pruning ranks every weight by |w| and zeros out the smallest ones until you hit a target sparsity (% of weights set to 0). The surviving weights are untouched. Slide the target up and watch the smallest-magnitude cells drop to grey (zeroed) as the coral threshold sweeps right across the |w| color bar.

For a hospital deployment, this is how you ship a segmentation model that fits on the edge box next to the scanner. You can usually delete 70–80% of the weights and lose almost nothing on the validation set — the accuracy curve is flat. Push past the knee (~85–90%) and it falls off a cliff: you have started cutting load-bearing weights, not just dead ones. The sweet spot is the largest sparsity still on the plateau — a smaller, faster model with no clinically meaningful drop. (Sparse weights also store and multiply faster — only the nonzeros cost anything.)

50%
teal = kept |w|grey = zeroedcoral = prune threshold
💡 Why it mattersTrained networks are massively over-parameterized: magnitude pruning zeroes out the smallest-magnitude weights (a cheap proxy for "least important"), shrinking memory and FLOPs so models fit on edge devices and serve faster. With structured or N:M (e.g. 2:4) sparsity, those zeros translate into real hardware speedups on Ampere+ tensor cores rather than just smaller checkpoints.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed to compress LLMs and CNNs for on-device and low-latency serving, often paired with quantization; in medical imaging it slims segmentation/classification backbones (e.g. U-Net/nnU-Net-style models) so they run on bedside scanners, endoscopy carts, or point-of-care hardware. NVIDIA 2:4 sparsity and one-shot pruners like Wanda/SparseGPT make ~50% weight removal practical with little or no retraining.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (global L1 pruning + the |w|>thr formula)▶
import torch
import torch.nn.utils.prune as prune

# --- Idiomatic: PyTorch's built-in global magnitude pruning -----------------
# Zero the smallest-|w| weights across these layers until 70% are gone.
params = [(m, class="s">"weight") for m in (model.enc1, model.enc2, model.bottleneck)]
prune.global_unstructured(params, prune.L1Unstructured, amount=class="n">0.70)
for m, name in params:
    prune.remove(m, name)            # bake mask into .weight (drop reparam)

# --- From scratch: exactly what L1Unstructured.compute_mask does -------------
def magnitude_prune(w: torch.Tensor, sparsity: float) -> torch.Tensor:
    flat = w.abs().flatten()                          # score every weight by |w|
    k = round(sparsity * flat.numel())                # PyTorch uses round(), not int()
    if k == class="n">0:
        return w
    kill = torch.topk(flat, k, largest=False).indices # the k smallest-|w| -- exactly k
    mask = torch.ones_like(flat)
    mask[kill] = class="n">0                                     # zero precisely those k (tie-safe)
    return w * mask.view_as(w)                         # survivors untouched

# Faithful from-scratch run on a FRESH (unpruned) bottleneck copy:
W = model.bottleneck.weight.detach().clone()
print((magnitude_prune(W, class="n">0.70) == class="n">0).float().mean())  # -> 0.70
distill.py — soften teacher logits, train the student to match
Blue = teacher logits (fixed). Teal bars = soft targets at τ; coral = the runner-up "dark-knowledge" class. Dashed line = the one-hot hard label.

Knowledge distillation — train a small student on a big teacher's soft labels

A large teacher outputs logits over the classes. Instead of training a small student on the one-hot ground-truth label, distillation trains it to match the teacher's softened probabilities p=softmax(z/τ)p = softmax(z / \tau )p=softmax(z/τ). A temperature τ > 1 flattens the distribution so the small probabilities the teacher assigns to the wrong classes become visible — and copyable.

Those small probabilities are "dark knowledge": the teacher quietly says this enhancing glioma also looks a bit like a meningioma or a post-op cavity, and nothing like a normal brain. The hard argmax keeps only the winner (entropy = 0); the soft target carries this whole similarity structure, so the student learns far more per example.

For deployment this is the compression lever: a 100M-parameter teacher can hand its behaviour to a student small enough to run on the scanner console or a single on-prem GPU — keeping accuracy while shrinking memory and latency at the point of care. It pairs naturally with pruning and quantization, and with self-supervised pretraining (DINO/MAE) which is how the teacher learned cheaply in the first place. The distillation loss is the KL between teacher and student soft targets, scaled by τ2\tau ^{2}τ2 to keep gradient magnitudes stable.
1.00

τ → 0 collapses the soft target back to the one-hot hard label (entropy → 0, no extra signal). τ ≫ 1 pushes it toward uniform (entropy → ln N). The sweet spot in between is where the relational "which wrong classes are plausible" signal is richest — that is what the student copies.

softmax(z/τ)dark knowledgeKL · τ² losscompress for edge
💡 Why it mattersA small student trained on a teacher's soft probability distribution (or logits) learns the teacher's "dark knowledge" — the relative confidence across classes — and so generalizes far better than the same student trained on hard one-hot labels alone. This lets you ship a model that is 5-50x smaller and cheaper to run while keeping most of the big model's accuracy, which is the only practical way to deploy strong models on phones, edge devices, or under tight latency/cost budgets.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins essentially every fast small model in production: DistilBERT/TinyBERT for cheap NLP, the Llama-3/Gemma-2 small variants distilled from larger siblings, and white-box distillation of GPT-4-class outputs into open models. In medical imaging it compresses heavy segmentation/diagnosis nets (e.g. distilling a large nnU-Net or SAM teacher into a lightweight student) for on-device or point-of-care inference, and DINOv2's small models are distilled from a ViT-g teacher.

▸ Code PyTorch — soft-target KD loss (what actually runs)▶
import torch.nn.functional as F

def distillation_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, target, tau=class="n">4.0, alpha=class="n">0.5):
    # soft targets: flatten BOTH distributions by the temperature  p = softmax(z / tau)
    p_teacher = F.softmax(teacher_logits / tau, dim=-class="n">1)        # teacher's "dark knowledge"
    log_p_student = F.log_softmax(student_logits / tau, dim=-class="n">1)
    # KL(teacher || student) on the softened logits; tau**2 keeps the gradient scale
    # matched to the hard-label term (soft grads shrink ~1/tau**2).  Hinton et al. 2015.
    kd = F.kl_div(log_p_student, p_teacher, reduction=class="s">"batchmean") * (tau * tau)
    # student still sees the real one-hot label at tau=1 (what argmax would keep)
    ce = F.cross_entropy(student_logits, target)
    return alpha * kd + (class="n">1.0 - alpha) * ce

# teacher is frozen at inference temperature; only the small student updates
with torch.no_grad():
    teacher_logits = teacher(x)        # big net, eval mode, no grad
student_logits = student(x)            # small net we actually deploy
loss = distillation_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, target, tau=class="n">4.0)
loss.backward()                        # gradients flow only into the student
finetune.py — LoRA: freeze W, learn only ΔW = B·A
Faint slate = frozen W (d×d). Teal = B (d×r), coral = A (r×d) — the only trainable weights. Bottom-right = their product ΔW = B·A, a genuine rank-r matrix. Drag the rank.

LoRA — fine-tune a giant model by training two thin matrices

A pretrained weight matrix W is d×d. Full fine-tuning re-trains all d2d^{2}d2 of its entries. LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) freezes W entirely and learns only a low-rank update ΔW=B⋅A\Delta W = B\cdot AΔW=B⋅A, where B is d×r and A is r×d with rank r ≪ d. At inference the model uses W+B⋅AW + B\cdot AW+B⋅A. The product of a (d×r) and an (r×d) matrix can have rank at most r, so ΔW\Delta WΔW is forced to be low-rank — and that is the whole point.

Drag rank r. Trainable parameters are 2⋅d⋅r2\cdot d\cdot r2⋅d⋅r instead of d2d^{2}d2; the bar tracks how much of the ideal full update ΔW\Delta WΔW the rank-r factorization captures. Because real weight updates have a steeply decaying spectrum, even a tiny r recovers almost all of it — r=4 already captures >98% here.

This is the modern recipe for adapting a frozen medical foundation model to a new task on a single GPU. A 3D CT/MRI encoder may carry hundreds of millions of pretrained weights; retraining them for a new tumor type risks catastrophic forgetting and demands huge compute and data. LoRA instead bolts a handful of thin B/A factors onto each attention/projection layer — at d=4096 that is >99% fewer trainable parameters — so a hospital can specialize a shared foundation model to its own scanner and protocol from a small labeled set, ship just the megabytes-sized adapters, and keep the original weights untouched.
4
W frozenΔW = B·Arank r ≪ d2dr ≪ d²cheap finetune
💡 Why it mattersFine-tuning every weight of a multi-billion-parameter model is ruinously expensive in compute and storage; LoRA freezes the base model and learns only a low-rank update ΔW = B·A per layer, cutting trainable parameters by 100-10,000× and shrinking each checkpoint to a few MB. This makes adapting a giant model affordable on a single GPU, and lets you hot-swap dozens of task-specific adapters over one shared frozen backbone instead of storing a full copy per task.
▸ Where it’s usedLoRA (and its 4-bit variant QLoRA) is the default way to fine-tune LLMs like Llama and Mistral on commodity GPUs, and to specialize Stable Diffusion / SDXL into custom styles and characters that ship as tiny shareable adapter files. In medical imaging it is used to adapt foundation models — e.g. parameter-efficient tuning of SAM/MedSAM, CLIP, and ViT backbones to new modalities and organs (CT, MRI, pathology) without full retraining or large labeled datasets.

▸ Code PyTorch / PEFT — what actually runs▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model  # idiomatic: wraps every target Linear

class LoRALinear(nn.Module):                  # the essence PEFT builds under the hood
    def __init__(self, base: nn.Linear, r=class="n">4, alpha=class="n">8):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = base.requires_grad_(False)        # W is FROZEN — never updated
        d_out, d_in = base.weight.shape
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(r, d_in) * class="n">0.01)  # r×d, Gaussian init
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d_out, r))        # d×r, zeros → ΔW=0 at start
        self.s = alpha / r                                  # scaling α/r
    def forward(self, x):
        # y = W·x + (α/r)·(B·A)·x  — ΔW = B·A is rank ≤ r, only 2·d·r params train
        return self.base(x) + self.s * (x @ self.A.T) @ self.B.T

# idiomatic equivalent: freeze the backbone, inject adapters into attention projections
cfg = LoraConfig(r=class="n">4, lora_alpha=class="n">8, target_modules=[class="s">"q_proj", class="s">"v_proj"])
model = get_peft_model(backbone, cfg)         # trainable params drop from d² to ~2·d·r
model.print_trainable_parameters()            # e.g. >99% fewer trainable at d=4096
fedavg.py - Federated training
Plane = model-weight space. Teal dots = each hospital's local model; coral X = its private optimum; ringed dot = averaged global model. Only weights cross the dashed links - never scans.

Federated learning (FedAvg)

Four hospitals hold private scans they are not allowed to share. Each trains the same model on its own data, drifting toward its local optimum (coral X). Once per round, every site uploads only its weight vector; the server takes the plain average (FedAvg) and broadcasts that single global model back. Drag Round to watch the global dot converge - the raw data never moves.

This is exactly how you train one OncoSeg model across hospitals under HIPAA / GDPR: scans stay behind each institution's firewall, and only gradients/weights - which carry far less identifiable signal - leave the building. The faithful part: with quadratic local losses centered at each site's optimum, the global FedAvg solution is provably the mean of the per-site optima, and the distance to it shrinks by a fixed factor (1-lr)E every round. Fewer local epochs E = gentler steps = more rounds to converge; this is the real communication-vs-compute trade-off in cross-silo FL.
0
3
data stays localweights averagedglobal broadcast
💡 Why it mattersFederated learning trains a shared model across many sites by exchanging only weight updates, never the raw data — FedAvg averages each client's locally-trained weights (weighted by sample count) into a global model each round. This lets hospitals or phones jointly train on data they are legally or practically forbidden to pool (HIPAA/GDPR, patient privacy, bandwidth), turning siloed datasets into one larger effective training set.
▸ Where it’s usedWidely used in mobile keyboards (Google Gboard next-word prediction) and on-device personalization, and a major thrust in medical imaging where data cannot leave the hospital — e.g. the multi-institution NVIDIA Clara/MONAI FL tumor and COVID-lung studies and the EXAM model trained across 20 sites. It also underpins privacy-sensitive finance and IoT/edge deployments.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs each FedAvg round▶
import copy, torch

def fedavg_round(global_model, client_loaders, n_k, local_epochs=class="n">3, lr=class="n">0.1):
    g = global_model.state_dict()
    agg = {k: torch.zeros_like(v, dtype=torch.float64) for k, v in g.items()}
    N = float(sum(n_k))                                   # total samples across silos
    for loader, nk in zip(client_loaders, n_k):           # each hospital, data stays local
        local = copy.deepcopy(global_model)               # start from broadcast global w
        opt = torch.optim.SGD(local.parameters(), lr=lr)
        local.train()
        for _ in range(local_epochs):                     # E local epochs on private scans
            for x, y in loader:
                opt.zero_grad()
                loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(local(x), y)
                loss.backward(); opt.step()
        for k, v in local.state_dict().items():           # only weights/buffers leave silo
            agg[k] += (nk / N) * v.double()               # FedAvg: w_g = Σ_k (n_k/N)·w_k
    new = {}
    for k, v in g.items():                                # cast back; keep int buffers intact
        new[k] = agg[k].to(v.dtype) if v.is_floating_point() else v.clone()
    global_model.load_state_dict(new)                     # broadcast new global model
    return global_model
train.py — torch.cuda.amp
FP16 magnitude axis (log10). Hollow grey = raw gradient, teal = after ×S. Coral bands = underflow / overflow.

Mixed precision & loss scaling

Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) does the heavy matmuls in FP16 — half the memory, ~2× the throughput on tensor cores — while keeping an FP32 master copy of the weights for the actual update. The catch: FP16 can only represent magnitudes down to its smallest subnormal, 2-24 ≈ 6e-8. Any gradient smaller than that flushes to exactly 0 and that learning signal is lost forever.

Loss scaling rescues them. Multiply the loss by a large factor S (a power of two) before backward()backward()backward(); by the chain rule every gradient is scaled by the same S, shifting the whole cloud up into FP16's representable band. Right before the FP32 master-weight update you divide the gradients back by S — so the math is unchanged, you've only borrowed dynamic range. Drag the slider: watch the sub-floor gradients climb out of the underflow zone. Push S too far and the largest gradient hits the 65504 ceiling → Inf; a real dynamic loss scaler detects that, halves S and skips the step.

Per the OncoSeg training review, the notebook trained in pure FP32 and was the exact memory/throughput win it was missing. A 3D multi-scale tumor volume is enormous; AMP roughly halves activation memory, letting you fit a larger patch or batch (better BatchNorm/Dice statistics) and train faster on the same hospital GPU. Dice-style losses on tiny lesions produce very small gradients — precisely the regime where loss scaling prevents silent underflow that would otherwise stall learning on the smallest, most clinically important tumors.
2^0 = 1
FP16 floor 2⁻²⁴≈6e-8ceiling 65504FP32 master copy
💡 Why it mattersStoring activations and gradients in FP16/BF16 instead of FP32 roughly halves memory and doubles throughput on Tensor Cores, but FP16's narrow exponent range silently underflows small gradients to zero; loss scaling multiplies the loss by a large factor so those gradients survive, then unscales before the optimizer step. The result is near-FP32 accuracy at a fraction of the compute and memory cost, often the difference between a model fitting on a GPU or not.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the default in virtually all modern training: LLM pretraining/fine-tuning, diffusion models, and large 3D medical-imaging networks (volumetric U-Nets in nnU-Net/MONAI) where activation memory is the bottleneck. BF16 (no loss scaling needed) dominates on A100/H100, while FP16 + dynamic loss scaling remains common on consumer and older GPUs and for low-latency inference.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (torch.amp autocast + GradScaler)▶
import torch
from torch.amp import autocast, GradScaler

scaler = GradScaler(class="s">"cuda")            # holds the dynamic loss scale S (a power of two)

for vol, mask in loader:               # vol: (B,1,D,H,W) 3D tumor patch
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    with autocast(class="s">"cuda", dtype=torch.float16):   # only ops/activations inside run in FP16
        logits = model(vol)                       # params stay FP32; autocast casts ops, not weights
        loss = dice_ce_loss(logits, mask)         # tiny-lesion grads risk FP16 underflow (<2^-14 loses precision; 0 below 2^-24)
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()      # backprop on S*loss => every grad *= S (chain rule), lifts them off the underflow floor
    scaler.unscale_(opt)               # divide the (already-FP32) .grad tensors back by S, in place
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), class="n">1.0)   # clip on true (unscaled) grads
    scaler.step(opt)                   # if any grad is Inf/NaN, this step is SKIPPED
    scaler.update()                    # overflow -> halve S; clean streak -> double S (the dynamic scaler)
cell_graph_gnn.py — k-NN message passing
Coral = tumor nuclei, teal = immune nuclei. The ringed node is the cell being updated; lines = its k nearest-neighbor edges; its inner core recolors to the aggregated feature.

Cell-graph GNN

Instead of one image patch, model the tissue as a graph: each detected nucleus is a node carrying a feature (here a scalar “tumor-ness” score), and edges connect each node to its k nearest spatial neighbors. A single GNN message-passing step replaces a node’s feature with the mean of its k neighbors’ features — a mean-pool aggregation — the core idea behind GCN & GraphSAGE-mean (which additionally keep the node’s own feature and apply a learned weight + nonlinearity; dropped here for clarity). Slide k to grow the neighborhood and watch the highlighted tumor cell’s feature get pulled toward its surroundings.

The highlighted cell is a tumor nucleus (original feature 0.85) but it sits inside a ring of immune cells. With small k, all neighbors are immune, so message passing rewrites its feature down to ~0.16 — the model now “knows” this tumor cell is immune-infiltrated. This tumor-microenvironment context is invisible to a per-patch CNN cropped on that single nucleus; it only emerges from the spatial graph. Raise k past the immune ring (k≥7) and the nearby tumor cells re-enter, nudging the feature back up — a direct view of how neighborhood size sets the receptive field of a cell-graph model.
3
nodes = nucleiedges = k-NNupdate = mean(neighbors)
💡 Why it mattersTumors are fundamentally about tissue organization — which cells touch which, and how immune, stromal, and malignant cells are spatially arranged — yet CNNs on pixel patches discard this relational structure. A cell-graph GNN builds nodes from segmented nuclei (with morphology/marker features) and edges from spatial proximity, then message-passes over them, letting the model reason directly about the tumor microenvironment for interpretable, topology-aware prediction.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed in computational/digital pathology on H&E and multiplexed (CODEX/IMC/Visium) whole-slide images for cancer grading, survival and treatment-response prediction, biomarker discovery, and characterizing tumor-immune spatial niches; the same cell/tissue-graph paradigm also underlies spatial-omics analysis and graph-based tissue classification.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch_geometric.nn import knn_graph
from torch_geometric.utils import scatter

# pos: [N,2] nucleus coordinates,  x: [N,1] "tumor-ness" feature per nucleus
pos = torch.tensor(nuclei_xy, dtype=torch.float)
x   = torch.tensor(tumorness, dtype=torch.float).unsqueeze(class="n">1)

# edges = each node -> its k nearest spatial neighbors (the lines in the canvas)
edge_index = knn_graph(pos, k=k, loop=False)        # [2, E]; row=src(neighbor), col=dst(center)
src, dst = edge_index

# ONE message-passing step: new feature = MEAN of the k neighbors' features
# h_i = (1/|N(i)|) * sum_{j in N(i)} x_j   <-- exactly what the widget animates
h = scatter(x[src], dst, dim=class="n">0, dim_size=x.size(class="n">0), reduce=class=class="s">"s">class="s">'mean')

# This pure mean is GraphSAGE-mean's NEIGHBOR aggregation (random-walk norm D^-1 A).

macenko.py — match a scanner's colour to a fixed reference
Same tissue, three renders: SOURCE (lab-B cast) → NORMALIZED (Macenko) vs the fixed REFERENCE. Bars = mean colour distance ΔE to reference.

Macenko stain normalization — beating the scanner colour cast

Send one glass slide to two labs and the H&E images come back different colours: scanner optics, dye lots and protocols give every site its own cast. A model trained on lab-A pinks then sees lab-B purples as a brand-new distribution. Macenko et al. (2009) fixes this without touching the network: work in optical density OD=−log10(I/I0)OD = -log_{10}(I/I_{0})OD=−log10​(I/I0​), estimate each image's two-vector stain basis Ms=H,EM_{s} = {H,E}Ms​=H,E, deconvolve to per-stain concentrations C=Ms−1⋅ODC = M_{s}^{-1}\cdot ODC=Ms−1​⋅OD, rescale those concentrations so their robust (99th-percentile) maximum matches a fixed reference, then recompose in the reference basis M_ref. The output wears the reference's colours but keeps the source's tissue structure.

This is a domain-shift fix, the histology twin of MRI intensity normalization in demo 03. Drag the cast: the raw SOURCE marches away from the REFERENCE (red ΔE bar climbs), yet the NORMALIZED output stays pinned at ΔE≈0 (teal bar) for every cast — because by construction it is the reference's stain matrix at the reference's concentration scale. Run this as a deterministic pre-processing step and a hospital can deploy one model across every scanner it owns.

💡 Why it mattersH&E whole-slide images vary wildly in colour because of differing scanners, staining batches, reagents and labs, and CNNs trained on one site's colour cast often collapse on another's. Macenko normalization estimates each slide's stain vectors via SVD of the optical-density colour cloud and re-projects them onto a reference, removing scanner/batch colour shift so models generalise across institutions.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is a standard preprocessing or augmentation step in computational pathology pipelines — tumour/tissue segmentation, mitosis detection, grading, and biomarker/MSI prediction — and underpins multi-site challenges (e.g. CAMELYON metastasis detection, TCGA cohorts) and foundation-model training where slides come from many scanners.
