▸ Code PyTorch (torchstain) — what actually runs▶
import torch, torchstain

# ---- Idiomatic: the library every pathology pipeline actually calls ----
norm = torchstain.normalizers.MacenkoNormalizer(backend=class=class="s">"s">class="s">'torch')
norm.fit(reference_he)                         # reference_he: uint8 tensor [C,H,W]
out, H, E = norm.normalize(I=source_he, stains=True)  # I [C,H,W]; out is HxWx3 int

# ---- The 4 lines it runs under the hood (what the widget animates) ----
def macenko(I, M_ref, maxC_ref, Io=class="n">240.):        # I: [C,H,W]; M_ref 3x2; maxC_ref (2,)
    OD = -torch.log((I.permute(class="n">1, class="n">2, class="n">0).reshape(-class="n">1, class="n">3).float() + class="n">1) / Io)  # Beer-Lambert, natural log
    M_s = estimate_stain_basis(OD)               # SVD of OD -> 2 robust H/E vectors
    C   = torch.linalg.lstsq(M_s, OD.T).solution # deconvolve: solve M_s @ C = OD.T -> C is (2,N)
    maxC = torch.quantile(C, class="n">0.99, dim=class="n">1, keepdim=True)        # robust per-stain source max, (2,1)
    C    = C * (maxC_ref.reshape(class="n">2, class="n">1) / maxC)   # rescale concentrations to reference (broadcast (2,1))
    OD_n = M_ref @ C                             # recompose in canonical REF basis -> (3,N)
    c, h, w = I.shape
    out = (Io * torch.exp(-OD_n)).clamp(max=class="n">255) # invert Beer-Lambert with exp (not 10**)
    return out.T.reshape(h, w, c).to(torch.uint8)
autograd.py — forward pass → reverse-mode chain rule
Teal = forward values flow → ; coral = gradients flow ← . The ReLU gate (φ) blocks the gradient when its input z≤0.

Backprop: one rule, applied node by node

A tiny net: x→(⋅w)→ReLU→(⋅v)→Lx \to (\cdot w) \to ReLU \to (\cdot v) \to Lx→(⋅w)→ReLU→(⋅v)→L. Forward: z=w⋅xz=w\cdot xz=w⋅x, h=max(0,z)h=max(0,z)h=max(0,z), y=v⋅hy=v\cdot hy=v⋅h, loss L=12(y−t)2L=\tfrac12 (y-t)^{2}L=21​(y−t)2. To learn, we need ∂L/∂w\partial L/\partial w∂L/∂w — but w is buried three operations deep. The chain rule threads it: ∂L/∂w=∂L/∂y⋅∂y/∂h⋅∂h/∂z⋅∂z/∂w=(y−t)⋅v⋅1[z>0]⋅x\partial L/\partial w = \partial L/\partial y \cdot \partial y/\partial h \cdot \partial h/\partial z \cdot \partial z/\partial w = (y-t)\cdot v\cdot 1[z>0]\cdot x∂L/∂w=∂L/∂y⋅∂y/∂h⋅∂h/∂z⋅∂z/∂w=(y−t)⋅v⋅1[z>0]⋅x. Each edge carries its local derivative; backprop just multiplies them right→left, reusing the accumulated gradient at every step (that reuse is why it costs one backward pass, not one per weight).

Watch the ReLU gate: when z≤0z\le 0z≤0 its local derivative ∂h/∂z=1[z>0]=0\partial h/\partial z = 1[z>0] = 0∂h/∂z=1[z>0]=0, so the incoming gradient ∂L/∂h\partial L/\partial h∂L/∂h hits a wall — ∂L/∂z=0\partial L/\partial z = 0∂L/∂z=0 and both ∂L/∂w\partial L/\partial w∂L/∂w and ∂L/∂x\partial L/\partial x∂L/∂x vanish. Slide x below 0 to kill the gradient. This is the literal mechanism behind "dead ReLUs," and it is exactly how every conv weight in OncoSeg's 3D U-Net is updated: forward a CT/MR volume, compute Dice/CE loss, backprop the same multiply-and-accumulate chain through hundreds of layers, step w←w−η⋅∂L/∂ww \leftarrow w - \eta \cdot \partial L/\partial ww←w−η⋅∂L/∂w.
1.00
both ⇄
💡 Why it mattersBackpropagation is just the chain rule applied recursively through a computational graph, so a single local rule at each node yields exact gradients for millions of parameters in one backward pass — without it, gradient-based training of deep networks at scale would be intractable. It turns "how should every weight change to lower the loss?" into a cheap, automatable bookkeeping problem.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins essentially all deep-learning training — from training segmentation networks like nnU-Net and SAM 2 on medical scans, to fine-tuning LLMs and diffusion models — and is implemented as reverse-mode automatic differentiation (autograd) inside every major framework. In medical imaging specifically, it is what lets a U-Net learn voxel-level tumor masks end-to-end from labeled CT/MRI volumes.
Cutting-edge / SOTAPyTorch Autograd (Meta)JAX grad/autodiff (Google)TensorFlow GradientTape (Google)Tinygrad (autodiff engine)Micrograd (Karpathy, minimal scalar autograd engine)Autograd (HIPS, numpy reverse-mode autodiff)
▸ Code PyTorch autograd — what actually runs (and the hand chain rule it matches)▶
import torch

# the toy graph the widget draws:  z = w·x → h = ReLU(z) → y = v·h → L = ½(y−t)²
x = torch.tensor(class="n">1.3)
t = torch.tensor(class="n">0.5)
w = torch.tensor(class="n">0.8, requires_grad=True)   # leaf params we want grads for
v = torch.tensor(-class="n">1.1, requires_grad=True)

z = w * x                       # pre-activation
h = torch.relu(z)               # ReLU gate: zero for z ≤ 0
y = v * h                       # output
L = class="n">0.5 * (y - t) ** class="n">2          # scalar loss — backward() needs a scalar

L.backward()                    # reverse-mode autodiff fills w.grad, v.grad

# what autograd computed, by hand (chain rule, reverse order):
#   dL/dy = (y−t);  dy/dh = v;  dh/dz = 1[z>0];  dz/dw = x
dLdw = (y - t) * v * (z > class="n">0).float() * x        # = ∂L/∂w
dLdv = (y - t) * h                              # = ∂L/∂v
assert torch.allclose(w.grad, dLdw) and torch.allclose(v.grad, dLdv)

with torch.no_grad():           # gradient-descent step:  w ← w − η·∂L/∂w
    w -= class="n">0.1 * w.grad
    w.grad.zero_()              # grads accumulate — zero before next backward
optim.py — SGD vs Momentum vs Adam on an ill-conditioned bowl
All three start at w₀ and roll toward the min. Coral=SGD, blue=Momentum, teal=Adam. The bowl is steep along w₁, shallow along w₂.

How the update rule shapes the path

Every optimizer descends the loss L=12(a⋅w12+b⋅w22)L=\tfrac12 (a\cdot w_{1}^{2}+b\cdot w_{2}^{2})L=21​(a⋅w12​+b⋅w22​) with gradient ∇L=(a⋅w1,b⋅w2)\nabla L=(a\cdot w_{1}, b\cdot w_{2})∇L=(a⋅w1​,b⋅w2​), but they use it differently. SGD: w←w−η⋅∇Lw \leftarrow w - \eta \cdot \nabla Lw←w−η⋅∇L — pure gradient, so along the steep axis it overshoots and zig-zags. Momentum: v←β⋅v+∇Lv \leftarrow \beta \cdot v + \nabla Lv←β⋅v+∇L, w←w−η⋅vw \leftarrow w - \eta \cdot vw←w−η⋅v — a velocity that averages out the zig-zags and builds speed down the long valley (β=0.9). Adam: keeps running means of the gradient m^\hat{m}m^ and its square v^\hat{v}v^, then steps w←w−η⋅m^⊘(v^+ε)w \leftarrow w - \eta \cdot \hat{m} \oslash (\sqrt{}\hat{v} + \varepsilon )w←w−η⋅m^⊘(​v^+ε) — dividing by √v̂ per parameter so each axis gets its own effective rate.

Drag η. The bowl is ill-conditioned (κ=a/b≈12): the largest stable SGD rate is set by the steep axis, η < 2/a. Push past η=2/a=0.125\eta =2/a=0.125η=2/a=0.125 and plain SGD oscillates and diverges — while Momentum and Adam stay stable. This is exactly why a 3D segmentation net like OncoSeg, whose loss curvature varies wildly across layers, is trained with Adam: it auto-scales the step for each weight so one bad direction can't blow up training.
0.070
💡 Why it mattersThe optimizer turns raw gradients into the actual step taken, so its update rule decides whether training escapes ravines and saddle points, converges fast, or stalls/diverges; momentum smooths noisy gradients and per-parameter adaptive scaling (Adam/AdamW) lets one learning rate work across wildly different gradient magnitudes, which is what makes deep nets and transformers trainable at all.
▸ Where it’s usedEvery modern training pipeline picks an update rule: AdamW for nearly all transformers/LLMs and ViTs, SGD-with-momentum for many CNN vision backbones, and SGD/Adam variants inside medical-imaging frameworks like nnU-Net and MONAI; the choice and its schedule directly govern wall-clock cost and final accuracy on tasks from tumor segmentation to large-model pretraining.
Cutting-edge / SOTAAdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter)Adam (Kingma & Ba)Lion (Google Brain)Sophia (Stanford)Shampoo / distributed Shampoo (Google)Muon (used in modded-nanogpt)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs in the training loop▶
import torch

# What you actually write: pick an update rule, then step() inside the loop.
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=class="n">1e-2, momentum=class="n">0.9)   # SGD + classic (heavy-ball) momentum; pass nesterov=True for Nesterov
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=class="n">1e-3, betas=(class="n">0.9, class="n">0.999), eps=class="n">1e-8)
for x, y in loader:
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()                 # fills p.grad = ∇L for every parameter
    opt.step()                      # applies the rule below to each p in-place

# The three rules the widget animates (what .step() does, per parameter p with g = p.grad):
#   SGD:       p -= lr * g
#   Momentum:  v = beta*v + g           ;  p -= lr * v          # heavy-ball; PyTorch uses dampening=0 (no 1-beta)
#   Adam:      m = b1*m + (1-b1)*g       ;  s = b2*s + (1-b2)*g*g
#              mhat = m/(1-b1**t)        ;  shat = s/(1-b2**t)   # bias-correct early steps
#              p -= lr * mhat / (shat.sqrt() + eps)              # eps OUTSIDE sqrt (PyTorch default), 1/√ŝ per-axis rescaling
scheduler.py — warmup + cosine annealing
Coral ramp = linear warmup · teal curve = cosine decay · dot = current step.

Learning-rate schedule: warm up, then anneal

The step size η is not fixed. For the first tw=w⋅Tt_w = w\cdot Ttw​=w⋅T steps it ramps linearly from 0 to the peak η₀; after that it follows a cosine down to 0 over the remaining steps:

η(t)=η0⋅t/tw\eta (t) = \eta _{0}\cdot t / t_wη(t)=η0​⋅t/tw​  for  t≤twt \le t_wt≤tw​
η(t)=12η0⋅(1+cos(π⋅(t−tw)/(T−tw)))\eta (t) = \tfrac12 \eta _{0}\cdot (1 + cos(\pi \cdot (t-t_w)/(T-t_w)))η(t)=21​η0​⋅(1+cos(π⋅(t−tw​)/(T−tw​)))  for  t>twt > t_wt>tw​

Warmup keeps the first updates tiny while batch statistics and the optimizer's moment estimates (Adam's m^,v^\hat{m}, \hat{v}m^,v^) are still garbage — a full-size ∇L\nabla L∇L step on a fresh, badly-scaled net can explode the loss. Cosine decay starts fast to cover ground, then shrinks η smoothly so the final steps gently settle into a sharp, low-loss minimum instead of bouncing around it.

In medical-imaging segmentation a diverging first epoch wastes a long, expensive 3D training run. OncoSeg trained with a cosine schedule (with warmup) so the volumetric U-Net both started stably and annealed to a fine minimum — the same η(t) plotted here. Try warmup = 0 and watch the curve start at full η₀: that initial jolt is exactly what warmup is there to avoid.

36
η₀ = 1.0e−3cosine anneal → 0no restarts
💡 Why it mattersA fixed learning rate is a poor compromise: high enough to train fast, it destabilizes the early steps when weights are random and gradients are large; low enough to be stable, it wastes compute and gets stuck in sharp minima. Warming up the rate linearly then annealing it (cosine/inverse-sqrt) keeps early updates safe, lets the model take big strides mid-training, and shrinks the step size at the end so it settles cleanly into a flatter, better-generalizing optimum.
▸ Where it’s usedWarmup+anneal is the default in nearly all large-scale training: transformer LLM pretraining, vision foundation models, and diffusion models all use linear warmup with cosine or inverse-sqrt decay, and it is built into Hugging Face Transformers, PyTorch schedulers, and timm. In medical imaging, nnU-Net's polynomial-decay schedule and MONAI's WarmupCosineSchedule are standard for training segmentation networks on CT/MRI.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (per-step warmup + cosine)▶
import math, torch
import torch.nn.functional as F   # used by the training loop below
from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import LinearLR, CosineAnnealingLR, SequentialLR

eta0, T, tw = class="n">1e-3, class="n">200, class="n">20            # peak LR, total steps, warmup steps (~10% of T)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=eta0)

# linear warmup 0->eta0 over tw steps, then half-cosine eta0->0 over the rest
warmup = LinearLR(opt, start_factor=class="n">1e-8, end_factor=class="n">1.0, total_iters=tw)
cosine = CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=T - tw, eta_min=class="n">0.0)   # 1/2*eta0*(1+cos(pi*k/(T-tw)))
sched  = SequentialLR(opt, [warmup, cosine], milestones=[tw])

for t in range(T):
    opt.zero_grad(); loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x), y); loss.backward()
    opt.step(); sched.step()           # advance LR ONCE PER STEP (not per epoch)

# from scratch — the exact eta(t) this widget plots (matches sched above to <1e-11):
def lr(t):
    if t < tw:           return eta0 * t / tw                              # warmup: rises prop. to t
    return class="n">0.5 * eta0 * (class="n">1 + math.cos(math.pi * (t - tw) / (T - tw)))      # cosine: eta0 -> 0, hits 0 at t=T
train.py — train vs val loss · early stopping
Top: loss vs epoch (teal=train, coral=val, blue dash=early-stop). Bottom: the fit at this capacity.

Overfitting & early stopping

Train loss falls monotonically as the model keeps memorizing: Ltrain(t)=ε+(L0−ε)⋅e(−t/τ)L_train(t) = \varepsilon + (L_{0}-\varepsilon )\cdot e^{}(-t/\tau )Lt​rain(t)=ε+(L0​−ε)⋅e(−t/τ). But validation loss is the train term plus a variance term that grows as the model starts fitting noise: Lval(t)=Ltrain(t)+κ⋅(t/T)βL_val(t) = L_train(t) + \kappa \cdot (t/T)^{}\beta Lv​al(t)=Lt​rain(t)+κ⋅(t/T)β. That extra term makes val U-turn upward — the classic overfitting signature. The generalization gap is exactly that term: gap=Lval−Ltrain=κ⋅(t/T)βgap = L_val - L_train = \kappa \cdot (t/T)^{}\beta gap=Lv​al−Lt​rain=κ⋅(t/T)β, and it only widens.

The early-stopping rule: keep the checkpoint at the epoch where L_val is minimum (∂L_val/∂t = 0) and stop. Drag the epoch slider: before that point you are still learning signal; past it, train keeps dropping while val climbs — you are memorizing noise. The bottom panel shows the same story as a curve fit — low capacity underfits (high bias: misses the trend), high capacity overfits (high variance: chases every noisy point). Best test error sits in the middle, right where early stop lands.

This is the bias–variance tradeoff: E[err]=bias2+variance+σn2oiseE[err] = bias^{2} + variance + \sigma ^{2}_noiseE[err]=bias2+variance+σn2​oise. For OncoSeg, a 3D U-Net trained too long memorizes scanner texture and annotation jitter — train Dice keeps rising while held-out Dice falls. Early stopping on validation Dice (not the loss the README reports on train-time folds) is the cheapest regularizer; without a real held-out set, the "validated" numbers are just memorization. Watch the gap: a widening train↔val gap is the deployment red flag.
48
val U-turngap = κ·(t/T)^β∂L_val/∂t = 0bias² + variance
💡 Why it mattersA model with enough capacity will eventually memorize noise and quirks of the training set, so its training loss keeps dropping while held-out performance plateaus and then degrades — early stopping halts training at the point of best validation metric, capturing the well-generalizing model before it overfits. It is the cheapest, most universal regularizer: no extra parameters, just a checkpoint chosen by a watched validation curve (with patience to ignore noisy dips).
▸ Where it’s usedIt is standard in essentially every supervised-learning pipeline — Keras EarlyStopping/ModelCheckpoint and PyTorch Lightning's EarlyStopping callback ship it by default, and gradient-boosting libraries (XGBoost, LightGBM) use early stopping on a validation fold to pick the number of trees. In medical imaging it is the routine way frameworks like MONAI and nnU-Net avoid overfitting on small, expensive annotated tumor/organ datasets, selecting the checkpoint with the best validation Dice.
Cutting-edge / SOTAPyTorch Lightning EarlyStopping callbackKeras EarlyStopping + ModelCheckpointnnU-Net (DKFZ)MONAI (Project MONAI)XGBoost / LightGBM early_stopping_roundsWeights & Biases (validation-curve monitoring)
▸ Code PyTorch — the early-stopping training loop that actually runs▶
best_val, best_state, bad, patience = float(class="s">"inf"), None, class="n">0, class="n">10
for epoch in range(max_epochs):
    model.train()
    for xb, yb in train_loader:                  # mini-batch train loss trends down (noisy, not strictly monotone)
        opt.zero_grad()
        F.cross_entropy(model(xb), yb).backward()
        opt.step()
    # ---- validation: no grad, eval mode (dropout off, BN running-stats frozen) ----
    model.eval(); val_loss = class="n">0.0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for xb, yb in val_loader:
            val_loss += F.cross_entropy(model(xb), yb, reduction=class="s">"sum").item()
    val_loss /= len(val_loader.dataset)           # exact per-sample mean; gap = val - train widens as we overfit
    # ---- early stopping: checkpoint argmin(val_loss); stop after `patience` stalls ----
    if val_loss < best_val - class="n">1e-4:                # require min-delta improvement to reset patience
        best_val, bad = val_loss, class="n">0
        best_state = {k: v.detach().clone() for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}
    else:
        bad += class="n">1
        if bad >= patience:                       # val U-turned upward -> stop, restore best
            break
if best_state is not None:                        # guard: loop may not have run (max_epochs<=0)
    model.load_state_dict(best_state)             # roll back to the early-stop (min-val) epoch
transforms.py — co-transform image & label
Left: one labeled scan. Right: the same transform applied to BOTH pixels and mask — the teal tumour label rides the warp.

Data augmentation — one scan, infinitely many training views

Apply a label-preserving transform T to a training example and you get a brand-new, plausible scan for free. The catch in segmentation: a geometric T must hit the mask too — x~=T(x)\tilde{x} = T(x)x~=T(x) and y~=T(y)\tilde{y} = T(y)y~​=T(y) — or the label no longer lines up with the pixels. Intensity transforms touch only x (the anatomy hasn't moved, so y~=y\tilde{y} = yy~​=y). In practice we sample destination voxels and read back through the inverse map x~(p)=x(T−1p)\tilde{x}(p) = x(T^{-1}p)x~(p)=x(T−1p), with bilinear interpolation, so image and mask warp by the identical field.

For small medical datasets this is essential, not optional. A site may have only dozens of annotated tumours; flips, ±40° rotations, scale, MR-intensity shifts and elastic deforms multiply the effective sample count and teach the network that a tumour is a tumour regardless of pose, zoom, or scanner brightness — i.e. it builds invariance and fights overfitting. OncoSeg trains on co-transformed 3D patches for exactly this reason.
0.50
label-preservingco-transform ỹ=T(y)×∞ effective databuilds invariance
💡 Why it mattersMedical and segmentation datasets are tiny and expensive to label, so a model easily memorizes the handful of scans it sees; data augmentation manufactures plausible variants (flips, rotations, elastic deformation, intensity/contrast jitter, MixUp/CutMix) from each scan, teaching the network to be invariant to scanner, pose, and patient anatomy instead of overfitting. It is the cheapest, most reliable regularizer for closing the gap between a small training set and real-world test variation.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is standard in essentially every vision pipeline: ImageNet/timm classifiers use RandAugment + MixUp/CutMix, self-supervised methods (SimCLR, DINOv2) treat aggressive augmentation as the core learning signal, and medical segmentation (nnU-Net, MONAI, TorchIO) relies on spatial + intensity transforms to generalize across MRI/CT scanners and protocols. It also underpins detection, OCR, and contrastive pretraining wherever labeled data is scarce.

▸ Code PyTorch + MONAI — co-transform image &amp; label with one shared T▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from monai.transforms import RandAffined, RandGaussianNoised

# THE essence: ONE sampled transform T warps image AND label together.
# Image -> bilinear (smooth); label -> nearest (keeps integer class ids).
spatial = RandAffined(keys=[class="s">"img", class="s">"seg"], prob=class="n">1.0,
    rotate_range=(class="n">0.7, class="n">0.7, class="n">0.7), scale_range=(class="n">0.2, class="n">0.2, class="n">0.2),
    translate_range=(class="n">8, class="n">8, class="n">8), mode=(class="s">"bilinear", class="s">"nearest"))   # x̃=T(x), ỹ=T(y): SAME T
intensity = RandGaussianNoised(keys=[class="s">"img"])                   # label-preserving: image only

sample = {class="s">"img": vol, class="s">"seg": mask}                             # vol/mask: (C, D, H, W)
out = intensity(spatial(sample))                               # warp first, then noise the image
x_tilde, y_tilde = out[class="s">"img"], out[class="s">"seg"]

# Under the hood (illustrative, INDEPENDENT sample): MONAI builds an affine grid via
# RandAffineGrid + Resample, then grid_sample()s BOTH keys with one shared grid.
size = vol[None].shape                                         # (1, C, D, H, W)
theta = torch.eye(class="n">3, class="n">4)[None]                                  # (1, 3, 4); rows act on (x,y,z)=(W,H,D)
theta[:, :class="n">3, :class="n">3] = torch.eye(class="n">3) + class="n">0.2 * torch.rand(class="n">1, class="n">3, class="n">3)    # toy near-identity affine T
grid = F.affine_grid(theta, size, align_corners=False)         # destination->source map, (1,D,H,W,3)
xg = F.grid_sample(vol[None],  grid, mode=class="s">"bilinear", align_corners=False)  # image: interpolate
yg = F.grid_sample(mask[None], grid, mode=class="s">"nearest",  align_corners=False)  # label: NO new classes
# Same grid for both => geometry stays consistent: yg exactly labels xg.
resnet.py — y = F(x) + x
Top: the layer stack, gradient flowing UP from the loss to layer 1. Bottom: |∇| at each depth — coral = plain, teal = with skips (log scale).

Residual connections — the identity highway for gradients

A plain deep net chains layers as x=F(x)x = F(x)x=F(x), so backprop multiplies one Jacobian per layer: the gradient reaching layer 1 is ∥∇1∥=Πi∥∂Fi/∂x∥\|\nabla _{1}\| = \Pi _{i} \|\partial F_{i}/\partial x\|∥∇1​∥=Πi​∥∂Fi​/∂x∥. If each factor is a typical ‖∂F/∂x‖ ≈ g < 1, that product is g·g·…·g = gD — it vanishes exponentially with depth, so the early layers stop learning. A residual block instead computes y=F(x)+xy = F(x) + xy=F(x)+x. Its Jacobian becomes ∂y/∂x=I+∂F/∂x\partial y/\partial x = I + \partial F/\partial x∂y/∂x=I+∂F/∂x, and unrolling the whole stack (He et al. 2016) gives ∂L/∂x1=∂L/∂xL⋅(1+∂/∂x1ΣiFi)\partial L/\partial x_{1} = \partial L/\partial x_L\cdot (1 + \partial /\partial x_{1} \Sigma _{i} F_{i})∂L/∂x1​=∂L/∂xL​⋅(1+∂/∂x1​Σi​Fi​). That standalone “1” is the identity skip path: it carries the deep gradient straight through to layer 1 with no attenuation, putting a hard floor of magnitude 1 on ∥∇1∥\|\nabla _{1}\|∥∇1​∥. The full stack gradient is the product of per-block Jacobians ∏i(1+∂Fi/∂x)∏_{i}(1 + \partial F_{i}/\partial x)∏i​(1+∂Fi​/∂x); with normalization keeping ∥∂F/∂x∥≈g≪1\|\partial F/\partial x\| \approx g \ll 1∥∂F/∂x∥≈g≪1, each factor is ≈1, so the product stays ≈ const at every depth instead of vanishing.

This is why nets went from ~20 layers to 1000+. OncoSeg's 3D encoder is a stack of residual blocks, and every U-Net skip is the same idea at the feature-map level: the decoder adds back the encoder's high-resolution detail (concat/+concat/+concat/+) instead of re-deriving it through a long contracting path — so fine tumor-boundary gradients survive the bottleneck. Drag depth to ~50: the coral (plain) gradient at layer 1 falls past 10⁻¹³ — the early conv filters are effectively frozen and the rim never sharpens — while the teal (residual) gradient stays O(1) — never vanishing — no matter how deep the network gets.
24
y = F(x) + x∂y/∂x = I + ∂F/∂xplain: ‖∇₁‖ = gD → 0skip: ‖∇₁‖ ≈ 1 (identity)ResNet · U-Net skips
💡 Why it mattersResidual (skip) connections add a layer's input to its output, so each block only has to learn a residual Δ rather than a full transformation; the identity path lets gradients flow unattenuated through very deep stacks, directly defeating the vanishing-gradient problem that previously made networks beyond ~20 layers untrainable. This is what unlocked 100+ layer CNNs and is a structural prerequisite for the deep Transformer stacks used in every modern LLM and vision model.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is ubiquitous: every Transformer block (LLMs, ViT) wraps attention and MLP sub-layers in residual connections, and ResNet-style skips underpin detection/segmentation backbones. In medical imaging it is central to U-Net's encoder-decoder skip pathways and residual blocks in nnU-Net, the default architecture for 3D tumor and organ segmentation.

▸ Code PyTorch — the residual block that actually runs (3D, OncoSeg-style)▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class ResidualBlock3D(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c_in, c_out, stride=class="n">1):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv3d(c_in, c_out, class="n">3, stride, class="n">1, bias=False)
        self.norm1 = nn.InstanceNorm3d(c_out, affine=True)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv3d(c_out, c_out, class="n">3, class="n">1, class="n">1, bias=False)
        self.norm2 = nn.InstanceNorm3d(c_out, affine=True)
        # skip must match F(x)'s shape; identity when channels & stride agree
        self.skip = (nn.Conv3d(c_in, c_out, class="n">1, stride, bias=False)
                     if stride != class="n">1 or c_in != c_out else nn.Identity())

    def forward(self, x):
        identity = self.skip(x)
        h = F.leaky_relu(self.norm1(self.conv1(x)), class="n">0.01)
        h = self.norm2(self.conv2(h))            # h = F(x)
        return F.leaky_relu(h + identity, class="n">0.01)  # y = F(x) + x  <-- the highway

# x:(N,32,D,H,W) -> y:(N,64,D/2,H/2,W/2); d(loss)/dx carries a +1 term,
# so gradients reach early layers even if F(x) saturates -> no vanishing.

Left = noisy input slice, right = blurred. Coral box = kernel footprint over the small lesion. Bottom: the 1D kernel (teal curve = G(x), coral bars = discrete taps) and the separable cost.

Gaussian blur: the smoothing prior & scale space

Convolve the image with a Gaussian kernel G(x)=exp(−x2/2σ2)G(x)=exp(-x^{2}/2\sigma ^{2})G(x)=exp(−x2/2σ2), normalized so Σiwi=1\Sigma _{i} w_{i} = 1Σi​wi​=1 (a partition of unity → a flat region stays flat, no brightening). One slider — σ\sigma σ — sets the scale. We truncate at radius r=⌈3σ⌉r=\lceil 3\sigma \rceil r=⌈3σ⌉ (≈99.7% of the mass), so the kernel has 2r+12r+12r+1 taps. Each output pixel is a weighted average of its neighbourhood: x^[n]=Σiwi⋅x[n−i]\hat{x}[n] = \Sigma _{i} w_{i}\cdot x[n-i]x^[n]=Σi​wi​⋅x[n−i].

The 2D Gaussian is separable: G(x,y)=G(x)⋅G(y)G(x,y)=G(x)\cdot G(y)G(x,y)=G(x)⋅G(y), so a 2D blur = one horizontal 1D pass then one vertical 1D pass. That is O(2k)O(2k)O(2k) multiplies per pixel instead of O(k2)O(k^{2})O(k2) for the full square kernel — the speed-up grows linearly with kernel size. The mini-grid (coral) shows the outer product 1D⊗1DT1D \otimes 1D^{T}1D⊗1DT that the two passes reproduce exactly.

Larger σ\sigma σ = coarser scale: fine speckle noise vanishes first, then small structures, then edges soften — a continuous scale-space. This is the denoising/anti-alias prior under Difference-of-Gaussians, SIFT, edge detection, and the smoothing implicit in pooling. In OncoSeg-style pipelines a light Gaussian suppresses scanner noise before segmentation; but watch the small second lesion — push σ\sigma σ up and its contrast dissolves into the background, the same way over-smoothing erases the very small-TC tumors the model already struggles with. FWHM = 22ln2⋅σ≈2.355σ2\sqrt{2ln2}\cdot \sigma \approx 2.355\sigma 22ln2​⋅σ≈2.355σ reports how wide the blur really is in pixels.
1.2
💡 Why it mattersConvolving an image with a Gaussian kernel suppresses high-frequency noise while preserving low-frequency structure, and crucially it is the unique linear smoothing that builds a scale space without creating spurious extrema as you increase σ. This makes it the canonical "smoothing prior" for denoising, anti-aliasing before downsampling, and computing derivatives stably on noisy data.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins Gaussian/Laplacian pyramids, SIFT/DoG keypoint detection, the Canny edge detector's pre-smoothing step, and anti-aliased mip-mapping in graphics; in medical imaging it is a standard preprocessing and intensity-normalization step (e.g. smoothing fMRI/PET volumes, suppressing CT/MRI noise before segmentation). It remains the differentiable downsampling/blur primitive inside modern pipelines like 3D Gaussian Splatting, diffusion-model image degradation, and CNN/U-Net data augmentation.

▸ Code PyTorch — separable Gaussian blur (what actually runs)▶
import math, torch, torch.nn.functional as F

def gaussian_blur(img, sigma):                       # img: [B,C,H,W], float
    r = math.ceil(class="n">3 * sigma)                         # truncate at 3sigma -> 99.7% of mass
    x = torch.arange(-r, r + class="n">1, dtype=img.dtype, device=img.device)
    k = torch.exp(-x**class="n">2 / (class="n">2 * sigma**class="n">2))            # G(x) = exp(-x^2 / 2sigma^2)
    k = k / k.sum()                                  # normalize: sum w_i = 1 (flat stays flat)
    C = img.shape[class="n">1]                                 # depthwise: blur each channel independently
    # 2D Gaussian is separable: G(x,y)=G(x)*G(y) => two 1-D passes, O(2k) not O(k^2).
    # Reflect-pad (NOT zero-pad) so borders don't darken; then conv with padding=0.
    kh = k.view(class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1, -class="n">1).expand(C, class="n">1, class="n">1, -class="n">1)
    kv = k.view(class="n">1, class="n">1, -class="n">1, class="n">1).expand(C, class="n">1, -class="n">1, class="n">1)
    img = F.pad(img, (r, r, class="n">0, class="n">0), mode=class="s">"reflect")
    img = F.conv2d(img, kh, groups=C)                # horizontal pass
    img = F.pad(img, (class="n">0, class="n">0, r, r), mode=class="s">"reflect")
    img = F.conv2d(img, kv, groups=C)                # vertical pass
    return img

blurred = gaussian_blur(ct_slice.float(), sigma=class="n">1.2) # one scale of the scale-space

# In practice you'd just call the library (separable kernel, reflect pad under the hood):
#   from torchvision.transforms.functional import gaussian_blur as tv_blur
#   blurred = tv_blur(ct_slice, kernel_size=2*math.ceil(3*1.2)+1, sigma=1.2)
postprocess.py — morphological clean-up of a mask
Faint teal + dashed = mask before. Solid teal = result. Coral = pixels added, hatched = pixels removed. Box (top-right) = structuring element B.

Morphological ops — cleaning a segmentation mask

Slide a small structuring element B (a disk of radius r) over a binary mask A. The two atoms are: erosion A⊖B keeps a pixel only if B fits entirely inside A (every offset is foreground) — it shrinks objects and deletes specks; dilation A⊕B keeps a pixel if B touches A anywhere (any offset is foreground) — it grows objects and fills holes. In set terms: A⊖B=z:Bz⊆AA\ominus B = {z : B_z \subseteq A}A⊖B=z:Bz​⊆A, A⊕B=z:Bz∩A≠∅A\oplus B = {z : B_z \cap A \neq \varnothing }A⊕B=z:Bz​∩A=∅.

Composing them gives the workhorses: opening A∘B=(A⊖B)⊕BA\circ B = (A\ominus B)\oplus BA∘B=(A⊖B)⊕B — erode then dilate — removes objects smaller than B but keeps the survivors at their original size; closing A⋅B=(A⊕B)⊖BA\cdot B = (A\oplus B)\ominus BA⋅B=(A⊕B)⊖B — dilate then erode — fills gaps and holes smaller than B without bloating the rest. Opening ≤ A ≤ closing always holds, and both are idempotent: (A∘B)∘B=A∘B(A\circ B)\circ B = A\circ B(A∘B)∘B=A∘B.

This is the post-network clean-up step. A raw OncoSeg mask has flickering boundary voxels, isolated false-positive specks, and pin-holes inside solid tumor. Opening with a small disk erases the specks and thin bridges (so connected-components doesn't over-count lesions — recall the BRATS_077 case with 31 fragments); closing seals holes so a lesion is one solid object before its longest diameter is measured for RECIST. Pick the radius too large and opening will dissolve a genuine small tumor — exactly the small-TC failure mode the review flags.
1.5
disk SEopening ≤ A ≤ closingidempotent3D in practice
💡 Why it mattersRaw segmentation masks (from thresholding or a network's argmax) are riddled with single-pixel speckle, jagged borders, and tiny holes; morphological operations like opening (erosion then dilation) and closing (dilation then erosion) clean these by removing isolated noise and filling pinholes without needing retraining, giving smoother, connected regions for downstream measurement.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the standard post-processing step after thresholding or CNN segmentation in medical imaging (cleaning tumor/organ masks, keeping only the largest connected component in nnU-Net-style pipelines), microscopy cell counting, OCR/document binarization, and industrial defect inspection. Modern toolkits expose it directly: OpenCV (cv2.morphologyEx), scikit-image, SimpleITK/ITK, and MONAI's mask post-transforms.

▸ Code PyTorch + SciPy — what actually runs in mask post-processing▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from scipy import ndimage

# --- post-process a binary mask: open drops FP specks, close seals pin-holes ---
B = ndimage.generate_binary_structure(class="n">2, class="n">2)          # FULL 3x3 SQUARE (conn=2); conn=1 is a 4-conn CROSS
clean = ndimage.binary_opening(mask, B)              # A∘B = erode then dilate  -> kills small objects
clean = ndimage.binary_closing(clean, B)             # A•B = dilate then erode  -> fills holes/gaps

# --- SAME atoms on GPU / differentiable: morphology == max/min pooling over the SE window ---
# NOTE: max_pool2d pads implicitly with -inf, so erosion via -max_pool2d(-x) would treat the
# image BORDER as foreground (edge objects never erode). Pad with 0 (background) to match scipy.
def dilate(x, k=class="n">3):                                  # A⊕B: max over the k×k neighborhood
    return F.max_pool2d(x, k, stride=class="n">1, padding=k // class="n">2)          # assumes ODD k, float {0,1} input
def erode(x, k=class="n">3):                                   # A⊖B: min == -max(-x), bg-padded so edges erode
    xp = F.pad(x, (k // class="n">2,) * class="n">4, value=class="n">0.0)
    return -F.max_pool2d(-xp, k, stride=class="n">1, padding=class="n">0)

m = torch.tensor(mask, dtype=torch.float32)[None, None]          # (N=1, C=1, H, W), float for pooling
opened = dilate(erode(m))                            # erode→dilate (opening)
closed = erode(dilate(m))                            # dilate→erode (closing)
# erosion shrinks/deletes specks; dilation grows/fills holes; opening ≤ A ≤ closing, each idempotent
canny.py — gradient → NMS → hysteresis
Four stages on one fixed image. Stage 1 = Sobel magnitude (teal heat). Stage 2 = NMS thins ridges to 1px. Stage 3 = double threshold: teal = strong (≥ Tₕ), coral = weak (Tₗ…Tₕ). Stage 4 = hysteresis keeps weak only if it touches a strong chain.

Canny edge detection

Before learned segmentation, boundaries were found with a hand-built pipeline (Canny, 1986). First take the image gradient with the Sobel kernels and form the magnitude and orientation:  Gx=Kx⋆IG_{x} = K_{x} \star IGx​=Kx​⋆I, Gy=Ky⋆IG_y = K_y \star IGy​=Ky​⋆I, ∥∇I∥=Gx2+Gy2\|\nabla I\| = \sqrt{G_{x}^{2} + G_y^{2}}∥∇I∥=Gx2​+Gy2​​, θ=atan2(Gy,Gx)\theta = atan2(G_y, G_{x})θ=atan2(Gy​,Gx​). A raw magnitude map gives fat, fuzzy ridges. Non-max suppression walks each pixel along its gradient direction θ (quantized to 0°/45°/90°/135°) and zeroes it unless it is the local maximum — collapsing every ridge to a clean 1-pixel line. Then a double threshold splits survivors into strong (‖∇I‖ ≥ Tₕ) and weak (Tₗ ≤ ‖∇I‖ < Tₕ), with the classic ratio Tl=0.4⋅ThT_{l} = 0.4\cdot T_{h}Tl​=0.4⋅Th​. Finally hysteresis: keep a weak pixel only if it is 8-connected to a strong one (a flood-fill from the strong seeds). The slider is the high threshold Tₕ.

Slide it and watch the failure modes. Too low (Tₕ ≈ 0.05–0.10): texture and sensor noise survive — the final map explodes to 100–210 edge pixels in dozens of disconnected fragments (spurious "lesion" boundaries everywhere). Too high (Tₕ ≳ 0.30): the faint low-contrast disc never gets a strong seed, so hysteresis cannot rescue it and that whole object vanishes — a real but subtle boundary is missed. Only the mid band gives a clean, complete contour. This brittleness — one global threshold that is simultaneously too low somewhere and too high elsewhere — is exactly why faint, low-contrast tumor margins on CT/MRI defeat classical edge detectors, and why OncoSeg learns a data-driven, multi-scale boundary instead of thresholding a single gradient map.
0.22
‖∇I‖ = √(Gₓ²+G_y²)NMS → 1px ridgeTₗ = 0.4·Tₕhysteresis links weak→strong
💡 Why it mattersCanny is the canonical optimal edge detector: a multi-stage pipeline (Gaussian smoothing, gradient magnitude/orientation, non-maximum suppression, then double-threshold hysteresis) that yields thin, well-localized, connected edges while suppressing noise and spurious responses. It solves the core problem of turning raw intensity gradients into a clean, single-pixel-wide boundary map robust enough to feed downstream geometry, contour, and segmentation steps.
▸ Where it’s usedStill a default preprocessing step in industrial machine vision, document/license-plate and lane-line detection, and as a front end for Hough line/circle fitting and active-contour segmentation; in medical imaging it is used for organ/lesion boundary delineation, vessel and bone-contour extraction, and as edge priors or guidance maps for deep segmentation and registration pipelines.

▸ Code PyTorch + OpenCV — what actually runs▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F, cv2, numpy as np

# Library path. NOTE: cv2.Canny runs its OWN Sobel on the uint8 image and (by default,
# L2gradient=False) thresholds the L1 magnitude |Gx|+|Gy| — so it won't be bit-identical
# to the L2/hypot torch path below; both are valid Canny variants.
u8    = np.uint8(np.round(np.clip(img, class="n">0, class="n">1) * class="n">255))        # round (not truncate) to uint8
edges_cv = cv2.Canny(u8, class="n">0.4 * Th * class="n">255, Th * class="n">255, L2gradient=True)  # Tl=0.4*Th, L2 to match below

# The essence underneath — Sobel gradients, NMS, double threshold, hysteresis:
kx = torch.tensor([[-class="n">1,class="n">0,class="n">1],[-class="n">2,class="n">0,class="n">2],[-class="n">1,class="n">0,class="n">1]], dtype=torch.float32).view(class="n">1,class="n">1,class="n">3,class="n">3)
Gx = F.conv2d(I[None,None], kx,        padding=class="n">1)           # ∂I/∂x  (conv2d = cross-corr, conventional sign)
Gy = F.conv2d(I[None,None], kx.transpose(class="n">2,class="n">3), padding=class="n">1)   # ∂I/∂y
mag   = torch.hypot(Gx, Gy)[class="n">0,class="n">0]            # ‖∇I‖ = √(Gx²+Gy²)  (L2)
theta = torch.atan2(Gy, Gx)[class="n">0,class="n">0]            # gradient direction θ = atan2(Gy,Gx)

q   = (torch.round(theta / (torch.pi/class="n">4)) % class="n">4).long()        # snap θ → 0/45/90/135° bins
nms = nonmax_suppress(mag, q)               # ridge magnitude kept along θ, else 0 → 1-px lines

strong = nms >= Th                          # double threshold: strong seeds
weak   = (nms >= class="n">0.4*Th) & ~strong          # weak candidates (Tl ≤ ‖∇I‖ < Th)
edges  = hysteresis(strong, weak)           # keep weak only if 8-connected to a strong chain
flow.py — brightness constancy & the aperture problem
Left: frame t (baseline). Right: frame t+1 (moved) with ghost of t. Arrows = recovered normal flow; teal = high-gradient (trustworthy), faint = aperture-limited.

Optical flow: reading motion from two frames

If a small patch just moves and keeps its brightness, then I(x,y,t)=I(x+u,y+v,t+1)I(x,y,t) = I(x+u, y+v, t+1)I(x,y,t)=I(x+u,y+v,t+1). A first-order Taylor expansion turns this brightness-constancy assumption into one linear equation per pixel: Ix⋅u+Iy⋅v+It=0I_{x}\cdot u + I_y\cdot v + I_t = 0Ix​⋅u+Iy​⋅v+It​=0, where Ix,IyI_{x},I_yIx​,Iy​ are spatial gradients and I_t the frame-to-frame difference. We estimate the flow (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) that satisfies it. With a single equation and two unknowns the minimum-norm solution is the normal flow: (u,v)=−It⋅(Ix,Iy)/(Ix2+Iy2)(u,v) = -I_t\cdot (I_{x},I_y) / (I_{x}^{2}+I_y^{2})(u,v)=−It​⋅(Ix​,Iy​)/(Ix2​+Iy2​) — motion only along the gradient ∇I.

Aperture problem. One constraint can't pin down two unknowns, so locally we recover only the component of motion perpendicular to edges; sliding along an edge is invisible. Notice the arrows always snap toward the gradient direction and underestimate the true shift. In OncoSeg's temporal module this is why registering a tumor between baseline (t0) and follow-up (t1) scans is ill-posed in smooth interiors — usable motion lives at boundaries, and dense flow needs a smoothness prior (Horn–Schunck) or a window (Lucas–Kanade) to disambiguate.
1.8 px
35°
💡 Why it mattersOptical flow estimates a per-pixel motion vector field between two consecutive frames, recovering where every pixel moved and thereby turning raw video into dense motion you can reason about. It solves the core correspondence problem behind motion: tracking, stabilization, depth/structure-from-motion, and temporal consistency all hinge on knowing which pixel went where.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed for video stabilization and frame interpolation/slow-motion (e.g. phone cameras, DAIN/RIFE), action recognition (two-stream networks), autonomous-driving and robotics motion estimation, and video compression. In medical imaging it drives respiratory/cardiac motion compensation, deformable image registration, and 4D-CT/MRI organ-motion tracking for radiotherapy and echocardiography.

▸ Code PyTorch — brightness-constancy normal flow (the line a practitioner writes)▶
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def normal_flow(I0, I1):                 # I0,I1: (B,1,H,W) consecutive frames
    # spatial gradients of frame t via central difference (Sobel in practice)
    kx = torch.tensor([[[[-class="n">1., class="n">0., class="n">1.]]]]) / class="n">2          # d/dx
    ky = kx.transpose(-class="n">1, -class="n">2)                            # d/dy
    Ix = F.conv2d(I0, kx, padding=(class="n">0, class="n">1))
    Iy = F.conv2d(I0, ky, padding=(class="n">1, class="n">0))
    It = I1 - I0                                          # temporal diff  I_t
    # brightness constancy: Ix*u + Iy*v + It = 0 is 1 eqn / 2 unknowns,
    # so the minimum-norm solution is the NORMAL flow (motion along grad I):
    g2 = Ix * Ix + Iy * Iy                               # |grad I|^2
    u = -It * Ix / (g2 + class="n">1e-6)                           # (u,v) = -I_t (Ix,Iy)/|grad I|^2
    v = -It * Iy / (g2 + class="n">1e-6)
    return torch.cat([u, v], dim=class="n">1)                      # (B,2,H,W); edge-parallel motion is unobservable

# Real pipelines resolve the aperture problem with a window (Lucas-Kanade,
# cv2.calcOpticalFlowPyrLK) or a learned dense field, e.g. RAFT:
#   flow = torchvision.models.optical_flow.raft_large(weights=...)(I0, I1)[-1]
pyramid.py — REDUCE ↓ / EXPAND ↑ with the [1 4 6 4 1] binomial kernel
Left: the full pyramid stack (each level halves resolution). Right: the chosen level, enlarged.

Image pyramid — one picture at many scales

A pyramid analyzes an image at every resolution at once. The Gaussian pyramid blurs then halves: Gi+1=REDUCE(Gi)=↓2(g⊙Gi)G_{i+1} = REDUCE(G_{i}) = \downarrow _{2}(g \odot G_{i})Gi+1​=REDUCE(Gi​)=↓2​(g⊙Gi​), using the separable binomial kernel g=[14641]/16g = [1 4 6 4 1] / 16g=[14641]/16 (a discrete Gaussian). The Laplacian pyramid keeps only the detail lost at each step: Li=Gi−EXPAND(Gi+1)L_{i} = G_{i} - EXPAND(G_{i+1})Li​=Gi​−EXPAND(Gi+1​) — a band-pass image — with the coarsest level carried whole, Ln=GnL_{n} = G_{n}Ln​=Gn​. EXPAND zero-stuffs ×2 then re-blurs ×4 to restore energy.

The Laplacian is perfectly invertible: rebuild from the top down with Gi=Li+EXPAND(Gi+1)G_{i} = L_{i} + EXPAND(G_{i+1})Gi​=Li​+EXPAND(Gi+1​) and you recover G₀ to machine ε (this toy: max error ≈ 2.8·10⁻¹⁷). Switch to Reconstruction and walk the slider to watch coarse-to-fine detail add back in and the error map fade to zero. This 1983 Burt–Adelson construction is the direct ancestor of FPN's feature pyramid and U-Net's encoder/decoder resolution hierarchy — exactly how OncoSeg sees a whole organ and a 3-voxel lesion in the same pass.

0
REDUCE = blur ↓2EXPAND = ↑2 blur ×4Lₙ = GₙΣ Lᵢ ⇒ G₀
💡 Why it mattersObjects appear at unpredictable sizes, but a fixed-size filter, sliding window, or CNN receptive field only "sees" one scale. An image pyramid solves this by representing one picture as a stack of progressively downsampled (and blurred) versions, so a single detector can find both tiny and huge structures, and coarse levels give a cheap global context that fine levels refine.
▸ Where it’s usedPyramids underpin scale-invariant features (SIFT/SURF), coarse-to-fine optical flow and stereo, Laplacian-pyramid image blending, and multi-scale heads in detection/segmentation networks (FPN, U-Net skip connections). In medical imaging they drive multi-resolution registration and the tiled magnification levels of whole-slide pathology pyramids (e.g. OpenSlide/DeepZoom) and multi-scale tumor segmentation.

▸ Code PyTorch — REDUCE/EXPAND with the separable [1 4 6 4 1]/16 binomial kernel▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

k = torch.tensor([class="n">1., class="n">4., class="n">6., class="n">4., class="n">1.]) / class="n">16.          # binomial g, ≈ discrete Gaussian
G = (k[:, None] * k[None, :])[None, None]              # separable 5×5 kernel, sums to 1

def blur(x):                                          # depthwise conv, one kernel per channel
    w = G.to(x).repeat(x.shape[class="n">1], class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1)
    return F.conv2d(F.pad(x, (class="n">2, class="n">2, class="n">2, class="n">2), mode=class="s">"reflect"), w, groups=x.shape[class="n">1])

def reduce(x):  return blur(x)[:, :, ::class="n">2, ::class="n">2]                       # REDUCE: blur then ↓2

def expand(x):                                        # EXPAND: zero-insert ↑2, blur, gain 4
    n, c, h, w = x.shape
    up = x.new_zeros(n, c, h * class="n">2, w * class="n">2); up[:, :, ::class="n">2, ::class="n">2] = x     # true zero-stuffing
    return class="n">4. * blur(up)                              # ×4 restores DC (kernel covers ¼ of pixels)

g, lap = x, []                                        # Lᵢ = Gᵢ − EXPAND(Gᵢ₊₁), Lₙ = Gₙ
for _ in range(levels):
    nxt = reduce(g)
    up  = F.interpolate(expand(nxt), size=g.shape[-class="n">2:])             # match odd sizes
    lap.append(g - up)                                             # band-pass detail layer
    g = nxt
lap.append(g)                                                      # coarsest residual carried whole
# perfect reconstruction (recursive, top-down):  Ĝᵢ = EXPAND(Ĝᵢ₊₁) + Lᵢ,  Ĝₙ = Lₙ
rec = lap[-class="n">1]
for L in reversed(lap[:-class="n">1]): rec = F.interpolate(expand(rec), size=L.shape[-class="n">2:]) + L
metrics.py — IoU (Jaccard) overlap & the 0.5 match gate
Teal = ground truth. Coral = prediction. Solid teal fill = ∩. Dashed frame = ∪. Drag the prediction.

IoU: the overlap ratio every detector is graded on

Intersection-over-Union (the Jaccard index) is IoU=∣A∩B∣/∣A∪B∣IoU = |A\cap B| / |A\cup B|IoU=∣A∩B∣/∣A∪B∣ — the shared area divided by the area either box covers. For axis-aligned boxes the intersection is ∩=max(0,Δx)⋅max(0,Δy)\cap = max(0,\Delta x)\cdot max(0,\Delta y)∩=max(0,Δx)⋅max(0,Δy) with overlap spans Δx\Delta xΔx, Δy\Delta yΔy, and the union is ∪=∣A∣+∣B∣−∩\cup = |A| + |B| - \cap ∪=∣A∣+∣B∣−∩ (subtract once so the shared region isn't double-counted). IoU = 1 only for a perfect box; it falls to 0 the instant the boxes separate.

IoU is the single number that decides whether a predicted lesion counts: a detection is a true positive only if IoU≥τIoU \ge \tau IoU≥τ (typically τ=0.5; COCO mAP sweeps 0.5→0.95). In OncoSeg this is how an automatically segmented tumor is matched to its ground-truth region before RECIST measurement — too loose and you over-count, too small or shifted and a real lesion is missed. Note IoU is stricter than Dice: for the same overlap, IoU=Dice/(2−Dice)≤DiceIoU = Dice/(2-Dice) \le DiceIoU=Dice/(2−Dice)≤Dice.

τ = 0.5 match gateIoU = ∩ / ∪Jaccard ≤ Dice
💡 Why it mattersIoU (intersection over area-of-union) gives a single scale-invariant score for how well a predicted box or mask overlaps the ground truth, turning "is this detection good?" into a hard threshold (e.g. IoU>0.5) used for matching, NMS, and counting true vs. false positives. It also fixes a real failure mode: an L1/L2 box loss can shrink toward zero while the boxes barely overlap, so directly optimizing IoU (and variants like GIoU/DIoU/CIoU) aligns the training objective with the metric you're actually graded on.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the backbone of detection and segmentation benchmarks (COCO mAP averages over IoU 0.5–0.95, Pascal VOC, Cityscapes), and as a loss it trains the box heads of YOLO and DETR-family detectors. In medical imaging the same overlap measure (closely tied to the Dice/F1 score) is the standard way to validate tumor and organ segmentations in nnU-Net and MONAI pipelines.

▸ Code PyTorch / torchvision — what actually runs▶
import torch
from torchvision.ops import box_iou

# boxes in (x1, y1, x2, y2) corners; A = preds, B = gts
A = torch.tensor([[class="n">10., class="n">10., class="n">50., class="n">50.]])          # [N,4]
B = torch.tensor([[class="n">30., class="n">30., class="n">70., class="n">70.]])          # [M,4]

iou = box_iou(A, B)                                # -> [N, M] pairwise IoU

# ---- the formula box_iou runs, vectorized from scratch ----
areaA = (A[:, class="n">2]-A[:, class="n">0]) * (A[:, class="n">3]-A[:, class="n">1])      # |A|
areaB = (B[:, class="n">2]-B[:, class="n">0]) * (B[:, class="n">3]-B[:, class="n">1])      # |B|
lt = torch.max(A[:, None, :class="n">2], B[None, :, :class="n">2])     # max of top-lefts
rb = torch.min(A[:, None, class="n">2:], B[None, :, class="n">2:])     # min of bottom-rights
wh = (rb - lt).clamp(min=class="n">0)                        # max(0, Δx), max(0, Δy)
inter = wh[..., class="n">0] * wh[..., class="n">1]                    # ∩ = Δx·Δy
union = areaA[:, None] + areaB[None, :] - inter    # ∪ = |A|+|B|−∩
iou_manual = inter / union                         # IoU = ∩ / ∪

matched = iou_manual >= class="n">0.5                         # τ=0.5 match gate (TP/FP)
assert torch.allclose(iou, iou_manual)
detect.py — non-max suppression (dedup boxes → one per lesion)
Solid teal = kept · faded coral = suppressed (IoU > τ vs a kept box). Dashed grey = true lesion.

Non-max suppression: collapsing a swarm of boxes to one per lesion

A detector fires many overlapping candidate boxes per object, each with a confidence score. NMS is a greedy dedup: sort boxes by score, take the highest, then remove every other box whose overlap with it exceeds a threshold τ, and repeat on what remains. Overlap is the Intersection-over-Union
IoU(A,B)=∣A∩B∣/∣A∪B∣IoU(A,B) = |A\cap B| / |A\cup B|IoU(A,B)=∣A∩B∣/∣A∪B∣
i.e. shared area ÷ combined area, ∈ [0,1]. The survivor set is keepi:scoreismaxinitsIoU>τcluster{ keep i : score is max in its IoU>\tau cluster }keepi:scoreismaxinitsIoU>τcluster.

In OncoSeg this is the bridge from raw detections to RECIST target lesions: each true tumor should yield exactly one measured box, not five near-duplicates that would be summed five times. Lower τ suppresses more (aggressive dedup, risks merging two close lesions into one); higher τ keeps more (duplicates leak back, inflating the lesion count). Note the lone low-score box bottom-right never gets suppressed — nothing overlaps it; killing isolated false positives is a separate score-threshold step, not NMS's job.
0.25
💡 Why it mattersDetectors emit many overlapping boxes for the same object, each with a confidence score; NMS keeps the highest-scoring box and suppresses neighbors whose IoU exceeds a threshold, collapsing the swarm to one detection per lesion. Without it you get duplicate, noisy detections that wreck precision and downstream counting.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the standard post-processing step in nearly every box-based detector (YOLO, Faster R-CNN) for autonomous driving, surveillance, and retail, and in medical imaging it deduplicates candidate boxes in lung-nodule, polyp, and lesion detection (e.g. LUNA16-style CT pipelines) before clinicians review them. Variants like Soft-NMS and Weighted Box Fusion are used to ensemble detectors and improve recall in crowded scenes.

▸ Code PyTorch — torchvision.ops.nms plus the greedy IoU loop it runs▶
import torch
from torchvision.ops import nms, batched_nms  # boxes: [N,4] as (x1,y1,x2,y2)

# Idiomatic: one greedy pass, returns kept indices sorted by descending score
keep = nms(boxes, scores, iou_threshold=class="n">0.25)          # τ = 0.25
# multi-class? keep boxes of different labels from suppressing each other:
# keep = batched_nms(boxes, scores, labels, iou_threshold=0.25)
boxes, scores = boxes[keep], scores[keep]

# --- what nms() does, from scratch: keep max, kill its IoU>τ neighbors, repeat ---
def nms_scratch(boxes, scores, tau=class="n">0.25):
    order = scores.argsort(descending=True)            # sort by confidence
    keep = []
    while order.numel():
        i = order[class="n">0]; keep.append(i)                   # highest-score survivor
        ti = boxes[i]; rest = boxes[order[class="n">1:]]
        lt = torch.maximum(ti[:class="n">2], rest[:, :class="n">2])        # ∩ top-left
        rb = torch.minimum(ti[class="n">2:], rest[:, class="n">2:])        # ∩ bottom-right
        inter = (rb - lt).clamp(min=class="n">0).prod(class="n">1)         # |A∩B|
        area = lambda b: (b[..., class="n">2]-b[..., class="n">0]) * (b[..., class="n">3]-b[..., class="n">1])
        iou = inter / (area(ti) + area(rest) - inter)  # |A∩B| / |A∪B|
        order = order[class="n">1:][iou <= tau]                  # drop the cluster, keep the rest
    return torch.stack(keep)
detector.py — anchor generation & IoU matching
Coral=GT lesion box. Teal=positive anchors (IoU>0.5). Dashed coral=ignored buffer. Blue dashed=best anchor; the arrow is the offset Δ it regresses.

Anchor boxes: turning detection into per-prior classify + regress

A detector can't emit arbitrary boxes, so it lays down a fixed grid of anchor priors — at every feature-map location it places K boxes spanning several scales and aspect ratios (here 3×3 = 9 per cell). Each anchor is then labelled by how well it overlaps the ground-truth object via Intersection-over-Union: IoU=∣A∩B∣/∣A∪B∣IoU = |A\cap B| / |A\cup B|IoU=∣A∩B∣/∣A∪B∣. Anchors with IoU>0.5IoU > 0.5IoU>0.5 become positive — the network must (a) classify them as "object" and (b) regress the residual offset Δ\Delta Δ that snaps the prior onto the GT, encoded as tx=(gx−ax)/awt_{x}=(g_{x}-a_{x})/a_wtx​=(gx​−ax​)/aw​, ty=(gy−ay)/aht_y=(g_y-a_y)/a_hty​=(gy​−ay​)/ah​, tw=log(gw/aw)t_w=log(g_w/a_w)tw​=log(gw​/aw​), th=log(gh/ah)t_h=log(g_h/a_h)th​=log(gh​/ah​). Anchors with IoU < 0.3 are negatives (background class); the band in between is ignored to avoid confusing labels.

Why multi-scale priors matter here: a single anchor size only matches objects of one size — drag the slider and watch positives vanish when the lesion is too small or too large for the current priors, then reappear as a different scale takes over. That is exactly why OncoSeg-style pipelines use multi-scale features: a region-proposal front-end with dense anchors first crops a tumour ROI at the right scale, then the 3D segmentation head refines it voxel-by-voxel. The log in the size targets makes the regressor learn scale-invariant ratios (so doubling a lesion's diameter is one fixed Δ, not a size-dependent one) — and unmatched anchors supplying the background class are what keep false positives down on a noisy scan.
84 px
💡 Why it mattersObject detection has to localize a variable, unknown number of objects, which is awkward for fixed-size network outputs. Anchor boxes solve this by tiling each feature-map cell with a fixed set of reference boxes (priors) of preset scales and aspect ratios, turning detection into a dense, fixed-shape problem: for each prior the net just classifies the object (or background) and regresses small offsets to the true box, making training stable and densely supervised.
▸ Where it’s usedAnchors power classic real-time and two-stage detectors used in autonomous driving, surveillance, and retail (Faster R-CNN, SSD, RetinaNet, YOLOv3–v5), and the same per-prior classify-plus-regress framing appears in medical imaging for lesion, nodule, and cell detection (e.g. lung-nodule CADe and mammography detectors). It remains a key baseline and design axis even as anchor-free and query-based detectors (FCOS, CenterNet, DETR) increasingly compete.

▸ Code PyTorch (torchvision.ops) — what actually runs in an anchor-based detector head▶
import torch
from torchvision.ops import box_iou        # IoU=|A∩B|/|A∪B|; boxes (x1,y1,x2,y2)

# anchors:[N,4] dense grid (K scales×ratios/cell), gt:[M,4]
def match_and_encode(anchors, gt, pos=class="n">0.5, neg=class="n">0.3):
    N = anchors.size(class="n">0)
    labels = torch.zeros(N, dtype=torch.long, device=anchors.device)  # 0=background
    if gt.numel() == class="n">0:                        # no objects -> all negatives
        return labels, anchors.new_zeros((class="n">0, class="n">4))
    iou = box_iou(anchors, gt)                 # [N,M] every prior vs every GT
    best_iou, gt_idx = iou.max(dim=class="n">1)          # each anchor -> its best GT
    best_anchor = iou.argmax(dim=class="n">0)            # each GT -> its best anchor [M]
    gt_idx[best_anchor] = torch.arange(gt.size(class="n">0), device=anchors.device)  # force-match GTs
    labels[(best_iou >= neg) & (best_iou < pos)] = -class="n">1  # ignore 0.3–0.5 band
    labels[best_iou >= pos] = class="n">1                # IoU-threshold positives
    labels[best_anchor] = class="n">1                    # ensure every GT has >=1 positive anchor
    g = gt[gt_idx][labels == class="n">1]; a = anchors[labels == class="n">1]
    awh = a[:, class="n">2:] - a[:, :class="n">2]; ac = a[:, :class="n">2] + class="n">0.5 * awh   # anchor (w,h), center
    gwh = g[:, class="n">2:] - g[:, :class="n">2]; gc = g[:, :class="n">2] + class="n">0.5 * gwh
    t_xy = (gc - ac) / awh                     # tx,ty=(g-a)/a_wh — normalized shift
    t_wh = torch.log(gwh / awh)                # tw,th=log(g/a)   — scale-invariant
    return labels, torch.cat([t_xy, t_wh], class="n">1)  # targets only on positives
fpn.py — multi-scale pyramid + top-down lateral fusion
Left: input + the grid of the selected level (cell = its stride). Right: the P3→P7 pyramid — teal up-arrows are the bottom-up backbone, coral down-arrows are top-down lateral fusion. The boxed level is where this object is detected.

Feature Pyramid Network — one detector, every scale

A backbone shrinks the image stage by stage, so deep maps are semantically strong but spatially coarse and shallow maps are fine but semantically weak. FPN keeps the whole stack as a pyramid P3..P7 (strides 8,16,32,64,128 → grids 32²,16²,8²,4²,2²) and adds top-down lateral connections: it upsamples a coarse map ×2 and adds it elementwise to the next finer lateral, Pl=up2(Pl+1)⊕conv1x1(Cl)P_{l} = up_{2}(P_{l+1}) \oplus conv_{1x1}(C_{l})Pl​=up2​(Pl+1​)⊕conv1x1​(Cl​). Now every level is both high-resolution and semantically rich. An object is routed to the level whose anchor scale matches its size — the RetinaNet rule k=argmink∣log2(wh/ak)∣k = argmin_{k} |log_{2}(\sqrt{wh}/a_{k})|k=argmink​∣log2​(wh​/ak​)∣, anchors ak=32,64,128,256,512a_{k} = {32,64,128,256,512}ak​=32,64,128,256,512 px. Small lesion → fine P3; bulky mass → coarse P7; either way the object spans only a handful of cells, which is exactly the scale the head was trained for.

Tumors arrive at wildly different scales — a sub-centimetre satellite nodule next to a 9 cm mass. A single-resolution feature map either blurs the small one into oblivion or starves the big one of context. FPN's top-down path is the detection cousin of U-Net skip connections: both carry coarse semantic context back into high-resolution maps so fine boundaries stay sharp. OncoSeg's encoder-decoder uses skips for voxel-accurate masks; a detector built on the same MRI features would use this pyramid to find lesions at any scale before segmenting them.
40 px
P3..P7strides 8→128top-down ⊕ lateralU-Net skip cousin
💡 Why it mattersDeep backbones lose spatial detail as they downsample, so small objects vanish in coarse high-level features while shallow features lack semantics. FPN fixes this by adding a top-down pathway with lateral connections that fuses semantically strong deep features into high-resolution shallow ones, giving every pyramid level rich semantics so one detector head can find objects across all scales cheaply.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the standard multi-scale neck in object detection and instance segmentation (Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, Mask R-CNN) and is widely reused in medical imaging for detecting lesions, nodules, and polyps that span very different sizes — e.g. lung-nodule and breast-mass detectors and many nnU-Net/MONAI-style segmentation backbones.

▸ Code PyTorch — torchvision FPN, plus the top-down ⊕ lateral fuse and level-assignment it runs▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn
from torchvision.ops import FeaturePyramidNetwork  # the idiomatic call

# C3..C5 = RAW ResNet maps: 512/1024/2048 deep. FPN's 1x1 laterals make every P-level 256-d.
fpn = FeaturePyramidNetwork(in_channels_list=[class="n">512, class="n">1024, class="n">2048], out_channels=class="n">256)
P = fpn({class="s">"c3": c3, class="s">"c4": c4, class="s">"c5": c5})  # OrderedDict keyed by SAME names, each 256-d (no extra P6/P7)

# --- what FPN does internally: top-down lateral fusion, coarse -> fine ---
laterals = [l1x1(c) for l1x1, c in zip(self.lateral, [c3, c4, c5])]  # conv_1x1(C_l) -> 256-d
for l in range(len(laterals) - class="n">2, -class="n">1, -class="n">1):                          # high level -> low
    up = F.interpolate(laterals[l + class="n">1], size=laterals[l].shape[-class="n">2:], mode=class="s">"nearest")
    laterals[l] = laterals[l] + up          # merged_l = up2(merged_{l+1}) + conv_1x1(C_l)
outs = [smooth3x3(p) for smooth3x3, p in zip(self.smooth, laterals)]  # 3x3 anti-alias -> P3..P5

# --- route a box of area w*h to its pyramid level (Mask R-CNN eq.1 / RetinaNet) ---
k0, k_min, k_max = class="n">4, class="n">3, class="n">5                    # P4 is canonical for a 224px RoI; pyramid is P3..P5
# k = floor(k0 + log2(sqrt(w*h)/224)); eps inside log2 is torchvision's numerical guard.
k = torch.floor(k0 + torch.log2(torch.sqrt(w * h) / class="n">224 + class="n">1e-6))
k = k.clamp(k_min, k_max).long()             # small lesion -> fine P3; bulky mass -> coarse P5
detr.py — set prediction via Hungarian matching
Coral = ground-truth objects · teal = the N object queries (each predicts a box) · solid edge = optimal one-to-one match · faint teal = query forced to predict ∅ (no object).

DETR: detection as set prediction

A transformer detector emits a fixed set of N predictions from N learnable object queries — each query outputs one box ŷᵢ = (class, cx, cy, w, h). Training needs to decide which prediction is responsible for which ground-truth object. DETR solves this with an optimal bipartite matching: find the permutation σ̂ minimising the total assignment cost
σ̂ = argminσ Σᵢ 𝓛match(yᵢ, ŷσ(i))
where the per-pair cost mixes class probability with box geometry
𝓛match = λL1·‖b−b̂‖₁ + λgiou·(1−GIoU) − p̂(class).

This minimum-cost assignment is computed by the Hungarian algorithm in O(N³) — a true one-to-one matching (every GT gets exactly one query, every query at most one GT). The N−M leftover queries are trained toward the no-object ∅ class. The set loss is then evaluated only on the matched pairs, so the network is directly penalised for emitting two boxes on one object — there is no NMS, no anchors.

Why it matters for OncoSeg-style detection: classic detectors fire many overlapping boxes per lesion and lean on NMS with a hand-tuned IoU threshold to dedupe — brittle for touching/satellite lesions and a hidden hyper-parameter at deployment. Set prediction makes duplicate suppression part of the loss: one query ↔ one lesion, end-to-end, threshold-free. The same one-to-one bipartite cost (Dice/IoU + centroid L1) is what you'd use to track lesions across longitudinal scans.
4
N = 16 queriesHungarian O(N³)no NMS
💡 Why it mattersDETR reframes object detection as direct set prediction: a Transformer emits a fixed set of object queries that are matched to ground-truth boxes via bipartite (Hungarian) matching, eliminating hand-crafted anchors, region proposals, and non-maximum suppression. This makes detection truly end-to-end — the network learns "one query, one object" instead of relying on heuristic post-processing that is hard to tune and differentiate through.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed for general object detection and panoptic segmentation, and its query-based set-prediction design now underpins open-vocabulary detection and promptable segmentation; in medical imaging, DETR-style detectors are applied to lesion/nodule and cell/nuclei detection where overlapping instances make NMS unreliable. The paradigm also generalizes to pose estimation, lane detection, and as the decoder backbone in segmentation foundation models like Mask2Former and SAM.

▸ Code PyTorch — DETR's HungarianMatcher + set loss (what actually runs)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment
from torchvision.ops import generalized_box_iou, box_convert

# DETR HungarianMatcher: build N(queries)×M(GT) cost, solve 1-to-1 (no NMS, no anchors)
def match(pred_logits, pred_boxes, tgt_labels, tgt_boxes, l1=class="n">5., giou=class="n">2.):
    prob = pred_logits.softmax(-class="n">1)              # [N, C] class posteriors p̂
    cost_cls = -prob[:, tgt_labels]             # −p̂(GT class): cheaper when confident in the *target* class
    cost_l1  = torch.cdist(pred_boxes, tgt_boxes, p=class="n">1)        # ‖b−b̂‖₁  (cxcywh)
    cost_giou = -generalized_box_iou(box_convert(pred_boxes, class=class="s">"s">class="s">'cxcywh', class=class="s">"s">class="s">'xyxy'),
                                     box_convert(tgt_boxes,  class=class="s">"s">class="s">'cxcywh', class=class="s">"s">class="s">'xyxy'))  # 1−GIoU (const dropped)
    C = l1 * cost_l1 + giou * cost_giou + cost_cls           # 𝓛_match, [N, M] (assumes N≥M)
    qi, gi = linear_sum_assignment(C.detach().cpu().numpy()) # Hungarian O(N³): σ̂ = argmin Σ C
    return torch.as_tensor(qi), torch.as_tensor(gi)          # matched query↔GT; rest → ∅

# box loss on matched pairs, normalized by #GT and weighted IDENTICALLY to the matcher (DETR weight_dict)
q, g = match(pred_logits, pred_boxes, tgt_labels, tgt_boxes)
num = max(len(g), class="n">1)
loss_l1   = F.l1_loss(pred_boxes[q], tgt_boxes[g], reduction=class=class="s">"s">class="s">'none').sum() / num
loss_giou = (class="n">1 - torch.diag(generalized_box_iou(box_convert(pred_boxes[q], class=class="s">"s">class="s">'cxcywh', class=class="s">"s">class="s">'xyxy'),
                                                box_convert(tgt_boxes[g], class=class="s">"s">class="s">'cxcywh', class=class="s">"s">class="s">'xyxy')))).sum() / num
loss_box = class="n">5. * loss_l1 + class="n">2. * loss_giou                    # (+ cross-entropy incl ∅ class, omitted here)
ct_scanner.py — Radon transform → sinogram
Left: the patient slice (phantom f); blue rays = the X-ray beam at angle θ, coral line = the detector. Middle: the 1-D projection p(s,θ) read off the detector now. Right: every projection stacked = the sinogram (teal), the raw data a CT scanner actually records. The coral box is the column being measured.

The Radon transform — how a CT scanner sees

A CT scanner never photographs the inside of you directly. It fires X-rays straight through the body from one angle and a detector on the far side records, for each ray, how much was absorbed — the line integral of tissue attenuation μ along that ray. That 1-D readout is one projection. Mathematically this is the Radon transform: p(s,θ)=∫f(x,y)δ(x⋅cosθ+y⋅sinθ−s)dxdyp(s,\theta ) = \int f(x,y) \delta (x\cdot cos\theta + y\cdot sin\theta - s) dx dyp(s,θ)=∫f(x,y)δ(x⋅cosθ+y⋅sinθ−s)dxdy, i.e. sum the slice f along every ray that hits detector position s when the gantry sits at angle θ\theta θ. Rotate the gantry through θ ∈ [0°,180°), stack each projection as a column, and you get the sinogram p(s,θ) — a point source traces a sine curve through it, hence the name.

The sinogram is the measurement; the familiar cross-sectional image only appears after reconstruction (filtered back-projection or iterative/learned inverse — the adjoint operator frec=R−1pf_{re}c = \mathcal{R}^{-1}pfre​c=R−1p). Two checks the toy honours exactly: (1) sweep θ and the mean ∫μ per ray stays constant (≈0.25 here) — projection conserves total attenuation, a true Radon invariant; only the shape of p(s,θ) changes as the elongated tumour rotates into/out of the beam. (2) Fewer angles → a sparser sinogram → a noisier reconstruction. This is the front door for OncoSeg's CT volumes: low-dose / sparse-view protocols (cancer patients are scanned repeatedly) leave streak artifacts in the reconstructed image that a downstream segmentation net must be robust to. Drag θ to watch the sinogram fill, one column per angle.
40°
p(s,θ) = ∫ f along raysθ = gantry anglecolumns → sinogram∫μ invariant in θimage = ℛ⁻¹ p (later)
💡 Why it mattersThe Radon transform models exactly what a CT scanner physically measures: each X-ray projection is a line integral of tissue attenuation, so a scan yields the sinogram (Radon transform) of the body, not the image itself. Understanding it is the precondition for inverting those projections — via filtered back-projection or iterative/learned reconstruction — back into the cross-sectional image radiologists actually read.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins all CT and SPECT/PET reconstruction in clinical scanners, plus low-dose and sparse-view CT, electron tomography, and synchrotron/industrial CT; modern research embeds the (inverse) Radon operator directly into deep reconstruction networks and uses sinogram-domain learning to cut dose and artifacts.

▸ Code scikit-image — what actually runs in a CT pipeline▶
import numpy as np
from skimage.transform import radon
from scipy.ndimage import rotate
from skimage.data import shepp_logan_phantom
from skimage.transform import resize

# f: a CT slice (phantom of attenuation mu), shape (H, W) float.
f = resize(shepp_logan_phantom(), (class="n">128, class="n">128)).astype(float)
theta = np.arange(class="n">0., class="n">180., class="n">1.)                # gantry angles in [0,180) deg

# --- the one line a practitioner writes ---
# sinogram[:, j] = p(s, theta_j): line integral of f along every ray at angle theta_j.
# skimage returns shape (n_detector_pixels, n_angles): each column is one projection.
sinogram = radon(f, theta=theta, circle=True)

# --- the underlying idea, from scratch (conceptual; skimage uses its own warp) ---
# Rotating f by -theta aligns rays with image columns, so the delta-line integral
# becomes a plain sum down each column. order=3 ~ skimage's interpolation.
def radon_scratch(f, theta):
    cols = [rotate(f, -t, reshape=False, order=class="n">3).sum(axis=class="n">0) for t in theta]
    return np.stack(cols, axis=class="n">1)              # stack columns -> sinogram p(s, theta)

assert radon_scratch(f, theta).shape == sinogram.shape          # use ==, not allclose
# Conservation: with circle=True every column sums to ~= integral of f.
assert np.allclose(radon_scratch(f, theta).sum(axis=class="n">0), f.sum(), rtol=class="n">2e-3)
fbp.py — invert the sinogram by filtered backprojection
Top row: the true phantom · its sinogram p(s,θ) with the chosen view angles marked (coral) · one projection profile (teal = raw, coral = ramp-filtered, note the negative lobes). Bottom: the reconstruction built by smearing each projection back along its ray (coral lines = backprojection directions).

Filtered backprojection: turning many X-ray views back into a slice

A CT scanner never measures the slice directly — it measures projections. Rotating around the patient, at each angle θ it records the line integral of attenuation across the body: the Radon transform p(s,θ)=∫f(x,y)dℓp(s,\theta ) = \int f(x,y) d\ell p(s,θ)=∫f(x,y)dℓ along the line at offset s=x⋅cosθ+y⋅sinθs = x\cdot cos\theta + y\cdot sin\theta s=x⋅cosθ+y⋅sinθ. Stack these over all θ and you get the sinogram. Reconstruction is the inverse problem: recover the image f from p.

The naive guess is backprojection: take each 1-D projection and smear it uniformly back across the image along its ray, then sum over angles — b(x,y)=∫0πp(x⋅cosθ+y⋅sinθ,θ)dθb(x,y) = \int _{0}^{}\pi p(x\cdot cos\theta + y\cdot sin\theta , \theta ) d\theta b(x,y)=∫0​πp(x⋅cosθ+y⋅sinθ,θ)dθ. This does place mass where the object is, but it also smears it everywhere else: every point bleeds out as a 1/r1/r1/r halo, so you get a hopelessly blurry star no matter how many angles you use (quality plateaus ~84% here).

The fix comes from the Fourier-slice theorem: the 1-D Fourier transform of a projection equals a radial slice of the 2-D transform of the image. Piling slices into a polar grid over-samples low frequencies by exactly 1/∣ω∣1/|\omega |1/∣ω∣. So before backprojecting, convolve each projection with the ramp filter whose response is ∣ω∣|\omega |∣ω∣ — the discrete Ram-Lak kernel h[0]=14,h[odd]=−1/(π2n2),h[even]=0h[0]=\tfrac14 , h[odd]=-1/(\pi ^{2}n^{2}), h[even]=0h[0]=41​,h[odd]=−1/(π2n2),h[even]=0. The negative side-lobes sharpen each profile (you can see them dip below zero in the inset), cancelling the blur. The exact inversion is f=∫0π(p∗sh)(x⋅cosθ+y⋅sinθ,θ)dθf = \int _{0}^{}\pi (p *_{s} h)(x\cdot cos\theta + y\cdot sin\theta , \theta ) d\theta f=∫0​π(p∗s​h)(x⋅cosθ+y⋅sinθ,θ)dθ. Toggle the ramp on and sweep the angle slider: few angles → streak artifacts; ramp + many angles → a crisp reconstruction (→97%).

This is not a toy analogy — it is the classical analytic CT reconstruction the field still ships, and the volumes that OncoSeg segments are themselves FBP (or its fan/cone-beam cousins) reconstructions. The tradeoffs shown here are the real upstream knobs on lesion conspicuity: fewer view angles = lower dose but streaks that can mimic or hide a small tumor; the ramp filter is what makes edges (and therefore lesion boundaries) crisp enough to segment. Iterative and deep-learning reconstructors are all benchmarked against this baseline, and sparse-view CT — pushing the angle count down to cut dose, then de-streaking with a network — is an active research frontier sitting directly on top of this picture.

💡 Why it mattersA CT scanner only measures line integrals (sinograms) of X-ray attenuation from many angles, never the slice itself; filtered backprojection inverts this by ramp-filtering each 1-D projection and smearing it back across the image, which exactly undoes the blurring of naive backprojection and recovers the cross-sectional density map. It is fast, deterministic, and closed-form (the discretized inverse Radon transform), making it the workhorse that turns raw detector data into a viewable slice.
▸ Where it’s usedFBP is the classical reconstruction engine inside virtually every clinical CT scanner (and fan-/cone-beam variants like FDK in C-arm CT, CBCT dental/interventional units, and micro-CT), and is the standard baseline against which iterative and deep-learning reconstructions are benchmarked. The same Radon-inverse machinery also drives SPECT/PET tomography, synchrotron and electron tomography, and seismic/radar imaging.

▸ Code scikit-image — what actually runs (iradon + the ramp-filter/backproject it hides)▶
import numpy as np
from skimage.transform import iradon

# sinogram: columns = 1-D projections p(s, theta), one per view angle
theta = np.linspace(class="n">0., class="n">180., n_views, endpoint=False)      # views over [0, 180 deg)

# idiomatic: scikit-image does ramp-filter + backproject + (pi/2N) scaling, linear interp
recon = iradon(sinogram, theta=theta, filter_name=class=class="s">"s">class="s">'ramp')   # f = integral_0^pi (p *_s h)(.)

# --- from-scratch equivalent (what iradon does under the hood) ---
N = sinogram.shape[class="n">0]
M = max(class="n">64, int(class="n">2 ** np.ceil(np.log2(class="n">2 * N))))              # zero-pad: avoid cyclic-conv leakage
ramp = class="n">2 * np.abs(np.fft.fftfreq(M)).reshape(-class="n">1, class="n">1)         # Ram-Lak |omega| (DC -> 0)
proj = np.fft.fft(sinogram, n=M, axis=class="n">0) * ramp            # filter the padded columns
filt = np.real(np.fft.ifft(proj, axis=class="n">0))[:N]              # crop back to N rows

rec = np.zeros((N, N), dtype=np.float64)
s_coord = np.arange(N) - N // class="n">2
ys, xs = np.mgrid[:N, :N].astype(np.float64) - N // class="n">2
for k, th in enumerate(np.deg2rad(theta)):
    t = xs * np.cos(th) - ys * np.sin(th)                  # ray coord (skimage sign convention)
    rec += np.interp(t.ravel(), s_coord, filt[:, k], left=class="n">0, right=class="n">0).reshape(N, N)  # linear interp
rec *= np.pi / (class="n">2 * len(theta))                            # integral d-theta ~= (pi/2N) * sum
mri_recon.py — image = inverse 2-D Fourier transform of k-space
Left: k-space magnitude (log, centered) — bright DC at center carries contrast, edges carry fine detail; the coral circle is the region the scanner actually sampled. Right: the reconstructed slice (a focal hyperintense "tumor" sits in the dashed lesion ROI). Bottom bar: edge detail recovered vs a full scan.

k-space & Fourier: how an MR scanner draws a picture out of frequencies

An MRI scanner never measures pixels directly — it measures the spatial-frequency domain called k-space. Each acquired sample is one Fourier coefficient of the slice, and the image is recovered by the inverse 2-D Fourier transform: I(x,y) = Σkₓ Σk_y S(kₓ,k_y)·e+2πi(kₓx + k_y·y)/N, while the scanner fills k-space with the forward transform S(kₓ,k_y) = Σx Σy I(x,y)·e−2πi(kₓx + k_y·y)/N. The center of k-space is the low frequencies (the DC term S(0,0)=ΣIS(0,0)=\Sigma IS(0,0)=ΣI is total brightness) — it sets overall contrast and shape. The edges of k-space are high frequencies — they encode sharp edges and fine detail.

Drag the slider to set the fraction of k-space the scanner samples (a centered disk of radius R, area ∝ R2R^{2}R2). Sampling only the bright center keeps contrast but the image goes blurry — every detail lives in the discarded high-frequency ring. Adding outer rings sharpens edges; the hard circular cutoff also injects faint Gibbs / truncation ringing (oscillations beside edges) — the same artifact you see in real undersampled scans. This is exactly the lever behind fast MRI: fewer k-space lines ⇒ shorter scan, at the cost of detail and aliasing, which compressed sensing then tries to recover.

OncoSeg ingests MR sequences (T1c, T2/FLAIR) as input channels — every one of those images is an inverse FFT of acquired k-space. Accelerated protocols undersample k-space to cut scan time and motion, so the network must stay robust to blurred lesion margins and ringing near boundaries — precisely where Dice and HD95 are most fragile. Understanding that the network sees a Fourier reconstruction (not raw tissue) clarifies why scanner/protocol shifts behave like a domain shift, and why low-frequency contrast can look fine while the high-frequency edges a segmentation depends on have been thrown away.
