💡 Why it mattersAn MR scanner never measures pixels directly — it samples the spatial-frequency domain (k-space), and the image is recovered by an inverse 2D/3D Fourier transform, so understanding k-space is what lets you reason about resolution (k-space edges), contrast (k-space center), aliasing, and motion/phase artifacts. It also explains how you can deliberately undersample k-space to scan faster, with the missing frequencies filled in by parallel imaging or deep-learning reconstruction.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins every clinical MRI sequence and every accelerated/compressed-sensing protocol (e.g. faster brain, cardiac, and abdominal scans), as well as MRI reconstruction research on undersampled k-space; the same Fourier-sampling view also appears in CT, radio interferometry, and any phase-contrast or k-space-trajectory (radial/spiral) imaging.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (torch.fft.ifft2)▶
import torch
import torch.fft as fft

# kspace: complex (H, W) tensor the scanner acquires, already DC-centered for display.
# Forward model (how it got there):  kspace = fftshift(fft2(image))
def reconstruct(kspace, radius_frac=class="n">1.0):
    H, W = kspace.shape
    # fftshift puts DC (k=0) at index N//2, so center the keep-disk there (NOT (N-1)/2).
    cy, cx = H // class="n">2, W // class="n">2
    yy, xx = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H).float(), torch.arange(W).float(), indexing=class="s">"ij")
    R = radius_frac * min(H, W) / class="n">2
    mask = ((yy - cy) ** class="n">2 + (xx - cx) ** class="n">2) <= R ** class="n">2     # 1 = sampled, 0 = skipped
    ks = kspace * mask                                      # undersample -> blur + Gibbs ringing

    # THE line: image = inverse 2-D FFT of k-space.  I = (1/N) Sum S(k) e^{+2pi i k.x/N}
    # ifftshift undoes the centering before the transform; magnitude = displayed slice.
    image = fft.ifft2(fft.ifftshift(ks))
    return image.abs()

# NOTE: the mask is the INSCRIBED disk, so radius_frac=1 keeps only ~pi/4 of k-space
# (corners dropped). Use radius_frac >= 2**0.5 for true full sampling / exact recon;
# small radius -> low-freq contrast only, edges lost.
img = reconstruct(kspace, radius_frac=class="n">0.30)
register.py — rigid SSD alignment
Top: fixed (teal) vs moving (coral) overlay. Bottom: SSD cost landscape vs θ — marker slides into the basin as you align.

Image registration

Two scans of the same anatomy never land in the same coordinate frame — the patient shifts and rotates between acquisitions. Registration recovers a transform T that maps the moving image onto the fixed one, then resamples: warped(p) = M(R(θ)⋅p+tR(\theta )\cdot p + tR(θ)⋅p+t), with rotation R(θ)=[[cosθ,−sinθ],[sinθ,cosθ]]R(\theta ) = [[cos \theta , -sin \theta ],[sin \theta , cos \theta ]]R(θ)=[[cosθ,−sinθ],[sinθ,cosθ]] and translation t=(dx,dy)t = (dx, dy)t=(dx,dy). We score the fit with an intensity similarity cost — here the sum of squared differences, SSD(T)=(1/N)Σi(F(pi)−M∘T(pi))2SSD(T) = (1/N) \Sigma _{i} (F(p_{i}) - M\circ T(p_{i}))^{2}SSD(T)=(1/N)Σi​(F(pi​)−M∘T(pi​))2. Slide dx,dy,θdx, dy, \theta dx,dy,θ to drive SSD toward its single minimum: at the true transform the two images coincide and SSD→0SSD \to 0SSD→0. That is exactly what an optimizer does — descend ∇T SSD until the basin bottoms out.

In OncoSeg this is the gate before any comparison. Baseline and follow-up CT/MR — or PET aligned to CT — must share one frame, or a voxel-wise subtraction map and every RECIST diameter measure apparent "tumor change" that is really just repositioning. The checkerboard makes it visceral: across each seam, vessels and tumor edges must line up — if they jump, you are measuring motion, not biology. Multi-modal scans use a different cost (mutual information) since intensities don't match across modalities, but the optimization picture is identical: warp, score, descend. The cost landscape below also shows the catch — gradient descent can stall in a shallow local minimum, which is why clinical pipelines use multi-resolution pyramids and good initialization.

💡 Why it mattersImage registration finds the spatial transform that aligns two or more images into a common coordinate frame, so pixels/voxels that depict the same anatomy or scene point line up. Without it you cannot reliably fuse multi-modal scans (e.g. PET+CT, MR+US), track change across time (tumor shrinkage between visits), correct motion, or map a patient onto an atlas — alignment errors directly corrupt every downstream measurement.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins multi-modal fusion and longitudinal follow-up in radiology and radiotherapy planning (deformable CT/MR alignment), atlas-based segmentation and normalization in neuroimaging, image-guided surgery and biopsy, plus non-medical uses like panorama stitching, satellite/remote-sensing co-registration, SLAM, and aligning histology to radiology. Learning-based deformable registration now does in seconds what classical iterative optimization took minutes to do.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (differentiable rigid warp + SSD descent)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# fixed, moving: (1,1,H,W). Optimize rigid params (theta,dx,dy) by descending SSD.
theta = torch.zeros(class="n">1, requires_grad=True)        # rotation (rad)
trans = torch.zeros(class="n">2, requires_grad=True)        # (dx,dy) in normalized [-1,1] coords
opt = torch.optim.Adam([theta, trans], lr=class="n">5e-2)

for _ in range(class="n">200):
    c, s = torch.cos(theta), torch.sin(theta)     # shape (1,); slices below keep shapes equal
    # affine_grid wants the OUTPUT->INPUT map M: grid(p_out) = M @ [p_out; 1]
    M = torch.stack([c, -s, trans[class="n">0:class="n">1], s, c, trans[class="n">1:class="n">2]]).reshape(class="n">1, class="n">2, class="n">3)
    grid = F.affine_grid(M, moving.shape, align_corners=False)        # sampling coords in moving
    warped = F.grid_sample(moving, grid, align_corners=False)         # warped(p)=moving(M @ [p;1])
    ssd = ((fixed - warped) ** class="n">2).mean()                             # SSD = (1/N) Sum (F - warped)^2
    opt.zero_grad(); ssd.backward(); opt.step()
# theta,trans now parameterize the fixed->moving RESAMPLING map (the inverse of the
# moving->fixed motion); invert M if you need the moving->fixed transform itself.
# SSD is valid only for same-modality images.

# Production (3-D, multimodal) uses MONAI/ITK with mutual information, e.g.
#   monai.transforms, or itk-elastix's elastix_registration_method(fixed, moving, "rigid")
register.py — Mattes mutual information
Left: fixed CT (teal) with the moving MR (coral) slid by Δx. Top-right: joint histogram p(a,b) — it sharpens to tight clusters as the slices align. Bottom: I(A;B) vs Δx peaks at alignment.

Mutual information — the multimodal alignment metric

To register a CT to an MRI you cannot subtract pixels: the same bone is bright in CT but dark on MR, so sum-of-squared-differences and correlation are meaningless across modalities. Information theory gives the fix. Treat the two overlapping images as random variables A (CT intensity) and B (MR intensity); their joint histogram p(a,b) records how often value a in one image coincides with value b in the other. Mutual information measures how much knowing one intensity tells you about the other: I(A;B)=ΣiΣjp(a,b)⋅log2[p(a,b)/(p(a)⋅p(b))]I(A;B) = \Sigma _{i}\Sigma _{j} p(a,b)\cdot log_{2}[ p(a,b) / (p(a)\cdot p(b)) ]I(A;B)=Σi​Σj​p(a,b)⋅log2​[p(a,b)/(p(a)⋅p(b))], equivalently I=H(A)+H(B)−H(A,B)I = H(A) + H(B) - H(A,B)I=H(A)+H(B)−H(A,B). When the slices align, each tissue's CT value maps consistently to one MR value, so the joint histogram collapses onto a few tight clusters, joint entropy H(A,B) drops, and I(A;B) is maximal. Misalign them and pixels from different tissues get paired at random — the histogram smears, H(A,B) rises, and I(A;B) falls. Registration is therefore just: find the transform T that maximizes I(A;B).

Drag Δx to misregister, and watch the joint histogram blur while I(A;B) slides off its peak; return to Δx=0 and it snaps back to a sharp maximum. The decisive point: MI peaks at alignment regardless of the intensity relationship — here the CT↔MR map is even inverted for bone, so the Pearson correlation at perfect alignment is only r≈0.24 and SSD/correlation would never find the answer, yet MI does. This is exactly why MI is the default similarity metric for multimodal registration (ITK/Elastix/ANTs Mattes-MI). In OncoSeg's response pipeline, baseline and follow-up scans from different scanners or sequences are co-registered by maximizing MI before tumor volumes are compared — without that alignment, a longitudinal ΔV is just noise.

▸ Where it’s usedIt is the standard similarity metric for fusing CT, MR and PET in radiotherapy planning, neurosurgical navigation, PET-CT attenuation correction and atlas-to-patient registration, and the same objective drives InfoNCE contrastive representation learning that aligns image and text or two augmented views

▸ Code Python — SimpleITK Mattes MI registration + the from-scratch I(A;B) it maximizes▶
import SimpleITK as sitk
import numpy as np

# --- Idiomatic: ITK/Elastix-style multimodal registration via Mattes MI ---
# NOTE: ImageRegistrationMethod MINIMIZES the metric; SimpleITK negates MI, so
# the optimizer descends on -MI, i.e. it maximizes I(A;B). Mattes MI is a SMOOTH,
# DIFFERENTIABLE Parzen-window (B-spline KDE) estimate -- not a hard histogram --
# which is exactly why gradient descent works here.
R = sitk.ImageRegistrationMethod()
R.SetMetricAsMattesMutualInformation(numberOfHistogramBins=class="n">50)
R.SetOptimizerAsRegularStepGradientDescent(learningRate=class="n">1.0, minStep=class="n">1e-4, numberOfIterations=class="n">200)
R.SetInitialTransform(sitk.TranslationTransform(fixed.GetDimension()))  # fixed=CT, moving=MR
R.SetInterpolator(sitk.sitkLinear)
T = R.Execute(fixed, moving)   # finds T that maximizes I(A;B) (minimizes -MI)

# --- From scratch: a HARD-BINNED MI estimator (illustrative; NOT Mattes' KDE form) ---
def mutual_info(a, b, bins=class="n">50):
    pab, _, _ = np.histogram2d(a.ravel(), b.ravel(), bins=bins)  # counts
    pab = pab / pab.sum()                 # joint p(a,b); sharpens to tight clusters at alignment
    pa, pb = pab.sum(class="n">1, keepdims=True), pab.sum(class="n">0, keepdims=True)  # marginals
    m = pab > class="n">0
    # I(A;B) = Σ p(a,b)·log2[ p(a,b) / (p(a)·p(b)) ]  == H(A)+H(B)-H(A,B)
    return np.sum(pab[m] * np.log2(pab[m] / (pa @ pb)[m]))
preprocess.py — CT windowing (HU → grey)
Same axial slice, one window. Right strip = HU→grey ramp; dashed = window edges; coral dots = tissues inside the window.

CT windowing: making ±2000 HU fit in 256 greys

A CT voxel is a Hounsfield Unit — calibrated radiodensity where air = −1000, water = 0, dense bone ≳ +1000. That spans ~3000+ values, but a monitor (and your eye) resolves far fewer greys. A display window picks a slice of the HU range — center level L, span width W — and stretches it across black→white, clipping everything outside:

display(HU)=clip((HU−L)/W+12,0,1)display(HU) = clip( (HU - L)/W + \tfrac12 , 0, 1 )display(HU)=clip((HU−L)/W+21​,0,1)

So HU=L−W/2→blackHU = L-W/2 \to blackHU=L−W/2→black, HU=L→50%greyHU = L \to 50\% greyHU=L→50%grey, HU=L+W/2→whiteHU = L+W/2 \to whiteHU=L+W/2→white. Narrow W = high contrast over a thin HU band (subtle soft-tissue differences pop); wide W = low contrast but everything from air to bone is visible at once.

40 HU
400 HU
Why radiologists re-window the same scan many times: a brain window (L40/W80) reveals grey/white-matter contrast but blows out bone to pure white; a lung window (L−600/W1500) shows nodules in air but flattens soft tissue to one grey. No single window shows everything — hence the preset buttons on every PACS workstation. This is the clinical cousin of OncoSeg's intensitynormalizationintensity normalizationintensitynormalization: the network learns features only across the HU band you feed it, so the clip/normalize window you choose at preprocessing decides which tissues (and which low-contrast tumors near ~+55 HU) are even representable before training. Pick it wrong and a lesion is clipped to black or white before the model ever sees it.
💡 Why it mattersCT scanners record tissue density in Hounsfield Units spanning roughly -1000 (air) to +3000 (dense bone), but displays and most 8-bit pipelines only resolve 256 grey levels, so showing the full range would compress bone and soft tissue into a few indistinguishable shades. Windowing picks a center (level) and span (width) and linearly maps just that HU band to 0-255, dumping the rest to black/white — this is what lets a radiologist see lung detail, brain bleeds, or liver lesions that would otherwise be invisible, and it's also the de-facto normalization step before feeding CT into a CNN.
▸ Where it’s usedEvery clinical CT/PACS workstation ships preset windows (lung, mediastinum/soft-tissue, bone, brain, liver), and the same windowing transform is the standard preprocessing for deep-learning CT pipelines — e.g. nnU-Net clamps each task to a learned HU intensity range, and MONAI exposes ScaleIntensityRange/CT-window transforms for tumor, organ, and lesion segmentation. It is also baked into the DICOM standard itself via the Window Center/Width and VOI LUT tags.

▸ Code PyTorch + MONAI — what actually runs in preprocess.py▶
import torch
from monai.transforms import ScaleIntensityRange

# Brain window: level L=40 HU, width W=80 HU
L, W = class="n">40.0, class="n">80.0
lo, hi = L - W / class="n">2, L + W / class="n">2   # window edges: [0, 80] HU → black, white

# hu: raw CT volume in Hounsfield Units, shape (C, D, H, W)
hu = torch.randint(-class="n">1000, class="n">1200, (class="n">1, class="n">16, class="n">256, class="n">256)).float()

# --- idiomatic: MONAI preprocessing transform (clip + rescale to [0,1]) ---
window = ScaleIntensityRange(a_min=lo, a_max=hi, b_min=class="n">0.0, b_max=class="n">1.0, clip=True)
grey = window(hu)               # exactly the per-voxel map below, fused

# --- from-scratch equivalent (the formula the widget draws) ---
# display(HU) = clip((HU − L)/W + ½, 0, 1)   ≡   clip((HU − lo)/(hi − lo), 0, 1)
grey_manual = torch.clamp((hu - L) / W + class="n">0.5, class="n">0.0, class="n">1.0)

assert torch.allclose(grey, grey_manual, atol=class="n">1e-5)
# grey is what the network sees: HU outside [lo,hi] saturate to 0/1 (clipped).
gan.py - adversarial training
Teal = real pdata, coral = fake pg, blue = D(x)=P(real). Dots = samples.

GAN: a two-player minimax game

Two networks fight. The generator G maps noise z→x̂ trying to fake the real data; the discriminator D outputs D(x)=P(real) and tries to catch fakes. They optimize minG maxD Ex∼pdata[log D(x)] + Ez[log(1−D(G(z)))]. For a fixed G the best critic is the optimal discriminator D*(x) = pdata(x) / (pdata(x) + pg(x)). Plug it back in and G is minimizing 2·JSD(pdata ‖ pg) − log4. The unique global optimum is pg = pdata, where D∗(x)=12D*(x) = \tfrac12 D∗(x)=21​ everywhere (the critic is reduced to a coin flip) and JSD=0JSD = 0JSD=0. Drag the training step and watch the coral cloud slide onto the teal one while the blue D-curve flattens to the dashed ½ line.

Why it matters for OncoSeg-style imaging: labeled tumor volumes are scarce and scanners disagree. GANs synthesize realistic lesions to augment tiny training sets, harmonize CT/MRI appearance across sites (CycleGAN-style domain transfer), and the adversarial loss sharpens segmentation/translation outputs. The same D≈½, JSD→0 signature is your convergence check — if D stays confident (D(real)≫D(fake)), the generator is still losing and the synthetic scans are detectable artifacts, not training-worthy data. Mode collapse (the coral cloud covering only one real peak) is the classic failure to watch for.
0.00
D* = pdata/(pdata+pg)optimum: pg=pdataD→½ · JSD→0
💡 Why it mattersA GAN pits a generator against a discriminator in a minimax game, training the generator to fool a critic rather than fit an explicit likelihood — which lets it learn sharp, high-frequency image detail that pixel-wise MSE losses tend to blur away. This adversarial signal solves the problem of synthesizing realistic samples (and translating between domains) when you have no paired ground truth or no tractable density to optimize.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed for photorealistic image synthesis and editing (StyleGAN faces), unpaired domain translation (CycleGAN), and super-resolution (Real-ESRGAN); in medical imaging they generate synthetic scans for data augmentation and privacy, harmonize cross-scanner MRI/CT, and do CT-to-MRI synthesis and low-dose denoising. The adversarial loss also survives inside modern diffusion pipelines as the discriminator that powers fast few-step distillation (e.g. ADD/SDXL-Turbo).

▸ Code PyTorch — the two-player update that actually runs▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# One adversarial step. minimax value: V = E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))]
# D ascends V; G descends it. BCE-with-logits IS that log term: -[y·logσ(o)+(1-y)·log(1-σ(o))]
def gan_step(G, D, x_real, z, optD, optG):
    x_fake = G(z)                                            # one generator forward, reused for G step
    # --- update D: maximize log D(x) + log(1 - D(G(z)))  (real->1, fake->0) ---
    d_real = D(x_real); d_fake = D(x_fake.detach())          # detach -> no grad into G here
    loss_D = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(d_real, torch.ones_like(d_real)) \
           + F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(d_fake, torch.zeros_like(d_fake))
    optD.zero_grad(); loss_D.backward(); optD.step()

    # --- update G: non-saturating  maximize log D(G(z))  ==  fool D into label 1 ---
    d_gen = D(x_fake)                                        # grad flows G <- D (x_fake kept its graph)
    loss_G = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(d_gen, torch.ones_like(d_gen))
    optG.zero_grad(); loss_G.backward(); optG.step()
    return loss_D.item(), loss_G.item()
# At the Nash equilibrium D*(x)=½ everywhere → V = -log4, G's samples ≈ p_data.
vae.py — encode → sample (reparameterize) → decode
Teal = posterior q(z|x)=N(μ,σ); dashed = prior N(0,1). Coral dot = the sampled z (it jitters: that is the reparameterization noise). Right grids: input x vs reconstruction x̂. Bar = recon vs β·KL.

Variational Autoencoder — a latent space you can sample from

An autoencoder squeezes x through a bottleneck and rebuilds it. A VAE makes that bottleneck probabilistic: the encoder emits not a point but a Gaussian q(z∣x)=N(μ,σ)q(z|x)=N(\mu ,\sigma )q(z∣x)=N(μ,σ). We draw a code with the reparameterization trick z=μ+σ⊙ε,ε∼N(0,1)z = \mu + \sigma \odot \varepsilon , \varepsilon \sim N(0,1)z=μ+σ⊙ε,ε∼N(0,1) — the randomness lives in ε, so gradients still flow through μ and σ. The decoder turns z back into x^\hat{x}x^. Training minimizes L=∥x−x^∥2+β⋅KL(N(μ,σ)∥N(0,1))L = \|x-\hat{x}\|^{2} + \beta \cdot KL(N(\mu ,\sigma )\|N(0,1))L=∥x−x^∥2+β⋅KL(N(μ,σ)∥N(0,1)): a reconstruction term plus a pull dragging every posterior toward the unit Gaussian prior, with KL in closed form KL=12Σk(μk2+σk2−1−lnσk2)KL = \tfrac12 \Sigma _{k}(\mu _{k}^{2} + \sigma _{k}^{2} - 1 - ln \sigma _{k}^{2})KL=21​Σk​(μk2​+σk2​−1−lnσk2​).

That KL term is the whole point. It forces neighbouring codes to overlap the prior, so the latent space becomes smooth and continuous — you can then sample z∼N(0,1) and decode plausible new images, or interpolate between two scans and watch anatomy morph cleanly. The β knob trades the two goals: β→0 collapses σ→0 (a deterministic autoencoder) → razor-sharp recon but a punctured, ungeneratable latent; large β drives σ→1, μ→0 → a beautifully regular, sampleable manifold but a blurry x̂. In OncoSeg this is how you build a generative tumor-shape prior: learn the manifold of normal/abnormal anatomy, sample synthetic lesions for augmentation, or flag out-of-distribution scans by their reconstruction error. (The μ/σ here follow the exact ELBO optimum μₖ*=2mₖ/(2+β), σ²*=β/(2+β) for a toy Gaussian model — drag β and the recon↑ / KL↓ tradeoff is the real one.)
1.00
reparam: z=μ+σ⊙εKL(N(μ,σ)‖N(0,1))ELBO = recon + β·KLstructured latent → sample
💡 Why it mattersA VAE forces the encoder to map inputs onto a smooth, continuous probabilistic latent space (regularized toward a prior via the KL term), so you can sample new, plausible data and interpolate between examples — something a plain autoencoder's arbitrary, holey latent space can't do. This makes it the workhorse for generative modeling, anomaly detection (low likelihood = outlier), and as the perceptual compressor inside modern latent-diffusion pipelines.
▸ Where it’s usedIn production, a VAE is the latent compressor (the "VAE") inside Stable Diffusion / SDXL and most latent-diffusion models, turning pixels into the compact space the diffusion model actually denoises. In research and medicine it powers unsupervised lesion/anomaly detection on brain MRI and chest imaging, molecule and protein generation, and learned image/video compression.

▸ Code PyTorch — the real VAE forward pass + ELBO (what actually trains)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

def forward(enc, dec, x, beta=class="n">1.0):
    # encoder emits the posterior q(z|x)=N(mu, sigma^2); predict log(sigma^2) for stable, unconstrained sigma
    mu, logvar = enc(x).chunk(class="n">2, dim=-class="n">1)              # each (B, latent_dim); enc must output 2*latent_dim

    # reparameterization trick: z = mu + sigma * eps, eps~N(0,1) -> gradients flow through mu, logvar
    std = torch.exp(class="n">0.5 * logvar)                     # sigma = exp(logvar/2)
    z   = mu + std * torch.randn_like(std)            # rsample(); randomness isolated in eps

    x_hat = dec(z)                                    # decoder maps z -> reconstruction

    # VAE loss = -ELBO = reconstruction + beta * KL(N(mu,sigma^2) || N(0,1)); sum over latent dims, mean over batch
    # (Gaussian-decoder NLL up to the usual 0.5/const absorbed into beta)
    recon = F.mse_loss(x_hat, x, reduction=class=class="s">"s">class="s">'none').flatten(class="n">1).sum(class="n">1)
    kl    = -class="n">0.5 * (class="n">1 + logvar - mu.pow(class="n">2) - logvar.exp()).sum(class="n">1)   # 1/2 Σ(mu^2 + sigma^2 - 1 - ln sigma^2)
    loss  = (recon + beta * kl).mean()                # minimize negative ELBO
    return x_hat, loss, recon.mean(), kl.mean()

# to generate: sample the prior and decode  ->  x_new = dec(torch.randn(n, latent_dim))
flow_matching.py — learn a velocity field, integrate noise → data with Euler steps
Coral dots = noise x₀ (t=0). Teal blobs = data modes x₁ (t=1). Faint teal arrows = velocity field v(x,t); trails = the integrated transport.

Flow matching / rectified flow — generate by transporting noise along straight paths

Diffusion learns to denoise over dozens of stochastic steps. Flow matching instead learns a deterministic velocity field v(x,t)v(x,t)v(x,t) that transports a sample as time runs t:0→1t: 0 \to 1t:0→1, governed by the ODE dx/dt=v(x,t)dx/dt = v(x,t)dx/dt=v(x,t). We pick the simplest possible bridge between a noise sample x0x_{0}x0​ and a data sample x1x_{1}x1​ — a straight line: xt=(1−t)⋅x0+t⋅x1x_{t} = (1-t)\cdot x_{0} + t\cdot x_{1}xt​=(1−t)⋅x0​+t⋅x1​, whose conditional velocity is the constant u=x1−x0u = x_{1} - x_{0}u=x1​−x0​. The network is trained by regression (no likelihoods, no noise schedule): minE∥v(xt,t)−(x1−x0)∥2min E\|v(x_{t},t) - (x_{1}-x_{0})\|^{2}minE∥v(xt​,t)−(x1​−x0​)∥2. The field it learns is the marginal velocity v(x,t)=E[x1−x0∣xt=x]v(x,t) = E[ x_{1} - x_{0} | x_{t} = x ]v(x,t)=E[x1​−x0​∣xt​=x]. At sample time we just integrate it forward with explicit Euler steps: x←x+v(x,tk)⋅Δtx \leftarrow x + v(x,t_{k})\cdot \Delta tx←x+v(x,tk​)⋅Δt, Δt=1/steps\Delta t = 1/stepsΔt=1/steps.

This widget computes the exact marginal velocity in closed form (Gaussian noise → a weighted mixture of data modes), so the physics is real, not faked. Drag steps: with just 4–8 Euler steps the coral noise cloud already lands cleanly on the teal data modes — where diffusion needs dozens of denoising steps. That speed is the whole point: rectified flow (Liu 2022) and conditional flow matching (Lipman 2023) are the SOTA successors to diffusion and power Stable Diffusion 3, Flux and SiT. Because the paths are nearly straight (path-length ÷ chord ≈ 1), few-step integration barely strays from the true ODE solution. The catch lives at steps = 1: a single step lands at the prior mean E[x1]E[x_{1}]E[x1​] — the honest failure mode that motivates more steps or reflow. For OncoSeg this is the fast generative engine: synthesize realistic lesion appearances for augmentation, or sample plausible tumor masks as a segmentation prior, in a handful of forward passes — cheap enough to actually deploy.

💡 Why it mattersFlow matching trains a generative model by regressing a velocity field that moves samples along (nearly) straight ODE paths from noise to data, sidestepping the slow stochastic many-step sampling and tricky noise-schedule tuning of classic diffusion. Because the learned trajectories are close to straight lines, you can integrate the ODE in very few steps — or even one with rectified-flow "reflow" — giving high-quality samples at a fraction of the inference cost.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins today's leading text-to-image/video systems (Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX, Meta Movie Gen) and is increasingly used for fast image and protein/molecule generation, robot action policies, and speech synthesis; in medical imaging it drives few-step CT/MRI reconstruction, denoising, and modality translation where sampling speed matters.

▸ Code PyTorch — flow-matching training loss + Euler ODE sampling, what actually runs▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# v_theta(x, t): MLP/U-Net regressing the velocity field. x:(B,D), t:(B,1) -> (B,D)
def train_step(v_theta, x1, opt):           # x1: real data batch (B, D)
    x0 = torch.randn_like(x1)               # noise endpoint  x0 ~ N(0, I)
    t  = torch.rand(x1.size(class="n">0), class="n">1, device=x1.device)   # t ~ U(0,1)
    xt = (class="n">1 - t) * x0 + t * x1              # linear interpolant  x_t = (1-t)x0 + t x1
    u  = x1 - x0                            # conditional target velocity (constant along the path)
    loss = F.mse_loss(v_theta(xt, t), u)    # min E|| v(x_t,t) - (x1 - x0) ||^2
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return loss.item()

@torch.no_grad()                            # sample: integrate the ODE dx/dt = v(x,t), t: 0 -> 1
def sample(v_theta, n, D, steps=class="n">8, device=class=class="s">"s">class="s">'cuda'):
    x  = torch.randn(n, D, device=device)   # start from noise  x = x0
    dt = class="n">1.0 / steps
    for k in range(steps):                  # explicit (forward) Euler
        t = torch.full((n, class="n">1), k * dt, device=device)
        x = x + v_theta(x, t) * dt          # Euler update  x <- x + v(x, t_k)·Δt
    return x                                 # x ≈ data sample  x1
metrics.py — ROC curve & AUC (operating-point-free eval)
Left: score histograms (coral = tumor-positive voxels, blue = negatives) with the moving threshold t. Right: every threshold maps to one (FPR, TPR) point — the dot — and the swept locus is the ROC.

ROC & AUC: scoring a classifier without committing to a threshold

A model outputs a continuous score s∈[0,1] (e.g. p(tumor) per voxel). To make a hard call you pick a threshold t and predict positive when s≥ts \ge ts≥t. Two rates fall out: TPR=TP/(TP+FN)TPR = TP/(TP+FN)TPR=TP/(TP+FN) (sensitivity — caught positives) and FPR=FP/(FP+TN)FPR = FP/(FP+TN)FPR=FP/(FP+TN) (false alarms = 1−specificity). Slide t and the operating point (FPR,TPR)(FPR, TPR)(FPR,TPR) traces the ROC curve. Its area is AUC=∫01TPRd(FPR)AUC = \int _{0}^{1} TPR d(FPR)AUC=∫01​TPRd(FPR), which equals the ranking probability P(s+>s−)P(s^{+} > s^{-})P(s+>s−) — the chance a random positive outscores a random negative.

Move t: the dot slides along the curve, trading sensitivity for specificity, but the curve — and the AUC — never change. That is the point: AUC judges how well scores separate the classes, independent of where a clinician later sets the alarm. In OncoSeg a tumor/normal voxel head with AUC 0.5 is coin-flipping (diagonal); 1.0 perfectly ranks every positive above every negative. Raise class separation to watch the histograms pull apart and the curve bow toward the top-left corner.
0.50
0.55
💡 Why it mattersA ROC curve traces true-positive vs. false-positive rate across every possible decision threshold, and AUC summarizes that whole trade-off as one threshold-free number (the probability a random positive outscores a random negative), so you can rank and compare classifiers before deciding where to set the operating point. This matters most when the threshold depends on downstream cost or prevalence — e.g. a tumor screener tuned for high sensitivity vs. a confirmatory test tuned for specificity.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the default discrimination metric for medical-imaging diagnosis and CAD systems (radiology, dermatology, pathology, retinal screening — and a regulatory staple in FDA submissions), credit-risk and fraud scoring, and information-retrieval ranking; AUROC is reported by scikit-learn, TorchMetrics and MONAI, though on heavily imbalanced data practitioners increasingly pair it with the precision-recall curve / AUPRC.

▸ Code scikit-learn — what actually runs (plus the trapezoid + Mann–Whitney identities)▶
import torch
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score

# logits -> per-voxel p(tumor); flatten the volume to score every voxel
scores = torch.sigmoid(model(vol)).flatten().cpu().numpy()   # s in [0,1]
labels = mask.flatten().cpu().numpy().astype(int)            # 1 = tumor, 0 = normal

# idiomatic: sweep every threshold -> (FPR, TPR) locus + area under it
fpr, tpr, thr = roc_curve(labels, scores)                    # fpr ASCENDING (thr high->low)
auc = roc_auc_score(labels, scores)                          # AUC = integral TPR d(FPR)

# from scratch (the two formulas the widget animates):
# fpr is ascending, so the integral is already positive -> NO minus sign
auc_trapz = torch.trapz(torch.tensor(tpr), torch.tensor(fpr)).item()  # ∫ TPR d(FPR)

# AUC == P(random positive scored above random negative)  -> Mann–Whitney U
pos, neg = scores[labels == class="n">1], scores[labels == class="n">0]
wins = (pos[:, None] > neg[None, :]).sum() + class="n">0.5 * (pos[:, None] == neg[None, :]).sum()
auc_rank = wins / (pos.size * neg.size)                       # ties count as half a win

assert abs(auc - auc_trapz) < class="n">1e-6 and abs(auc - auc_rank) < class="n">1e-6  # three views, one number
metrics.py — precision / recall / F1 under class imbalance
Teal = PR curve (every threshold). Coral dot = current operating point; faint coral = the F1 iso-contour through it. Blue dashed = prevalence baseline.

Precision, recall & F1 — the right metric for rare tumour voxels

Move the decision threshold and a single classifier becomes many. Of the voxels it calls tumour, what fraction really is? — P=TP/(TP+FP)P = TP / (TP + FP)P=TP/(TP+FP). Of the voxels that truly are tumour, what fraction did it catch? — R=TP/(TP+FN)R = TP / (TP + FN)R=TP/(TP+FN). Raising the threshold trades recall away for precision; lowering it does the reverse. Their harmonic mean balances both: F1=2⋅P⋅R/(P+R)F1 = 2\cdot P\cdot R / (P + R)F1=2⋅P⋅R/(P+R), maximal only when neither is sacrificed.

The plot sweeps the threshold across the same two score distributions — abundant negatives, a 2% sliver of positives — and traces precision against recall. Drag the slider to ride the curve: at threshold 0 you flag everything (R = 1) but precision collapses to the prevalence (0.02); at threshold 1 precision → 1 but recall → 0. The coral dot is your operating point, the teal tick marks the F1 peak.

Under heavy imbalance, ROC lies by omission. A 2%-tumour scan gives AUROC ≈ 0.89 (looks excellent) while AUPRC ≈ 0.26 — because the huge true-negative mass makes the false-positive rate tiny even when false positives outnumber true positives. The PR curve's baseline is the prevalence, not 0.5, so it shows the real cost of crying "tumour" on healthy tissue. For rare-class segmentation like OncoSeg, F1 / Dice and the PR curve — not accuracy or ROC — are the honest scoreboard, and the operating threshold is tuned to the F1 peak (or the clinical precision/recall the use-case demands).
0.50
P = TP/(TP+FP)R = TP/(TP+FN)F1 = 2PR/(P+R)2% prevalence
💡 Why it mattersWhen tumour voxels are a tiny fraction of the volume, accuracy is misleading: a model that predicts "all background" scores >99% yet finds nothing. Precision, recall and their harmonic mean F1 ignore the dominant true-negatives and instead trade off missed lesions (recall) against false alarms (precision), making them the honest objective for class-imbalanced detection and segmentation.
▸ Where it’s usedStandard for evaluating medical segmentation and lesion detection (F1/Dice as the per-voxel reporting metric in BraTS, LiDC, KiTS challenges), and for any rare-event task such as fraud detection, defect inspection, information retrieval, and object detection where mAP is computed by integrating the precision-recall curve.

▸ Code sklearn precision_recall_curve + the TP/FP/FN counts behind one PR point▶
import torch
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score

# scores: model's P(tumour) per voxel (after sigmoid); y: 0/1 ground truth
scores = torch.sigmoid(logits).flatten()          # (N,) in [0,1]
y = labels.flatten().int()                          # (N,) ~2% positive

# sweep EVERY threshold; sklearn sorts scores desc & accumulates TP/FP
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(y.numpy(), scores.numpy())
# AP = sum_n (R_n - R_{n-1}) * P_n  (step-wise; NOT trapezoidal auc(rec,prec))
ap = average_precision_score(y.numpy(), scores.numpy())

# from-scratch at one threshold tau (what each curve point IS):
tau = class="n">0.5
pred = scores >= tau
tp = (pred & (y == class="n">1)).sum().float()
fp = (pred & (y == class="n">0)).sum().float()
fn = (~pred & (y == class="n">1)).sum().float()
P = tp / (tp + fp + class="n">1e-8)          # precision = TP / (TP + FP)
R = tp / (tp + fn + class="n">1e-8)          # recall    = TP / (TP + FN)
F1 = class="n">2 * P * R / (P + R + class="n">1e-8)    # harmonic mean — low if either is sacrificed

# F1-optimal operating point. prec/rec have len(thr)+1: last point is the
# synthetic (rec=0, prec=1), so [:-1] aligns with thr exactly.
f1_curve = class="n">2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec + class="n">1e-8)
tau_star = thr[f1_curve[:-class="n">1].argmax()]   # tune on a VALIDATION split, not 0.5 / test
metrics.py — Confusion matrix · recall (row) vs precision (column)
Rows = true class, columns = predicted. Teal diagonal = correct; coral off-diagonal = errors. R = recall (row), P = precision (column).

Confusion matrix: where the model mistakes which class

A 4-class tissue classifier (Background, Edema, Tumor Core, Enhancing) is scored by counting, for every true class i, how its NiN_{i}Ni​ voxels were predicted. Cell MijM_{ij}Mij​ = #(true=i, pred=j). The diagonal MiiM_{ii}Mii​ is correct; everything off it is an error. Two complementary scores read it in orthogonal directions: recall reads a row — Ri=Mii/ΣjMijR_{i} = M_{ii} / \Sigma _{j} M_{ij}Ri​=Mii​/Σj​Mij​ (of the real i's, how many did we catch?) — while precision reads a column — Pj=Mjj/ΣiMijP_{j} = M_{jj} / \Sigma _{i} M_{ij}Pj​=Mjj​/Σi​Mij​ (of everything we called j, how many were truly j?). Overall accuracy is the diagonal mass over the total: acc=ΣiMii/ΣijMijacc = \Sigma _{i} M_{ii} / \Sigma _{ij} M_{ij}acc=Σi​Mii​/Σij​Mij​.

Drop accuracy and watch each row's mass leak off the diagonal — counts don't vanish, they migrate into the cells the model confuses. Raise confusability and that leaked mass concentrates: errors collapse onto the most look-alike neighbor (Tumor Core ⇄ Enhancing here), exactly the failure radiologists fear. Notice the asymmetry — Background's huge support keeps its precision high even as recall falls, while the small Enhancing class loses both first. That is why OncoSeg reports per-region Dice/recall, never a single accuracy: a 90%-accurate model can still miss most of the enhancing tumor, and only the confusion matrix exposes which class it confuses for which.

💡 Why it mattersA confusion matrix breaks a single accuracy number into the full grid of true-vs-predicted classes, exposing which classes a model swaps (e.g. confusing benign tumor for malignant) so you can see directional, class-specific failures that aggregate metrics hide. It is the substrate from which precision, recall, specificity, and F1 are derived, and is essential under class imbalance where high accuracy can mask near-total failure on the minority class.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed everywhere classifiers are evaluated: triaging error patterns in medical imaging (tumor grading, diabetic-retinopathy and chest-X-ray screening, pathology), spam/fraud detection, and content moderation, where off-diagonal cells decide which mistakes are clinically or operationally acceptable. It also drives per-class debugging in large vision/NLP benchmarks and threshold tuning for deployment.

▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (bincount confusion matrix → recall/precision/accuracy)▶
import torch

C = class="n">4  # classes: BG, Edema, Core, Enh
true = labels.flatten()          # (N,) int64 in [0,C)
pred = logits.argmax(class="n">1).flatten()  # (N,) hard prediction per voxel

# Confusion matrix M[i,j] = #(true=i, pred=j) via one bincount over flattened pairs.
# This is exactly the count torchmetrics/mmseg use; row=true, col=pred.
idx = true * C + pred                                  # fold (i,j) -> single bin
M = torch.bincount(idx, minlength=C * C).reshape(C, C)  # (C, C) counts
# equivalent: M = torchmetrics.functional.confusion_matrix(pred, true, "multiclass", C)

diag = M.diag().float()                  # M_ii  = correct per class
recall    = diag / M.sum(dim=class="n">1)          # R_i = M_ii / Σ_j M_ij   (read a ROW)
precision = diag / M.sum(dim=class="n">0)          # P_j = M_jj / Σ_i M_ij   (read a COLUMN)
accuracy  = diag.sum() / M.sum()         # Σ_i M_ii / Σ_ij M_ij    (diagonal mass)

# Hardest off-diagonal mistake (true -> pred the model confuses most):
off = M.clone(); off.fill_diagonal_(class="n">0)
i, j = divmod(int(off.argmax()), C)      # e.g. Core -> Enh under high confusability
evaluate.py — bootstrap 95% CI on mean Dice
Top: the n=16 held-out per-subject Dice scores (the only data we have). Below: the bootstrap distribution of the mean as B resamples accumulate; teal band = 95% CI [2.5, 97.5] percentiles.

Bootstrap confidence interval — a number without error bars is a guess

You evaluate on n test subjects and report meanDice=0.81mean Dice = 0.81meanDice=0.81. But that single number is itself a random draw — run on a different 16 patients and you'd get something else. The nonparametric bootstrap (Efron, 1979) estimates that sampling spread using only the data in hand: draw a resample of size n with replacement from the scores, recompute the statistic θ^∗β=(1/n)⋅Σixi∗\hat{\theta }*_{\beta} = (1/n)\cdot \Sigma _{i} x_{i}*θ^∗β​=(1/n)⋅Σi​xi​∗, repeat B times, then read the empirical 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the {θ̂*₁…θ̂*ᵦ} as the 95% CI. The spread of that bootstrap cloud is the standard error: SE≈Σ(θ^∗β−θˉ∗)2/BSE \approx \sqrt{\Sigma (\hat{\theta }*_{\beta} - \bar{\theta }*)^{2} / B}SE≈Σ(θ^∗β​−θˉ∗)2/B​, which here tracks the textbook s/ns/\sqrt{n}s/n​.

This is the direct fix for the review's single-run, no-CI problem. OncoSeg headlines a point Dice and an ECE = 0.0101 computed from one subject and 5 MC samples, then claims significance — with no interval to say whether the gap survives sampling noise. Drag B: at B≈10 the CI jumps around wildly (Monte-Carlo noise ∝ 1/√B); by B≈1000–2000 it locks in at width ≈ 0.14. Note the percentile CI is asymmetric here — the low-Dice failure cases pull the left tail out — which a symmetric ±1.96·SE bar would hide. The cost is trivial: report 0.81[0.74,0.88]0.81 [0.74, 0.88]0.81[0.74,0.88] and the reader can judge the claim.

💡 Why it mattersA single point metric (Dice 0.87, AUC 0.91) hides how much it would swing on a different test set; the bootstrap resamples your existing predictions with replacement thousands of times to estimate that sampling variability, turning a bare number into a confidence interval. This is what lets you say whether model A genuinely beats model B or whether the gap is within noise — no parametric distribution assumption needed.
▸ Where it’s usedStandard practice for reporting 95% CIs and paired comparisons in medical-imaging challenges (segmentation Dice/HD95, detection AUROC) and clinical-AI papers, plus A/B test deltas, click-through rates, and ranking metrics in industry. Tools like scikit-learn, SciPy's bootstrap, and the MICCAI MetricsReloaded / challengeR pipelines build it directly into leaderboard and significance reporting.

▸ Code NumPy + SciPy — the percentile bootstrap that draws the teal CI band▶
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import bootstrap

# per-subject held-out Dice — the only data we have (n=16)
dice = np.array([class="n">0.91,class="n">0.88,class="n">0.94,class="n">0.62,class="n">0.85,class="n">0.79,class="n">0.93,class="n">0.55,
                 class="n">0.90,class="n">0.87,class="n">0.71,class="n">0.96,class="n">0.83,class="n">0.48,class="n">0.89,class="n">0.92])
theta_hat = dice.mean()                      # point estimate to report
B = class="n">2000                                      # # of bootstrap resamples
rng = np.random.default_rng(class="n">0)

# --- vectorized nonparametric bootstrap of the mean (Efron 1979) ---
# resample n scores WITH replacement, B times, recompute the statistic
idx   = rng.integers(class="n">0, dice.size, size=(B, dice.size))   # (B, n) indices in [0,n)
boot  = dice[idx].mean(axis=class="n">1)                            # θ̂*_b  per resample, shape (B,)
lo, hi = np.percentile(boot, [class="n">2.5, class="n">97.5])    # empirical 2.5/97.5 pctiles -> 95% PERCENTILE CI
se     = boot.std(ddof=class="n">1)                    # SE = spread of the bootstrap cloud

# scipy one-liner, SAME percentile method (note: scipy's *default* is BCa, which we
# override here). For skewed/small n, prefer method='BCa' (bias & skew corrected).
ci = bootstrap((dice,), np.mean, n_resamples=B, method=class=class="s">"s">class="s">'percentile',
               confidence_level=class="n">0.95, random_state=class="n">0).confidence_interval
# (manual vs scipy use independent RNG streams, so CIs match only up to MC noise)

print(fclass="s">"Dice = {theta_hat:.3f}  class="n">95% CI [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]  SE={se:.3f}")
evaluate.py — k-fold cross-validation
Top: dataset split into k folds; the coral fold is held out for validation this round, teal folds train. Bottom: per-fold scores with the mean line and ±1σ band.

k-fold cross-validation: an error bar for your score

Shuffle the data, cut it into k equal folds, then run k rounds: round i trains on the other k−1 folds and validates on fold i. Every sample is validated exactly once. The reported estimate is the average of the k held-out scores, with a spread: CV=(1/k)⋅ΣisiCV = (1/k)\cdot \Sigma _{i} s_{i}CV=(1/k)⋅Σi​si​ and σ=(1/(k−1))⋅Σi(si−CV)2\sigma = \sqrt{ (1/(k-1))\cdot \Sigma _{i} (s_{i} - CV)^{2} }σ=(1/(k−1))⋅Σi​(si​−CV)2​. The number you publish is CV±σCV \pm \sigma CV±σ, not a single lucky split.

On a single train/val split, a 200-patient oncology cohort can give a Dice that swings several points just from which patients landed in val. k-fold spends the whole dataset on evaluation: each patient is held out once, so the mean is a far more honest estimate and σ tells you how split-sensitive the model is. Crank k up and the folds get smaller, so each per-fold score gets noisier and σ across folds actually grows — k=5 or 10 is the standard bias/variance/compute sweet spot, not the σ-minimizer. That is why small medical datasets (like OncoSeg's tumor cohorts) report 5-fold CV rather than one split, and why a model-comparison claim without an error bar is not yet trustworthy.
5
1
💡 Why it mattersA single train/test split gives one point estimate whose value swings with the luck of the split, so you can't tell a real improvement from sampling noise. k-fold rotates every sample through the test set once, turning that single number into a mean ± standard deviation — an error bar that exposes variance, overfitting, and whether model A truly beats model B.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the default protocol for reporting Dice/accuracy in medical-imaging challenges and small-data regimes (e.g. nnU-Net's built-in 5-fold CV, MONAI pipelines), for hyperparameter search in scikit-learn, and for honest leaderboard scores on Kaggle and in any paper where a single split would be unreliable. Stratified and grouped variants keep class balance or prevent patient/site leakage across folds.
Cutting-edge / SOTAnnU-Net (DKFZ) — built-in 5-fold CVscikit-learn (StratifiedKFold / GroupKFold / cross_val_score)MONAI (Project MONAI)Optuna (cross-validated hyperparameter search)MLflow (experiment tracking of CV runs)
▸ Code scikit-learn — what actually runs (k-fold, Dice ± σ)▶
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold  # use GroupKFold/StratifiedKFold if patients/classes matter

def cross_validate(dataset, k=class="n">5, seed=class="n">0):
    # shuffle once, then cut into k nearly-equal folds (first n%k folds get +1); each sample held out once
    data = np.asarray(dataset, dtype=object)            # coerce list/paths -> fancy-indexable array
    kf = KFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    scores = []
    for fold, (train_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(kf.split(data)):
        model = train(data[train_idx])                  # fit on the k-1 training folds
        s = evaluate(model, data[val_idx])              # Dice on the held-out fold i -> s_i
        scores.append(s)
    scores = np.asarray(scores, dtype=float)
    cv  = scores.mean()                                 # CV = (1/k)*Sum_i s_i
    std = scores.std(ddof=class="n">1)                            # sigma = sqrt( Sum_i (s_i-CV)^2 / (k-1) )
    return cv, std, scores

cv, std, per_fold = cross_validate(cohort, k=class="n">5)
print(fclass="s">"Dice = {cv:.3f} +/- {std:.3f}  (per-fold: {np.round(per_fold,class="n">3)})")
# report CV +/- sigma, not one lucky split; std() uses ddof=1 for the sample (k-1) estimator
gradcam.py — where did the CNN look?
Left: input CT slice. Right: Grad-CAM overlay (teal = evidence FOR the chosen class; ⊕ marks the peak). Bottom: the K feature maps Aₖ and their gradient weights αₖ (teal αₖ>0, coral αₖ<0).

Grad-CAM — a saliency map of the class evidence

A CNN's last conv block emits K feature maps Aₖ(i,j) — each a spatial detector for some learned pattern (a lesion core, an organ, a bright rim). A global-average-pool + linear head then scores each class: yc=Σkwkc⋅GAP(Ak)y^{c} = \Sigma _{k} w^{c}_{k} \cdot GAP(A_{k})yc=Σk​wkc​⋅GAP(Ak​). Grad-CAM asks: how much does the class score rise if map Aₖ lights up? That is the gradient flowing back into the map, averaged over space: αk=(1/Z)Σij∂yc/∂Ak(i,j)\alpha _{k} = (1/Z) \Sigma _{ij} \partial y^{c}/\partial A_{k}(i,j)αk​=(1/Z)Σij​∂yc/∂Ak​(i,j) with Z=H⋅WZ = H\cdot WZ=H⋅W. For this GAP+linear head that average is exactly αk=wkc/Z\alpha _{k} = w^{c}_{k}/Zαk​=wkc​/Z. Weight every map by its αₖ, sum, and clip the negatives: Lc=ReLU(Σkαk⋅Ak)L^{c} = ReLU(\Sigma _{k} \alpha _{k}\cdot A_{k})Lc=ReLU(Σk​αk​⋅Ak​). The result is a coarse, conv-resolution heatmap of where the evidence for class c sits — upsample it onto the scan and you can literally point at the region the network used.

This is how you audit an OncoSeg-style model before it touches a patient. Slide through the classes: for Tumor core the heat collapses onto the lesion; for Peritumoral edema it jumps to the surrounding organ; for Healthy tissue it spreads to background. Same image, same maps — only the gradient weights αₖ change, and the localization follows. The ReLU matters: with it OFF you see the signed CAM, where coral cells are evidence against the class (negative αₖ on the lesion map). Turning ReLU ON keeps only what argues for the class — exactly Selvaraju et al. (2017). A map that lights up the right anatomy is reassuring; one that fires on a scanner artifact or table edge is a red flag you want to catch before deployment.
Tumor core
ReLU on
αₖ = wᶜₖ / ZZ = H·WLᶜ = ReLU(Σₖ αₖ·Aₖ)Σ rawCAM = yᶜcoral = evidence against
💡 Why it mattersDeep classifiers are black boxes: a CNN can output "malignant" with high confidence but give no reason. Grad-CAM solves this by weighting the last conv feature maps by the gradients of the target class flowing into them, producing a coarse heatmap that shows which pixels drove the decision — turning a scalar prediction into spatial evidence you can sanity-check, debug for shortcut learning, and present to a clinician without retraining or modifying the network.
▸ Where it’s usedStandard tool for sanity-checking and debugging image classifiers — exposing "shortcut" learning (e.g. a model keying on text overlays or rulers instead of pathology), localizing disease in chest X-rays, dermoscopy, and digital pathology for weakly-supervised localization, and producing the regulatory/clinical-trust heatmaps shown alongside CAD predictions. Widely used in deep-learning papers, the pytorch-grad-cam toolkit, and Captum/MONAI explainability pipelines.

▸ Code PyTorch — Grad-CAM via forward/backward hooks (what actually runs)▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

acts, grads, handles = {}, {}, []
model.eval()
target = model.layer4  # last conv block emitting K feature maps A_k
handles.append(target.register_forward_hook(lambda m, i, o: acts.__setitem__(class="s">"A", o)))
handles.append(target.register_full_backward_hook(lambda m, gi, go: grads.__setitem__(class="s">"g", go[class="n">0])))
try:
    logits = model(x)                       # x: (1,C,H,W) -> y: (1,n_classes)
    model.zero_grad()
    logits[class="n">0, c].backward()                 # seed grad of class-c score y^c only

    A = acts[class="s">"A"]                           # (1,K,h,w) feature maps A_k
    g = grads[class="s">"g"]                          # (1,K,h,w) = d y^c / d A_k(i,j)
    alpha = g.mean(dim=(class="n">2, class="n">3), keepdim=True)  # alpha_k = (1/Z) sum_ij d y^c/d A_k
    cam = F.relu((alpha * A).sum(dim=class="n">1))    # L^c = ReLU(sum_k alpha_k * A_k) -> (1,h,w)

    cam = F.interpolate(cam[:, None], size=x.shape[-class="n">2:],
                        mode=class="s">"bilinear", align_corners=False)  # upsample to input
    cam = (cam - cam.amin()) / (cam.amax() - cam.amin() + class="n">1e-8)  # -> [0,1]
    cam = cam.detach()                      # drop autograd graph for downstream use
finally:
    for h in handles: h.remove()            # avoid leaking/duplicating hooks
integrated_gradients.py — path integral from baseline x'
Left: input lesion patch x (teal = pixel value). Right: per-pixel IG attribution (coral = supports F). Track = the straight path x'→x; dots = the N gradient samples. Bar = Σᵢ IGᵢ filling toward the completeness target F(x)−F(x').

Integrated gradients — attribution that obeys an axiom

A raw saliency map ∂F/∂x is just the gradient at the input. But neurons saturate: once a feature is strong, its local gradient flattens to ~0, so the pixel that caused the prediction can get zero credit. Integrated Gradients fixes this by walking a straight line from a neutral baseline x' (a black image) to the input x and averaging the gradient all along the way:

IGᵢ = (xᵢ − x'ᵢ) · ∫₀¹ ∂F/∂xᵢ |x'+α(x−x') dα

The slider sets N, the number of Riemann samples approximating that integral: IGᵢ ≈ (xᵢ−x'ᵢ)·(1/N)·Σk=1..N ∂F/∂xᵢ|α=k/N. More steps ⇒ a finer sum ⇒ a sharper, more faithful map.

The killer property is completeness: summing the attributions returns the model's score gain exactly — ΣiIGi=F(x)−F(x′)\Sigma _{i} IG_{i} = F(x) - F(x')Σi​IGi​=F(x)−F(x′). With few steps the coarse sum undershoots (watch the coral bar fall short of the teal target and the gap shrink ~1/N as you slide right). For OncoSeg this is the difference between a heatmap a radiologist can trust — every unit of predicted tumor likelihood is accounted for by specific voxels — and a pretty-but-unverifiable saliency picture. IG needs only gradients (one backward pass per step), no architecture changes, which is why it is a default for auditing medical-imaging models.

axiomaticcompleteness Σ=F(x)−F(x')baseline = blackgradient-basedmodel-agnostic
💡 Why it mattersIntegrated Gradients solves the saturation and noise problems of raw gradient saliency by integrating gradients along a straight path from a neutral baseline to the input, giving a principled per-pixel/per-feature attribution that provably satisfies completeness (attributions sum to the model's output gap vs. the baseline) and other axioms like sensitivity and implementation invariance. This turns "where did the network look" from an unstable heatmap into an auditable, theoretically grounded explanation.
▸ Where it’s usedWidely used to explain deep classifiers and rank feature importance in vision, NLP, tabular, and genomics models; in medical imaging it highlights which voxels or regions drive a tumor/disease prediction, supporting model debugging, bias auditing, and regulatory documentation. It is a standard primitive in production XAI toolkits and is used in clinical-AI validation and computational-biology (e.g., DeepLIFT/IG attributions over DNA sequences).

▸ Code PyTorch + Captum — what actually runs▶
import torch
from captum.attr import IntegratedGradients

# Captum's DEFAULT IG uses the TRAPEZOID rule (method="riemann_trapezoid"),
# not a right Riemann sum -> reproduce that exactly so completeness holds.
ig = IntegratedGradients(model)
attr, delta = ig.attribute(x, baselines=x_base, target=cls,
                           n_steps=N, return_convergence_delta=True)
# delta ~ 0  <=>  Σ attr == F(x) - F(x')   (completeness axiom)

# --- exact from-scratch path integral (trapezoidal, matches Captum default) ---
alphas = torch.linspace(class="n">0.0, class="n">1.0, N).view(N, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1)   # BOTH endpoints, α∈[0,1]
path = x_base + alphas * (x - x_base)        # straight line x'->x, N samples
path.requires_grad_(True)
F = model(path)[:, cls].sum()                # one batched backward pass
g = torch.autograd.grad(F, path)[class="n">0]          # ∂F/∂(input) at each interpolated point
w = torch.full((N, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1, class="n">1), class="n">1.0 / (N - class="n">1))   # trapezoid weights, Σw = 1
w[class="n">0] *= class="n">0.5; w[-class="n">1] *= class="n">0.5                     # half-weight the endpoints
avg_grad = (g * w).sum(dim=class="n">0, keepdim=True)   # ≈ ∫₀¹ ∂F/∂x dα  (O(1/N²) accurate)
ig_map = (x - x_base) * avg_grad             # IGᵢ = (xᵢ−x'ᵢ)·∫ ∂F/∂xᵢ dα
torch.allclose(ig_map, attr, atol=class="n">1e-4)      # now True (right-Riemann was ~3e-3 off)
# If you instead want a RIGHT Riemann sum (linspace(1/N,1,N), simple mean),
# pass method="riemann_right" to ig.attribute and expect only O(1/N) agreement.
rollout.py — Attention rollout: tracing CLS → patch influence
Teal heatmap = how much the [CLS] token influences each patch after composing L layers. Coral ring = the object (tumor). Drag the slider to roll more layers.

Attention rollout: what a ViT is really looking at

A single layer's attention map A is misleading — every layer also passes information straight through its residual connection. Rollout corrects this: per layer it forms A~=12A+12I\tilde{A} = \tfrac12 A + \tfrac12 IA~=21​A+21​I (half attention, half identity), then composes layers by matrix multiplication: R = ÃL · ÃL−1 ⋯ Ã1. Because each A~\tilde{A}A~ is row-stochastic (rows sum to 1), so is R — the [CLS] row R[CLS,⋅]R[CLS, \cdot ]R[CLS,⋅] is a genuine probability distribution over input patches: "how much does each patch flow into the output token."

Watch the contrast: raw last-layer CLS attention smears across the image (≈30% on the tumor), but as you compose layers the rollout concentrates onto the object (≈66%). This is exactly how ViT/DINO/VLM saliency maps are made — and why a clinician-facing OncoSeg explanation should use rollout, not a single attention head, to claim "the model focused here." The CLS-row sum staying at 1.00 is your sanity check that nothing leaked.
8
💡 Why it mattersA single ViT attention map is misleading because information mixes across many layers and is dominated by residual (skip) connections, so raw attention does not show what actually reached the final prediction. Attention rollout (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020) recursively multiplies the per-layer attention matrices — adding the identity to account for residuals — to estimate how much each input patch ultimately influences the [CLS] token, yielding a far more faithful saliency map.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed to debug and audit ViT classifiers — checking whether a model attends to the lesion rather than scanner artifacts or text overlays in chest X-ray, histopathology, and dermatology models, and to localize objects weakly-supervised in DINO/DINOv2 self-supervised features. It is a standard sanity-check and figure-generation tool in vision-transformer research and in regulated medical-imaging model validation.
Cutting-edge / SOTAAttention Rollout (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020)Transformer Interpretability Beyond Attention Visualization / Chefer et al. CVPR 2021 (LRP + rollout)pytorch-grad-cam (jacobgil, ViT support)DINO / DINOv2 attention maps (Meta)Captum (PyTorch)Hugging Face Transformers (output_attentions)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (Abnar & Zuidema attention rollout)▶
import torch

# attns: list of L tensors [B, heads, N, N] — one softmaxed attention map per ViT block
# (grab them via forward hooks on each block's attn, or timm's attn_drop output)
def attention_rollout(attns):
    B, _, N, _ = attns[class="n">0].shape
    eye = torch.eye(N, device=attns[class="n">0].device).expand(B, N, N)
    R = eye.clone()                                   # identity = start of the chain
    for A in attns:
        A = A.mean(dim=class="n">1)                             # fuse heads: average over the head axis -> [B,N,N]
        A = class="n">0.5 * A + class="n">0.5 * eye                       # Ã = ½A + ½I : add the residual stream
        A = A / A.sum(dim=-class="n">1, keepdim=True)           # renormalize so each row stays a distribution
        R = A @ R                                     # compose layers: R_l = Ã_l · R_{l-1}  (matmul)
    return R                                          # row-stochastic; row i = how token i draws from inputs

R = attention_rollout(attns)                          # [B, N, N]
cls_saliency = R[:, class="n">0, class="n">1:]                            # CLS row, drop CLS->CLS -> mass over each patch
gh = gw = int(cls_saliency.shape[-class="n">1] ** class="n">0.5)
heatmap = cls_saliency.reshape(-class="n">1, gh, gw)            # fold patch tokens back to the 2-D image grid
# heatmap.sum() over patches ≈ CLS->CLS complement; the CLS row of R sums to 1.0 (sanity check)
pca.py — eigen-axes of the covariance & 1-D projection
Left: grey cloud, dashed 1-σ covariance ellipse, teal PC₁ / coral PC₂ (length = √λ), blue PC₁ rail, coral residual drops. Right: every point collapsed to its 1-D code z = PC₁·x; teal bar = variance kept.

PCA: rotate to the axes of maximum variance

Center the data, form the covariance Σ=(1/n)⋅Σi(xi−xˉ)(xi−xˉ)T\Sigma = (1/n)\cdot \Sigma _{i} (x_{i}-\bar{x})(x_{i}-\bar{x})^{T}Σ=(1/n)⋅Σi​(xi​−xˉ)(xi​−xˉ)T, then eigendecompose it: Σvk=λkvk\Sigma v_{k} = \lambda _{k} v_{k}Σvk​=λk​vk​. The eigenvectors v1,v2v_{1},v_{2}v1​,v2​ are the principal axes (orthogonal, sorted by λ); each eigenvalue λk\lambda _{k}λk​ is exactly the variance of the data measured along that axis. PC₁ is the single direction that captures the most spread — projecting onto it, z=v1T(x−xˉ)z = v_{1}^{T}(x-\bar{x})z=v1T​(x−xˉ), is the best 1-D summary of a 2-D point. Fraction kept = λ1/(λ1+λ2)\lambda _{1}/(\lambda _{1}+\lambda _{2})λ1​/(λ1​+λ2​); the discarded coral drop-lines are the reconstruction error PC₂ would have stored.

Rotate the cloud and watch the axes spin to follow it while λ₁, λ₂ and %-variance stay frozen — PCA is rotation-invariant, it finds intrinsic structure, not the coordinate frame you happened to use. Raise the aspect (make the blob round) and PC₁'s share collapses toward 50%: no preferred direction left to compress. This is the engine behind decorrelation and linear dimensionality reduction — the same trick that turns thousands of OncoSeg radiomic / deep features per lesion into a handful of variance-ranked components for visualization, denoising, and batch-effect removal before downstream response modeling.
20°
0.30
💡 Why it mattersPCA finds an orthogonal rotation of the data into directions (eigenvectors of the covariance) ordered by how much variance they capture, so you can compress, denoise, or visualize high-dimensional data while losing the least information. It turns correlated, redundant features into a few uncorrelated axes — solving the curse of dimensionality and exposing dominant structure that raw coordinates hide.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed everywhere as a preprocessing and exploratory step: 2D/3D visualization (often before t-SNE/UMAP), eigenfaces and image compression, genomics population-structure analysis (e.g. genotype PCA), and whitening features before clustering or regression. In medical imaging it underlies statistical shape/appearance models (active shape models), radiomics feature reduction, and denoising of MRI/CT and diffusion data.
Cutting-edge / SOTAscikit-learn PCA / IncrementalPCA / TruncatedSVD (randomized SVD, Halko et al.)PyTorch torch.pca_lowrank (randomized low-rank SVD, Halko et al.)UMAP / openTSNE (PCA-initialized embeddings)PCAngsd & PLINK --pca (genomics PCA)RAPIDS cuML PCA / IncrementalPCA (GPU)
▸ Code PyTorch — what actually runs (SVD of centered data = PCA)▶
import torch

# X: (n, d) feature cloud — e.g. flattened tumor-patch embeddings
Xc = X - X.mean(class="n">0, keepdim=True)                  # center: subtract the mean

# --- idiomatic: SVD gives the principal axes directly (no n*n covariance) ---
U, S, Vt = torch.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
components = Vt                                    # rows of Vt = eigenvectors of Σ
explained = S**class="n">2 / (S**class="n">2).sum()                    # var along PCk / total var

# --- from-scratch equivalent: Σ = (1/n)·Xcᵀ·Xc, then eigendecompose ---
# cov = Xc.T @ Xc / (Xc.shape[0] - 1)             # the d×d covariance matrix
# evals, evecs = torch.linalg.eigh(cov)           # ascending; PC1 = evecs[:, -1]
# (singular value Sₖ² = (n-1)·eigenvalue λₖ — same axes, same variances)

pc1 = components[class="n">0]                                # axis of maximum variance
z = Xc @ pc1                                       # 1-D code: project onto PC1 (z = PC1·x)
print(fclass="s">"variance kept by PC1: {explained[class="n">0].item():.class="n">1%}")
embedding.py — t-SNE / UMAP of a learned feature space
45 high-D vectors from 3 seeded clusters, mapped to 2-D. Watch points organize as the embedding optimizes. Within-cluster shape is meaningful; the empty space between clusters is not.

t-SNE / UMAP — neighborhoods, not distances

A deep encoder turns each image (or patch) into a high-D feature vector. To see that space we squash it to 2-D — but PCA only keeps global variance and smears overlapping clusters. t-SNE/UMAP instead preserve who is near whom. For each point t-SNE fits a Gaussian whose width σᵢ is tuned so its neighbor distribution hits a target perplexity: pⱼ|ᵢ = exp(−‖xᵢ−xⱼ‖²/2σᵢ²) / Σₖ exp(·). In 2-D it uses a heavy-tailed Student-t kernel qᵢⱼ ∝ (1+‖yᵢ−yⱼ‖²)⁻¹ and minimizes KL(P∥Q)=Σijpij⋅log(pij/qij)KL(P\|Q) = \Sigma _{ij} p_{ij}\cdot log(p_{ij}/q_{ij})KL(P∥Q)=Σij​pij​⋅log(pij​/qij​) by gradient descent. Perplexity ≈ the effective number of neighbors each point listens to.

This is how you sanity-check a frozen pathology foundation model (UNI, Virchow) or any OncoSeg encoder: embed thousands of patches, run t-SNE/UMAP, and look for cleanly separated clusters by tissue type — that means the features are linearly probe-able and a tiny head will work. Two traps to teach: (1) perplexity too small → clusters shatter into specks (you "see" structure that is just noise); too large (→ N) → distinct clusters merge. (2) The gap size between clusters and a cluster's overall position carry no metric meaning — never read "tumor is far from stroma, close to immune" off a t-SNE plot. Use it to spot batch effects and mislabels, not to measure distances.

💡 Why it mattersNeural-net feature spaces are too high-dimensional to inspect directly, and linear methods like PCA crush the local structure that matters. t-SNE and UMAP project embeddings to 2-3D by preserving each point's neighborhood (who is close to whom) rather than absolute distances, revealing clusters, manifolds, and outliers — but the price is that cluster sizes, inter-cluster gaps, and global geometry are not trustworthy and shift with perplexity/n_neighbors.
▸ Where it’s usedStandard for visually QA-ing learned embeddings — exploring CNN/ViT/DINOv2 feature spaces, sanity-checking class separation, and spotting label noise or batch effects. In medical imaging and biology it underpins single-cell RNA-seq atlases (Seurat, Scanpy), digital-pathology tile clustering, and inspecting tumor/radiomics feature embeddings before downstream modeling.

import torch
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
import umap  # pip install umap-learn

# Z: (N, D) features straight out of a frozen encoder (UNI / Virchow / your OncoSeg backbone)
Z = encoder(patches).flatten(class="n">1).detach().cpu().numpy().astype(class="s">"float32")  # e.g. (10000, 768)

# --- what practitioners actually run -------------------------------------
emb = TSNE(n_components=class="n">2, perplexity=class="n">30, metric=class="s">"euclidean",
           init=class="s">"pca").fit_transform(Z)                  # (N, 2) for plotting
emb_umap = umap.UMAP(n_components=class="n">2, n_neighbors=class="n">30, min_dist=class="n">0.1).fit_transform(Z)

# --- the core t-SNE objective the widget visualizes (toy: ONE shared sigma) ---
X = torch.tensor(Z); Y = torch.randn(len(Z), class="n">2, requires_grad=True)
D2 = torch.cdist(X, X) ** class="n">2                               # ‖xᵢ−xⱼ‖²
P  = torch.exp(-D2 / (class="n">2 * sigma**class="n">2)); P.fill_diagonal_(class="n">0) # Gaussian affinities (real t-SNE bisects a per-point σᵢ)
P  = P / P.sum(class="n">1, keepdim=True)                           # pⱼ|ᵢ: each row sums to 1
P  = (P + P.t()) / (class="n">2 * len(Z))                           # symmetrize CONDITIONALS → pᵢⱼ (sums to 1)
for _ in range(class="n">1000):
    Qn = class="n">1.0 / (class="n">1.0 + torch.cdist(Y, Y) ** class="n">2)             # Student-t kernel: qᵢⱼ ∝ (1+‖yᵢ−yⱼ‖²)⁻¹
    Qn.fill_diagonal_(class="n">0); Q = Qn / Qn.sum()
    loss = (P * (P.clamp_min(class="n">1e-12) / Q.clamp_min(class="n">1e-12)).log()).sum()  # KL(P‖Q)
    loss.backward(); Y.data -= class="n">200.0 * Y.grad; Y.grad = None            # toy GD on the 2-D layout
cluster.py — Lloyd's algorithm (k-means)
Left: points recolour by nearest-centroid assignment; bold × = centroids, faint trail = their migration. Right: inertia J falling each iteration.

k-means clustering — unsupervised grouping by similarity

Given points {xᵢ} and a chosen k, k-means seeks centroids {μⱼ} minimising the within-cluster scatter J = Σᵢ ‖xᵢ − μc(i)‖² (the inertia), where c(i)=argminj∥xi−μj∥c(i)=argmin_{j}\|x_{i}-\mu _{j}\|c(i)=argminj​∥xi​−μj​∥. There is no closed form, so Lloyd's algorithm alternates two cheap steps until labels stop changing: (1) assign every point to its nearest centroid, then (2) update each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it, μⱼ = (1/|Cⱼ|) Σi∈Cⱼ xᵢ. Each step can only lower (or hold) J — assignment minimises J for fixed μ, the mean minimises J for fixed labels — so the curve on the right is monotonically non-increasing and the method converges to a local optimum. Drag the iteration slider to watch points recolour and centroids slide from their seeded ring toward the blob centres.

This is the workhorse of unsupervised medical-imaging analysis: cluster voxels in a (T1, T2, FLAIR) intensity space to separate tissue types — CSF, grey/white matter, tumour core vs oedema — with no labels at all, a fast first pass before a supervised model like OncoSeg refines the boundary. Two caveats the widget makes visible: J always drops, so a lower J does not mean a better clustering — push k up and J keeps falling even past the 3 true blobs (over-segmentation); and the result depends on initialisation. Set k=3 (matching the data) for the cleanest, lowest-J solution.

💡 Why it mattersk-means partitions unlabeled data into k groups by iteratively minimizing within-cluster variance, giving a fast, scalable way to discover structure (color regions, tissue types, prototype "codewords") when no labels exist. It turns a vague "what natural groups are here?" question into concrete centroids you can threshold, recolor, or quantize against.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed for image color quantization and palette extraction, superpixel/region pre-segmentation, vector quantization for codebooks (VQ-VAE, RVQ in audio/image tokenizers), and customer/feature segmentation. In medical imaging it seeds intensity-based tissue clustering (e.g. brain MRI gray/white/CSF separation) and color-deconvolution clustering in digital pathology, often as a lightweight initializer before supervised models.

▸ Code PyTorch — Lloyd's two steps (assign + update), plus the sklearn one-liner▶
import torch
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# Idiomatic: scikit-learn runs Lloyd (+ k-means++ seeding) for you.
labels = KMeans(n_clusters=class="n">3, n_init=class="n">10).fit_predict(X.cpu().numpy())

# From scratch — the two alternating steps the widget animates:
def lloyd(X, k, iters=class="n">50):           # X: (N, D)
    mu = X[torch.randperm(len(X))[:k]].clone()    # seed k centroids (N,D)->(k,D)
    c  = torch.cdist(X, mu).argmin(class="n">1)             # initial assignment, (N,)
    for _ in range(iters):
        new_mu = torch.stack([                    # UPDATE: μⱼ = mean(C_j)
            X[c == j].mean(class="n">0) if (c == j).any() else mu[j] for j in range(k)
        ])
        mu = new_mu
        new_c = torch.cdist(X, mu).argmin(class="n">1)      # ASSIGN: c(i)=argminⱼ‖xᵢ−μⱼ‖
        if torch.equal(new_c, c): break           # labels stable -> converged
        c = new_c
    # c and mu are now mutually consistent (c = argmin against final mu),
    # so inertia J=Σ‖xᵢ−μ_c(i)‖² is the true objective at the returned solution.
    J = (X - mu[c]).pow(class="n">2).sum()                  # squared dists -> inertia (↓ each iter)
    return c, mu, J
infonce.py — pull the positive pair together, push negatives apart
Teal = anchor z (view A). Coral = positive z⁺ (view B, same image). Grey = negatives z⁻ⱼ (other images). Drag training step to watch them sort themselves on the unit circle.

InfoNCE: learning by comparison, with no labels

Take one image, make two random augmentations (crop, flip, jitter) — that is a positive pair. Every other image in the batch is a negative. An encoder maps each view to an L2-normalized embedding, so similarity is pure cosine: sim(u,v)=u⋅vsim(u,v) = u\cdot vsim(u,v)=u⋅v. The InfoNCE loss is a softmax cross-entropy that treats "which of these is my positive?" as an N+1-way classification: L=−log[exp(sim+/τ)/(exp(sim+/τ)+Σjexp(simj−/τ))]L = -log [ exp(sim^{+}/\tau ) / ( exp(sim^{+}/\tau ) + \Sigma _{j} exp(sim_{j}^{-}/\tau ) ) ]L=−log[exp(sim+/τ)/(exp(sim+/τ)+Σj​exp(simj−​/τ))]. Minimizing L pulls z and z⁺ together (numerator up) while pushing every z⁻ away (denominator down).

This is the engine behind SimCLR / MoCo and the self-supervised pretraining of modern foundation models — including medical-imaging encoders. With unlabeled MRI/CT/WSI, two augmented views of the same scan must agree while different patients are repelled, so the network discovers tissue, anatomy and texture structure before any radiologist label exists. A few annotated scans then fine-tune a tiny head — exactly how OncoSeg-style backbones get data-efficient. Temperature τ is the key knob: small τ sharpens the contrast (heavily penalizing hard negatives), large τ softens it (a hedged, lower-resolution comparison). Drag the training step and watch L collapse as the geometry sorts itself out.
30%
0.20

The denominator sums over the positive and all negatives, so InfoNCE is literally −logsoftmax(sim/τ)+-log softmax(sim/\tau )_{+}−logsoftmax(sim/τ)+​ — cross-entropy where the "correct class" is the matching view. Lower L ⇔ higher p(positive). With N negatives, a uniform-chance start gives L ≈ log(N+1)log(N+1)log(N+1).

L2-normalizedcosine = dotsoftmax(sim/τ)SimCLR · MoColabel-free
💡 Why it mattersInfoNCE lets a network learn useful representations without any labels: by pulling matched ("positive") views of the same example together and pushing apart "negatives", it turns a noise-contrastive softmax into a tractable lower bound on mutual information. This solves the cost and scarcity problem of annotation — critical in domains like medical imaging where expert labels are expensive and rare.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins self-supervised pretraining for vision (SimCLR/MoCo), image-text alignment (CLIP), and audio/video encoders, and is widely used to pretrain on large unlabeled medical-image archives (CT/MRI/pathology) before fine-tuning on small labeled sets. The same objective also trains modern text-embedding and retrieval models for semantic search and RAG.

▸ Code PyTorch — SimCLR NT-Xent: the InfoNCE loss that actually runs▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

def info_nce(z1, z2, tau=class="n">0.2):                 # z1,z2: (B,D) two augmented views of the same B images
    z = torch.cat([F.normalize(z1, dim=class="n">1),     # L2-normalize -> dot product IS cosine sim
                   F.normalize(z2, dim=class="n">1)], class="n">0)  # stack 2B embeddings
    sim = z @ z.t() / tau                       # (2B,2B) cosine sim / temperature = the LOGITS (tau applied here, once)
    sim.fill_diagonal_(float(class=class="s">"s">class="s">'-inf'))           # mask self-similarity -> exp(-inf)=0 drops it from the softmax denom

    B = z1.size(class="n">0)
    # for row i, the positive is its OTHER view: i<->i+B. Everything else (incl. other view's negatives) is a negative.
    targets = torch.arange(class="n">2 * B, device=z.device)
    targets = (targets + B) % (class="n">2 * B)           # -> [B..2B-1, 0..B-1]
    # NT-Xent / InfoNCE == softmax cross-entropy on the logits: -log( exp(sim[i,i+]) / sum_{j!=i} exp(sim[i,j]) )
    # NOTE: sim is ALREADY divided by tau, so cross_entropy must NOT divide again (do not write sim/tau here).
    return F.cross_entropy(sim, targets)        # mean over 2B rows; pulls z<->z+ together, pushes all z- apart

# usage in a SimCLR step:
# z1, z2 = encoder(aug(x)), encoder(aug(x));  loss = info_nce(z1, z2, tau=0.2);  loss.backward()
reinforce.py — ascend ∇θ J = 𝔼[∇θ log πθ(a)·R]
Top: reward landscape R(a) (teal) and the Gaussian policy π(a)=N(μ,σ²) (coral); ticks = sampled actions, size ∝ reward. Bottom: expected reward J(θ) rising over training.

Policy gradient: reward-weighted imitation of your own actions

A policy is a distribution over actions. Here it is a 1-D Gaussian πθ(a)=N(μ,σ2)\pi \theta (a)=N(\mu ,\sigma ^{2})πθ(a)=N(μ,σ2) with parameters θ=(μ,logσ)\theta =(\mu , log \sigma )θ=(μ,logσ). We want to maximize the expected reward J(θ)=𝔼a~πθ[R(a)]. The policy-gradient theorem gives a gradient we can actually estimate from samples: ∇θJ=E[∇θlogπθ(a)⋅R(a)]\nabla \theta J = \mathbb{E}[\nabla \theta log \pi \theta (a)\cdot R(a)]∇θJ=E[∇θlogπθ(a)⋅R(a)]. In words: sample an action, see its reward, then nudge θ to make high-reward actions more probable and low-reward actions less probable — reward-weighted imitation of your own behavior.

For a Gaussian policy the score function is exact: ∂logπ/∂μ=(a−μ)/σ2\partial log \pi /\partial \mu = (a-\mu )/\sigma ^{2}∂logπ/∂μ=(a−μ)/σ2 and ∂logπ/∂(logσ)=(a−μ)2/σ2−1\partial log \pi /\partial (log \sigma ) = (a-\mu )^{2}/\sigma ^{2} - 1∂logπ/∂(logσ)=(a−μ)2/σ2−1. Drag training step: the mean μ\mu μ climbs toward the high-reward action a∗a*a∗, and once reward concentrates near the mean the variance term goes negative so σ\sigma σ shrinks — the policy stops exploring and commits. The bottom curve is the true J=E[R]J=\mathbb{E}[R]J=E[R], rising from ≈0.08 to ≈0.94.

This is the seed of modern alignment and control. RLHF and its successors (PPO, GRPO) optimize a language policy with exactly this reward-weighted log-prob gradient, where R is a learned human-preference reward — it is how Claude-style assistants are tuned. The same update trains continuous robot policies. We subtract a baseline b=𝔼[R] (variance reduction, still unbiased: 𝔼[∇log π·b]=0) and use the exact expected gradient via Gauss–Hermite quadrature, so the trajectory is deterministic and the learning curve is reproducible — the discipline you'd want before letting a reward-tuned agent touch a clinical workflow.
