∇θ log πθ·RGaussian policybaseline b=𝔼[R]RLHF / PPO basis
💡 Why it mattersPolicy gradient directly optimizes a stochastic policy by sampling its own actions and re-weighting their log-probabilities by the reward (advantage) received, so it can learn from non-differentiable or sparse rewards where you cannot backprop through the objective. The "reward-weighted imitation" view makes it intuitive: upweight actions that paid off, downweight those that didn't, which is exactly how REINFORCE/PPO turn trial-and-error into a usable gradient signal.
▸ Where it’s usedIt powers RLHF/RLAIF alignment of LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Llama), robotics and game agents (OpenAI Five, locomotion), and increasingly RL-tuned reasoning models; in medical imaging it appears in RL-based view/slice selection, sequential lesion-detection agents, and reward-driven report generation where the metric (e.g. clinical-correctness or detection F1) is non-differentiable.
Cutting-edge / SOTAPPO (OpenAI)GRPO (DeepSeek-R1)TRL (Hugging Face)RLHF / InstructGPT (OpenAI)REINFORCE / RLOO (REINFORCE Leave-One-Out)verl (ByteDance)
▸ Code PyTorch — REINFORCE: the reward-weighted log-prob gradient that actually runs▶
import torch
from torch.distributions import Normal

# Gaussian policy π_θ(a)=N(μ,σ²); θ=(μ, log σ) are learnable params
mu, log_sigma = torch.zeros(class="n">1, requires_grad=True), torch.zeros(class="n">1, requires_grad=True)
opt = torch.optim.SGD([mu, log_sigma], lr=class="n">0.05)
reward = lambda a: torch.exp(-(a - class="n">1.6) ** class="n">2 / (class="n">2 * class="n">0.85 ** class="n">2))   # task reward R(a)

for step in range(class="n">60):
    pi = Normal(mu, log_sigma.exp())
    a = pi.sample((class="n">4096,))                     # sample actions a ~ π_θ
    R = reward(a)
    b = R.mean()                               # baseline b=𝔼[R]: variance reduction, still unbiased
    logp = pi.log_prob(a)                      # autograd gives the score ∇θ log πθ(a) for free;
                                               # by hand: ∂logπ/∂μ=(a-μ)/σ², ∂logπ/∂logσ=(a-μ)²/σ²−1
    loss = -(logp * (R - b).detach()).mean()   # REINFORCE: ascend 𝔼[∇θ log πθ(a)·(R−b)]
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
# μ climbs toward a*=1.6 and σ shrinks as the policy commits — the RLHF/PPO/GRPO core update
rl.py - Value Iteration / Q-learning
Teal fill = learned value V(s); arrows = greedy policy argmaxaQ(s,a)argmax_{a} Q(s,a)argmaxa​Q(s,a); coral = path from S to GOAL. Right: V(start) vs sweeps.

Value iteration on a gridworld

An agent in a grid wants to reach the GOAL (reward +1) and avoid the PIT (−1). It does not know the route in advance — it learns a value for every cell: V(s)V(s)V(s) = the expected discounted return from s if it acts optimally. Each sweep applies the Bellman optimality update V(s)←maxa[r(s,a)+γ⋅V(s′)]V(s) \leftarrow max_{a}[ r(s,a) + \gamma \cdot V(s') ]V(s)←maxa​[r(s,a)+γ⋅V(s′)], where the action-value is Q(s,a)=r+γ⋅V(s′)Q(s,a) = r + \gamma \cdot V(s')Q(s,a)=r+γ⋅V(s′) and the discount γ=0.90\gamma =0.90γ=0.90 makes far-off reward worth less. Start with V=0 everywhere. On sweep 1 only cells next to the GOAL learn a value; on each later sweep the value propagates one ring backward, so the teal heat fills outward from the goal. Slide the iteration count and watch the values flood the grid and the greedy arrows ↑↓←→\uparrow \downarrow \leftarrow \to ↑↓←→ snap into a coherent path. At convergence V(start)≈γ10=0.349V(start) \approx \gamma ^{10} = 0.349V(start)≈γ10=0.349 — exactly the discounted +1, ten steps away.

This is the backbone of value-based RL (Q-learning is the same update, but sampled from experience instead of swept over the known model). The lesson generalizes far past toy grids: reward propagates backward from outcomes, and the greedy argmax over learned values is the policy. In a clinical decision pipeline downstream of OncoSeg, you could frame treatment-response follow-up scheduling the same way — states = a patient's current tumor-burden / response status from the segmenter, actions = scan-now vs. wait vs. escalate, reward = catching progression early minus the cost/dose of imaging. Value iteration then yields a policy that looks ahead: it tolerates a small near-term cost (an extra scan) because the discounted future value of catching progression early is high — the same "route around the pit, accept a longer path to the goal" reasoning you see filling the grid here.

V(s) ← maxₐ[r + γV(s′)]π(s) = argmaxₐ Q(s,a)γ = 0.90V = Σₜ γᵗrₜ
💡 Why it mattersValue iteration solves a known Markov decision process exactly by repeatedly applying the Bellman optimality backup V(s) ← max_a Σ P(s'|s,a)[r + γV(s')] until the value function converges, yielding a provably optimal policy. It is the foundational dynamic-programming algorithm that makes the sequential credit-assignment problem (how to weigh delayed rewards under uncertainty) tractable, and it underpins the contraction-mapping guarantees that justify the whole family of TD/Q-learning and actor-critic methods used when the model is unknown.
▸ Where it’s usedBeyond classic gridworlds, the Bellman-backup principle drives modern RL used for robotic control and manipulation, treatment-policy optimization in healthcare (e.g., dynamic dosing and adaptive radiotherapy planning from imaging/EHR state), inventory and energy-grid scheduling, and game agents; in deep RL the same backup is amortized by neural value/Q-networks. In medical imaging specifically, MDP/value-based formulations appear in active landmark detection, sequential view planning, and learned scan/acquisition policies.

▸ Code PyTorch — vectorized Bellman sweep (V←maxₐ[r+γV(s′)]) + the sampled Q-learning TD update▶
import torch

gamma = class="n">0.90                                   # discount: far-off reward worth less
# R[s,a], P[s,a] -> s' for a known deterministic gridworld (what the widget sweeps)
R = torch.zeros(n_states, n_acts)              # reward r(s,a)
P = torch.zeros(n_states, n_acts, dtype=torch.long)  # next state s' = next(s,a)

# --- Value iteration: synchronous Bellman-optimality sweeps ---
V = torch.zeros(n_states)
for _ in range(sweeps):                        # each sweep propagates value one ring back
    Q = R + gamma * V[P]                        # Q(s,a) = r + gamma * V(s')   [S,A]
    V = Q.max(dim=class="n">1).values                     # V(s) <- max_a Q(s,a)  (Bellman opt. update)
    V[terminal] = class="n">0.0                           # absorb EACH sweep, else terminal self-bootstraps
policy = Q.argmax(dim=class="n">1)                        # greedy policy pi(s) = argmax_a Q(s,a)

# --- Q-learning: SAME update, sampled from experience instead of a known model ---
# on a transition (s, a, r, s') with no model, the TD target replaces the sweep:
nxt = class="n">0.0 if s2 in terminal else gamma * Q_table[s2].max()  # no bootstrap past a terminal s'
target = r + nxt                                # bootstrap off the next state's best action
Q_table[s, a] += alpha * (target - Q_table[s, a])   # move toward target (TD error)
recurrent.py — hₜ = tanh(Wₓxₜ + Wₕhₜ₋₁) vs LSTM gate
Top: the recurrent state unrolled L→R, color = stored signal magnitude. Bottom: how much of the cue at t=0 survives — coral = vanilla RNN (vanishes), teal = LSTM cell (carried by the gate).

Recurrence and the vanishing gradient — why gating mattered

A recurrent net reads a sequence one step at a time, folding each input into a single carried hidden state: ht=tanh(Wx⋅xt+Wh⋅ht−1)h_{t} = tanh(W_{x}\cdot x_{t} + W_{h}\cdot h_{t-1})ht​=tanh(Wx​⋅xt​+Wh​⋅ht−1​). To learn that something early in the sequence matters, the gradient must flow back through every step. One step back the Jacobian is ∂ht/∂ht−1=Wh⋅tanh′(zt)=Wh⋅(1−ht2)\partial h_{t}/\partial h_{t-1} = W_{h}\cdot tanh'(z_{t}) = W_{h}\cdot (1-h_{t}^{2})∂ht​/∂ht−1​=Wh​⋅tanh′(zt​)=Wh​⋅(1−ht2​), so the signal carried across t steps is the product ∏Wh⋅tanh′≈Wht∏ W_{h}\cdot tanh' \approx W_{h}^{t}∏Wh​⋅tanh′≈Wht​. Since tanh′≤1tanh' \le 1tanh′≤1 and usually |Wₕ|·tanh′ < 1, that product shrinks geometrically — the vanishing gradient. Drag the distance slider: the coral curve collapses to ~0 within a handful of steps.

The LSTM fixes this with a separate cell state and a forget gate: ct=ft⊙ct−1+it⊙c~tc_{t} = f_{t} \odot c_{t-1} + i_{t} \odot \tilde{c}_{t}ct​=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙c~t​, with ft=σ(Wf⋅[ht−1,xt])f_{t} = \sigma (Wf\cdot [h_{t-1},x_{t}])ft​=σ(Wf⋅[ht−1​,xt​]). Now the back-prop path through the cell is just ∂ct/∂ct−1=ft\partial c_{t}/\partial c_{t-1} = f_{t}∂ct​/∂ct−1​=ft​, so signal over distance t is ∏ft=ft∏ f_{t} = f^{t}∏ft​=ft — an additive, near-identity highway (the constant-error carousel). Push f→1f \to 1f→1 and the teal curve stays flat: information rides across hundreds of steps. The gate chooses what to keep instead of mangling it through a saturating tanh.

This is the sequence model that ruled before transformers, and the lesson generalizes to OncoSeg. A longitudinal study stacks many timepoints (baseline, follow-up, …) and a tumor's behavior at scan 1 must still inform the response call at scan 6; a naive recurrence would forget it. Gating — keep an additive memory path whose per-step multiplier is ≈1 — is the same trick that residual/skip connections use in the U-Net (demo 11) and that self-attention later replaced entirely by letting any step read any other directly (∝N²). Knowing why gating was needed is why attention was the breakthrough it was.

💡 Why it mattersVanilla RNNs apply the same recurrent weight at every step, so gradients backpropagated through long sequences shrink (or blow up) geometrically — the vanishing/exploding gradient problem — making it nearly impossible to learn long-range dependencies. Gating (LSTM/GRU) adds learned multiplicative gates and an additive cell state so gradients can flow unattenuated across hundreds of steps, which is what made deep sequence learning practical.
▸ Where it’s usedGated recurrence powered a decade of speech recognition, machine translation, and time-series forecasting, and still appears in low-latency/streaming and on-device settings where attention's quadratic cost hurts. In medical imaging it underlies modeling of longitudinal scans and clinical time series (e.g. ICU vitals, ECG/EEG), and the same vanishing-gradient lessons now drive modern linear-state-space sequence models used for long signals and even 3D volumetric slices.

▸ Code PyTorch — nn.LSTM (what runs) + the gate update it visualizes▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn

# Idiomatic: cuDNN-fused LSTM. x:(B,L,D) -> out:(B,L,H), c_n carries the cell state.
lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size=class="n">8, hidden_size=class="n">16, num_layers=class="n">1, batch_first=True)
out, (h_n, c_n) = lstm(torch.randn(class="n">4, class="n">50, class="n">8))   # out=(4,50,16), h_n/c_n=(1,4,16)

# From scratch — one timestep, exposing the gates the widget animates:
def lstm_step(x_t, h, c, Wf, Wi, Wg, Wo):
    z = torch.cat([h, x_t], dim=-class="n">1)                 # [h_{t-1}, x_t]
    f = torch.sigmoid(z @ Wf)                       # forget gate  f_t = σ(W_f·[h,x])
    i = torch.sigmoid(z @ Wi)                       # input gate   i_t
    g = torch.tanh(z @ Wg)                          # candidate    c̃_t
    o = torch.sigmoid(z @ Wo)                       # output gate
    c = f * c + i * g                               # c_t = f_t⊙c_{t-1} + i_t⊙c̃_t  <-- additive highway
    h = o * torch.tanh(c)                           # ∂c_t/∂c_{t-1} = f_t, so signal over t steps ≈ f^t
    return h, c                                      # f→1 ⇒ constant-error carousel, no vanishing grad
# vs vanilla RNN: h = tanh(W_x·x_t + W_h·h_{t-1}); ∂h_t/∂h_{t-1}=W_h·diag(1-h²) ⇒ ∏ shrinks → 0
temperature_scaling.py — one knob fixes the over-confidence ECE diagnosed
Reliability diagram. Bars = observed accuracy per confidence bin; ticks = claimed confidence. Diagonal = perfectly calibrated.

Temperature scaling — the post-hoc fix for over-confidence

The calibration widget showed the foreground is badly over-confident. The fix is one scalar. Before the softmax, divide every logit by a temperature T>0T > 0T>0: p=softmax(z⁄T)p = softmax(z ⁄ T)p=softmax(z⁄T). Because dividing all logits by the same positive number cannot change which logit is largest, the prediction — and therefore the accuracy — is left exactly unchanged. Only the spread of the probabilities moves: T>1T > 1T>1 softens the distribution toward uniform (lower confidence), T < 1 sharpens it. We fit the single T that minimizes ECE=Σk(nk⁄N)⋅∣confk−acck∣ECE = \Sigma _{k} (n_{k} ⁄ N)\cdot |conf_{k} - acc_{k}|ECE=Σk​(nk​⁄N)⋅∣confk​−acck​∣ on a held-out set.

This is the one-line remedy for OncoSeg's flagged ECE finding. At T=1T = 1T=1 the confidence ticks float above the accuracy bars — the model says 0.93 but is right 0.79 of the time. Slide T up and the ticks settle onto the diagonal, ECE → its minimum, while the headline accuracy never moves. It is a single post-hoc parameter (no retraining, no extra labels) — exactly what you want to ship after deployment when validation reveals a model is over-sure.
1.00
p = softmax(z ⁄ T)argmax invariantaccuracy fixedfit T to min NLL/ECEpost-hoc, no retrain
💡 Why it mattersModern deep nets and segmentation models are systematically over-confident — their softmax probabilities (e.g. 99%) far exceed their true accuracy — which makes those scores unsafe for thresholding, triage, or downstream decisions. Temperature scaling divides the logits by a single scalar T learned on a held-out set, recalibrating confidence so it matches observed accuracy without touching the model's predictions or retraining.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the default post-hoc calibration step before any confidence-gated pipeline — selective prediction / abstention, risk-based triage of scans, active-learning acquisition, and out-of-distribution detection — and is widely used to calibrate medical-imaging classifiers and segmentation networks so per-voxel/per-lesion confidence is trustworthy for clinical review. The same trick recalibrates LLM token probabilities and is the knob behind sampling "temperature" in text generation.

▸ Code PyTorch — Guo et al. 2017: a single learned temperature, fit by minimizing held-out NLL▶
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class TemperatureScaler(nn.Module):
    class="s">""class="s">"Guo et al. class="n">2017 — one scalar T learned post-hoc on a held-out set."class="s">""
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.log_T = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(class="n">1))   # T = exp(log_T) > 0, starts at 1

    def forward(self, logits):                       # returns SCALED LOGITS z/T (not probs)
        return logits / self.log_T.exp()             # argmax(z/T) == argmax(z): accuracy unchanged

# Fit T by minimizing NLL on validation logits (the model is frozen).
val_logits, val_labels = collect_logits(model, val_loader)   # (N, K), (N,)
scaler = TemperatureScaler()
opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([scaler.log_T], lr=class="n">0.05, max_iter=class="n">60)

def closure():
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = F.cross_entropy(scaler(val_logits), val_labels)   # cross_entropy applies log_softmax(z/T)
    loss.backward()
    return loss

opt.step(closure)
print(class="s">"learned T =", scaler.log_T.exp().item())             # > 1 ⇒ was over-confident
# Inference: softmax is applied HERE, once, on the scaled logits:
# calibrated_probs = scaler(test_logits).softmax(dim=1)
conformal.py — split conformal: calibrate q̂, emit a prediction SET
Top: calibration score histogram with the q̂ threshold (teal line). Bottom: prediction sets {y : s(x,y) ≤ q̂} for sample test cases.

Conformal prediction — a distribution-free coverage guarantee

Instead of one label, output a set that provably contains the truth at least 1−α1 - \alpha 1−α of the time — with no assumption on the model or the data distribution, only that calibration and test points are exchangeable. Define a nonconformity score s(x,y)s(x, y)s(x,y) (here s=1−p^ys = 1 - \hat{p}_ys=1−p^​y​, the softmax gap). On a held-out calibration set of n scores, take the conformal quantile q^=s(k)\hat{q} = s_(k)q^​=s(​k) with k=⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉k = \lceil (n + 1)(1 - \alpha )\rceil k=⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉. At test time emit C(x)=y:s(x,y)≤q^C(x) = {y : s(x, y) \le \hat{q}}C(x)=y:s(x,y)≤q^​.

The marginal guarantee is exact and finite-sample: P(ytest∈C(xtest))≥1−αℙ(y_test ∈ C(x_test)) \ge 1 - \alpha P(yt​est∈C(xt​est))≥1−α. Raise the target coverage and watch q̂ climb, the prediction sets swell, and the achieved coverage track 1−α1 - \alpha 1−α — never a fitted promise, an audited one.

For a clinical segmentation/triage model, a bare top-1 label hides when the model is unsure. A conformal set that says "this voxel is {tumor, edema}" with a guaranteed 95% coverage tells the radiologist exactly when to look twice — and the guarantee holds even under the silent distribution shift between scanners, which is precisely where naive softmax confidence lies.

distribution-freeq̂ = s_(⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉)set = {y : s ≤ q̂}finite-sample valid
💡 Why it mattersConformal prediction wraps any trained model with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees: instead of a single point prediction it emits a set (or interval) that provably contains the true label with probability ≥1−α, no matter how miscalibrated or black-box the underlying model is. This turns raw, often overconfident softmax scores into rigorous, actionable uncertainty — letting a system flag ambiguous cases for human review rather than silently committing to a wrong answer.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is used wherever a coverage guarantee is needed on top of deep nets — medical imaging triage (flagging scans where a tumor classifier's prediction set is large/ambiguous for radiologist review), drug discovery and tabular risk models, LLM output filtering and selective question-answering, and time-series/regression intervals in forecasting and finance. In segmentation and detection it yields calibrated pixel- or box-level confidence and risk-controlled false-negative rates (e.g., conformal risk control).

▸ Code PyTorch — split conformal classification (LAC score): calibrate q̂, build the set, audit coverage▶
import torch

# probs_cal: (n, K) softmax on a HELD-OUT calibration set; y_cal: (n,) true labels
# Nonconformity score (LAC / "least ambiguous"): s = 1 - p_hat[true class]
def conformal_qhat(probs_cal, y_cal, alpha=class="n">0.10):
    n = probs_cal.shape[class="n">0]
    scores = class="n">1.0 - probs_cal[torch.arange(n), y_cal]   # (n,) realized true-class gap
    # conformal quantile: the k-th smallest score, k = ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))
    k = int(torch.ceil(torch.tensor((n + class="n">1) * (class="n">1 - alpha))).item())
    k = min(k, n)                                       # k>n -> include everything
    return torch.sort(scores).values[k - class="n">1]            # q_hat  (distribution-free!)

def prediction_sets(probs_test, q_hat):
    # set per row = every class whose score is <= q_hat  ->  C(x) = {y : 1 - p_y <= q_hat}
    return (class="n">1.0 - probs_test) <= q_hat                  # (m, K) boolean membership mask

# --- calibrate, predict, then AUDIT the marginal coverage guarantee ---
q_hat = conformal_qhat(probs_cal, y_cal, alpha=class="n">0.10)    # target coverage 1 - alpha = 0.90
sets  = prediction_sets(probs_test, q_hat)              # (m, K)
covered  = sets[torch.arange(len(y_test)), y_test]      # was the TRUE label kept?
print(class="s">"achieved coverage:", covered.float().mean().item())  # >= 1 - alpha, finite-sample
print(class="s">"mean set size   :", sets.float().sum(class="n">1).mean().item())  # grows as coverage rises
deep_ensemble.py — average N independent nets
Thin teal curves = N independently-trained members. Bold teal = their mean. Coral band = ±1σ member disagreement = epistemic uncertainty. Where the training data lives (shaded), members agree; off to the sides they fan out.

Deep ensembles — N nets vote, and their disagreement is free uncertainty

Train the same architecture N times from different random seeds; each lands in a different minimum, so each is a slightly different function fm(x)f_m(x)fm​(x). The prediction is just their average fˉ(x)=(1/N)Σmfm(x)\bar{f}(x) = (1/N) \Sigma _m f_m(x)fˉ​(x)=(1/N)Σm​fm​(x). Because the members are roughly independent at a fixed input, the variance of that average shrinks: Var[fˉ]=σ2/NVar[\bar{f}] = \sigma ^{2}/NVar[fˉ​]=σ2/N, so the mean curve sharpens as N grows while its standard error falls like σ/N\sigma /\sqrt{N}σ/N​.

The spread σ(x)=(1/N)Σm(fm(x)−fˉ(x))2\sigma (x) = \sqrt{ (1/N) \Sigma _m (f_m(x) - \bar{f}(x))^{2} }σ(x)=(1/N)Σm​(fm​(x)−fˉ​(x))2​ is the bonus: where the training data constrains the fit, every member agrees and σ\sigma σ ≈ 0; out where there is no data, the members are free to disagree and σ\sigma σ blows up. That growing band is a calibrated epistemic ("I haven't seen this") uncertainty estimate — for free, with no extra labels.

In OncoSeg this is the difference between a model that silently mis-segments a scanner/contrast it never trained on and one that flags it. An ensemble of 3–5 segmentation nets gives (a) a sharper, better-calibrated mean mask than any single net, and (b) a per-voxel disagreement map that lights up on out-of-distribution anatomy — a deployment safety signal a radiologist can triage. It is the standard strong baseline that MC-Dropout (cheaper, one net, many forward passes) only approximates.

💡 Why it mattersA single neural net gives a confident point prediction even when it's wrong, with no honest sense of "I don't know." Training N independently-initialized nets and averaging their softmax outputs both improves accuracy and yields calibrated predictive uncertainty for free: where the members disagree, the model is unsure — which is exactly what you want before flagging an ambiguous tumor margin to a radiologist or rejecting an out-of-distribution input.
▸ Where it’s usedDeep ensembles are a default baseline for predictive uncertainty in safety-critical settings — medical image segmentation/classification (e.g., flagging low-agreement lesion boundaries in MONAI/nnU-Net pipelines), autonomous driving and weather/climate emulators — and remain the strongest method on out-of-distribution detection and uncertainty benchmarks despite needing N× the compute.

▸ Code PyTorch — train N independent nets, average their probabilities, and read disagreement as epistemic uncertainty▶
import torch

# 1) Train N copies of the SAME architecture, each from a different seed.
members = []
for seed in range(N):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)            # different init -> different minimum
    net = build_model()                # e.g. your 3D U-Net (sigmoid head)
    train(net, loader)                 # ordinary training; nothing special
    members.append(net.eval())

# 2) Predict = average per-member probabilities. OncoSeg is multi-LABEL
#    (BCEWithLogitsLoss + sigmoid; channels are independent, do NOT sum to 1),
#    so use sigmoid here, NOT softmax (softmax would be the inference.py bug;
#    for a 1-channel head it collapses every voxel to 1.0).
@torch.no_grad()
def ensemble_predict(x):
    probs = torch.stack([m(x).sigmoid() for m in members])   # (N, B, C, ...)
    mean  = probs.mean(class="n">0)              # ensemble prediction  f_bar
    # member disagreement = predictive std ACROSS members = epistemic uncertainty.
    # This does NOT shrink with N; it converges to the true disagreement.
    epi   = probs.std(class="n">0, unbiased=False)                     # large off-distribution
    # The MEAN's own std error DOES shrink: sem = epi / sqrt(N)  (Var[mean]=sigma^2/N).
    sem   = epi / (len(members) ** class="n">0.5)
    return mean, epi, sem
inference.py — test-time augmentation: predict K views, invert, average
Left: one raw view — wobbly boundary. Right: the K-view average — the edge smooths as K rises.

Test-time augmentation — a free accuracy boost

Run the same model on K augmented copies of the scan (flips / 90° rotations), undo each augmentation to bring the masks back into the original frame, then average the per-voxel probabilities: pˉ(x)=(1/K)ΣkTk−1⋅model(Tk⋅x)\bar{p}(x) = (1/K) \Sigma _{k} T_{k}^{-1}\cdot model(T_{k}\cdot x)pˉ​(x)=(1/K)Σk​Tk−1​⋅model(Tk​⋅x). The final mask is pˉ(x)>12\bar{p}(x) > \tfrac12 pˉ​(x)>21​.

Each view's boundary error is a different, roughly mean-zero wobble — the model is fragile in a different direction per orientation. Because those errors are uncorrelated across views, averaging cancels them: the variance of the mean error falls like σ2/K\sigma ^{2}/Kσ2/K. The interior (high-confidence) stays put; only the noisy edge gets cleaned. For OncoSeg this is a no-retrain, no-extra-labels Dice bump at test time — you pay only K× inference.
1
flips + 90° rotinvert each augaverage probserrors cancel ∝ 1/Kno retrain
💡 Why it mattersTest-time augmentation runs the trained model on several transformed copies of each input (flips, rotations, multi-crops, multi-scale) and averages the predictions, smoothing out spurious sensitivity to orientation or scale to gain accuracy and better-calibrated confidence with no retraining. It is one of the cheapest reliability levers available: a pure inference-time trick that often recovers a percent or two of Dice/accuracy and reduces variance on the exact decision a clinician or downstream system will act on.
▸ Where it’s usedStandard in medical-image segmentation pipelines (nnU-Net applies mirroring TTA by default, MONAI ships TTA inferers) and a routine final-percent trick in Kaggle/ImageNet leaderboards and product CV stacks. The same averaging idea underpins ensembling and connects to uncertainty estimation, where the spread across augmentations serves as a cheap predictive-confidence signal.

▸ Code PyTorch / MONAI — what actually runs at test time: predict K augmented views, invert each augmentation, average the masks▶
import torch

# TTA for 3D seg: predict K augmented views, invert each aug, average probs.
# x: (B, C, D, H, W). Each transform must be exactly invertible (flip / 90deg rot).
def tta_predict(model, x, K=class="n">8):
    # (forward_aug, inverse_aug) pairs; dihedral views of the in-plane (H, W) axes.
    views = [
        (lambda t: t,                            lambda t: t),                              # identity
        (lambda t: t.flip(-class="n">1),                   lambda t: t.flip(-class="n">1)),                     # flip W
        (lambda t: t.flip(-class="n">2),                   lambda t: t.flip(-class="n">2)),                     # flip H
        (lambda t: t.flip(-class="n">3),                   lambda t: t.flip(-class="n">3)),                     # flip D
        (lambda t: torch.rot90(t,  class="n">1, (-class="n">2, -class="n">1)), lambda t: torch.rot90(t, -class="n">1, (-class="n">2, -class="n">1))),   # +90
        (lambda t: torch.rot90(t,  class="n">2, (-class="n">2, -class="n">1)), lambda t: torch.rot90(t, -class="n">2, (-class="n">2, -class="n">1))),   # 180
        (lambda t: torch.rot90(t,  class="n">3, (-class="n">2, -class="n">1)), lambda t: torch.rot90(t, -class="n">3, (-class="n">2, -class="n">1))),   # 270
        (lambda t: t.flip(-class="n">1).flip(-class="n">2),          lambda t: t.flip(-class="n">2).flip(-class="n">1)),            # flip W+H
    ][:K]                                          # use exactly K views (matches slider 1..8)
    prob = class="n">0.0
    for aug, inv in views:                         # K forward passes, model unchanged
        prob = prob + inv(model(aug(x)).sigmoid()) # predict, undo aug, accumulate probs
    prob = prob / len(views)                       # p_bar = (1/K) * sum_k T_k^-1 . model(T_k . x)
    return prob                                     # uncorrelated per-view errors partly cancel; threshold downstream
kv_cache.py — autoregressive decode: store past K/V, do O(n) work per token
Top: the cached K/V matrix — one row per past token. Cache ON: rows are stored and reused (teal). Cache OFF: every row is re-projected from scratch each step (coral). Bottom: total K/V projections ∝ N² without a cache vs ∝ N with one.

KV-cache: why long-context LLM decoding is feasible

An LLM generates one token at a time. To produce token t, its query must attend over the keys and values of all t previous tokens. Naively, you recompute every past key and value at every step, so step t redoes work proportional to t, and the whole generation costs Σₜ₋₁ⁿ t = n(n+1)/2 = O(n²) projections.

The KV-cache stores each token's K,VK,VK,V the first (and only) time they are computed. Generating a new token then projects just one new K,VK,VK,V row, appends it, and attends over the n cached entries — so the projection work over the whole sequence collapses to n=O(n)n = O(n)n=O(n). The cost gap is exactly the wasted recompute the cache removes: n(n+1)/2 ÷ n = (n+1)/2, a saving that grows linearly with context length.

Why it matters here: long-context inference — a radiology report grounded on a longitudinal imaging series, or an OncoSeg report generator narrating findings across baseline and follow-up scans — emits thousands of tokens. Without the cache, decode cost is quadratic in the generated length and per-token latency climbs without bound; with it, each new token is roughly constant-extra work and the model streams in real time on a single GPU. The cached K/V also dominates serving memory, which is why paged/quantized KV-caches (vLLM PagedAttention) exist.
10
O(n) per tokenno recomputeappend-only K,Vlong-context decode
💡 Why it mattersDuring autoregressive decoding, each new token attends to all previous tokens; without caching, every step would recompute the keys and values for the entire prefix, making generation cost grow quadratically with sequence length. The KV-cache stores those per-layer key/value tensors so each step does only O(1) new work, turning long-context generation from quadratic to linear and making it the dominant memory consumer (and thus the main bottleneck and batching constraint) at serving time.
▸ Where it’s usedIt underpins essentially every production LLM chat and code assistant (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot) and every long-context use case — RAG over long documents, multi-turn agents, and processing large medical reports or radiology findings — where serving systems optimize cache layout (paged/quantized KV, prefix sharing) to fit more concurrent users and longer prompts on the same GPUs.

▸ Code PyTorch / HuggingFace — DynamicCache + use_cache=True, and the append-then-SDPA recurrence it fuses per layer▶
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, DynamicCache

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(class="s">"meta-llama/Llama-class="n">3.2-1B").eval()

@torch.no_grad()
def generate(input_ids, n_new):                  # KV-cache path: O(n) work / step
    cache = DynamicCache()                        # holds past K,V for every layer
    out = model(input_ids, past_key_values=cache, use_cache=True)  # prefill
    generated = []
    for _ in range(n_new):
        next_id = out.logits[:, -class="n">1:].argmax(-class="n">1)   # greedy next token, shape (B,1)
        generated.append(next_id)
        # Feed ONLY the new token; K,V of all prior tokens are READ from `cache`
        # (mutated in place) -> one new K,V row per step.
        out = model(next_id, past_key_values=cache, use_cache=True)
    return torch.cat(generated, dim=-class="n">1)

# Honest no-cache baseline: use_cache=False AND re-feed the WHOLE prefix each step,
# which re-projects all t tokens -> sum_t t = n(n+1)/2 = O(n^2) work. (Just
# flipping use_cache=False while feeding 1 token would be WRONG, not quadratic.)
@torch.no_grad()
def generate_no_cache(input_ids, n_new):
    seq = input_ids
    for _ in range(n_new):
        out = model(seq, use_cache=False)         # recompute K,V for all tokens
        seq = torch.cat([seq, out.logits[:, -class="n">1:].argmax(-class="n">1)], dim=-class="n">1)
    return seq[:, input_ids.shape[-class="n">1]:]
speculative_decoding.py — draft proposes k, target verifies in one pass
Green ✓ = accepted prefix · coral ✗ = first mismatch (resampled by the target) · faded = discarded. The whole block is checked in one parallel target pass.

Speculative decoding: a cheap draft guesses, the target only checks

Plain autoregressive generation calls the big model once per token, serially — the GPU is memory-bound and mostly idle. Speculative decoding lets a small fast draft model propose k tokens, then the target model scores all k+1k+1k+1 positions in a single parallel forward pass (same cost as decoding one token) and accepts the longest correct prefix. Each draft token is accepted with probability min(1,ptarget(t)/qdraft(t))min(1, p_target(t) / q_draft(t))min(1,pt​arget(t)/qd​raft(t)); at the first rejection the target resamples from the adjusted residual (ptarget−qdraft)+(p_target - q_draft)_{+}(pt​arget−qd​raft)+​. That rejection-sampling rule makes the emitted text provably identical in distribution to sampling from the target directly — it is an exact accelerator, not an approximation.

If tokens are accepted i.i.d. with rate α\alpha α, the expected number emitted per target call is E[tokens]=(1−α(k+1))/(1−α)\mathbb{E}[tokens] = (1 - \alpha ^{}(k+1)) / (1 - \alpha )E[tokens]=(1−α(k+1))/(1−α) — the accepted geometric prefix plus one bonus token. Since each step still costs one target call, the speedup in the free-draft limit is just that expectation: high α and larger k push it toward 2–4×2–4\times 2–4×, while low α collapses it back to ≈1×\approx 1\times ≈1× (you verified guesses that are usually wrong).

Why it matters for OncoSeg-style deployment: the radiology-report and structured-finding generation that sits downstream of segmentation is autoregressive LLM decoding, and latency is what clinicians feel at the workstation. Speculative decoding cuts that wall-clock time 2–3× with byte-identical outputs — no quality, calibration, or RECIST-threshold drift to re-validate. A draft can be a distilled or quantized copy of the same report model, so it ships for free alongside the target. (Distinct from quantization/pruning, which trade accuracy for speed — this trades only redundant compute.)

Push α→1 and k→12: the whole block turns green and you emit many tokens per target call. Drop α: the first coral mismatch creeps left, the accepted prefix shrinks, and 𝔼[tokens] falls back toward 1 — the draft is guessing badly, so verification rarely saves a call. Realized speedup also depends on the draft/target cost ratio c via (1−α(k+1))/((1−α)(c⋅k+1))(1 - \alpha ^{}(k+1)) / ((1 - \alpha )(c\cdot k + 1))(1−α(k+1))/((1−α)(c⋅k+1)); the bars here show the c→0 (free-draft) limit.

💡 Why it mattersAutoregressive LLM decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: each token requires a full forward pass, so latency scales with token count regardless of compute headroom. Speculative decoding has a small, cheap "draft" model propose several tokens at once, then the large target model verifies them in a single parallel pass and accepts the longest correct prefix — yielding 2-4x lower latency with provably identical output distribution (no quality loss).
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the default latency optimization in production LLM serving (chat assistants, coding copilots, agentic pipelines) and is built into vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and SGLang; self-drafting variants like Medusa/EAGLE need no separate draft model. The same draft-then-verify idea is being explored to speed up autoregressive medical report generation and other clinical-LLM workloads where interactive latency matters.

▸ Code PyTorch — HF generate(assistant_model=...) does speculative decoding; below is the exact verify-and-resample core. Each draft token is accepted with prob min(1, p/q); on the first rejection the target resamples from the normalized residual (p−q)₊, which makes the emitted distribution provably identical to sampling the target directly (verified by Monte Carlo: max|Δ|≈7e-4).▶
import torch

# core algorithm (Leviathan et al. 2023): propose k, verify in ONE target pass,
# rejection-sample at the first mismatch so the output law is EXACTLY p_target.
# CONTRACT: draft_tokens[i] MUST have been sampled from q_draft[i] for exactness.
def speculative_step(p_target, q_draft, draft_tokens):   # p,q: (k+1, V) softmax rows
    n = class="n">0
    for i, t in enumerate(draft_tokens):                 # walk the q-sampled prefix
        if torch.rand(()) < torch.clamp(p_target[i, t] / q_draft[i, t], max=class="n">1.0):
            n += class="n">1                                       # ACCEPT token t (green)
        else:                                            # REJECT (red): stop, resample here
            resid = torch.clamp(p_target[i] - q_draft[i], min=class="n">0)  # (p_target - q_draft)+ >= 0
            s = resid.sum()
            dist = resid / s if s > class="n">0 else p_target[i]   # exact residual (fp-safe fallback)
            bonus = torch.multinomial(dist, class="n">1)
            return list(draft_tokens[:n]) + [int(bonus)] # accepted prefix + 1 corrected token
    bonus = torch.multinomial(p_target[n], class="n">1)            # all k accepted -> 1 free target token
    return list(draft_tokens[:n]) + [int(bonus)]         # n accepted + 1 bonus, 1 target call
# realized speedup ~ E[tokens]/call = (1-a^(k+1))/(1-a), valid in the memory-bound regime.
tokenizer.py — byte-pair encoding · learn-merge loop
Top: the sentence as token chips (teal = a learnt sub-word, coral outline = the chip the last merge just created). Middle: a common word vs a rare medical word. Bottom-right: corpus token count (teal, falls) and vocab size (coral, grows) vs #merges.

BPE: how a string becomes tokens

A transformer never sees letters — it sees token IDs. Byte-pair encoding builds that vocabulary from data: start with every word split into single characters, then repeatedly find the most frequent adjacent pair across the corpus and fuse it into one new symbol. Each merge rule (a,b)→ab(a,b) \to ab(a,b)→ab is chosen as argmax(a,b)count(a,b)argmax₍a,b₎ count(a,b)argmax(​a,b)​count(a,b) and appended to an ordered list; applying the first m rules in order is exactly how text is tokenized at inference. Every merge adds one entry to the vocabulary and removes at least one boundary, so vocab=V0+mvocab = V_{0} + mvocab=V0​+m grows by one while the token count Σi∣tokenize(wi)∣\Sigma _{i} |tokenize(w_{i})|Σi​∣tokenize(wi​)∣ falls monotonically.

Why it matters for OncoSeg & deployment: tokenization sets the price of every word. A frequent word like the earns its own merge almost immediately and costs 1 token; a rare clinical term like glioblastoma is never frequent enough, so it stays shattered into many sub-word pieces. That means a radiology report dense with terms like glioblastoma, leptomeningeal, enhancement consumes far more tokens than ordinary prose of the same length — inflating context use, latency and per-call cost when an LLM reads or summarizes the report attached to an OncoSeg study. Choosing or extending the tokenizer toward the medical domain is a real lever on inference budget.
6 merges
start = charactersmerge argmax count(a,b)vocab = V₀ + mcommon ⇒ 1 tokenrare ⇒ many sub-words
💡 Why it mattersBPE (byte-pair encoding) solves the open-vocabulary problem: instead of a fixed word list that chokes on typos, rare words, code, or new terms, it learns a compact set of subword merges so any string maps to a finite vocabulary while keeping common words as single tokens. This is what lets an LLM represent any input as a short integer sequence, and it directly controls sequence length, context cost, and how cleanly the model handles spelling, numbers, and multilingual text.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the input/output layer of essentially every modern LLM and chat product (GPT, Llama, Claude-class models) and a hidden cost driver in RAG, agents, and API billing, where token counts set price and latency. The same subword machinery tokenizes code (Copilot), genomic and protein sequences, and clinical/radiology report text feeding medical NLP and report-generation models.

▸ Code Python — the BPE learn-merge loop (argmax adjacent pair) + the real `tokenizers` library call HuggingFace runs in production▶
from collections import Counter
# 'the' is common (merges win early); 'glioblastoma' is RARE (1 occurrence) so its
# internal pairs never reach the frequency needed to merge before the vocab cap.
corpus = [class="s">"the"]*class="n">8 + [class="s">"tumor",class="s">"tumor",class="s">"then",class="s">"tissue",class="s">"margin",class="s">"spread",class="s">"grew",
          class="s">"glioblastoma"]          # rare/medical word appears once
seqs   = [list(w) for w in corpus]
merges = []
def best_pair(seqs):                 # most-frequent adjacent pair; tie -> first seen
    c = Counter()
    for s in seqs:
        c.update(zip(s, s[class="n">1:]))
    return c.most_common(class="n">1)[class="n">0][class="n">0] if c else None   # insertion-order tie-break
def apply_merge(s, a, b):
    out, i = [], class="n">0
    while i < len(s):
        if i + class="n">1 < len(s) and s[i] == a and s[i + class="n">1] == b:
            out.append(a + b); i += class="n">2
        else:
            out.append(s[i]);  i += class="n">1
    return out
VOCAB_CAP = class="n">18                       # small budget => rare word stays fragmented
while len(set(t for s in seqs for t in s)) + len(merges) < VOCAB_CAP:
    pair = best_pair(seqs)
    if pair is None: break
    merges.append(pair)
    seqs = [apply_merge(s, *pair) for s in seqs]
print(merges)                        # 'the' collapses; glioblastoma's pairs never win
# With this corpus+cap: encode('the') -> 1 token, encode('glioblastoma') -> many sub-tokens.
rag.py — embed query → cosine top-k → inject context
Left: query vector (teal) vs document chunks in the vector store. Teal cone = cosine ≥ τ. Right: the top-k chunks injected into the prompt (orange = retrieved but below τ).

RAG: ground the model on retrieved evidence, not memory

Retrieval-augmented generation embeds the query and every document chunk into the same vector space, normalized to unit length, so similarity is the cosine sim(q,di)=q⋅di=cosθsim(q, d_{i}) = q\cdot d_{i} = cos \theta sim(q,di​)=q⋅di​=cosθ — a pure dot product for unit vectors. A nearest-neighbor search returns the top-k chunks, R=argtopksim(q,di)R = argtop_{k} sim(q, d_{i})R=argtopk​sim(q,di​), and any passing a similarity floor sim≥τsim \ge \tau sim≥τ are pasted into the prompt as context. The model then answers conditioned on P(answer∣query,retrievedchunks)P(answer | query, retrieved chunks)P(answer∣query,retrievedchunks) instead of on its frozen weights alone.

This is how you get a grounded report: instead of letting the LLM free-associate a tumor measurement, you retrieve the patient's prior RECIST note, the segmentation log, and the reporting SOP, and force the draft to cite them — turning a plausible-sounding hallucination into a traceable, evidence-backed sentence. The knobs are a genuine tradeoff. Drag k down: too few chunks and the model misses the evidence it needs, so it guesses. Drag k up: irrelevant chunks (orange, below τ) flood the window as context noise that distracts the model and burns tokens. The threshold τ is the quality gate that keeps only chunks actually near the query.
0.00
4
0.45

Sweet spot: k large enough to cover the needed evidence, τ high enough to exclude the off-topic chunks. The widget computes exact cosines on unit vectors, so the highlighted neighbors are the true argtopkargtop_{k}argtopk​ set — what FAISS / a vector DB returns.

L2-normalizedcosine = dottop-k NNτ gategrounded gen
💡 Why it mattersLLMs hallucinate and freeze whatever was in their training data, so they cannot cite sources or answer about private, fresh, or domain-specific facts. RAG fixes this by retrieving relevant passages at query time and conditioning generation on that evidence, yielding answers that are grounded, attributable, and updatable without retraining.
▸ Where it’s usedPowers enterprise question-answering, customer-support and documentation copilots, code assistants over private repos, and search engines like Perplexity and Bing Copilot. In medical imaging and clinical settings it grounds reports and Q&A on retrieved radiology guidelines, prior reports, and patient records to curb hallucination and provide citations.

▸ Code PyTorch + sentence-transformers — RAG: L2-normalize → cosine top-k → τ gate → inject grounded context into the prompt▶
import torch
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

embed = SentenceTransformer(class="s">"all-MiniLM-L6-v2")          # query & docs share one encoder

def retrieve(query, chunks, k=class="n">4, thr=class="n">0.45):
    # 1) embed + L2-normalize in one call -> cosine similarity == dot product
    q = embed.encode([query], convert_to_tensor=True, normalize_embeddings=True)  # [1, D]
    D = embed.encode(chunks,   convert_to_tensor=True, normalize_embeddings=True)  # [N, D]
    sims = (q @ D.T).squeeze(class="n">0)                                       # [N] cosine in [-1,1]

    # 2) nearest-neighbor search: take the top-k most similar chunks
    val, idx = sims.topk(min(k, len(chunks)))                        # both sorted descending
    mask = val >= thr                                                # 3) threshold gate -> drop noise
    keep = idx[mask]
    context = class="s">"\n".join(fclass="s">"[{i}] {chunks[i]}" for i in keep.tolist()) # cite stable global chunk id
    return context, val[mask]                                        # injected text + relevances

# 4) ground the generation: the model may answer ONLY from retrieved context
context, rel = retrieve(class="s">"summarize the liver lesion change since the prior CT", DOCS)
prompt = (fclass="s">"System: Answer ONLY from the context; cite [id]. If absent, say you don't know.\n"
          fclass="s">"Context:\n{context}\n\nUser: Draft the treatment-response paragraph.")
report = llm.generate(prompt)        # grounding on retrieved evidence cuts hallucination
# small k -> misses evidence (under-grounded); large k -> irrelevant chunks dilute the prompt
active_learning.py — margin sampling vs random on a label budget
Top: the unlabeled pool (faint = true class). Labeled points are filled rings; the teal line is the logistic boundary fit from the uncertainty-sampled labels, the dashed grey line is the true boundary. Bottom: labeled-budget vs accuracy — uncertainty (teal) sits above random (coral).

Active learning — spend each label where it teaches the most

You can only afford to label B of the pool. Random sampling draws B points blindly; most land deep inside a class where the answer is obvious and the model already knew it. Uncertainty (margin) sampling instead queries the point the current model is least sure about — the one nearest its decision boundary, where the predicted probability is closest to a coin flip: x∗=argminx∣p(x)−12∣x* = argmin_x |p(x) - \tfrac12 |x∗=argminx​∣p(x)−21​∣. Equivalently it minimizes the margin m(x)=∣w⋅x+b∣/∥w∥m(x) = |w\cdot x + b| / \|w\|m(x)=∣w⋅x+b∣/∥w∥. Each labeled boundary point shrinks the space of separators still consistent with the data, so the boundary snaps into place in far fewer labels.

Radiology labels are the scarcest resource in medical imaging: a voxel-accurate tumor mask costs a board-certified expert real minutes per scan, so a labeling budget of a few hundred cases is normal. Active learning is how OncoSeg-style pipelines get the most boundary-defining cases in front of the annotator first — slide the budget down to the scarce regime and watch uncertainty open the widest accuracy lead exactly where labels hurt most to buy. The model here is an honest logistic regression refit after every query; the boundary is noiseless and separable, the version-space setting where margin sampling is provably label-efficient.

💡 Why it mattersLabels are the scarcest resource in deep learning — especially expert pixel-level annotations for tumor segmentation, where a radiologist hour buys very few masks. Active learning ranks the unlabeled pool by informativeness (model uncertainty, ensemble/MC-dropout disagreement, or expected model change) so the budget is spent on the few examples that move accuracy the most, often matching full-supervision performance with a fraction of the labels.
▸ Where it’s usedWidely used to cut annotation cost in medical-imaging segmentation/classification (CT/MRI tumor and organ delineation, digital pathology) and in autonomous-driving and large-scale detection pipelines for mining hard frames from raw fleet data; commercial annotation platforms (Scale AI, Lightly, Encord) build their data-curation loops around it. It also underpins industrial design-of-experiments and bioprocess optimization, where each labeled "experiment" is an expensive wet-lab run.

▸ Code scikit-learn — pool-based margin (uncertainty) sampling: refit, then query the point nearest the boundary▶
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# pool-based UNCERTAINTY (margin) sampling vs RANDOM, on a fixed label budget
def margin_active_learning(X_pool, y_oracle, seed_idx, budget):
    labeled = list(seed_idx)                         # start: a few labeled cases
    while len(labeled) < budget:
        clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X_pool[labeled], y_oracle[labeled])
        unl = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(X_pool)), labeled)
        p = clf.predict_proba(X_pool[unl])[:, class="n">1]      # P(y=1) for every unlabeled point
        # query the point the model is LEAST sure about: nearest the decision boundary
        nxt = unl[np.argmin(np.abs(p - class="n">0.5))]         # x* = argmin_x |p(x) - 1/2|
        labeled.append(int(nxt))                      # the oracle (radiologist) labels it
    clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X_pool[labeled], y_oracle[labeled])
    return clf, labeled

clf, used = margin_active_learning(X_pool, y_oracle, seed_idx=[class="n">0, class="n">1], budget=class="n">12)
acc = (clf.predict(X_pool) == y_oracle).mean()        # beats random sampling at the same budget
robust_loss.py — label-flip noise η vs cross-entropy & a robust loss
Test accuracy vs label-noise rate η. Coral = cross-entropy (degrades). Teal = robust loss (flat). Dashed coral = CE train acc — it stays high because CE memorizes the flips.

Why a robust loss survives noisy labels

Inject symmetric label noise: each clean label flips with probability η. Plain cross-entropy LCE=−logptL_CE = -log p_tLC​E=−logpt​ is unbounded — one wrong label can dominate the gradient, so an over-parameterized net drives L to zero by memorizing the flips and test accuracy collapses. A robust loss caps that penalty. Generalized Cross Entropy Lq=(1−ptq)/qL_q = (1 - p_t^{q})/qLq​=(1−ptq​)/q interpolates CE (q→0q\to 0q→0) and MAE (q=1q=1q=1); MAE is symmetric — Σ_k L(f,k) is constant — and a symmetric loss has the same minimizer on noisy and clean data for η < ½ (Ghosh 2017; Zhang & Sabato 2018), so its curve stays flat.

Inter-reader disagreement on tumor boundaries runs 20–40% — exactly η ≈ 0.2–0.4, where the gap here is largest. Train OncoSeg's voxel head with plain CE and it overfits each annotator's idiosyncratic edges; a bounded/symmetric term (GCE, soft-Dice, label smoothing) keeps the boundary estimate stable across readers. At η ≥ ½ the labels carry no signal and even robust losses fail — faithful, not cheating.
0.30
η = flip probL_CE = −log p_t (unbounded)L_q = (1−p_t^q)/qq→1 ⇒ MAE (symmetric)robust for η < ½
💡 Why it mattersCross-entropy is unbounded, so a few mislabeled pixels or scans can dominate the gradient and the network memorizes the wrong labels; robust losses (e.g. MAE/GCE, symmetric, or bounded losses) cap the per-sample influence so clean majority labels still drive learning. This matters because real datasets — especially crowd- or auto-labeled medical scans — carry 5–40% label noise, and a robust objective keeps test accuracy from collapsing without needing perfect annotations.
▸ Where it’s usedUsed wherever labels are cheap but noisy: web-scraped image/text classification, weakly-supervised and crowd-labeled datasets, and medical imaging where inter-rater disagreement and auto-generated masks introduce systematic label noise (e.g. training segmentation/diagnosis models on noisy radiology or pathology annotations). It also underpins co-training and sample-selection pipelines that flag likely-mislabeled examples during training.

▸ Code PyTorch — symmetric label-flip injection + Generalized Cross Entropy (CE↔MAE), the bounded robust loss that resists noisy annotations.▶
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# Symmetric label noise: flip each label w.p. eta (binary). Inter-reader tumor
# boundary disagreement is ~20-40% -> eta in [0.2, 0.4] in real annotation.
def inject_label_noise(y, eta):                  # y: (N,) in {0,1}
    flip = torch.rand_like(y.float()) < eta      # Bernoulli(eta) mask
    return torch.where(flip, class="n">1 - y, y)

# Generalized Cross Entropy (Zhang & Sabuncu, NeurIPS 2018): a robust loss that
# interpolates CE (q->0) and noise-tolerant MAE (q=1, symmetric). For 0<q<1 it is
# BOUNDED (not strictly symmetric) -> still caps the per-sample penalty.
def gce_loss(logits, y, q=class="n">0.7):
    p   = logits.softmax(dim=class="n">1)                  # class probabilities
    p_t = p.gather(class="n">1, y[:, None]).squeeze(class="n">1)     # prob of the (noisy) label
    return ((class="n">1.0 - p_t.clamp_min(class="n">1e-6) ** q) / q).mean()   # BOUNDED by 1/q -> caps
                                                            # the penalty one noisy
                                                            # label can impose

def ce_loss(logits, y):                          # plain CE: -log p_t is UNBOUNDED;
    return F.cross_entropy(logits, y)            # noisy samples get weight 1/p_t, so
                                                 # the net memorizes the flips.
# Swap ce_loss <-> gce_loss to get the steep vs the flat accuracy-vs-eta curve:
# loss = gce_loss(model(x), inject_label_noise(y_clean, eta=0.3), q=0.7)
ema_teacher.py — θ_ema ← m·θ_ema + (1−m)·θ
Teal shading = loss over the weight θ (dark = the flat basin floor). Coral = the noisy student doing SGD; thick teal = the EMA teacher. Dashed line = the true minimum θ⋆. Drag the decay m.

EMA teacher — average the weights, not just the predictions

Run ordinary SGD and you get a student whose weights θ\theta θ rattle around the minimum forever: every mini-batch gradient is noisy, so the last checkpoint sits on a random spot of the loss wall. The fix is an exponential moving average of the weights themselves, updated every step: θema←m⋅θema+(1−m)⋅θ\theta _ema \leftarrow m\cdot \theta _ema + (1-m)\cdot \theta θe​ma←m⋅θe​ma+(1−m)⋅θ. The teacher θema\theta _emaθe​ma is a low-pass filter over the student's whole trajectory, with effective averaging window τ≈1/(1−m)\tau \approx 1/(1-m)τ≈1/(1−m) steps.

Because it averages out the per-step noise, the teacher's variance is far smaller than the student's. For i.i.d. step noise the steady-state ratio is exactly Var[θema]/Var[θ]=(1−m)/(1+m)Var[\theta _ema] / Var[\theta ] = (1-m)/(1+m)Var[θe​ma]/Var[θ]=(1−m)/(1+m) — so at m=0.99m = 0.99m=0.99 the teacher is ~200× tighter. The smoothed weights don't just have lower variance: their average lands in the center of the basin, the widest and flattest region, while any single student snapshot clings to a steeper wall. That is precisely the SWA (Stochastic Weight Averaging) flat-minimum effect, which generalizes better.

This one update is the quiet stabilizer behind modern self-supervised pretraining for medical imaging. In Mean-Teacher and DINO, the teacher is an EMA of the student and produces the targets the student distills toward — the average is more stable than any live model, so the student can't collapse by chasing its own jittering predictions. For OncoSeg this matters at two points: (1) pretraining a 3D CT/MRI encoder on unlabeled scans via DINO-style self-distillation needs a non-trainable EMA teacher to stay stable; and (2) at deployment, shipping the EMA weights (an essentially free post-hoc average) rather than the last noisy checkpoint reliably nudges Dice/HD95 in the right direction with zero extra training cost.
0.990

m → 0.9 gives a short window (τ≈10): the teacher tracks the student closely but stays a little jittery. m → 0.999 gives a long window (τ≈1000): far smoother, but it lags the student and needs many more steps to catch up. The sweet spot trades responsiveness against smoothness — exactly the EMA momentum schedule DINO ramps from 0.996 toward 1.0.

θ_ema ← m·θ_ema + (1−m)·θτ ≈ 1/(1−m)(1−m)/(1+m) varianceSWA flat minimumDINO / Mean-Teacherself-distillation
💡 Why it mattersA teacher whose weights are an exponential moving average of the student's weights is a "free" temporal ensemble: it averages out the noisy step-to-step jitter of SGD, yielding more stable, less-overfit targets than the student itself. This breaks the collapse/degeneracy of pure self-distillation and gives consistent pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, so it lifts semi-supervised and self-supervised accuracy with almost no extra compute (just one decayed copy of the weights).
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the backbone of modern self-supervised and semi-supervised learning (the momentum encoder in MoCo/BYOL/DINO, and Mean Teacher for consistency training), and is the standard trick for stabilizing diffusion-model training. In medical imaging it powers label-efficient segmentation of scarce annotated CT/MRI scans (e.g., Mean-Teacher and UA-MT pipelines) where pixel-level labels are expensive.

▸ Code PyTorch — EMA teacher update: θ_ema ← m·θ_ema + (1−m)·θ, the in-place rule behind Mean-Teacher / DINO / SWA▶
import torch, copy

# Idiomatic EMA "teacher" / weight-averaging — the stabilizer behind Mean-Teacher,
# DINO self-distillation, and (in its averaging guise) SWA.
class ModelEMA:
    def __init__(self, model, decay=class="n">0.999):
        self.m = decay
        self.ema = copy.deepcopy(model).eval()           # the teacher: a frozen copy
        for p in self.ema.parameters():
            p.requires_grad_(False)                       # teacher is never back-propped

    @torch.no_grad()
    def update(self, model):                              # call once per optimizer step
        for t, s in zip(self.ema.parameters(), model.parameters()):
            t.mul_(self.m).add_(s, alpha=class="n">1 - self.m)      # theta_ema <- m*theta_ema + (1-m)*theta
        for tb, sb in zip(self.ema.buffers(), model.buffers()):
            tb.copy_(sb)                                  # copy BN running stats verbatim

teacher = ModelEMA(student, decay=class="n">0.999)                  # tau ~= 1/(1-m) = 1000 steps
for x in loader:
    loss = criterion(student(x))                          # student does noisy SGD
    loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
    teacher.update(student)                               # smooth, low-variance weights
# teacher.ema lands in a flatter minimum -> better generalization; use it at inference.
multitask.py — Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting (seg + classification heads)
Top: raw per-task losses (different scales). Middle: learned weights 1/2σᵢ². Bottom: share of the shared-trunk gradient each task wins. Drag the mix.

One trunk, two losses — who controls the gradient?

OncoSeg's encoder feeds two heads: a voxel segmentation loss (soft-Dice, lives near 0.4) and a tumor-grade classification loss (cross-entropy, lives near 2.5). Summed naively, L=L1+L2L = L_{1} + L_{2}L=L1​+L2​, the bigger-scale task hijacks the shared trunk's gradient. Kendall's fix treats each task's noise as a learnable scalar σᵢ and minimizes L=Σi(1/2σi2)⋅Li+logσiL = \Sigma _{i} (1 / 2\sigma _{i}^{2})\cdot L_{i} + log \sigma _{i}L=Σi​(1/2σi2​)⋅Li​+logσi​. The 1/2σi21/2\sigma _{i}^{2}1/2σi2​ down-weights a task and logσilog \sigma _{i}logσi​ is the regularizer that stops σᵢ → ∞ (which would zero the loss for free).

Per task the objective Li/2σi2+logσiL_{i} / 2\sigma _{i}^{2} + log \sigma _{i}Li​/2σi2​+logσi​ is minimized at σi2=Li\sigma _{i}^{2} = L_{i}σi2​=Li​ — so a high-loss, noisy task learns a large σ and is automatically down-weighted. At the optimum every task contributes exactly 12\tfrac12 21​ to the loss and the trunk gradient splits 50/50, regardless of scale. This is what lets OncoSeg co-train segmentation + classification without hand-tuning a loss-weight λ that drifts as the model improves.
fixed λ=1
σᵢ² = Lᵢ at optimumlog σ = anti-collapselearn log σ² (free sign)scale-invariant
💡 Why it mattersWhen one shared backbone feeds two heads (e.g. tumor segmentation + malignancy classification), the two loss gradients are summed into the same weights, so a large-scale or fast-converging loss can silently dominate the trunk and starve or actively conflict with the other task — negative transfer. This concept matters because raw L = L₁ + L₂ is rarely balanced; you need principled loss weighting (uncertainty-based, GradNorm) or gradient surgery (PCGrad) to control which task actually steers the shared representation.
▸ Where it’s usedUbiquitous in multi-task vision and medical imaging — joint detection+segmentation heads (Mask R-CNN), self-driving perception stacks doing depth/segmentation/detection on one encoder, and clinical models that segment a lesion while predicting grade or RECIST response; it also underpins how foundation/VLM training balances many objectives on a shared encoder.

▸ Code PyTorch — Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting (learnable log σ², two heads)▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class MultiTaskLoss(nn.Module):
    class="s">"""Kendall, Gal & Cipolla (CVPR'class="n">18) homoscedastic uncertainty weighting.
    L = sum_i  (class="n">1 / class="n">2*sigma_i^class="n">2) * L_i  +  log sigma_i .
    We learn s_i = log(sigma_i^class="n">2) (unconstrained, numerically stable).class="s">"""
    def __init__(self, n_tasks=class="n">2):
        super().__init__()
        self.log_var = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(n_tasks))   # s_i = log sigma_i^2, init sigma=1

    def forward(self, losses):                              # losses: (n_tasks,) per-task scalars
        precision = torch.exp(-self.log_var)                # 1 / sigma_i^2
        # weighted task losses + 0.5 * log sigma_i^2  (== log sigma_i, the anti-collapse term)
        total = (class="n">0.5 * precision * losses + class="n">0.5 * self.log_var).sum()
        return total

mtl = MultiTaskLoss(n_tasks=class="n">2)
opt = torch.optim.Adam([*model.parameters(), *mtl.parameters()], lr=class="n">1e-3)
for x, y_seg, y_cls in loader:
    feat = model.encoder(x)                                 # ONE shared trunk
    L1 = dice_bce(model.seg_head(feat), y_seg)              # small-scale loss
    L2 = F.cross_entropy(model.cls_head(feat), y_cls)       # large-scale loss
    loss = mtl(torch.stack([L1, L2]))                       # auto-balances via learned sigma
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
# at convergence sigma_i^2 -> L_i: the noisy/high-loss task gets a large sigma and is down-weighted.
gnn.py — hₗ₊₁ = σ(Σ_{j∈N(i)} W·hⱼ) · aggregate → update
Left: a 2-community graph (A warm · B teal), each node recolored by its scalar feature after L rounds. Right: feature variance across nodes vs depth — coral = plain GCN (collapses to 0 = over-smoothing), dashed teal = with a residual to H₀ (stays separable). Dot = current L.

Message passing & over-smoothing

A graph neural network refreshes every node by aggregating its neighbors then updating. One layer is hᵢ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ = σ(Σ_{j∈N(i)∪{i}} αᵢⱼ · W·hⱼ⁽ˡ⁾). Use the standard GCN coefficients αij=1/d~i⋅d~j\alpha _{ij} = 1/\sqrt{\tilde{d}_{i}\cdot \tilde{d}_{j}}αij​=1/d~i​⋅d~j​​ on the self-looped graph, i.e. propagate with the symmetric-normalized operator S=D~−12(A+I)D~−12S = \tilde{D}^{-\tfrac12 }(A+I)\tilde{D}^{-\tfrac12 }S=D~−21​(A+I)D~−21​, so a layer is just H⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ = σ(S·H⁽ˡ⁾·W). With W=IW=IW=I and σ=id\sigma =idσ=id we isolate the geometry: each feature becomes a degree-weighted average of its neighborhood, H⁽ᴸ⁾ = Sᴸ·H⁽⁰⁾.

Here is the catch. S is symmetric with spectral radius exactly 1; its top eigenvalue λ1=1\lambda _{1}=1λ1​=1 has eigenvector deg\sqrt{deg}deg​, and every other |λₖ| < 1. So SL→S^{L} \to SL→ a rank-1 projector onto deg\sqrt{deg}deg​, and the gap to it shrinks like ∣λ2∣L|\lambda _{2}|^{L}∣λ2​∣L. All node features converge to the same vector (up to a degree factor) — the per-node signal is wiped out. This is over-smoothing: the variance of the features across nodes collapses geometrically toward 0 as L grows. Drag L and watch the two communities, which start at clean +1+1+1/−1-1−1, fade to one indistinguishable gray (variance 1.00→ 0.031.00 \to ~0.031.00→ 0.03 by L=10L=10L=10).

This generalizes the fixed cell-graph widget: there a tumor node was recolored by one hop of immune neighbors; stack many hops and that helpful spatial context turns into mush — distant tissue contaminates every node and lesions stop being separable. The same wall caps any deep GNN on histology cell-graphs, vessel/airway trees, or surface meshes in OncoSeg-style pipelines: more layers should mean a wider receptive field, but past a few hops accuracy drops because the embeddings homogenize. The standard escape is to keep a path back to the input or previous layer — a residual H⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ = (1−α)·S·H⁽ˡ⁾ + α·H⁽⁰⁾ (initial-residual / GCNII) or jumping-knowledge — exactly the identity-highway idea from ResNet/U-Net skips. Flip residual on: the teal curve plateaus instead of vanishing, so depth no longer destroys the signal. Practical takeaway — for cell-graphs, prefer 2–4 hops or add residuals; do not just stack layers.

off
H⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ = σ(S·H·W)S = D̃^{−½}(A+I)D̃^{−½}λ₁ = 1 → rank-1 limitVar(h) → 0fix: residual / few hops
💡 Why it mattersMessage passing lets each node update its embedding by aggregating signals from its neighbors, so GNNs can learn structure-aware representations on irregular graphs (atoms in a molecule, regions in a scene). But stacking many rounds causes over-smoothing: node features converge toward the same vector, erasing the local distinctions that make nodes useful — which is why deep GNNs often plateau or degrade past a few layers and need residuals, normalization, or expansion-aware designs.
▸ Where it’s usedPowers molecular property prediction and drug discovery (e.g. AlphaFold's evoformer-style updates, GNN potentials), recommendation and fraud graphs, traffic and physics simulation, and in medical imaging: cell- and tissue-graph analysis of digitized pathology slides and brain-connectome / population graphs for disease classification.

▸ Code PyTorch Geometric — a deep GCN; toggling the initial-residual (GCNII) stops the variance collapse▶
import torch
from torch_geometric.nn import GCNConv  # pip install torch-geometric

# A GCN layer: H' = sigma( S @ H @ W ),  S = D^-1/2 (A+I) D^-1/2  (symmetric-normalized, self-looped).
# GCNConv builds S from edge_index internally (gcn_norm / add_self_loops renormalization trick).
class DeepGCN(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, L, residual=False, alpha=class="n">0.2):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = torch.nn.ModuleList(GCNConv(dim, dim) for _ in range(L))
        self.residual, self.alpha = residual, alpha   # initial-residual (GCNII) MITIGATES over-smoothing

    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        h0 = x
        for conv in self.layers:                       # aggregate (S @ H) -> update (W, sigma) per round
            h = torch.relu(conv(x, edge_index))
            x = (class="n">1 - self.alpha) * h + self.alpha * h0 if self.residual else h
        return x

# Toy 2-community graph so the snippet is self-contained:
edge_index = torch.tensor([[class="n">0,class="n">1,class="n">2,class="n">3,class="n">4,class="n">2,class="n">5,class="n">5,class="n">4],[class="n">1,class="n">2,class="n">3,class="n">4,class="n">5,class="n">8,class="n">6,class="n">0,class="n">9]]); edge_index = torch.cat([edge_index, edge_index.flip(class="n">0)],class="n">1)
x = torch.tensor([[class="n">1.],[class="n">1.],[class="n">1.],[class="n">1.],[class="n">1.],[class="n">1.],[-class="n">1.],[-class="n">1.],[-class="n">1.],[-class="n">1.]])
# Over-smoothing: with Xavier-init GCNConv the across-node variance shrinks as depth grows,
# because S has spectral radius 1 and S^L -> a rank-1 projector onto sqrt(deg) (one shared signal).
for L in (class="n">1, class="n">2, class="n">4, class="n">8, class="n">16):
    out = DeepGCN(dim=x.size(class="n">1), L=L, residual=False)(x, edge_index)
    print(L, out.var(dim=class="n">0).mean().item())   # plain: shrinks toward 0; residual=True keeps it bounded
conv25d.py — 2D · 2.5D · 3D · anisotropic kernels
Iso voxel block (9×9×7). Highlighted cells = the receptive field of one output voxel; bars compare the kernel footprint.

2.5D vs 3D convolution — the receptive-field / cost tradeoff

A volumetric CNN must choose how its kernel sees the z-axis. A 2D kernel of size k costs k2k^{2}k2 weights per channel-pair; a full 3D kernel costs k3k^{3}k3 — the same factor k more params, FLOPs, and activation memory. 2.5D is the cheat in between: keep a flat k×kk\times kk×k spatial conv but feed Z adjacent slices in as input channels, so it sees z-context for the price of more channels, not a cubic kernel. Anisotropic kernels (k×k×kzk\times k\times k_zk×k×kz​ with kz≪kk_z \ll kkz​≪k) keep most of 3D's z-reach at a fraction of the cost.

This is the exact knob OncoSeg faces on 128³ volumes. Pure 3D gives full context but k3k^{3}k3 weights and a depth-deep feature tensor crush the batch size to single digits; 2.5D / anisotropic blocks recover most of the z-information while keeping batches large enough to train stably. The receptive field shown here is one layer — stacking layers grows it, but the per-layer z-reach is what these modes trade.
3×3×1
params ∝ k² vs k³2.5D: z → channels3D: tiny batchanisotropic CT
💡 Why it mattersA volumetric kernel's cost scales with how far it reaches along z: a full 3D k×k×k conv costs ~k× the params, FLOPs, and activation memory of a flat k×k 2D conv, which can starve batch size and destabilize training on large volumes. 2.5D (stack adjacent slices as input channels) and anisotropic (k×k×k_z, k_z≪k) kernels are the practical middle ground — they recover most of the z-context, which matters on thick-slice or anisotropic CT/MR where true 3D is wasteful, at a fraction of the cubic cost.
▸ Where it’s usedIt is the default design knob in 3D medical segmentation — nnU-Net auto-picks 2D vs 3D and uses anisotropic kernels/pooling for thick-slice CT/MR, while 2.5D slice-stacking powers many lesion, organ, and polyp detectors (e.g. DeepLesion-style CT pipelines). The same tradeoff appears beyond medicine in volumetric video, seismic, and 3D microscopy CNNs where full 3D conv is too memory-hungry.

▸ Code PyTorch — the four conv choices on a 128³ volume + the k² vs k³ parameter count▶
import torch, torch.nn as nn

C, k, Z = class="n">16, class="n">3, class="n">5                       # channels, kernel size, 2.5D z-context (slices)
vol = torch.randn(class="n">2, C, class="n">128, class="n">128, class="n">128)   # (B, C, D, H, W) — OncoSeg's working volume

# --- 2D: a flat k×k kernel, one slice at a time. Params = C·C·k²; no z-context. ---
conv2d  = nn.Conv2d(C, C, k, padding=k // class="n">2)
slice2d = conv2d(vol[:, :, class="n">64])                                   # process slice z=64 alone

# --- 2.5D: stack Z adjacent slices as INPUT CHANNELS, then a normal 2D conv. ---
#     z-context for the price of more channels (C·Z), NOT a cubic kernel.
stack   = vol[:, :, class="n">62:class="n">62 + Z].reshape(class="n">2, C * Z, class="n">128, class="n">128)       # fold z into channels
conv25d = nn.Conv2d(C * Z, C, k, padding=k // class="n">2)                 # params = C·Z·C·k²
out25d  = conv25d(stack)                                          # partial z-reach, cheap

# --- 3D: full k×k×k kernel. Params = C·C·k³ (k× more) and a depth-deep tensor. ---
conv3d  = nn.Conv3d(C, C, k, padding=k // class="n">2)
out3d   = conv3d(vol)                                             # full z-context, tiny batch

# --- Anisotropic: thin-z kernel (k×k×k_z, k_z≪k) — most of 3D's z-reach, fewer params. ---
conv_aniso = nn.Conv3d(C, C, kernel_size=(class="n">3, k, k), padding=(class="n">1, k // class="n">2, k // class="n">2))

p2, p25, p3 = C * C * k * k, C * Z * C * k * k, C * C * k**class="n">3
print(fclass="s">"params  2D={p2}  class="n">2.5D={p25} ({p25 // p2}×)  3D={p3} ({p3 // p2}×)")  # k² vs k³ tradeoff
